Fallback locales are loaded solely by ApplicationController#set_locale via I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!, so code running outside a request (Sidekiq jobs, mailers, rake tasks, console) in a non-English locale will attempt fallback lookups against locale files that were never loaded and return 'translation missing' instead of the site-default/English string, unless a web request previously happened to load them in the same process. The fix must load the fallback chain inside the translation path (or ensure_loaded! must be invoked for all execution contexts), not just in a controller before_filter.

title: Fallback calculation crashes if default_locale is unset and depends on DB-backed settings during translation
body: FallbackLocaleList#[] calls SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym on every fallback lookup. If default_locale is nil/blank (fresh install, boot/rake/migration contexts before site settings are available, or a cleared setting), this raises NoMethodError on nil (or produces the invalid locale :""), turning an otherwise recoverable missing-translation case into an exception for any I18n.t call. It also makes the low-level I18n backend depend on a database-backed SiteSetting lookup during translation, including during initialization when the settings table may not exist yet. Guard nil/blank and avoid requiring SiteSetting availability for the :en fallback.

title: Fallback list recomputes SiteSetting lookup on every missing translation
body: I18n::Backend::Fallbacks invokes I18n.fallbacks[locale] each time it retries a lookup, and this implementation allocates a new array and calls SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym (a settings-store lookup) on every invocation, with no memoization. On pages/emails with many untranslated keys in a non-English locale this adds repeated settings lookups and allocations to the hot translation path, partially defeating the translation LRU-cache accelerator. Cache the computed chain per locale (invalidating when default_locale changes) or compute the default once.

title: No tests cover the new fallback chain or its interaction with lazy locale loading
body: This PR replaces Rails' config.i18n.fallbacks with a custom FallbackLocaleList, changes the backend module inclusion (pluralization + fallbacks), deletes the old pluralization initializer, and adds a lazy ensure_loaded! path, but adds no specs. There is no coverage proving: a missing key in a user locale falls back to the site locale then :en, fallback files are actually loaded on demand, pluralization still works through the fallback locale, or behavior outside ApplicationController. Given the lazy-loading accelerator makes fallback success dependent on which locales happen to be loaded, a regression would silently surface as 'translation missing' strings in production.

title: Fallback lookup crashes when SiteSetting/default locale is unavailable
body: FallbackLocaleList#[] unconditionally calls SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym on every fallback computation. Before the database/settings are ready (boot, rake tasks, migrations, asset precompilation, or a nil/blank default_locale) SiteSetting can raise or return nil, and nil.to_sym raises NoMethodError. Because the I18n fallbacks backend invokes this on translation lookups, a routine translation can crash boot or request handling instead of falling back to :en.

title: Fallback locales are only loaded for web requests, and missed fallbacks get cached
body: Fallback translations are loaded only by ApplicationController#set_locale calling I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!. Background jobs, mailers, console/rake code and other non-controller paths set I18n.locale without this call, and I18n.translate in lib/freedom_patches/translate_accelerator.rb only loads config.locale. In those contexts a key missing from the primary locale will be looked up in fallback locales whose YAML was never loaded, return a missing-translation string, and for argument-less translations that result is frozen into the LRU cache keyed only by key+locale+backend, poisoning later web requests until reload.

title: Translation cache ignores the dynamic fallback chain
body: The LRU cache key is "#{key}#{config.locale}#{config.backend.object_id}" but the resolved value now depends on FallbackLocaleList, i.e. on SiteSetting.default_locale at lookup time. If an admin changes the site default locale, or a translation is first resolved before its fallback locale is loaded, the cached value for the user locale remains stale/frozen and is served indefinitely (up to cache eviction/reload) instead of the translation from the new fallback locale.

title: I18n.fallbacks is replaced with a Hash that does not implement the Fallbacks API
body: I18n.fallbacks is assigned a plain Hash subclass whose [] always computes a new array and ignores stored entries. Code and gems expecting the I18n::Backend::Fallbacks object installed by Rails/i18n (e.g. assigning fallbacks per-locale with []=, reading defaults, or calling methods other than the newly added ensure_loaded!) will silently lose assignments or fail. In environments where Rails still sets config.i18n.fallbacks, Rails can also overwrite this object with a real Fallbacks instance that has no ensure_loaded!, making ApplicationController#set_locale raise NoMethodError.

title: Every fallback lookup performs a SiteSetting lookup
body: FallbackLocaleList#[] calls SiteSetting.default_locale on each invocation, and the fallbacks backend invokes [] for translation lookups (including repeated/missing keys). This adds a settings/cache lookup to hot I18n paths that the translate accelerator is specifically trying to keep fast, instead of computing and memoizing the chain per locale and invalidating it when the site locale changes.

title: Denial cache key omits identity type, allowing anonymous denials to poison renderer checks
body: userPermDenialCacheKey is built only from namespace, checkReq.UserUID, action, name and parent, and Check consults it before dispatching on IdentityType. Anonymous subjects (anonymous:0) and renderer subjects (render:0) both parse to UserUID "0", so an anonymous Check for dashboards:read on dash1 that is denied writes a denial entry under UID 0, and a subsequent render:0 Check for the same namespace/action/name/parent hits that entry at line 117 and returns Allowed:false without ever reaching getRendererPermissions, which is supposed to allow renderers to read all dashboards/folders. The same collision applies between user and service-account subjects sharing a UID string. The key must include the identity type (or the denial cache must not be applied to renderer/anonymous identities).

title: Denial cache key uses ambiguous underscore concatenation, allowing cross-resource collisions
body: userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates userUID, action, name and parent with '_' separators and no escaping or length prefixing. Dashboard/folder UIDs can contain underscores, so distinct tuples collide, e.g. (name="a_b", parent="c") and (name="a", parent="b_c") produce the same key, as do userUID/action boundary variants. A denial legitimately cached for one resource therefore returns Allowed:false for a different resource the user may actually have access to. Encode the components unambiguously (e.g. hash the tuple or use a separator that cannot appear and length-prefix fields).

title: Negative caching reintroduces stale denials for newly granted/created resources
body: After the new DB re-query, any !allowed result is cached in permDenialCache for shortCacheTTL (30s) and subsequent Checks short-circuit at line 117 without re-querying. If a user (or UI) checks a dashboard/folder before its permission row exists or before an admin grants access, and the grant/creation then happens, the creator/grantee is still denied for up to 30s - the exact stale-denial symptom this PR aims to fix for newly created dashboards/folders. It is also set when checkPermission failed only because the folder tree came from the still-cached folderCache (buildFolderTree is not refreshed on the DB fallback), so a stale tree produces a persistent 30s denial even after permissions are re-fetched.

title: List still trusts stale cached permissions with no freshness fallback
body: Unlike Check, which now falls back to getIdentityPermissions when cached permissions do not allow the requested resource, List at line 180 returns whatever getCachedIdentityPermissions returns (permissionCacheUsage hit) and never re-queries the DB. After a user creates or is granted a dashboard/folder, List - the API used to fetch visible resources - will omit the new resource until permCache expires (30s), so the PR's goal of letting creators fetch newly created dashboards/folders is not achieved for listing even though single-resource Check now works.

title: Denial cache key does not include identity type, allowing cross-identity poisoning
body: permDenialKey is built only from namespace, raw UserUID, action, name and parent. Anonymous subjects (anonymous:0) and the render service (render:0) both parse to UserUID "0", and user/service-account subjects can also share UID strings. A denial cached for anonymous:0 on dashboards:read/dash1 is therefore returned for render:0 on the same resource, even though getRendererPermissions would grant renderers read access to all dashboards/folders. The same collision can deny a user or service account based on another identity type's denial. The identity type (checkReq.IdentityType) must be part of the denial key.

title: Denial cache blocks newly granted permissions and defeats the fresh-DB recheck
body: Check returns immediately on a permDenialCache hit and never re-queries the DB, while the entry written at line 154 lives for shortCacheTTL (30s) and is never invalidated when permissions change or when permCache is refreshed (e.g. by a List or another Check that fetches fresh permissions). A user who checks a dashboard/folder before its permission grant is visible, then creates/receives access to it, remains denied for up to 30s despite this PR's stated goal of letting creators immediately access newly created resources via a DB requery on cached-permission misses.

title: Denial cache key uses ambiguous underscore delimiters for name and parent
body: userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates userUID, action, name and parent with '_' separators, but dashboard/folder UIDs legitimately contain underscores. Distinct tuples collide: (name="c_d", parent="e") and (name="c", parent="d_e") produce the identical key, as do userUIDs containing underscores combined with shifted name/parent segments. A denial for one resource can therefore incorrectly deny a different resource in a different folder for 30s. Fields should be encoded unambiguously (e.g. length-prefixed or escaped/hashed).

title: Every cached-permission miss for a distinct resource triggers a full DB permission fetch
body: When cached permissions do not allow the check, Check unconditionally calls getIdentityPermissions, and this PR removed the permCache lookups inside getUserPermissions/getAnonymousPermissions, so that call always queries basic role, teams and the permission store (singleflight only dedupes concurrent identical keys, not sequential calls). Checking many distinct resources the user legitimately cannot access (e.g. listing/probing dashboards) causes one full DB fetch per resource until each individual resource's denial entry is populated, largely negating permCache for negative checks and risking DB load under denied-request traffic.

title: Denial cache prevents newly granted/created resources from becoming accessible until TTL expiry
body: Check returns Allowed:false solely from permDenialCache before consulting fresh DB permissions, and no path clears a denial entry when permissions change or when getIdentityPermissions later refreshes permCache for another request. A user checked before creating/being granted a dashboard or folder (or before a grant propagates) is therefore still denied for the full shortCacheTTL (30s), partially defeating this PR's goal of letting creators immediately fetch newly created resources. Only TTL expiry unblocks them.

title: Denial is cached even when the denial may be caused by a stale folder tree
body: On the DB-recheck path, checkPermission -> checkInheritedPermissions still uses buildFolderTree's folderCache (30s TTL); permissions are refreshed but the folder hierarchy is not. A dashboard in a newly created/moved folder can thus be denied because ancestors are missing from the stale tree, and line 154 then promotes that possibly-stale result into permDenialCache for another TTL, extending the incorrect denial beyond the folder-cache expiry and making it immune to the permission refresh.

title: Denial cache key is ambiguous and shares the permission-cache key prefix
body: userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates namespace, userUID, action, name and parent with '_' and no escaping/length-prefixing, so distinct tuples such as (name='a_b', parent='c') and (name='a', parent='b_c') produce the same key; Grafana UIDs may contain underscores. A denial for one resource can therefore incorrectly deny a different resource. The key also uses the same 'perm_<uid>_<action>' prefix as userPermCacheKey in the same underlying cache, so crafted/extended components can collide with a permission entry (bool vs map JSON), causing spurious cache misses/corrupt entries.

title: List still returns stale cached permissions with no revalidation
body: List accepts getCachedIdentityPermissions as authoritative whenever present and never re-queries the DB, unlike Check which falls back when the cached set does not contain the requested resource. A newly created dashboard/folder (or newly granted scope) will therefore be omitted from List results until permCache expires, so the PR's stated fix for fetching newly created dashboards/folders does not work for list/fetch-many flows that rely on List.

title: Delete action is never shown in the ruler-less list view
body: canDelete is now computed from the Grafana Prometheus rule when rulerRule is absent, but the Delete menu item is additionally gated on `rulerRule &&`. The new GrafanaRuleListItem/RuleActionsButtons path passes only promRule and no rulerRule, so Delete never renders in the alert list view even for users with delete permission, despite the new prom-based ability returning allowed.

title: Pause action is never shown in the ruler-less list view
body: canPause is now computed from the Grafana Prometheus rule when rulerRule is absent, but the pause item is additionally gated on `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)`. Since the list view no longer loads ruler rules, rulerRule is undefined there, the type guard is false, and Pause/Unpause can never be rendered from the list view even when the prom-based ability allows it.

title: Silence drawer cannot open for Prometheus-only rules
body: AlertRuleMenu can now show Silence based on the Prometheus rule and sets showSilenceDrawer, but this component only renders SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is true. In the ruler-less list view `rule` is undefined, so clicking Silence notifications does nothing and users cannot silence Grafana rules from the list.

title: Grafana rule list items are rendered without a React key
body: The 'grafana' case returns <GrafanaRuleListItem> without `key={key}`, unlike the datasource and unknown cases. FilterView builds a stable artificial key (getGrafanaRuleKey) specifically to prevent key duplication/reconciliation problems in this mapped list; omitting it causes React key warnings and can reuse the wrong row state when rules are added, removed, or reordered during pagination/filtering.

title: Federated rule groups are no longer treated as immutable
body: useAllAlertRuleAbilities previously computed `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)` and used it to mark Update/Delete/Pause as unsupported. The refactored useAllRulerRuleAbilities hardcodes `isFederated = false` with a TODO, and useAllAlertRuleAbilities delegates to it. CombinedRule consumers (e.g. the existing rules table/details) can now offer edit/delete/pause for federated Mimir rule groups that must remain immutable.

title: Delete action never appears in the new ruler-less list view
body: canDelete is now computed as ruler-ability OR grafana-prom-ability (line 87), but the Delete menu item is still guarded by `canDelete && rulerRule`. In the new list view (GrafanaRuleListItem/FilterView/GrafanaGroupLoader) only promRule is passed and rulerRule is undefined, so Delete is never rendered even for users with delete permission, despite the new prom-based ability logic and the handleDelete plumbing. The delete capability added for prom rules is effectively dead in the view it was added for.

title: Pause action never appears in the new ruler-less list view
body: canPause is computed as ruler-ability OR grafana-prom-ability (line 83), but rendering requires `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)` and renders MenuItemPauseRule with the rulerRule. In the new list view rulerRule is undefined, so Pause/Unpause is never shown for Grafana rules even when the prom-based ability grants it. Pausing from the list view is lost by this PR.

title: Silence menu item does nothing in the new list view
body: AlertRuleMenu can now show Silence based solely on the prom-rule ability, and clicking it calls handleSilence which sets showSilenceDrawer=true here. However the drawer is only rendered when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is true, and `rule` (the ruler rule) is undefined in the ruler-less list view (GrafanaRuleListItem passes only promRule). Users see and click 'Silence notifications' and nothing happens.

title: Grafana rule list items rendered without React key
body: The grafana case in the rules.map() switch returns <GrafanaRuleListItem> without the `key={key}` prop that the previous GrafanaRuleLoader element and the sibling datasource case have. In a paginated/infinite-scroll list that concatenates batches, React will reconcile these items by index, causing incorrect component/state reuse when the list grows or changes and key-duplication warnings. Restore key={key} (or key on promRule.uid).

title: Federated rule groups are now treated as editable/removable
body: useAllAlertRuleAbilities previously computed isFederated via isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group) and marked such rules immutable (Update/Delete/Pause unsupported). The refactored useAllRulerRuleAbilities used by it hardcodes `const isFederated = false` with a TODO. CombinedRule consumers (existing rule list/details) for datasource-managed federated groups will now offer Edit/Delete/Pause to permitted users for rules that must be immutable, leading to failing or invalid ruler writes.

title: Delete menu item can never appear in the new rule list view
body: canDelete is now OR-computed from the Grafana prom-rule abilities so it can be true when only promRule is supplied (the new list view passes no rulerRule after GrafanaRuleLoader was removed), but rendering is still gated by `canDelete && rulerRule`. In GrafanaRuleListItem/RuleActionsButtons.V2 only promRule is passed, so rulerRule is undefined and Delete is never rendered for Grafana rules in the list view, even for users with delete permission. The same pattern breaks Pause at line 123 (`canPause && rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule) && ...`), so paused-state toggling is also unreachable there.

title: Silence drawer can never open in the new rule list view
body: AlertRuleMenu now enables Silence from the Grafana prom-rule abilities and calls handleSilence, which sets showSilenceDrawer=true here, but the drawer is only rendered when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is true. In the new list view `rule` (the ruler rule) is always undefined because GrafanaRuleListItem only passes promRule, so clicking 'Silence notifications' does nothing and no drawer mounts. The check/drawer need a prom-rule based path.

title: Grafana rule list items are rendered without a React key
body: The `grafana` case in the rules.map() switch returns <GrafanaRuleListItem> without `key={key}`, unlike the datasource case on line 165 and the previous GrafanaRuleLoader usage which had key={key}. FilterView already computes a unique KeyedRuleWithOrigin.key to prevent duplication; without it React falls back to index reconciliation, which can reuse the wrong list-item state (menus, drawers, pause state) when the infinite-scroll list appends/reorders rules and will emit key warnings.

title: Shard-split queries are interpolated twice
body: runShardSplitQuery() now maps every target through datasource.applyTemplateVariables(), and then splitQueriesByStreamShard() passes each shard sub-request to runSplitQuery(), which at querySplitting.ts:299 maps the same targets through applyTemplateVariables() again (the updated test even expects 5 calls for a single query: 1 here plus 1 per shard sub-request). applyTemplateVariables() is not guaranteed to be idempotent: a template-variable value containing a $-prefixed string, an $__auto/$__interval-derived step, or ad-hoc filter handling can be rewritten differently on the second pass, and the second pass runs after interpolateShardingSelector() has injected the __stream_shard__ matcher into the expression. Interpolate only once, e.g. by having runSplitQuery() skip interpolation for requests already interpolated by the shard path or by removing the interpolation here and relying on runSplitQuery().

title: Empty-expression filter runs before interpolation, not after
body: The targets are filtered with .filter((query) => query.expr) before .map(applyTemplateVariables). A target whose expression is only a template variable, e.g. expr='$myQuery', passes the filter, but if the variable interpolates to an empty string the resulting empty query is no longer filtered out; it is then classified by isLogsQuery(''), grouped, and sent to the backend in a sub-request instead of being ignored like other empty queries. Move the empty-expression check to after interpolation (keeping the pre-filter if needed to avoid interpolating empty strings).

title: Shard-split queries are interpolated twice
body: runShardSplitQuery() now interpolates every target with applyTemplateVariables(), but splitQueriesByStreamShard() then passes those targets through runSplitQuery(), which after this PR also calls applyTemplateVariables() for every sub-request. The updated test codifies this by expecting 5 calls for 1 initial query and 4 shard sub-requests. Double replacement can corrupt queries whose interpolated variable value legitimately contains '$' or variable-like text, and can re-evaluate interval/range variables a second time instead of preserving the value fixed at the start. Interpolate once at the shard entry point for selector extraction and make the delegated runSplitQuery() call skip re-interpolation, or remove the early interpolation where it is not needed for sharding.

title: Queries becoming empty after interpolation are no longer filtered
body: The targets are filtered with query.expr before applyTemplateVariables() runs, so a query whose expression consists of a template variable that resolves to an empty string (for example expr='$variable' with an empty variable) survives the empty-query check and is then grouped, classified by isLogsQuery(''), and sent to runQuery()/Loki as an empty expression instead of being ignored like other empty queries. The same ordering was introduced in runShardSplitQuery(). Filter again after interpolation, or move the expr check after the map.

title: Shard-split queries are interpolated twice
body: runShardSplitQuery() already maps every target through datasource.applyTemplateVariables() (shardQuerySplitting.ts:52) because it needs the interpolated selector to fetch __stream_shard__ values, and splitQueriesByStreamShard() then executes each shard group via runSplitQuery() (shardQuerySplitting.ts:163), which now maps the same targets through applyTemplateVariables() again at this line. Template replacement is therefore applied twice to every sharded query (the updated shard test even expects 5 calls for 1 target: 1 up-front plus 1 per shard sub-request). This is not guaranteed idempotent: applyTemplateVariables also injects request.filters (adhoc filters) into the expr, so the second pass can duplicate label matchers/line filters in the LogQL sent to Loki (duplicate matchers in a stream selector can be rejected), and variable values introduced by the first pass that contain '$...' sequences can be re-expanded against the sub-request. The shard path needs a way to tell runSplitQuery() that its targets are already interpolated (or to not pre-interpolate beyond what shard grouping requires) instead of interpolating unconditionally.

title: "Plugin Request Completed" log loses its traceID field
body: The old logRequest explicitly appended "traceID" (from tracing.TraceIDFromContext) to logParams. The new code replaces m.logger.Info with m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info and drops that append, while instrumentContext in contextual_logger_middleware.go only sets endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID and uname in the contextual attributes. Unless the underlying infra logger independently injects a traceID at log time, the completed-request log no longer carries traceID, breaking correlation between this log line and traces/other traceID-tagged logs.

title: TestLogger.FromContext discards the logger's recorded state
body: FromContext returns NewTestLogger(), a fresh instance, instead of returning the receiver (or a logger sharing its Logs). LoggerMiddleware now logs via m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...), so any test that constructs a TestLogger, passes it to the middleware, and then asserts on that instance's InfoLogs.Calls/Message/Ctx will observe zero calls because the log was recorded on the throwaway instance. The fake should return f (sharing state) so existing and future LoggerMiddleware tests can assert on the log output.

title: New ContextualLoggerMiddleware has no test coverage and the logger/context contract is untested
body: This PR adds ContextualLoggerMiddleware, moves instrumentContext into it, makes LoggerMiddleware depend on FromContext(ctx) picking up endpoint/pluginId/dsName/dsUID/uname from the context, and depends on middleware ordering in CreateMiddlewares for that to work. No test is added for the new middleware, and the renamed metrics_middleware_test.go only covers metrics. A regression in ordering or in instrumentContext (e.g. LoggerMiddleware running before the context is enriched) would silently drop all of those fields from "Plugin Request Completed" logs with no failing test.

title: TestLogger.FromContext discards all recorded logs
body: TestLogger.FromContext returns a brand-new NewTestLogger() instead of the receiver (or a logger sharing the receiver's state). LoggerMiddleware.logRequest now logs via m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...), so any test that injects a TestLogger and then asserts on that instance's InfoLogs/WarnLogs/etc. will observe zero calls because the log record was written to a throwaway instance. FromContext should return f (or a logger sharing f's Logs) so the fake remains usable for assertions.

title: "Plugin Request Completed" log loses its traceID field
body: The old logRequest explicitly appended "traceID" from tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false) to every completion log. This change removes that code, and neither the replacement path (grafanaInfraLogWrapper.FromContext in pkg/plugins/log/logger.go, which only converts the infra logger returned by FromContext) nor the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware.instrumentContext (which only sets endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID and uname) adds a traceID attribute. As a result the 'Plugin Request Completed' log line no longer carries traceID, breaking log-to-trace correlation that existed before; the traceID must be re-added either in logRequest or in instrumentContext.

title: TestLogger.FromContext discards all recorded log state
body: FromContext returns a brand-new TestLogger instead of the receiver (or a logger sharing the receiver's state). LoggerMiddleware now logs via m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...), so any test that injects a TestLogger and then asserts on InfoLogs/DebugLogs/etc. of the injected instance will observe zero calls because the log was recorded on the discarded new instance. This makes the fake unable to verify the new LoggerMiddleware path and can silently turn existing assertions vacuous or failing.

title: "Plugin Request Completed" log line loses traceID field
body: The old logRequest explicitly added traceID (via tracing.TraceIDFromContext) plus pluginId/endpoint/dsName/dsUID/uname as log parameters. The new version relies solely on m.logger.FromContext(ctx). The ContextualLoggerMiddleware only sets endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID and uname via log.WithContextualAttributes; it never adds a traceID, and neither does grafanaInfraLogWrapper.FromContext. Consequently the completed-request log no longer carries traceID, breaking correlation between this log line and traces that dashboards/alerts/log queries may rely on.

title: Adding FromContext to Logger interface breaks other implementations
body: Logger is an interface; adding the FromContext(context.Context) Logger method is a breaking change for every implementation outside the two updated in this PR (pkg/plugins/log/logger.go and fake.go), including mocks/fakes in other packages or downstream consumers. Such implementations will no longer satisfy plog.Logger and will fail to compile until updated. The PR should update/search for all in-repo implementations and call out the break, or avoid widening the interface (e.g. optional interface checked by type assertion in LoggerMiddleware).

title: New ContextualLoggerMiddleware has no test coverage
body: This new middleware is now solely responsible for putting endpoint/pluginId/dsName/dsUID/uname into the request context, and LoggerMiddleware depends on it to produce those fields. No test file for contextual_logger_middleware.go is added, and the renamed metrics_middleware_test.go (still named TestInstrumentationMiddleware) does not assert contextual attributes. A regression in instrumentContext (wrong keys, missing datasource/user fields, or reordering in CreateMiddlewares so LoggerMiddleware runs before it) would silently drop those fields from all plugin request logs without any test failing.

title: Device is cached before DB write, so a rejected device is admitted on retry
body: tagDeviceUI calls localCache.SetDefault(key) before anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice. When CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached for a new device, the cache entry remains for 29 minutes. The next Authenticate for the same device hits the cache at line 83, TagDevice returns nil, and client.go therefore returns a successful identity. The configured limit is thus only enforced on the very first request from a process, after which the over-limit device is allowed in.

title: Device-limit check is a non-atomic count-then-insert (TOCTOU)
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice does CountDevices in one DB session and then performs the INSERT/ upsert in a separate session without a transaction, lock, or unique-count constraint. Concurrent anonymous authentications (now synchronous in client.go, and potentially across multiple Grafana instances sharing the DB) can all observe count < deviceLimit and all insert, exceeding the limit. The limit is therefore not reliably enforced under parallel first-time devices.

title: Anonymous authentication now blocks on synchronous DB tagging with no timeout
body: Previously TagDevice ran in a goroutine with a 2-minute timeout on a background context and never blocked login. Now Authenticate synchronously calls TagDevice(ctx, ...) on the request path: every cache-miss anonymous request waits for a COUNT plus INSERT/UPDATE, and a slow/hung database can stall or, via request-context cancellation, abort authentication/tagging. This adds DB latency/load to anonymous page/API loads and removes the panic-recovery/timeout isolation the async path had.

title: Expired existing device is permanently rejected when limit is reached
body: When count >= limit, CreateOrUpdateDevice delegates to updateDevice, which only updates rows whose updated_at is within the last 30 days (anonymousDeviceExpiration). A device returning after >30 days is not included in CountDevices (its slot is free), but updateDevice affects 0 rows and returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. It can never refresh updated_at, so it stays expired and is rejected until the 61-day cleanup deletes it, even though it should be treated as a (re-)new device subject only to the current count.

title: New device_limit option is not declared in defaults/docs
body: cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit reads auth.anonymous/device_limit, but the PR adds no entry to conf/defaults.ini (or configuration documentation). Operators have no discoverable, documented way to set the feature the PR introduces, and Grafana's config-documentation/defaults consistency checks expect new settings to be declared there.

title: Frontend limit type does not match the value actually sent
body: AnonymousDeviceLimit is a plain int64, so the backend always serializes anonymousDeviceLimit as a number (0 when unlimited). The frontend declares it as `number | undefined` in grafana-data/grafana-runtime and defaults it to undefined, implying undefined means unset/unlimited. Consumers checking `=== undefined` will never see that state from a real server; unlimited is indistinguishable in type from a ( nonsensical ) limit of 0 unless they know the backend convention.

title: Rejected device is cached as successfully tagged, bypassing the limit on retry
body: tagDeviceUI inserts the device ID into localCache (29-minute TTL) before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice. When the store returns ErrDeviceLimitReached the caller denies authentication, but the cache entry remains, so the device's next request hits the cache at line 83, TagDevice returns nil, and Anonymous.Authenticate grants an identity even though the device was never recorded and the limit is still exceeded. A rejected client only has to retry once to bypass the device limit for the cache lifetime.

title: Device-limit check is a non-atomic count-then-insert race
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice counts devices in one query and then performs the INSERT ... ON CONFLICT upsert as a separate statement/session when count < deviceLimit. Concurrent requests (including from multiple Grafana instances sharing the database, where the per-instance local cache provides no coordination) can all observe count == limit-1 and all insert, exceeding the configured limit. The limit needs an atomic/serialized enforcement (transaction with locking, unique-window constraint, or serialized writer), not a check-then-act across two sessions.

title: Provider signature changed without regenerating Wire wiring
body: ProvideAnonymousDeviceService changed its second dependency from anonstore.AnonStore to db.DB, and ProvideAnonDBStore gained a deviceLimit argument, but no wire_gen.go/wire set changes are included in this PR. The checked-in generated wiring still constructs and passes an *AnonDBStore where a db.DB is now expected and still calls ProvideAnonDBStore with one argument, so the server build/wire generation fails until the injector is regenerated and the now-redundant store provider binding is reconciled.

title: Anonymous authentication now synchronously performs DB writes and loses panic isolation
body: Authenticate previously tagged devices in a background goroutine with a 2-minute detached-context timeout and a recover() for panics. It now calls TagDevice synchronously on the request context: a slow/count-query-backed store blocks every anonymous authentication (cache misses add a COUNT plus INSERT/UPDATE round trip), request cancellation aborts tagging, and a panic in tagging propagates into the auth path instead of being logged. This turns device bookkeeping into a latency and availability dependency of anonymous login.

title: New device_limit option is not declared in default/sample config or documentation
body: The code reads [auth.anonymous] device_limit via MustInt64(0), but this PR adds no entry to conf/defaults.ini or conf/sample.ini and no configuration documentation. Grafana convention declares every setting in defaults.ini (which also feeds config docs/overrides tooling); without it the new limit is undiscoverable for operators and omitted from generated config documentation, despite being the user-facing switch for this feature.

title: Rejected device is cached as tagged and bypasses the limit on retry
body: tagDeviceUI inserts the device ID into localCache (SetDefault with 29-minute TTL) before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice, and does not evict the entry when that call returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. The first request for a new device over the limit is rejected in client.go, but any retry within 29 minutes hits the cache at line 83, returns nil, and Authenticate then issues an anonymous identity even though the device was never stored. This makes the device limit trivially bypassable by reloading the page.

title: Limit check and insert are not atomic, so concurrent devices can exceed the limit
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice performs CountDevices and then, in a separate DB session, INSERT ... ON CONFLICT. Two or more concurrent first-time devices (especially from different Grafana instances, whose local caches are per-process) can all observe count < deviceLimit and all insert, exceeding the configured limit. The limit needs to be enforced atomically (e.g. in a transaction/lock or a single conditional statement) if it is meant to be a hard cap.

title: Anonymous authentication now synchronously blocks on device-tagging DB writes
body: Authenticate previously tagged the device in a background goroutine with a 2-minute timeout and a detached context; it now calls TagDevice synchronously with the request context on every cache miss. This adds a COUNT query plus an INSERT/UPDATE to the authentication hot path for anonymous requests, so DB slowness directly increases (or, when the request context is cancelled, breaks) anonymous request latency/availability, and removes the panic recovery that the goroutine provided.

title: updateDevice relies on RowsAffected, which can be 0 for a valid existing device on MySQL
body: When the limit is reached, existing devices are admitted solely by updateDevice, which treats RowsAffected==0 as ErrDeviceLimitReached. MySQL by default reports rows actually changed (not rows matched), so an UPDATE that sets identical values (e.g. same client_ip/user_agent and an updated_at equal at the column's timestamp precision) returns 0 and a legitimately counted device is rejected as if it were new. The existing-device-at-limit path is also not covered by the new test, which only asserts rejection of a second distinct device.

title: New device_limit setting is not declared in defaults/sample config or docs
body: AnonymousDeviceLimit is read from [auth.anonymous] device_limit, but the PR does not add the key to conf/defaults.ini / conf/sample.ini or the configuration documentation. Operators have no discoverable way to learn the option exists, its default (0 = unlimited), or that negative values are also silently treated as unlimited by the deviceLimit > 0 check in the store.

title: Frontend type says anonymousDeviceLimit may be undefined but backend always sends a number
body: GrafanaConfig declares anonymousDeviceLimit as 'number | undefined' and GrafanaBootConfig defaults it to undefined, but the Go DTO (pkg/api/dtos/frontend_settings.go) is a plain int64 without omitempty, so the server always serializes it (0 when unset). Frontend code distinguishing 'not configured' (undefined) from 'configured as 0/unlimited' will never observe undefined from a real boot payload, making the two states indistinguishable.

title: Cleanup ticker interval reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute without justification
body: The background cleanup ticker is changed from time.Minute*10 to time.Minute*1, so all cleanup jobs including the now multi-query annotation cleanup run 10x more often. This is unrelated to the deadlock fix described in the PR, is not mentioned in the description, and increases steady-state database and CPU load on every Grafana instance. Revert to 10 minutes or justify/configure the change separately.

title: Successful routine cleanup batches are logged at Error level with full ID lists
body: Lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576 and 579 use r.log.Error for normal progress messages on every batch, including batches where err is nil (the fetch error was already returned above) and batches with zero IDs. This will emit error-level logs on every cleanup run, trigger error alerting/log-based monitoring, and include the complete ids slice (bounded only by AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize, e.g. 32767 IDs in the new test), producing huge log lines and I/O overhead. These should be Debug/Info without the full ID list or only logged when an actual error occurs.

title: Placeholder-limit workaround only handles SQLite, leaving large batches broken on PostgreSQL
body: deleteByIDs inlines IDs only when the DB is SQLite and the configured batch size exceeds 999; otherwise it builds one '?' placeholder per ID. PostgreSQL has a 65535 bind-parameter limit (and drivers/DBs have similar limits), so a configured AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize above that limit makes DELETE ... IN (?,...,?) fail with too-many-parameters, whereas the previous single-statement DELETE had no bind parameters and worked for any batch size. The decision is also based on the configured batch size rather than len(ids). Chunk the delete by actual ID count or inline/chunk for all dialects.

title: SQLite ID inlining builds the IN list quadratically
body: For SQLite batches over 999, values is rebuilt with fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) for every ID, copying the entire accumulated string each iteration. With the tested batch size of 32767 (and larger allowed configurations) this is O(n^2) copying and allocations on the cleanup path. Build the list with strings.Builder / strconv instead.

title: Cleanup interval reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute without justification
body: The ticker interval is changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, making all cleanup jobs, including the batched annotation cleanup, run ten times as often. This is unrelated to splitting the annotation queries and can increase sustained database load, lock contention, and the chance of overlapping long-running cleanup work (the per-run timeout is 9 minutes). The interval should remain 10 minutes unless this change is intentional and justified.

title: Routine cleanup batches are logged at Error level with full ID lists
body: Every batch in CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags logs via r.log.Error, including successful batches and empty batches, and includes the complete ids slice and SQL condition. This will emit error-level records on every cleanup cycle, polluting error monitoring, and with large batch sizes (for example the 32767 case added in tests) creates very large log lines. Routine progress should be Debug/Info and should log counts, not all IDs.

title: Parameter-limit handling only special-cases SQLite and can stall cleanup on other databases
body: deleteByIDs builds one bind parameter per ID for every non-SQLite database. If AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is configured above the driver's parameter limit (for example SQL Server's 2100 or MySQL/PostgreSQL prepared-statement limits), the DELETE fails and untilDoneOrCancelled aborts, so cleanup cannot progress in subsequent batches. The previous subquery DELETE had no per-ID parameter limit. The delete should be chunked below the dialect's limit, or inlined/chunked safely for all supported databases, not only when SQLite's batch size exceeds 999.

title: SQLite ID list construction is quadratic for large batches
body: The SQLite branch builds the IN list with values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) inside a loop, repeatedly copying the growing string. For the tested batch size of 32767 this is O(n^2) copying and can allocate substantial memory/CPU on every batch. Use strings.Builder (already imported) or strconv.AppendInt into a byte buffer to build the list in linear time.

title: Cleanup ticker interval reduced 10x without justification
body: The global cleanup ticker is changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, so every cleanup job (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, invites, short URLs, query history, and annotations) now runs 10x more often, not just annotation cleanup. This unrelated change increases DB and filesystem load on all Grafana instances and partially works against the goal of reducing MySQL contention from annotation cleanup. It should be reverted or justified and scoped to annotations only.

title: Routine cleanup progress is logged at Error level with full ID lists
body: CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags log 'Annotations/Tags to clean' and 'cleaned ...' via r.log.Error on every batch, including successful batches where err is nil. This will emit error-level logs (often wired to alerting/error reporting) for normal operation and each message embeds the full ids slice, which can be tens of thousands of IDs for large batch sizes, creating huge noisy log lines. These should be Debug/Info level without dumping all IDs.

title: SQLite inline ID list is built with quadratic string concatenation
body: For SQLite with a large batch size, deleteByIDs builds the IN (...) list with `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` in a loop over all ids. Each iteration copies the entire accumulated string, so building a 32767-ID list (as exercised by the new test) is O(n^2) in bytes copied and can take seconds and large allocations before the DELETE runs. Use strings.Builder (already imported) to build the list linearly.

title: Async legacy writes inherit the request context and will usually be cancelled
body: Create (and the identical patterns in Delete, Update and DeleteCollection) launch `go func()` with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` derived from the incoming request ctx. When the handler returns the created object, the apiserver cancels the request context, so the legacy write racing the response will typically see context.Canceled and never persist. Mode 3's guarantee that legacy is kept in sync as a safety net is therefore broken; the fix is a detached context (e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx) plus timeout) with request-scoped values/logging preserved.

title: Same object/objInfo shared between returned result and async legacy goroutine
body: Create passes the same `obj` pointer to Storage.Create, returns `created` to the caller, and concurrently passes `obj` to Legacy.Create in the goroutine; Update similarly re-uses the same `objInfo` for both stores. Callers/serializers can mutate or read the returned object while the legacy goroutine reads/mutates it (data race), Storage.Create may have set ResourceVersion/UID on obj making a subsequent legacy Create reject it, and UpdatedObjectInfo is not required to be idempotent or safe to evaluate a second time against a different (legacy) old object. The previous implementation used updateWrapper to hand legacy the exact object written to unified storage; dropping that also risks legacy updates computed from stale legacy state with a unified-storage ResourceVersion, causing RV conflicts. Deep-copy/wrap the object for the legacy write before returning.

title: Storage failures are recorded as legacy metrics
body: On Storage.Create error this records `recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` instead of `recordStorageDuration`, and Update does the same at line 129. Storage failures will inflate legacy error/latency metrics and leave storage metrics missing, misleading the dashboards/alerts used to judge whether mode 3 can be trusted. DeleteCollection's async goroutine at line 166 conversely calls recordStorageDuration for the Legacy.DeleteCollection call, and Delete at line 106 passes `name` instead of `options.Kind` as the kind label on success, creating wrong/high-cardinality series.

title: Async legacy failures are never logged
body: The legacy goroutines only record a duration metric and discard the returned error (Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection). Previously legacy failures were logged with the object. Combined with the fire-and-forget design, a permanently failing legacy write (e.g. duplicate create, RV conflict, validation) leaves unified and legacy silently diverged with no log line to investigate; at minimum log errObjectSt inside each goroutine.

title: Mode 3 tests never verify the async legacy write and race its completion
body: Tests register legacy mock expectations but Create/Update return before the legacy goroutine runs and no test waits for or asserts the legacy call (no AssertCalled / channel / Eventually). The mock.Mock is shared with a goroutine that may execute after the subtest finishes, so expectations can be silently unfulfilled or the stray goroutine can panic/race a later subtest sharing the package-level fixtures. The playlist integration cases in pkg/tests/apis/playlist/playlist_test.go have the same issue: doPlaylistTests immediately asserts the legacy API reflects k8s creates/updates/deletes, which under async mode 3 is inherently racy and will be flaky.

title: Delete discards its enriched logger when building the context
body: Delete builds `log := d.Log.WithValues("name", name, "kind", ..., "method", method)` but then does `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` with the unenriched logger, unlike the other methods. Downstream storage/legacy code logging from ctx loses name/kind/method correlation for deletes. It should be NewContext(ctx, log).

title: Async legacy writes derive timeout context from cancelled request context
body: Create, Delete (line 110), Update (line 135) and DeleteCollection (line 163) start goroutines with context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...) where ctx is the incoming request context. The API server cancels that context as soon as the handler returns, which happens immediately after the goroutine is spawned, so the legacy write will almost always run with an already-cancelled context and fail/be aborted. The legacy store therefore silently diverges from unified storage, defeating the stated purpose of mode 3. The goroutine needs a detached context (e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx) or a background context preserving values) before applying the timeout.

title: Legacy Create receives the pre-create object instead of the object created in unified storage
body: Storage.Create returns 'created', which carries server-assigned name (generateName), UID, resourceVersion and creationTimestamp, but the goroutine passes the original input 'obj' to Legacy.Create. If the storage does not mutate 'obj' in place, legacy creates a different object (different generated name/UID) or rejects it, so the two stores hold divergent copies. It also races with the caller/storage continuing to use 'obj' after Create returns. The legacy call should use the object returned by unified storage (as the previous synchronous implementation effectively did).

title: Legacy Update reuses the same UpdatedObjectInfo instead of the unified-storage result
body: The previous implementation wrapped objInfo so Legacy.Update received the exact object produced and stored by unified storage. The new code passes the raw objInfo to both Storage.Update and, asynchronously, Legacy.Update, so UpdatedObject is evaluated a second time against the legacy store's old object. If the legacy copy is missing or stale (the normal case while mode 3 is being rolled out, or after a failed async create), the legacy update computes from the wrong base, fails on resourceVersion, or creates/updates divergent content. It also shares objInfo with a goroutine that outlives the request. The result 'res' from Storage.Update should be wrapped (updateWrapper) and passed to legacy, as before.

title: Async legacy failures are never logged
body: In Create, Delete, Update and DeleteCollection the goroutine only records a duration metric and discards the legacy error; the previous synchronous code logged legacy failures with the object context. Combined with the fire-and-forget design, a permanently failing legacy write (bad object, missing row, timeout) is invisible in logs and unrecoverable, so operators cannot detect or reconcile divergence between unified and legacy storage. Each goroutine should log the error (with kind/name) in addition to recording the metric.

title: Storage failures are recorded as legacy metrics in Create and Update
body: When Storage.Create fails, line 45 calls recordLegacyDuration, and when Storage.Update fails, line 129 does the same, even though legacy was never called and 'startStorage' measured the storage attempt. Storage error rates/latencies for create and update will be invisible while legacy metrics show phantom failures, misleading the dashboards used to judge dual-write health. These should call recordStorageDuration(true, ...).

title: Delete and DeleteCollection record metrics with wrong labels/recorder
body: Delete's success path calls recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, ...) passing the object name where every other call passes options.Kind, creating per-object-name time series (unbounded cardinality) and breaking kind-based aggregation. DeleteCollection's legacy goroutine at line 166 calls recordStorageDuration instead of recordLegacyDuration, so legacy delete-collection latency/errors are attributed to unified storage. Both misreport the metrics this PR relies on to observe async legacy writes.

title: Mode 3 tests never verify the asynchronous legacy writes
body: TestMode3_Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection return as soon as the unified-storage call succeeds and never wait for or assert on the spawned legacy goroutine (no AssertCalled/waitgroup/synchronisation); several cases don't even register a legacy expectation. The core new behaviour of mode 3 — that legacy is written, with the right object, after unified storage — is therefore untested, and the un-awaited goroutines can also race with subsequent subtests sharing the package-level mocks/fixtures (mock.Mock is not safe for unsynchronised concurrent use). Tests should synchronise on the legacy call and assert its arguments, including that legacy failures do not fail the request.

title: Async legacy writes inherit the request context and will usually be cancelled
body: Create (line 51), Delete (line 110), Update (line 135) and DeleteCollection (line 163) derive the legacy timeout context from ctx, which is the incoming request context embedded with the logger. The Kubernetes API handler cancels that context when the request returns, and Mode 3 returns immediately after spawning the goroutine. The legacy operation therefore races request completion and will often receive context.Canceled before writing, silently defeating the stated safety copy to legacy storage. The goroutine should derive from a detached context (for example context.WithoutCancel or a background context, preserving needed values) before applying the 10-second timeout.

title: Async Update reuses the same UpdatedObjectInfo instead of the object already written to unified storage
body: Storage.Update has already consumed objInfo to compute the updated object from the unified-storage version. The goroutine then passes the same objInfo to Legacy.Update, which will fetch the legacy (different) old object and call UpdatedObject again. That second computation can carry the unified-storage ResourceVersion/UID state and fail optimistic-concurrency or validation against legacy, or produce different content than what was committed to unified storage. The previous implementation wrapped objInfo in updateWrapper carrying the exact object returned by Storage.Update; dropping that wrapper is a regression for the dual-write update path.

title: Async Create passes the storage-mutated input object to legacy Create
body: d.Storage.Create(ctx, obj, ...) is commonly implemented by mutating the passed-in obj in place (setting ResourceVersion, UID, creation timestamp, generated name). The goroutine then passes that same obj to d.Legacy.Create. Legacy create can therefore see a non-empty ResourceVersion/UID and reject the create, or create a legacy record whose identity/RV does not match a fresh create. Legacy should receive a copy cleared/derived from the returned created object (as other dual-writer modes do by stripping ResourceVersion), and doing the copy after Storage.Create also needs to happen before the caller can mutate the returned object.

title: Storage failures and DeleteCollection legacy result are recorded against the wrong metric
body: On Storage.Create failure (line 45) and Storage.Update failure (line 129) the code calls recordLegacyDuration(true, ..., startStorage) even though legacy was never attempted, so storage errors pollute the legacy latency/error series and no storage error is recorded. In DeleteCollection the async legacy call at line 166 calls recordStorageDuration instead of recordLegacyDuration, so legacy delete-collection latency is counted as storage latency. Delete success at line 106 also passes `name` in place of the kind used by every other call, creating inconsistent/high-cardinality metric labels. This makes the mode-3 dashboards/alerts used to judge migration safety wrong.

title: Legacy async failures are never logged and a legacy panic crashes the process
body: All four async legacy goroutines only record a duration metric: the returned error is never logged (and in Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection there is not even a log line naming the object on failure), and there is no recover. Because mode 3 promises legacy is written 'just as a safe measure', an operator cannot discover from logs that the safety copy is failing, and a panic in Legacy storage code inside the detached goroutine is not recovered by the HTTP handler middleware and will crash the server process.

title: Mode 3 tests never verify the asynchronous legacy writes and share one mock for both stores
body: The tests construct legacyStoreMock and storageMock around the same *mock.Mock, so a call to either store satisfies indistinguishable expectations, and they never call AssertExpectations / AssertCalled for the legacy Create, Update or Delete paths (Delete/DeleteCollection tests do not even register legacy expectations). Because the legacy calls now run in unsynchronized goroutines, the tests pass even if legacy is never written, and if the goroutine fires after the test finishes it can race with subsequent tests reusing the package-level example objects/mock state. The async behaviour (legacy called, with what object, within the timeout) is the core feature of mode 3 and needs synchronised assertions (e.g. a channel/WaitGroup in the mock).

title: New mode 3 integration cases immediately assert legacy visibility and are racy
body: The new file/unified mode 3 subtests reuse doPlaylistTests, which creates/updates/deletes via the k8s API and then immediately checks the legacy API (getFromBothAPIs and the legacy list/search checks). Under the new implementation the legacy write is fire-and-forget with a 10-second window, so there is no happens-before guarantee when those legacy assertions run; the test will be flaky and can also pass spuriously if a later assertion happens to be late enough. The mode 3 integration case needs polling/eventual-consistency assertions for the legacy side (or to wait for the async write) rather than the synchronous checks used for modes 1/2.

title: Write lock is acquired without re-checking the cache and is held across file I/O
body: After acquiring entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock(), GetWebAssets does not check entryPointAssetsCache again before reloading. Concurrent callers that all missed the initial RLock fast path will queue on the write lock and then each sequentially repeat readWebAssetsFromFile (and overwrite the cache) while holding the lock across disk I/O. This serializes cold-start (and every Dev-mode) requests and performs redundant manifest reads instead of letting all but the first caller reuse the newly populated cache; add a double-checked cache test inside the write lock and return the cached value when another goroutine populated it.

title: No concurrent test covers the race being fixed
body: The change adds synchronization around the global entryPointAssetsCache but no test exercises concurrent GetWebAssets calls, so a regression (e.g. a future unsynchronized access to the cache) would not be caught even under `go test -race`. Add a test that calls GetWebAssets from multiple goroutines in parallel (covering both the cached fast path and the initial load) and run it with the race detector.

title: Missing double-checked cache lookup under the write lock
body: After releasing the read lock at line 43, multiple concurrent cache-miss callers can queue on the write lock. Once each caller acquires it, the code does not re-check entryPointAssetsCache, so every queued caller repeats the manifest file read (and any future CDN fetch) and overwrites the cache instead of returning the value populated by the first caller. Add a second cache check after acquiring the write lock for the non-Dev path.

title: No concurrent regression test for the data-race fix
body: This change introduces mutex protection for the shared entryPointAssetsCache global but adds no test that calls GetWebAssets concurrently. Without a test exercised under `go test -race`, a future refactor could remove or bypass the locking and silently reintroduce the race the PR is intended to fix.

title: Missing double-check under write lock causes duplicate loads and cache replacement
body: After acquiring the exclusive Lock at line 48, the code does not re-check entryPointAssetsCache. Two concurrent cold-cache callers in non-Dev mode can both pass the RLock check with ret==nil, then sequentially each perform readWebAssetsFromFile (and SetContentDeliveryURL) and overwrite entryPointAssetsCache, with the first caller returning a pointer that is no longer the cached one. This wastes I/O and can yield different EntryPointAssets instances to concurrent callers; re-checking `cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil` after Lock and returning it would make the fast path race-free and single-load.

title: Mutex only guards the pointer, shared mutable EntryPointAssets is still returned to all callers
body: GetWebAssets returns the same *dtos.EntryPointAssets pointer stored in the global cache to every caller. The new RWMutex protects only reading/writing the pointer variable, not the pointed-to struct/slices. Any caller that mutates the returned value (as this function itself does via result.SetContentDeliveryURL at line 64) races with concurrent readers of the cached object. The fix is incomplete unless callers are guaranteed never to mutate the result; returning a copy/clone on the cached path (or documenting/enforcing immutability) is needed to fully eliminate the shared-global-state race described in the PR.

title: enableSqlExpressions always returns false and unconditionally dereferences feature toggles
body: enableSqlExpressions computes enabled as the negation of IsEnabledGlobally(FlagSqlExpressions), then returns false on both branches, so the helper is dead, inverted-looking logic. It also unconditionally calls h.features.IsEnabledGlobally even though the result is discarded; an ExpressionQueryReader constructed with a nil FeatureToggles (as test and non-service callers can do) will panic on a SQL query instead of returning the intended 'not implemented' error. Replace the helper with an explicit unconditional rejection (or a nil-safe check) so the disablement is clear and cannot be accidentally re-enabled by 'fixing' one branch.

title: Legacy UnmarshalSQLCommand path is not explicitly gated like the reader path
body: The explicit SQL-expression rejection was added only to ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery in pkg/expr/reader.go. UnmarshalSQLCommand (the legacy rawNode unmarshalling path used by the older SSE pipeline) still calls NewSQLCommand with no disabled/feature check; it is currently blocked only incidentally because the stubbed sql.TablesList returns a generic 'not implemented' error, which surfaces as a misleading 'error reading SQL command' BadRequest. If TablesList/the stub DB is ever restored or changed, this entry point silently becomes reachable again. Add the same explicit rejection to UnmarshalSQLCommand/NewSQLCommand as defense-in-depth for CVE-2024-9264.

title: No regression test that SQL expressions are rejected on all entry points
body: This security change adds no test asserting that QueryTypeSQL is rejected when FlagSqlExpressions is enabled, nor that the legacy UnmarshalSQLCommand path is rejected, and it does not update the existing SQL-expression tests that exercise NewSQLCommand/TablesList/Execute (which now always fail via the stub DB). Without a regression test, a future refactor of enableSqlExpressions or the stub DB could re-enable the DuckDB-backed RCE/LFI surface unnoticed, and the current test suite is left failing or must be silently skipped. Add CVE regression tests for both parsing entry points and update/skip the obsolete happy-path SQL tests explicitly.

title: enableSqlExpressions always returns false and can panic on nil toggles
body: enableSqlExpressions computes enabled as the negation of IsEnabledGlobally, then returns false on both branches, so the feature flag is dead code and the intent is unreadable for anyone re-enabling SQL expressions later. It also dereferences h.features without a nil check: an ExpressionQueryReader constructed with nil FeatureToggles (as test and legacy callers do) will panic on a SQL query instead of returning the 'not implemented' error, turning a disabled-feature request into a server panic path.

title: No tests cover the disabled SQL-expression behaviour and existing SQL tests are left broken
body: The stub DB makes TablesList, RunCommands and QueryFramesInto always return 'not implemented', and reader.go now rejects QueryTypeSQL, but the PR adds or updates no tests. Existing tests that construct SQL commands via NewSQLCommand/UnmarshalSQLCommand will now fail with sql-invalid-sql instead of exercising SQL, and nothing verifies the security-critical contract that a SQL expression is rejected even when FlagSqlExpressions is enabled. The disabled paths in reader.go, sql_command.go and pkg/expr/sql should be covered (and obsolete SQL-execution tests removed or skipped) before merging a CVE fix.

title: Legacy UnmarshalSQLCommand path is not gated by the new disabled check
body: Only ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery checks enableSqlExpressions; UnmarshalSQLCommand (the legacy rawNode pipeline entry point) still calls NewSQLCommand unconditionally. It is only stopped indirectly because sql.TablesList now errors from the stub DB, so legacy callers get a misleading BadRequest 'error reading SQL command' rather than an explicit disabled/not-implemented error, and restoring a real DB implementation in pkg/expr/sql would silently re-enable SQL expressions through this path despite the CVE fix. Gate UnmarshalSQLCommand/NewSQLCommand with the same disabled check.

title: Legacy SQL command construction bypasses the new disabled check
body: UnmarshalSQLCommand still constructs a SQLCommand via NewSQLCommand without checking whether SQL expressions are disabled; only ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery in reader.go has the new gate. This legacy entry point is therefore protected only indirectly because the stub DB makes sql.TablesList fail, returning a misleading BadRequest 'error reading SQL command' instead of an explicit disabled/not-implemented rejection. If the DuckDB-backed DB implementation is restored or replaced, this path will silently re-enable the CVE-2024-9264 surface without passing through the reader check. Gate both construction paths (or remove/stub UnmarshalSQLCommand/NewSQLCommand) so disabling does not depend on a downstream stub error.

title: enableSqlExpressions is dead, inverted logic that always returns false
body: enableSqlExpressions computes enabled := !IsEnabledGlobally(FlagSqlExpressions), then returns false in the if branch and false unconditionally afterwards, so the feature-flag check has no effect and the function name/contract is misleading. The current behavior (always disabled) matches the PR intent, but a future maintainer trying to re-enable SQL expressions behind the flag will find flipping the toggle does nothing and may 'fix' the wrong branch, accidentally re-enabling it insecurely. Make the disable explicit (e.g. return false with a comment referencing the CVE/removal, or delete the helper and inline the rejection) instead of leaving inverted dead logic.

title: No regression test that SQL expressions are rejected even with the feature flag on
body: This is a security fix for CVE-2024-9264 (RCE/LFI via DuckDB SQL expressions), but the PR adds no test asserting that a QueryTypeSQL expression is rejected when FlagSqlExpressions is enabled, nor that the legacy UnmarshalSQLCommand path cannot execute SQL. Without such a test, restoring the go-duck dependency or simplifying enableSqlExpressions back to a plain flag check would reintroduce the vulnerability with no failing test. Add tests covering both entry points with the flag on and off.

title: go.work.sum churn is inconsistent with the go.mod/go.sum dependency removal
body: go.mod/go.sum drop go-duck and its transitive deps (apache/thrift, klauspost/asmfmt, minio/asm2plan9s, minio/c2goasm, JohnCGriffin/overflow), yet go.work.sum re-adds hashes for several of those same modules while dropping unrelated ones (Azure azblob, google go-replayers). This suggests the workspace sums were not regenerated with go work sync after the removal and may fail verification or resurrect the removed DuckDB transitive graph for other workspace modules. Regenerate and verify go.work.sum so the vulnerable dependency is actually gone from the whole workspace, not just the main module.

title: Concurrent BuildIndex calls for the same key can corrupt or leak indexes
body: BuildIndex no longer holds cacheMu during index creation and builder execution, and the cache is only populated at line 137 after the build completes. Concurrent callers for the same NamespacedResource (for example searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex, which has no per-key deduplication, racing the parallel startup builds in searchSupport.init) can therefore both pass GetIndex, both create a bleve index, and for file-backed indexes both call bleve.New on the same directory path, causing lock/already-exists failures or corruption; whichever finishes last silently overwrites cache[key] without closing the earlier index, leaking its file handles/memory. The lock needs to remain finer-grained but still deduplicate/serialize builds per key and close any replaced index.

title: TotalDocs iterates the index cache without holding cacheMu
body: TotalDocs ranges over b.cache without acquiring cacheMu.RLock. With BuildIndex now inserting into b.cache (lines 137-139) while other builds/searches may be running, and searchSupport.init now calling TotalDocs for its completion log after parallel builds, this concurrent map iteration versus map write can trigger Go's fatal 'concurrent map iteration and map write' panic and crash the process. TotalDocs should snapshot or iterate the cache under RLock (taking care not to hold it during slow DocCount calls if that reintroduces contention).

title: Failed startup Init leaks the server's background context and watch goroutines
body: NewResourceServer now calls s.Init(ctx) before returning, but on error it only logs and returns nil, err without calling s.cancel() or Stop. If initialization partially succeeds -- e.g. search.init succeeds and starts its WatchWriteEvents goroutine/poller in searchSupport.init, then initWatcher fails -- the constructed server is discarded yet its background context (created at line 229) is never cancelled, so the search watcher, backend poller, and any blob/backend resources keep running for a server that failed to start. Cleanup (cancel/Stop) should run on the Init error path.

title: Concurrent BuildIndex calls for the same key can create duplicate Bleve indexes
body: BuildIndex no longer holds cacheMu during index creation and only locks for the final cache assignment. Two concurrent builds for the same NamespacedResource (for example, eager startup indexing racing a Search or watch-event getOrCreateIndex call, or two concurrent lazy builds for a missing key) can both call bleve.New/NewMemOnly, both run the builder, and both write the cache entry. For file-backed indexes they use the same directory, which can fail with lock/already-exists errors or interfere with each other; for all indexes the overwritten index is never closed, leaking its resources and leaving one caller with an index that is no longer the cached/searchable one. The previous whole-build lock serialized this; the finer-grained lock needs per-key deduplication or a check-and-reserve entry under the lock before building.

title: TotalDocs iterates the index cache without holding cacheMu
body: TotalDocs ranges over b.cache without acquiring cacheMu while BuildIndex now concurrently inserts into that map at line 138 after releasing most of its work from the lock. searchSupport.init calls TotalDocs after starting the watch goroutine, and later lazy builds can also run concurrently, so this can race with a map write and cause a fatal 'concurrent map iteration and map write' panic that cannot be recovered. TotalDocs should snapshot the indexes under RLock (or hold RLock while counting) before calling DocCount.

title: NewResourceServer now blocks on full index building and leaks background work on init failure
body: NewResourceServer synchronously calls s.Init(ctx) with the server's background-derived context, so construction now blocks until lifecycle init, full search indexing, and watcher setup finish, and callers cannot cancel or time out that work with their own context. If Init fails part-way (for example after search.init has started its WatchWriteEvents goroutine, which uses context.Background(), or after lifecycle Init), NewResourceServer returns nil and an error without calling s.Stop/s.cancel, leaving the caller no handle to stop the lifecycle backend or background goroutines. Previously lazy Init let server construction succeed and deferred this cost/failure to first use; eager init needs cleanup on failure and a cancellable startup context.

title: Postgres module-server regression is hidden by skipping the test
body: The change adds an unconditional skip for GRAFANA_TEST_DB=postgres with only a TODO saying the test does not work in Drone. This removes the only integration coverage for running the storage-server target without an HTTP server exactly in the configuration affected by moving unified-storage initialization into server construction, so a postgres-specific startup/init failure can merge and remain undetected. The skip should be tied to a tracked failure/issue or the underlying Drone/postgres init problem should be fixed instead of silently dropping coverage.

title: TotalDocs iterates the index cache without holding cacheMu
body: TotalDocs ranges over b.cache without acquiring cacheMu, while BuildIndex now inserts into that map under only a brief lock at the end of a potentially long build. Concurrent index creation (startup initialization with multiple workers, or lazy getOrCreateIndex during Search) can therefore race with TotalDocs, causing a data race and potentially a fatal 'concurrent map iteration and map write' panic. TotalDocs should hold cacheMu.RLock while iterating, or snapshot the indexes first.

title: Concurrent BuildIndex calls for the same key are no longer serialized
body: Removing the whole-function cacheMu lock means two concurrent BuildIndex calls for the same NamespacedResource can both create a bleve index, run the builder, and then overwrite b.cache[key]. For file-backed indexes both calls use the same directory, so the second bleve.New can fail or conflict with the first; for memory indexes the overwritten index is leaked without being closed and in-flight searches may keep using a different instance than the cached one. The finer-grained locking needs a per-key build lock/singleflight, and any replaced index should be closed.

title: searchSupport.init mutates shared counters and err from errgroup goroutines
body: Inside group.Go, totalBatchesIndexed++ and '_, _, err = s.build(...)' mutate variables declared outside the goroutine. With initWorkers > 1 these run concurrently, so the counter increment is racy/lost and the shared err can be overwritten by a succeeding build after a failing one (or vice versa), meaning group.Wait may not reliably report the failing build and the span attribute may be wrong. Use an atomic counter and a local '_, _, err := s.build(...); return err' inside each goroutine.

title: Failed eager Init leaks the server background context and any started watch goroutine
body: NewResourceServer now calls s.Init(ctx) during construction and, on error, returns nil without calling s.cancel(). If search.init succeeded far enough to start its watch goroutine (which uses context.Background in searchSupport.init) or lifecycle/watcher setup partially started, those goroutines and the claims context created at line 229 are never cancelled because the caller never receives the server to Stop. Construction failure should cancel s.cancel() (and stop any partially started lifecycle/search watcher) before returning the error.

title: Call to isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() does not compile
body: UsernameForm.authenticate() calls isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() with no arguments, but the only method added to its superclass UsernamePasswordForm is isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user) at UsernamePasswordForm.java:160. There is no no-arg overload, so this file will fail compilation and the PR cannot build.

title: Conditional passkeys are now disabled on the initial login page
body: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel) now requires user != null, and authenticate() at line 115 and challenge(context,error,field) at line 137 use it to decide whether to call webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context). On a first (non-re-authentication) login the user is not yet identified, so context.getUser() is null, fillContextForm is never called, and the ENABLE_WEBAUTHN_CONDITIONAL_UI attribute, challenge and RP data are not set on the login form. This breaks discoverable/passkey-first login where the credential itself identifies the user, e.g. the existing webauthnLoginWithDiscoverableKey tests that expect automatic passkey login from the initial UsernamePasswordForm page. The condition should remain based on passkeys being enabled, with shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators() (now overridden to false for conditional UI) preventing display of a per-user authenticator list.

title: Call to non-existent no-arg isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() breaks compilation
body: UsernameForm.authenticate() calls isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() with no arguments, but the only method defined in its superclass UsernamePasswordForm (line 160) is isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user). There is no inherited no-arg overload, so this file will not compile. It should pass the current user, e.g. isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser()).
