There is no coverage that optimized pagination returns correct next/prev cursors for datetime keys, that negative offsets are rejected rather than crashing or leaking out-of-page rows, or that non-admin/non-optimized requests still work. Given the datetime-key and negative-slice failures above, tests exercising a real multi-page audit-log request with optimized_pagination=true would have caught the breakage before merge.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator is incompatible with datetime ordering
body: The endpoint orders AuditLogEntry by '-datetime', but OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key in paginator.py does math.floor/math.ceil directly on the attribute value and value_from_cursor returns the raw integer cursor value. For a datetime field this raises TypeError when build_cursor computes keys (and compares a datetime column against an int in build_queryset), so the new optimized_pagination=true path returns 500 instead of audit logs for every authorized admin who enables it. DateTimePaginator exists precisely to convert datetimes via timestamps; this paginator does not.

title: Negative-offset slicing of a Django queryset raises instead of paginating
body: When enable_advanced_features is set and a client supplies a cursor with a negative offset (Cursor.from_string accepts any int), the code does queryset[negative:stop]. Django querysets explicitly reject negative indexing with AssertionError ('Negative indexing is not supported'), contrary to the comment claiming the ORM handles it. A privileged user can therefore craft a cursor that 500s the audit-log endpoint, and the same unclamped is_prev offset at line 182/884 exposes BasePaginator users to the same crash.

title: organization_context.member may be None
body: enable_advanced is computed as request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access. For non-superuser requests where the organization context has no member (e.g. superuser-less API/token contexts that reach this endpoint, or members not yet resolved), evaluating .has_global_access on None raises AttributeError and 500s a previously working endpoint; the check is evaluated on every request, not only when optimized_pagination=true, because Python evaluates the right-hand side regardless of use_optimized's value only gated by the boolean expression order — actually enable_advanced is always computed before the if, so all non-superuser requests without a member regress.

title: Insert-time eviction silently discards earliest-ending spans from segments
body: Once a merged set exceeds a hardcoded 1000 members, zpopmin removes the lowest-scored members, where the score is now end_timestamp_precise. This silently deletes arbitrary child spans (those ending earliest) from a segment that will later be flushed as if complete, with no metric, log, or segment-too-large outcome as the previous flush-time check produced. It corrupts segment data rather than rejecting/skipping oversized segments, and the hardcoded 1000 also ignores SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans (default 1001) and any configured value.

title: SET-to-ZSET conversion breaks in-flight Redis segments during deployment
body: Existing span-buf:s:* keys in Redis are regular sets created by SADD. The new code unconditionally issues ZADD in process_spans, ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE/ZPOPMIN in add-buffer.lua, and ZSCAN in _load_segment_data against those same key names. Redis returns WRONGTYPE for these commands on set-typed keys, so during rollout every trace with an unflushed segment (up to redis_ttl=3600s old) errors in the consumer pipeline instead of being flushed; there is no key versioning, type check, or migration/drain step.

title: Flush-time max_segment_spans guard removed with no equivalent for non-Lua growth
body: _load_segment_data no longer enforces max_segment_spans (the metric/log/skip branch was deleted). The only remaining cap is the Lua insert path, which does not cover segments already stored as sets, keys built by the initial batched ZADD before per-span Lua runs interleaved with other batches, or future writers. Oversized segments can now be loaded and produced downstream unbounded by span count, reintroducing the memory/downstream-size risk the guard existed for.

title: Redirect chain traversal cut from 10000 to 1000 breaks deep segment trees
body: The loop that follows span-buf:sr redirects to find the canonical set for a span now stops after 1000 hops instead of 10000, and the comment explaining that deeper trees may not join correctly was removed. Segment trees deeper than 1000 redirects will resolve set_span_id to an intermediate span, so spans are split into multiple segments (flushed separately with wrong segment_id/is_segment attribution) — a silent correctness regression for deep traces that previously worked.

title: Required end_timestamp_precise turns malformed/legacy spans into poison pills
body: process_batch now does val['end_timestamp_precise'] with direct indexing for every message. Any span payload lacking that field (older producers, partial/relay variants the previous code tolerated since it never read the field) raises KeyError inside the batch function, failing the whole batch and causing redelivery of the same poison message indefinitely. The new Span field in buffer.py is also a required positional-or-keyword argument added before the defaulted is_segment_span, breaking any other Span(...) construction sites that don't pass it.

title: Negative queryset slicing is not supported by Django and will crash
body: When enable_advanced_features is true and a user-supplied cursor has a negative offset, this passes cursor.offset directly as a queryset slice start. Django querysets explicitly raise AssertionError ('Negative indexing is not supported'), contrary to the comment claiming the ORM handles it. The OptimizedCursorPaginator path in OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint is therefore a 500 for such cursors rather than advanced pagination, and cursors are attacker-controlled via Cursor.from_string.

title: BasePaginator now allows negative offsets for prev cursors on all endpoints
body: start_offset is only clamped with max(0, offset) when not cursor.is_prev; for is_prev cursors the raw user-supplied offset is used in queryset[start_offset:stop]. A crafted prev cursor with a negative offset makes Django raise AssertionError, turning normal paginated endpoints using BasePaginator into unhandled 500s. Previously offset was used as parsed too, but this change codifies/allows the negative case without validating it; offsets should be rejected/clamped for both directions.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator is incompatible with the datetime ordering used by its only caller
body: OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint instantiates OptimizedCursorPaginator with order_by='-datetime', but get_item_key does math.floor/math.ceil directly on the attribute value and value_from_cursor returns cursor.value unchanged. For AuditLogEntry.datetime the value is a datetime, so math.floor(datetime) raises TypeError when build_cursor computes keys, and even if it did not, value_from_cursor would feed an int millisecond timestamp into build_queryset comparisons against a datetime column instead of converting like DateTimePaginator does. The optimized audit-log path is broken on the first page.

title: ZUNIONSTORE defaults to SUM and corrupts end_timestamp scores for duplicate spans
body: The migration from SUNIONSTORE to ZUNIONSTORE uses the default aggregate SUM. If the same span payload exists in both the destination and merged set (retries/re-deliveries are expected in this consumer), its score becomes the sum of the two end_timestamp_precise values (~2x a Unix timestamp) instead of the span's end time. That corrupts eviction ordering in the same script: duplicated spans look far-future and are retained while non-duplicated earlier spans are popped. The union needs an explicit aggregate such as MAX (or weights 1,0 semantics) to preserve scores.

title: Insert-time ZPOPMIN silently discards the earliest-ending spans from a segment
body: When a segment exceeds 1000 spans, this pops span_count-1000 members with the smallest end_timestamp_precise scores with no metric, log, or dropped-segment marker. Those spans are permanently lost before flushing, so downstream receives an incomplete segment indistinguishable from a complete one; depending on timestamps this can drop children that ended early while keeping later spans. The previous Python-side behavior at least counted/logged oversized segments and skipped them explicitly rather than silently emitting a truncated segment.

title: Removal of max_segment_spans guard lets oversized segments load unbounded at flush
body: _load_segment_data no longer enforces self.max_segment_spans; only the byte-size guard remains. Segments created before this deploy (plain Redis SETs are also incompatible, see zadd change), segments written by old consumers during a rolling deploy, or any path that bypasses the Lua cap can now accumulate arbitrarily many small payloads and be fully materialized into memory in payloads[key], risking consumer OOM instead of the previous counted/logged skip. The Lua hardcoded 1000 also ignores the configurable max_segment_spans=1001 setting.

title: Changing span sets to sorted sets breaks in-flight segments stored as Redis SETs
body: process_spans now issues ZADD and the Lua script issues ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE/ZPOPMIN against span-buf:s:* keys, and _load_segment_data issues ZSCAN. Segments already buffered at deploy time are regular SETs (created by SADD/SUNIONSTORE) with a 3600s TTL; every one of these commands against them returns WRONGTYPE, failing process_spans/flush until the old keys expire and losing/delaying those in-flight segments. No migration, key versioning, or type handling is provided.

title: Redirect chain traversal limit cut from 10000 to 1000 without justification
body: The loop that follows span-buf:sr redirects to find the canonical segment set now stops after 1000 hops instead of 10000; the removed comment noted trees deeper than the limit may not be joined correctly. Deep segment trees between 1000 and 10000 redirects will be split into multiple segments (wrong segment_id/is_segment attribution downstream) — a silent correctness regression unrelated to the stated eviction optimization.

title: New required end_timestamp_precise lookup can poison-batch on messages lacking it
body: process_batch now does val['end_timestamp_precise'] unconditionally while constructing Span (and Span gained the field with no default). Any ingest-spans message missing that field — older producers, partially-formed spans, or schema variants previously accepted since only trace/span/project ids were read — raises KeyError for the whole batch, causing redelivery loops for that batch. Use a fallback (e.g. end_timestamp or message timestamp) or give Span a default.

title: No test covers eviction, score preservation, or the new paginator
body: The test changes only add the now-required end_timestamp_precise field to existing fixtures. Nothing exercises a segment exceeding 1000 spans (which spans get evicted, whether the root span survives), duplicate-payload merges preserving scores under ZUNIONSTORE, or OptimizedCursorPaginator/negative cursors. The core behavioral change of this PR — insert-time eviction — would pass CI even if it dropped the wrong spans or crashed.

title: Insert-time eviction silently discards spans and can produce incomplete segments
body: When a segment exceeds 1000 members, `zpopmin` silently removes the lowest-scored (earliest `end_timestamp_precise`) spans without any metric, log, or marker that the segment was truncated. The remaining segment is later flushed as if complete. This replaces the previous `_load_segment_data` behaviour of detecting oversized segments and logging/metric-ing `segment_span_count_exceeded`, and changes the cap from `max_segment_spans=1001` in Python to a hardcoded 1000 in Lua, so legitimate large segments lose spans invisibly.

title: Redirect chain traversal limit reduced from 10000 to 1000
body: The loop that follows `span-buf:sr:` redirects now stops after 1000 hops instead of 10000, and the comment explaining that deeper segment trees may not be joined correctly was removed. Segment trees deeper than 1000 will now be split into multiple segments (wrong `set_key`, wrong segment/root attribution) where they previously assembled correctly, with no test covering deep chains near the new limit.

title: SET-to-ZSET conversion breaks on existing Redis data during deployment
body: `process_spans` now `zadd`s to `span-buf:s:*` keys and the Lua script uses `zcard`/`zunionstore`, while `_load_segment_data` uses `zscan`. Any segment keys already stored as plain SETs by the previous version (written with `sadd`) will raise Redis WRONGTYPE errors when touched by the new code, so in-flight segments at deploy time will error out / be lost instead of being flushed. No migration, dual-read, or versioned key prefix is provided.

title: Flush-side max_segment_spans guard removed with no replacement for pre-existing/oversized keys
body: The check that skipped and logged segments with more than `max_segment_spans` spans was deleted from `_load_segment_data`. The only remaining cap is the new Lua insert-time cap of 1000, which does not apply to keys created before this change, keys written by still-running old consumers during a rolling deploy, or the `max_segment_bytes`-only path; such segments are now loaded and flushed regardless of span count, and `self.max_segment_spans` is left as dead configuration.

title: Required end_timestamp_precise lookup can crash the consumer on spans lacking the field
body: `val["end_timestamp_precise"]` raises `KeyError` for any ingest-spans message without that field (the existing consumer test payload did not include it until this PR added it). A single such message fails `process_batch` and, being redelivered, can poison-pill the batch instead of being handled or defaulted. The new `Span.end_timestamp_precise` field in buffer.py is likewise a required positional field, breaking any other `Span(...)` constructors that were not updated.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot handle the datetime ordering it is wired into
body: `get_item_key` does `math.floor(value)`/`math.ceil(value)` on the raw attribute, copying `Paginator` instead of `DateTimePaginator`. `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint` passes `order_by="-datetime"`, so `value` is a `datetime` and `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError` on the first result whenever `optimized_pagination=true` is used by a superuser/global-access member. The optimized audit-log path therefore 500s rather than paginating.

title: Negative cursor offsets reach queryset slicing despite Django forbidding negative indexing
body: Cursor values are client-supplied (`Cursor.from_string` accepts a negative offset), and with `enable_advanced_features=True` the code passes `cursor.offset` straight into `queryset[start_offset:stop]`, claiming in comments that 'the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' and that this is safe. Django querysets explicitly raise `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported`, so a crafted `cursor=...:-5:...` request crashes the endpoint (500/DoS); if the queryset were ever a plain sequence the same code would instead wrap around and return rows from the end of the result set, bypassing the intended page window. The same unguarded negative-offset path was left in `BasePaginator.get_result` (line 182) for `is_prev` cursors, affecting all existing paginators.

title: Unrelated, undocumented optimized_pagination switch changes audit-log API behaviour
body: This PR is described as a spans-buffer optimization, but it adds a new `optimized_pagination=true` query parameter and a superuser/`has_global_access` gate that swaps the audit-log endpoint to a different paginator class. That is an unreviewed API contract/behaviour change bundled into the spans change: cursor format and results now depend on the caller's privileges, and (per the paginator defects) the privileged path is broken, with no endpoint tests covering either branch.

title: No test exercises eviction, the 1000-span cap, or deep redirect chains
body: The test changes only add the now-required `end_timestamp_precise` argument to existing Span constructions (all with the identical timestamp 1700000000.0). Nothing inserts more than 1000 spans into one segment to verify which spans `zpopmin` evicts (including whether the root/segment span can be evicted, invalidating `has_root_span` flushing), nothing verifies ordering by differing `end_timestamp_precise` scores after `zunionstore` merges, and nothing covers redirect chains over 1000 hops. The core new behaviour of the PR is therefore untested, as is the new OptimizedCursorPaginator/audit-log path.

title: Upsampling eligibility uses the outer dataset instead of scoped_dataset
body: _get_event_stats receives scoped_dataset, which get_event_stats_factory may replace (e.g. dashboard discover-split passes split_dataset=discover or the original scoped dataset), but the eligibility check passes the closure variable `dataset` instead. The transform decision therefore does not describe the dataset actually queried: split/error queries can miss upsampling and transaction-like split queries can be transformed based on the wrong dataset, producing wrong counts or invalid sample_weight queries.

title: upsampled_count is enabled for the errors dataset but only registered in Discover
body: _should_apply_sample_weight_transform returns True unconditionally for sentry.snuba.errors, so count() is rewritten to upsampled_count() for dataset=errors requests. The new SnQLFunction is only added to Discover's function_converter in src/sentry/search/events/datasets/discover.py; the errors dataset has its own function converter and does not gain this function from that change. Errors-dataset timeseries requests for allowlisted projects will fail function resolution instead of returning upsampled counts.

title: sum(sample_weight) undercounts events whose sample_weight is NULL
body: The aggregate is sum(sample_weight) with no coalesce/fallback. Events stored before client error sampling was populated, or events without a sample rate, can have NULL sample_weight; ClickHouse sum ignores NULLs, so those events contribute 0 instead of 1. Once any allowlisted project is queried, historical/unsampled errors silently disappear from count() results instead of counting with weight 1 (e.g. sum(coalesce(sample_weight, 1))).

title: Substring check treats negated/non-error queries as error-focused
body: _is_error_focused_query returns True whenever the raw query text contains 'event.type:error', including '!event.type:error' (explicitly excluding errors), quoted/tag values containing that text, or a broader OR query that also includes transactions. For Discover this incorrectly rewrites count() to sum(sample_weight) for transaction/non-error results, yielding wrong totals or queries against rows without meaningful sample_weight. The parsed query conditions, not a substring search, need to establish that results are errors only.

title: upsampled_count is exposed as a public user-callable function
body: Unlike the internal count helpers around it, the new SnQLFunction is not marked private=True. Any user can therefore send yAxis=upsampled_count() directly on any Discover query/project, bypassing the endpoint's all-projects-allowlisted and error-only checks. On transaction queries this can fail on sample_weight or return misleading weighted counts; the function should be private so only the server-side rewrite can invoke it.

title: Cache key compresses project IDs into a single hash value
body: Eligibility is cached under hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids))) rather than the project IDs themselves. Different project sets whose tuple hash collides share one cached allowlist verdict for 60s, so a non-allowlisted set can be treated as allowlisted (or vice versa) and counts are silently weighted/unweighted incorrectly. invalidate_upsampling_cache repeats the same scheme and cannot disambiguate. Build the key from the joined sorted IDs instead of a lossy hash.

title: Accidental gitlink file added to the repository root
body: The PR adds a new root entry 'sentry-repo' containing 'Subproject commit a5d2909...', i.e. an accidental nested-repo gitlink rather than application code. Merging it creates a stray submodule-like entry without .gitmodules metadata, which breaks/clutters checkouts and tooling; it should be removed from the change.

title: Upsampled function is not registered for the errors dataset
body: _should_apply_sample_weight_transform returns True unconditionally for the errors dataset, so count() is rewritten to upsampled_count(), but the upsampled_count SnQLFunction added in this PR is only registered in src/sentry/search/events/datasets/discover.py. The errors dataset uses its own function converter, so an allowlisted query explicitly using dataset=errors will fail query validation/building with an unknown-function error instead of returning upsampled counts.

title: Eligibility check uses the outer dataset instead of scoped_dataset
body: is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects is passed the closure variable dataset rather than the scoped_dataset argument to _get_event_stats. The dashboard-widget split path calls _get_event_stats with split_dataset=discover or the original scoped dataset, so the decision is made for the wrong dataset: error split queries originating from metrics/discover datasets will not be upsampled, and conversely a transformation can be decided based on a dataset that is not actually executed.

title: Discover error detection inspects request.GET instead of the executed query and matches negations
body: _is_error_focused_query only looks at request.GET['query'] and does a substring check for 'event.type:error'. It ignores the query argument actually passed to _get_event_stats, including internally constructed dashboard-split queries such as '(...) AND !event.type:transaction', so legitimate error queries can be missed. The substring check also returns True for '!event.type:error' and for mixed queries such as 'event.type:error OR event.type:transaction', applying sum(sample_weight) to non-error/transaction rows where upsampling must not apply.

title: upsampled_count sums sample_weight without handling missing weights
body: The aggregate is toInt64(sum(sample_weight)) with no coalesce/ifNull fallback to 1. Events in allowlisted projects that predate client error sampling, were not client-sampled, or otherwise have a NULL/absent sample_weight contribute NULL rather than counting as one event; if all rows in a bucket are NULL the sum is NULL and toInt64(NULL) can error or produce no count. This silently undercounts (or breaks) ordinary count() queries after the rewrite, contrary to a plain count() for unsampled events.

title: Cache key uses Python hash() of project IDs and is collision-prone
body: The eligibility cache key is built with hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids))). hash() is not a stable, collision-resistant identifier for a set of projects: different project sets can collide and share a cached eligibility result, causing upsampling to be applied to non-allowlisted projects or withheld from allowlisted ones for 60 seconds. A deterministic key such as the comma-joined sorted IDs should be used instead. invalidate_upsampling_cache repeats the same flawed key and is also never called when the allowlist option changes.

title: Stray sentry-repo subproject file committed
body: This added file contains only 'Subproject commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a', i.e. an accidentally committed nested-repository/gitlink artifact pointing at the base commit. It is unrelated to error upsampling and will create a broken/unexpected submodule entry in the repository if merged.

title: Falsy client_sample_rate is dropped and existing sample_rate is overwritten
body: _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling guards with 'if client_sample_rate:', so a present value of 0/0.0 is silently ignored, and for any truthy value it unconditionally overwrites normalized_data['sample_rate'] even if a legitimate sample_rate was already supplied by the SDK/event. In tests this can mask the intended sampling metadata and produce events whose stored sample_weight does not reflect the fixture the author specified.

title: upsampled_count is only registered on Discover but is generated for the errors dataset
body: transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling rewrites count() to upsampled_count() whenever _should_apply_sample_weight_transform returns True, and that helper returns True unconditionally for the errors dataset. However the new SnQLFunction is only added to the Discover dataset's function_converter; the errors dataset has its own function converter without upsampled_count. Any events-stats request with dataset=errors on an allowlisted project will therefore fail query validation/building (unknown function) instead of returning upsampled counts.

title: Upsampling eligibility uses the outer dataset instead of scoped_dataset
body: _get_event_stats receives scoped_dataset (which the dashboard-widget split logic can change to discover or keep as the metrics dataset), but the eligibility check passes the closure variable `dataset` instead of scoped_dataset. When a metrics_performance/metrics_enhanced request is split into a Discover error query, upsampling is wrongly skipped; conversely a transaction-like split can be transformed based on the original dataset even though the executed dataset/query is not error data. The transform decision must be made for the dataset actually executed.

title: Substring check treats negated error filters as error-focused queries
body: _is_error_focused_query does a raw substring search for 'event.type:error', so queries such as '!event.type:error', '-event.type:error', or 'event.type:transaction OR !event.type:error' are classified as error-focused. The endpoint will then rewrite count() to sum(sample_weight) over predominantly transaction/non-error rows, where sample_weight is not meaningful/populated, returning zero or badly undercounted series instead of the real count.

title: sum(sample_weight) drops events that have no sample weight
body: The aggregate is toInt64(sum(sample_weight)) with no fallback for rows whose sample_weight is NULL. Allowlisted projects will normally contain historical events and events ingested without client sampling information; ClickHouse sum() ignores NULLs (and yields NULL/0 for an all-NULL bucket), so those events silently disappear from upsampled counts rather than counting as 1 each. A safe aggregate needs a per-row default such as coalesce(sample_weight, 1).

title: Cache key relies on Python hash() and the invalidation helper is never wired up
body: Eligibility is cached under a key built from hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids))) and invalidate_upsampling_cache recomputes the same expression, but no code path calls invalidate_upsampling_cache when the project allowlist option changes. Combined with hash-collision risk between different project sets, one project set can briefly serve another set's cached eligibility and, more importantly, allowlist removals keep upsampling (and additions keep not upsampling) until TTL expiry with no invalidation hook despite the helper suggesting otherwise. Use a deterministic, collision-resistant key (e.g. the joined project ids) and either call invalidation on option change or remove the dead helper.

title: Accidental gitlink/subproject file committed
body: This adds a file `sentry-repo` containing only 'Subproject commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a', i.e. an accidental nested-repository gitlink. It is unrelated to the upsampling feature, will confuse tooling/checkouts, and should be removed before merge.

title: Error-focus detection reads request.GET instead of the actual query being executed
body: _is_error_focused_query inspects request.GET['query'], but _get_event_stats executes the `query` argument passed through get_event_stats_data and the dashboard split logic, which can differ from the raw GET parameter (split code appends 'AND !event.type:transaction', callers can supply modified queries). Eligibility can therefore be decided from a different query than the one sent to Snuba, causing missed upsampling for split error queries or transforms applied to non-error executions. Pass the effective query string into the eligibility check instead of re-reading the request.

title: Table-widget feature flag renders an empty table instead of the widget data
body: When the organization has the `use-table-widget-visualization` feature, `tableResultComponent` renders `TableWidgetVisualization` with hard-coded `columns={[]}` and `tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}}`, discarding `result.data`, `result.meta`, `fields`, field aliases, custom renderers, and the widget title. Every dashboard table widget for a flagged organization therefore shows an empty table rather than its queried data. The real table result should be converted and passed through, or the flag branch should not replace the working table yet.

title: Error events can be paired with the wrong nodestore payload
body: `fetch_error_details` builds `node_ids` from `error_ids` but then pairs them with `zip(error_ids, events.values())`. `nodestore.backend.get_multi` returns a mapping keyed by node id, not a sequence guaranteed to align positionally with `error_ids`; if an event is missing or the mapping order differs, an error ID is combined with another event's title/message/timestamp (the `if data is not None` check does not fix mis-pairing). This corrupts the chronological error context sent to Seer. Look up each payload by its generated node id instead of zipping values.

title: Hidden span attributes are only hidden while searching
body: The new `HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES` list (`is_segment`, `project_id`, `received`) is applied only inside the branch that runs when `searchQuery` is non-empty. With no search text the function returns `sortAttributes(attributes)` unfiltered, so the supposedly hidden attributes are still displayed by default and only disappear after the user types a query. The hidden-attribute filter should be applied to the sorted list in both paths.

title: Mixed age/timestamp validation misses falsy-but-present values
body: `validate_timestamp` and `validate_age` check `self.initial_data.get("age")` / `get("timestamp")` for truthiness. A report containing `timestamp` plus `age: 0` (a valid, present age) passes validation because `0` is falsy, violating the serializer's own rule that the two fields must not coexist and letting ambiguous Working-Draft/Editor's-Draft reports through. Presence should be tested with `is not None` / `in` rather than truthiness.

title: Assemble analytics are recorded for rejected and feature-disabled requests
body: `analytics.record("preprod_artifact.api.assemble", ...)` runs before the `organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble` feature check and before request-body validation, so 404 feature-disabled responses and 400 invalid requests are counted as assemble events. This inflates adoption/usage metrics with requests that never assembled an artifact. The event should be recorded only after the feature gate (and ideally after validation succeeds), or carry a field distinguishing rejected requests.

title: Merged-PR template helpers are added to the wrong class
body: _truncate_title, get_environment_info, and get_merged_pr_single_issue_template are added to CommitContextIntegration, but GitHubPRCommentWorkflow and GitlabPRCommentWorkflow call self.get_merged_pr_single_issue_template(...) and self.get_environment_info(...) on the PR-comment workflow object, which does not inherit from CommitContextIntegration. Additionally, get_merged_pr_single_issue_template calls PRCommentWorkflow._truncate_title(...), but _truncate_title was defined on CommitContextIntegration, not PRCommentWorkflow. Generating a merged-PR suspect-issue comment will therefore raise AttributeError instead of producing the comment.

title: Feature-flagged table widget renders empty data instead of the query result
body: When the organization has the use-table-widget-visualization feature, tableResultComponent renders TableWidgetVisualization with hardcoded columns={[]} and tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}}. It discards result.data, result.meta, fields, eventView, fieldAliases, custom field renderers, and loading state that are passed to StyledSimpleTableChart in the non-flagged branch, so every dashboard table widget behind the flag will appear empty.

title: Hidden span attributes are only hidden while searching
body: HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES ('is_segment', 'project_id', 'received') is only checked inside the branch that runs when searchQuery is non-empty. When the search box is empty, sortedAndFilteredAttributes returns sortAttributes(attributes) without filtering, so the supposedly hidden attributes are still displayed by default and only disappear after the user types a search query.

title: Browser reports with neither age nor timestamp are accepted
body: BrowserReportSerializer makes both age and timestamp required=False, and validate_age/validate_timestamp only reject the case where both are present. A report with neither field therefore passes validation and is counted, even though the two supported Reporting API specs each require one of these fields and the previous dataclass required timestamp. The validators also use truthiness (self.initial_data.get('age')), so age=0 does not trigger the mutual-exclusion check when timestamp is also present.

title: Error events are paired with error IDs by zipping an unordered nodestore result
body: fetch_error_details builds node_ids from error_ids, calls nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids), then does zip(error_ids, events.values()). get_multi returns a mapping keyed by node id and does not guarantee insertion in error_ids order, and missing nodes are absent rather than represented by None. Consequently IDs can be paired with another event's data, and when any event is missing the zip shifts all subsequent pairings and silently drops trailing errors instead of filtering only the missing entry by its node id, corrupting the error context sent to Seer.

title: New table visualization is rendered with permanently empty data
body: When the 'use-table-widget-visualization' feature is enabled, tableResultComponent renders TableWidgetVisualization with columns=[] and a hard-coded tableData of data: [] and empty meta, instead of converting result.data/result.meta and the widget fields into tabular data. Every dashboard table widget for an organization with the flag enabled will therefore render an empty table regardless of the query results.

title: Reports with neither age nor timestamp, or with age=0 plus timestamp, pass validation
body: Both age and timestamp are declared required=False, so a report containing neither field is accepted even though each supported Reporting API format supplies exactly one of them. The cross-field validators also use truthiness (self.initial_data.get('age') / get('timestamp')), so a report with age=0 and a timestamp present passes despite the stated mutual-exclusion rule. The endpoint will count malformed reports as valid browser reports.

title: Hidden span attributes are only hidden while searching
body: HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES ('is_segment', 'project_id', 'received') is only applied inside the branch that runs when searchQuery is non-empty. With no search text the function returns sortAttributes(attributes) unfiltered, so the supposedly hidden internal attributes are still displayed in the Attributes section; the filter needs to be applied before/independently of the search-text filter.

title: Error events are ordered against segment timestamps using mismatched units
body: fetch_error_details takes 'timestamp' from the stored error event, which is an epoch value in seconds, while replay recording segment events carry rrweb timestamps in milliseconds. gen_request_data compares error_events[error_idx]['timestamp'] < event.get('timestamp', 0) directly, so in production every error (approx. 1.7e9) sorts before every segment event (approx. 1.7e12) and all errors are emitted at the start of the log stream regardless of when they occurred, corrupting the chronological context sent to Seer. The unit test masks this by using second-scale segment timestamps (1.5/2.0/3.0).

title: Assemble analytics event is recorded before feature-flag and validation checks
body: analytics.record('preprod_artifact.api.assemble', ...) runs unconditionally at the start of post(), before the 'organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble' feature check returns 404 and before request-body validation returns 400. Calls from organizations without the feature and malformed requests are therefore counted as assemble API usage, skewing adoption/usage analytics for the new event type.

title: Sender check crashes for integrations without sender metadata
body: The check unconditionally indexes integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]. Integrations created before this metadata was recorded, or created through build_integration when state did not contain a sender, do not have that key. Linking such an existing-but-unattached GitHub integration to an organization therefore raises KeyError/TypeError and returns a 500 instead of completing the installation or showing the intended installation-failed page.

title: Authenticated-user validation is bypassed when the Integration row does not yet exist
body: When Integration.objects.get() raises DoesNotExist, GitHubInstallation immediately advances the pipeline without comparing pipeline state github_authenticated_user to the GitHub app installer. Because the Integration row is normally created by an asynchronous GitHub installation webhook, a user who completes the Sentry pipeline before that webhook is processed (or when the webhook is missed/delayed) bypasses the new validation entirely, and build_integration does not fetch the installer identity from GitHub to perform the check later. This leaves a race-dependent hole in the security control added by this PR.

title: GitHub token exchange and user lookup failures are not converted to the installation error page
body: safe_urlopen is called outside the try/except, which only covers safe_urlread, and get_user_info(payload["access_token"]) at line 434 is also unguarded. Network errors, GitHub 5xx responses, or failures from the /user lookup can therefore propagate as unhandled exceptions and produce a 500 during installation instead of the PR's intended generic 'Invalid installation request' failure page.

title: Sender check crashes for integrations whose metadata has no sender
body: GitHubInstallation assumes integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] always exists when an Integration row exists without an OrganizationIntegration. That is not guaranteed: build_integration in this same provider only sets metadata["sender"] when state contains a sender, so integrations created through the normal pipeline (or older/orphaned integrations whose org link was removed) have no sender key. Re-linking such an installation raises KeyError/TypeError and returns a 500 instead of either proceeding or showing the invalid-installation error page.

title: Token exchange network errors are not handled
body: OAuthLoginView calls safe_urlopen outside any try/except (only safe_urlread is wrapped), and get_user_info on line 434 is also invoked without error handling. If GitHub times out, resets the connection, or the /user lookup fails with an exception, the installation pipeline raises an unhandled 500 rather than rendering the github-integration-failed error response that the PR intends for token-exchange failures; only a clean response body lacking access_token/login reaches the graceful path.

title: test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the not-found installation path
body: The test now stubs a 404 for /app/installations/{id} but drives the flow with a deliberately wrong state value (ddd023...), so OAuthLoginView returns the generic invalid-request error before GitHubInstallation/build_integration ever queries the installation. The assertion on "Invalid installation request." passes even if the 404 handling in build_integration ("The GitHub installation could not be found.") is broken or removed, leaving that branch untested under the new two-step pipeline.

title: Sender validation is bypassed when the Integration row does not exist yet
body: When Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id) raises DoesNotExist, GitHubInstallation.dispatch immediately calls pipeline.next_step() without comparing pipeline state github_authenticated_user against the installer/sender. The sender is only available from the webhook-created Integration, so this path is taken whenever the GitHub installation webhook has not yet created the Integration (a normal race between the install redirect and webhook delivery, and the path used by the ordinary fresh-install flow in the tests). An attacker who installed the app can therefore complete linking from a different authenticated GitHub account simply by finishing the pipeline before the webhook creates the row, defeating the validation this PR adds.

title: Missing sender metadata causes an unhandled KeyError
body: integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] assumes every pre-existing Integration row has a sender dict with a login. Integrations created before sender was recorded (or created without that metadata) have no such key, so re-adding such an installation to an organization after its OrganizationIntegration was removed raises KeyError/TypeError and returns a 500 instead of the graceful github-integration-failed page or a completed install. The lookup should use .get() chaining and decide explicitly how to handle absent sender data.

title: Token exchange network errors are not converted to the installation error page
body: safe_urlopen() is called outside the try block, which only wraps safe_urlread()/decoding. If GitHub's access-token endpoint is unreachable, times out, or returns an HTTP error that safe_urlopen raises for, the exception propagates out of OAuthLoginView.dispatch and produces a 500 rather than the 'Invalid installation request' failure page promised for bad/reused codes and token failures. get_user_info() on line 434 has the same unhandled-failure exposure for the subsequent /user call.

title: test_installation_not_found no longer tests the installation-not-found path
body: The rewritten test_installation_not_found supplies a deliberately wrong state (ddd023...) on the second request, so OAuthLoginView rejects it for state mismatch and asserts 'Invalid installation request.' The request never reaches GitHubInstallation/build_integration, so the stubbed 404 from GET /app/installations/{id} and the 'The GitHub installation could not be found.' IntegrationError path are no longer exercised despite the test name; a regression in 404 handling would pass unnoticed.

title: queued timestamp is evaluated once at import time
body: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` evaluates `timezone.now()` once when the dataclass is defined, so every AssignmentSource created without an explicit queued value shares the same import-time timestamp instead of its creation time. If this field is later used for debugging, ordering, or expiring stale sync suppression, all records will appear to have been queued at process start. It should be `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`.

title: to_dict returns a non-JSON-serializable datetime used in Celery kwargs
body: `to_dict()` uses `asdict(self)`, leaving `queued` as a datetime object. `sync_group_assignee_outbound` places that dict directly in `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async(kwargs=...)`, whose arguments must survive task serialization; a raw datetime is not JSON-serializable and can make enqueueing the outbound assignee task fail in production (eager in-process tests would not expose this). Serialize `queued` to an ISO string in to_dict and parse it back in from_dict, with a round-trip test `from_dict(source.to_dict())`.

title: assignment_source added to sync_status_outbound abstract instead of sync_assignee_outbound
body: The new `assignment_source` parameter was added to the abstract `sync_status_outbound`, but no status caller passes it; meanwhile `sync_assignee_outbound` task (sync_assignee_outbound.py:59-61) now calls every installation as `sync_assignee_outbound(..., assignment_source=parsed_assignment_source)` while the abstract `sync_assignee_outbound` at line 397 still declares only `external_issue, user, assign=True, **kwargs`. Concrete providers that implement the abstract signature without **kwargs will raise TypeError when the task runs, breaking assignee sync for them. Add the parameter to the assignee abstract (and audit concrete implementations) instead of, or in addition to, the unused status one.

title: queued timestamp is evaluated once at import time
body: The dataclass field is declared as `queued: datetime = timezone.now()`, so Python calls timezone.now() once when the class is defined/imported and reuses that same value as the default for every AssignmentSource created during the process lifetime. All instances will therefore report the (stale) process-start time instead of their creation time. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` so each instance gets a fresh timestamp.

title: Datetime in AssignmentSource.to_dict() is not JSON-serializable for the Celery task
body: assignment_source.to_dict() uses dataclasses.asdict(), which leaves `queued` as a datetime object. sync_group_assignee_outbound then passes that dict as `assignment_source_dict` in sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async(kwargs=...). Celery/Kombu serializes task kwargs as JSON, and a datetime is not JSON serializable, so enqueueing the outbound task will raise a serialization/EncodeError whenever an inbound webhook supplied an assignment_source (exactly the new code path). This propagates out of GroupAssignee.assign/deassign called from sync_group_assignee_inbound, breaking inbound assignment; the eager `self.tasks()` tests do not serialize kwargs, so they do not catch it. Serialize `queued` to an ISO string in to_dict() (and parse it back in from_dict()) or drop it from the wire format.

title: from_dict does not validate/coerce field types, so malformed payloads can silently disable cycle prevention
body: from_dict only catches ValueError/TypeError from the constructor call. A payload such as {"source_name": 123, "integration_id": "456", "queued": "not-a-date"} constructs successfully with wrongly-typed fields; integration_id as a string will never equal the integer org_integration.integration_id in IssueSyncIntegration.should_sync, so the sync-cycle guard is silently bypassed and the loop the PR aims to prevent can recur. Coerce/validate integration_id (and queued) explicitly and return None (or raise) on type mismatches.

title: queued timestamp is evaluated once at import time
body: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` calls timezone.now() when the dataclass class is defined, not when an AssignmentSource is constructed. Every instance created without an explicit queued value therefore shares the process/import-time timestamp instead of its creation time. If queued is later used for ordering, staleness, or debounce decisions, those decisions will be wrong; it should use field(default_factory=timezone.now).

title: AssignmentSource dict passed to Celery contains a non-JSON-serializable datetime
body: assignment_source.to_dict() uses dataclasses.asdict(), so the queued value remains a datetime object. That dict is placed directly in sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async(kwargs=...), whose arguments must be serializable by the task serializer. On the inbound-assignment path this will fail to enqueue the outbound task (e.g. with a serialization/EncodeError) instead of performing the filtered sync, whereas the eager self.tasks() tests do not exercise real serialization. queued should be serialized to an ISO string (and parsed back in from_dict) or removed from the wire dict.

title: New assignment_source kwarg is unconditionally passed to all sync_assignee_outbound implementations
body: The task now calls installation.sync_assignee_outbound(..., assignment_source=parsed_assignment_source) for every installation. The abstract method allows **kwargs, but concrete issue-sync implementations are not required to accept an assignment_source keyword (several define only external_issue, user and assign). For such implementations this unconditional new kwarg raises TypeError and breaks all outbound assignee syncs, not just ones originating from an inbound webhook. Either only pass it when supported, keep passing it via **kwargs-compatible signatures after updating all implementations, or drop it since the value is only needed for the should_sync check already performed here.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler can no longer be instantiated
body: MetricAlertDetectorHandler now subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler but its body is just `pass`, so it does not implement the abstract members counter_names, get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values, and build_occurrence_and_event_data. Detector.detector_handler does `group_type.detector_handler(self)`, which will now raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler` instead of returning a handler that evaluates to no results as before. Any detector of type metric_alert_fire processed through process_detectors will crash rather than be skipped/handled.

title: Stateful evaluate docstring still says it returns a list
body: StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate now returns `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]`, but its docstring still says it 'returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult'. This contradicts the new dict-keyed contract introduced by this PR and can mislead implementers/callers about deduplication by group key.

title: Multi-group test builds expected occurrence for group_2 with the wrong value
body: In test_state_results_multi_group the packet has group_2 value 10, but the expected occurrence/event for group_2 is built by calling build_mock_occurrence_and_event(..., "group_2", 6, ...) with group_1's value 6. The test only passes because build_mock_occurrence_and_event ignores `value` entirely, so it cannot catch a regression where StatefulDetectorHandler passes the wrong per-group value to build_occurrence_and_event_data; other TestEvaluate cases similarly expect value 6 while evaluating 8/100. The expected construction should use each group's actual value (and ideally assert the hook receives it).

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is now abstract and cannot be instantiated
body: MetricAlertDetectorHandler now subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler with a bare `pass`, but StatefulDetectorHandler declares abstract members counter_names, get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values, and the newly added build_occurrence_and_event_data, none of which are implemented here. Python will raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler` when Detector.detector_handler does `group_type.detector_handler(self)`, crashing process_detectors for any detector of type metric_alert_fire instead of previously evaluating to an empty result. Stub implementations (or leaving the handler non-stateful until it is implemented) are needed.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler can no longer be instantiated
body: MetricAlertDetectorHandler now subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler but its body is just `pass`, so it does not implement the inherited abstract members `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, or the newly added `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. StatefulDetectorHandler remains abstract, therefore `group_type.detector_handler(self)` in Detector.detector_handler raises `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler` instead of returning a handler. Previously this handler implemented `evaluate()` returning `[]` and could be instantiated as a no-op. Any detector of type `metric_alert_fire` processed through `process_detectors` will now crash detector processing (the TypeError is not caught by the `detector_handler` property or `process_detectors`). Either implement the abstract methods for metric alerts or keep a concrete no-op `evaluate`/provide default implementations in the base class.

title: Transformed monitor config copy is discarded in occurrence context
body: get_monitor_environment_context copies monitor.config into `config` and replaces `config["schedule_type"]` with the human-readable display value, but the returned context uses `monitor_environment.monitor.config` instead of `config`. The transformed copy is therefore discarded and incident occurrences contain the raw schedule_type value rather than the intended display value.

title: Hung flusher processes are never killed before replacement
body: Processes are created with multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, whose SpawnProcess class is not an instance of multiprocessing.Process (the default-context Process class) on Linux. The isinstance check therefore skips process.kill() for a hung flusher, after which _create_process_for_shards starts a replacement for the same shards. The hung and replacement processes can then concurrently flush the same Redis shards, racing flush/done_flush and potentially producing duplicate segments or interfering with each other's in-progress flushes.

title: Flusher processes are not terminated in join() due to the same isinstance check
body: As in the restart path, join() only calls process.terminate() when isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) is true, which is false for SpawnProcess objects created from the spawn context on Linux. join() can therefore return while flusher processes are still running after the deadline; a subsequent rebalance/strategy for the same shards can run concurrently with these orphaned (until parent exit) flushers and duplicate work.

title: --flusher-processes accepts zero and negative values without validation
body: The new click option accepts any int. A negative value flows to SpanFlusher where min(negative, len(assigned_shards)) yields a negative num_processes and range() produces no processes at all: spans are written to Redis and offsets committed but nothing ever flushes them, with no error. A direct flusher_processes=0 via the factory is instead silently converted by `max_processes or len(...)` to one process per shard, the opposite of the requested limit. The option/factory should reject values < 1.

title: Multi-process flusher test never verifies any segment is flushed
body: test_flusher_processes_limit only asserts process counts and shard distribution, then joins; it submits no spans and asserts no produced output. The threaded produce_to_pipe path with multiple shards sharing processes, per-process restart/health bookkeeping, and the spawn-process path used in production are all unexercised, so regressions that drop or duplicate segments when shards share a flusher (or when a flusher restarts) would pass CI.

title: Spawned flusher processes are never killed on hang/crash restart
body: Processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, whose SpawnProcess class is not an instance of multiprocessing.Process (both derive from BaseProcess). The isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) check at line 254 therefore always fails for the real (non-test) processes, so a hung process is never kill()ed before _create_process_for_shards starts a replacement for the same shards. Two flushers then concurrently call flush_segments/done_flush_segments on the same Redis shards, racing to produce the same segments to buffered-segments (duplicates) or expiring each other's work. The same broken isinstance check at line 346-347 means join() also never terminate()s a hung spawned process. Use multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess (or check for threading.Thread inversely) for these checks.

title: --flusher-processes accepts values that crash or are silently ignored
body: The new click option accepts any int with no validation. Passing a negative value flows through ProcessSpansStrategyFactory into SpanFlusher where max_processes stays negative, num_processes = min(negative, len(shards)) is negative, process_to_shards_map is empty, and 'i % self.num_processes' then raises KeyError/ZeroDivision-style failure while assigning shards, crashing consumer startup. Passing 0 is silently converted by 'max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)' in SpanFlusher.__init__ (line 51) into one process per shard, i.e. the opposite of what the operator requested and a surprising resource jump. Validate the option to be >= 1 (e.g. in the CLI option or SpanFlusher.__init__).

title: Redis memory backpressure double-counts clusters shared across flusher processes
body: submit() sums get_memory_info() over one SpansBuffer per flusher process (lines 298-303). Multiple shard buffers that map to the same Redis cluster each report that cluster's memory, so a cluster shared by shards in different processes is counted multiple times in both 'used' and 'available', while a cluster contained in a single process is counted once. Previously a single SpansBuffer covering all shards could deduplicate by cluster. The weighted used/available ratio is therefore skewed toward whichever cluster happens to be split across more processes, causing the hard backpressure (MessageRejected / pausing the consumer) to trigger too early or too late depending on shard-to-process assignment. Deduplicate memory infos by cluster/service before summing.

title: Hung flusher processes are never killed before being replaced
body: Processes are created with multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, whose SpawnProcess objects are not instances of multiprocessing.Process (the fork-context Process class). The new isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) guard therefore evaluates to False for every real flusher process. When _ensure_processes_alive detects a hang (is_alive() is True but healthy_since is stale), it skips process.kill() and immediately calls _create_process_for_shards for the same shards. The hung process keeps running alongside its replacement, so two processes can concurrently call flush_segments/done_flush_segments and produce for the same Redis shards, risking duplicate or racing segment flushes, while the hung process continues consuming resources. The guard should check against the spawn context's process type / BaseProcess, or duck-type on kill/terminate.

title: join() never terminates spawned flusher processes
body: join() uses the same isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) check before calling process.terminate(). Because the flushers are SpawnProcess objects from the spawn context, this check is always False in production, so any flusher that does not exit promptly after stopped is set is never terminated. join() waits until the deadline for each process in sequence and then silently returns with daemon processes still alive, leaking processes and potentially leaving flushers running against Redis/Kafka after the consumer strategy has shut down. Use the mp_context process base type or hasattr-based termination instead.

title: Negative or zero flusher-process configuration crashes or disables flushing
body: The CLI option --flusher-processes accepts any int with no validation. A negative value flows through factory.py into SpanFlusher, where max_processes stays negative (only 0/None fall back via `or`), num_processes = min(negative, len(shards)) is negative, process_to_shards_map is empty, and the shard assignment loop then raises KeyError/ZeroDivision-style failures when computing i % num_processes or indexing the map. If assigned_shards is empty, num_processes is 0 and no flusher process is ever created while submit() still forwards messages to the committer, so spans can be committed to Redis but never flushed. Validate flusher_processes >= 1 at the CLI/factory boundary and handle the no-shards case explicitly.

title: Multiprocess flusher test never exercises flushing or restart with multiple processes
body: test_flusher_processes_limit only asserts len(processes)/num_processes and that the shard map totals 4, then immediately joins without submitting any span or advancing drift, so it cannot catch regressions in per-process flushing, duplicate production when shards share a process, backpressure aggregation, or the process-restart path in _ensure_processes_alive. Given the PR's core change is parallel flushing and supervision, a test should push spans through a multi-process (at least multi-thread via produce_to_pipe) flusher and assert each segment is produced exactly once, and/or simulate a dead/hung process and assert it is replaced.

title: Shutdown abandons queued work items
body: FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown=True for every worker before calling q.shutdown(immediate=False). OrderedQueueWorker.run() only checks `while not self.shutdown` at the top of its loop, so a worker that finishes its current item exits immediately even if its queue still contains pending items, and a worker blocked in get() that returns an item may process at most one more. The remaining queued items are therefore never processed and their offsets never complete, contrary to the immediate=False drain semantics. On consumer shutdown/rebalance those messages must be redelivered (or are lost if later code marks them complete), defeating the claimed graceful shutdown.

title: Final offsets are never committed on close and closed pool is reused after rebalance
body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() sets shutdown_event and joins the commit thread before calling queue_pool.shutdown(), so any items drained/completed during pool shutdown are completed after the last _commit_loop iteration and are never passed to commit_function. Worse, the queue_pool is owned by ResultsStrategyFactory and the same pool is passed to every strategy from create_with_partitions(); close() shuts its queues down irreversibly (queue.shutdown()), so after an Arroyo partition rebalance/revocation the factory creates a new strategy backed by a dead pool. Subsequent FixedQueuePool.submit() puts raise queue.ShutDown, which SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() catches and then add_offset+complete_offset, causing offsets to be committed without the results ever being processed.

title: Unbounded queues provide no backpressure
body: FixedQueuePool creates plain queue.Queue() instances with no maxsize and submit() does an unconditional put(). The class/strategy docstrings claim 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but nothing ever blocks or rejects: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() is called by Arroyo for every polled message and will enqueue indefinitely if one subscription/queue is slow, growing memory unboundedly, holding WorkItem/message references, and building a huge outstanding-offset window that can stall commits and trigger max.poll.interval rebalances. A bounded queue (with blocking or Arroyo-appropriate rejection) is required.

title: OffsetTracker state is never reset on partition revocation
body: OffsetTracker keeps all_offsets/outstanding/last_committed/partition_locks forever and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy exposes no revocation/flush hook to clear a partition. If a partition is revoked and later reassigned (possibly at an offset <= the previously recorded last_committed, e.g. after a rebalance or offset reset), get_committable_offsets() starts at last_committed+1 and can never emit a commit until processing passes the stale high-water mark, so processed results go uncommitted and are redelivered; removed partitions also leak sets/locks for the life of the factory-owned pool.

title: Commit scan is O(offset window) every second
body: get_committable_offsets() runs every 1s in _commit_loop and, per partition, iterates `for offset in range(start, max_offset + 1)`, i.e. over the entire uncommitted offset window, allocating/scanning proportionally to backlog size. Combined with the unbounded queues, a large backlog (exactly the slow-item scenario this mode targets) makes each commit tick O(window) per partition and can consume a full thread/CPU while commits fall further behind. Tracking only the contiguous head (e.g. sorted outstanding minimum) would be O(1)/O(log n).

title: Group-to-queue assignment uses randomized hash()
body: get_queue_for_group() uses Python's built-in hash() on a str, which is randomized per process via PYTHONHASHSEED, despite the docstring calling it 'consistent hashing'. The mapping differs across consumer processes/restarts, so the same subscription is not consistently assigned as documented and distribution cannot be reasoned about or reproduced in tests/operations; within a fleet this also gives no stable sharding guarantee. Use a stable digest (e.g. hashlib/md5 already used elsewhere for grouping) modulo num_queues.

title: Strategy close permanently shuts down the factory-owned shared queue pool
body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()/terminate() calls queue_pool.shutdown(), but ResultsStrategyFactory owns one FixedQueuePool and reuses it for every create_with_partitions() call. Arroyo closes the processing strategy when partitions are revoked/rebalanced and then creates a new strategy for the next assignment; the new strategy reuses a pool whose workers have exited and whose queues have been shut down. Subsequent queue.put() calls raise queue.ShutDown, which submit() then mishandles (see its exception path), so processing after any rebalance is broken and can silently drop work. The pool should be owned/refcounted by the factory, recreated per assignment, or not shut down by the per-assignment strategy.

title: Graceful shutdown discards queued items instead of draining them
body: FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown=True before calling q.shutdown(immediate=False). OrderedQueueWorker.run() checks `while not self.shutdown` before each get(), so a worker that finishes its current item exits even if its queue still contains pending items, despite immediate=False intending a drain. Those unprocessed items are simply abandoned on strategy close (they will only be recovered by Kafka redelivery, if ever), contradicting the graceful-shutdown contract and delaying/losing in-flight processing on every deploy or rebalance.

title: Failed work items are marked complete and their offsets are committed
body: OrderedQueueWorker.run() catches every Exception from result_processor, logs it, and then unconditionally calls offset_tracker.complete_offset() in the finally block. The commit loop therefore treats a crashed/failed result as successfully processed and advances the Kafka offset past it, so the message is never redelivered or sent to a DLQ. This contradicts the strategy docstring claim 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' and causes permanent data loss for transient processing failures.

title: Any submit-time exception is swallowed and the offset is marked processed
body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() wraps decoding, grouping and queue submission in one try/except; on any exception it logs, then add_offset()+complete_offset() for that message. If grouping_fn raises, the queue is already shut down, or queue.put() fails, the message was never processed yet becomes committable, advancing the offset and dropping the result with no DLQ/InvalidMessage propagation to Arroyo. Only genuinely undecodable/filtered messages should be skipped this way; processing/submission failures must not be marked complete.

title: Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure despite the documented guarantee
body: FixedQueuePool creates plain queue.Queue() instances with no maxsize, and submit() never blocks or raises MessageRejected. The strategy therefore accepts messages from Arroyo as fast as they are polled and accumulates them in memory while a slow group blocks its queue, growing memory (and the OffsetTracker's all_offsets/outstanding sets, which are only pruned up to the blocked offset) without bound and risking max.poll.interval/OOM kills. This contradicts the class docstring claims of 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up'. Bounded queues plus MessageRejected on full are needed.

title: OffsetTracker state is never reset when partitions are revoked or reassigned
body: OffsetTracker keeps last_committed/all_offsets/outstanding per Partition for the life of the factory-owned pool, and nothing clears them when Arroyo revokes a partition or reassigns it (possibly to a different committed position, or back to this consumer later at a lower offset after a group reset/rebalance). get_committable_offsets() starts scanning at max(last_committed+1, min_offset), so with a stale last_committed higher than the newly assigned offsets, no offset for that partition can ever be committed again; stale outstanding entries likewise permanently block commits. Tracker state must be (re)initialized from the partitions/offsets passed to create_with_partitions and cleaned up on revocation.

title: wait_until_empty reports empty while items are still being processed
body: wait_until_empty()/get_stats() only sum Queue.qsize(), which counts items still waiting in the queue but not the item a worker has already dequeued and is currently processing. As soon as the last item is picked up, total_items becomes 0 and wait_until_empty returns True while processing (and its side effects) are still in flight, so callers/tests/shutdown logic relying on it can proceed or commit-check too early. Use the queue's unfinished_tasks/task_done accounting or an explicit in-flight counter instead of qsize.

title: Failed work items are marked complete and their offsets are committed
body: OrderedQueueWorker.run catches every exception from result_processor, logs it, and then unconditionally calls offset_tracker.complete_offset in the finally block. The commit loop can therefore advance past a message that was never successfully processed, contradicting the strategy's documented 'only commits after successful processing' guarantee and causing permanent data loss on transient processing failures instead of redelivery.

title: Unbounded queues provide no backpressure and can grow without limit
body: FixedQueuePool creates queue.Queue() with no maxsize, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit always returns immediately after put(). Despite the docstring claiming natural backpressure, the Arroyo consumer will keep polling Kafka and enqueueing messages as fast as it can fetch them even if workers are stuck or slow, leading to unbounded in-memory growth/OOM and a huge backlog of fetched-but-uncommitted offsets.

title: Strategy close/terminate discards queued work by shutting down the shared pool
body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() sets the commit shutdown event and immediately calls queue_pool.shutdown() without first waiting for queues to drain (wait_until_empty is never used). FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets worker.shutdown=True, so a worker exits at the top of its loop after its current item even if its queue still holds items. On Arroyo partition revocation/rebalance this abandons in-flight messages, and because the same pool is shared (see result_consumer factory), closing one strategy instance also kills the pool for any subsequently created strategy: queue.put then raises queue.ShutDown, which submit()'s catch-all converts into add+complete offset, silently committing unprocessed messages.

title: Catch-all in submit marks offsets complete for messages never enqueued
body: submit() wraps decoding, grouping and queue submission in one try/except and, on any exception, adds and immediately completes the offset. This conflates poison messages with transient failures: e.g. grouping_fn raising, queue shutdown raising queue.ShutDown, or the real decode_payload asserting on FilteredPayload (decode_payload asserts payload is not FilteredPayload) all cause the offset to become committable even though nothing was processed, silently dropping the message with only a log line.

title: Kafka offsets are committed from a background thread
body: _commit_loop runs in its own thread and calls commit_function (the Arroyo Commit callable supplied to create_with_partitions) from there. Arroyo processing strategies are driven single-threaded by StreamProcessor and the commit callable/consumer commit path is not documented as thread-safe; invoking it concurrently with the main consumer loop risks races with the processor's own ONCE_PER_SECOND commit logic and with partition assignment changes, potentially committing offsets for partitions no longer owned.

title: Group-to-queue assignment uses Python's randomized hash()
body: get_queue_for_group uses built-in hash(group_key) % num_queues. For str keys hash() is randomized per process via PYTHONHASHSEED, so the 'consistent hashing' claimed in the docstring is not stable across restarts or across consumer processes: the same subscription is assigned to a different queue whenever the process restarts, breaking the ordering/affinity guarantee the pool exists to provide relative to any other process or previous incarnation. A stable digest (e.g. md5/sha like other Sentry grouping code) is required.

title: Committable-offset scan is O(offset range) every second per partition
body: get_committable_offsets iterates range(start, max_offset+1) and is invoked every second by the commit loop. When one slow item blocks a partition (the exact scenario this PR targets), the outstanding window grows with throughput, so each scan walks an ever-larger range of integers doing two set lookups per offset, and all_offsets keeps every uncommitted offset in memory. A single stuck subscription can thus make commit processing progressively more expensive and delay commits for all partitions.

title: Queue pool and offset tracker are never reset on partition reassignment
body: The FixedQueuePool (and its OffsetTracker) is created once in the factory __init__ and reused for every create_with_partitions call. OffsetTracker state (all_offsets, outstanding, last_committed) is keyed only by Partition and is never cleared when partitions are revoked or reassigned, and last_committed starts at -1 regardless of the committed position Arroyo passes in the partitions mapping. After a rebalance, stale outstanding entries from the previous assignment can permanently block commits for a reassigned partition, or stale last_committed state can cause incorrect committable calculations for a partition this consumer no longer owns or newly owns at a different position.

title: Backup-code login can bypass password verification
body: Password verification above is skipped whenever credentials.totpCode is non-empty, while the new backup-code branch only checks credentials.backupCode and does not itself verify the password. A crafted credentials request containing a valid backup code plus any dummy totpCode therefore authenticates without knowing the account password. A backup code is meant to replace only the TOTP second factor, so this reduces account login to possession of a single long-lived backup code.

title: Backup-code consumption is not atomic, allowing concurrent replay
body: The code reads the encrypted backup-code array, checks indexOf, and later writes back the same array with one entry nulled. Two concurrent login attempts using the same code can both read the original array and pass the check before either update completes, so a supposedly single-use backup code can establish multiple sessions. Consumption needs an atomic/transactional update or locking to guarantee single use.

title: Backup-code comparison does not normalize case or surrounding whitespace
body: Generated codes are lowercase hex and are displayed/downloaded in XXXXX-XXXXX form, but verification only removes hyphens. A user who transcribes or pastes the correct code with uppercase A-F letters, or with surrounding whitespace, is rejected with IncorrectBackupCode. The same normalization issue exists in the disable endpoint, so valid backup-code holders can be locked out of both login and disabling 2FA.

title: Users who enabled 2FA before this feature can never obtain backup codes
body: The migration adds backupCodes as null for existing users, and setup returns TwoFactorAlreadyEnabled for anyone with twoFactorEnabled set. Such users are still offered the Lost access flow, receive MissingBackupCodes, and are told to generate codes in settings, but there is no settings action to generate or regenerate backup codes without first disabling 2FA with a working authenticator. That makes the recovery path unusable for the entire pre-existing 2FA user base.

title: No test exercises backup-code login, single-use consumption, or disabling with a backup code
body: The added e2e coverage only checks that the download and copy buttons exist/work during setup in the disable test. As the TODO acknowledges, nothing tests logging in with a backup code, rejecting an incorrect code, rejecting reuse of a consumed code, handling missing codes for legacy users, or disabling 2FA with a backup code. These are security-critical server paths in next-auth-options.ts and disable.ts and can regress without any test failing.

title: Password visibility toggle is removed from keyboard tab order globally
body: Adding tabIndex={-1} to the show/hide password button in the shared PasswordField makes that control unreachable by keyboard for every password field in the app, not just the 2FA setup form. Keyboard-only users can no longer toggle password visibility, an accessibility regression unrelated to backup codes.

title: Backup code can bypass password verification
body: Password verification is skipped whenever credentials.totpCode is non-empty, while the new branch at line 131 authenticates whenever credentials.backupCode is valid and ignores the TOTP code. An attacker can therefore send a dummy totpCode together with a valid backup code and no correct password and be logged in. A leaked or guessed backup code thus becomes a single-factor credential instead of a replacement second factor; password verification must also run when backupCode is supplied (or whenever the account has a password and this is not the password-less external-TOTP flow).

title: Backup-code consumption is not atomic, allowing concurrent reuse
body: The code reads the encrypted backup-code list, marks the matched entry null, and writes the whole list back without a transaction, conditional update, or lock. Two concurrent login requests using the same backup code can both read the list before either writes, both find the code, and both authenticate, violating the documented exactly-once property of backup codes. Consumption needs to be made atomic so only one request can claim a code.

title: Backup-code comparison does not normalize case or whitespace
body: Generated codes are lowercase hex, but verification only strips '-' via replaceAll before indexOf; it does not trim whitespace or lowercase the input. A user who types the code in uppercase (as suggested by the XXXXX-XXXXX placeholder), or pastes it with surrounding whitespace, is rejected with IncorrectBackupCode even though they entered the correct code. The same un-normalized comparison exists in the disable-2FA endpoint, so normalization should be applied consistently in both places.

title: Users with pre-existing 2FA can never obtain backup codes
