Federated Mimir rule groups in existing CombinedRule consumers will therefore be offered edit/delete actions that federated groups do not support.

title: Grafana recording rules can no longer be paused
body: The ruler-based ability used isGrafanaManagedAlertRule, which is true for both Grafana alerting and recording rules, for Pause/Restore. The new prom-based ability uses isAlertingRule instead, so Pause and Restore are unsupported for Grafana recording rules. Since the list view no longer supplies a ruler rule to provide the old ability, recording rules lose pause/unpause entirely.

title: Grafana rule list items are rendered without a React key
body: The switch previously rendered GrafanaRuleLoader with key={key}; the replacement GrafanaRuleListItem omits the key while the datasource and unknown branches keep theirs. In this dynamically appended/filtered list, index-based reconciliation can reuse the wrong component instance and its local state such as modals, drawers, and menus, in addition to producing React key warnings. Restore key={key} on GrafanaRuleListItem.

title: Interpolating before querySupportsSplitting can defeat the $__range split guard
body: runSplitQuery() now replaces template variables in query.expr at line 299 and only afterwards, at line 300, partitions queries with querySupportsSplitting(). That helper is documented at lines 282-288 to keep queries containing $__range, $__range_s or $__range_ms out of splitting so the backend can interpolate the range against the unsplit time range. If applyTemplateVariables() substitutes those range variables (as it does other variables such as $__auto/$step in the new test), the marker is gone before the check, the query is classified as splittable, and every time chunk is sent with the range value frozen from the original panel range, producing incorrect rate/range results instead of the intended single unsplit request. The splittability check needs to be done on the pre-interpolation expression or range variables must be provably preserved and covered by a test.

title: Shard-split queries are interpolated twice, once per shard group
body: runShardSplitQuery() interpolates every target with datasource.applyTemplateVariables() at line 52, adds the __stream_shard__ selector, and then delegates each shard group to runSplitQuery() (line 163), which after this change interpolates the same targets again at querySplitting.ts:299. The updated test codifies this: a single target now triggers applyTemplateVariables 5 times (1 initial + 1 per shard sub-request). Template interpolation with scopedVars and ad-hoc filters (request.filters is passed in both places) is not a guaranteed idempotent operation: variable values containing '$', $__auto/step derivation, and ad-hoc filter injection into the stream selector can be applied a second time to an already interpolated/shard-augmented expression, and the redundant work scales with the number of shard groups. runSplitQuery needs a way for the shard path to skip re-interpolation, or the shard path should not pre-interpolate beyond what shard grouping requires.

title: Empty-expression filtering now happens before interpolation in shard splitting
body: The filters at lines 50-51 run before the interpolation map at line 52, whereas the previous code interpolated first and then dropped queries with no expr. A target whose expr is only a template variable (e.g. expr: '$q') that expands to an empty string now passes the filter, is interpolated to '', and continues into groupTargetsByQueryType()/getSelectorForShardValues() and on to execution as an empty LogQL query instead of being ignored, causing shard-label fetching and/or a Loki parse error for a query that should have been dropped. The expr emptiness check should also (or instead) be applied to the interpolated result; the same filter-before-map pattern was introduced in runSplitQuery at querySplitting.ts:296-299.

title: Shard-split queries are interpolated twice, once per shard group
body: runShardSplitQuery() now interpolates every target with datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters), and splitQueriesByStreamShard() then passes each shard sub-request to runSplitQuery(), which interpolates the same targets again with the same scopedVars and filters. The updated shard test confirms this: one original query now causes applyTemplateVariables to be called 5 times. applyTemplateVariables is not just placeholder substitution for dashboard variables; it also applies request.filters/ad-hoc filters and variable formatting/escaping. Re-applying it can duplicate ad-hoc filters in the LogQL expression and can re-expand $-sequences introduced by the first replacement, corrupting the query or changing the stream selector, in addition to repeating the work for every shard group. Interpolation should happen once, e.g. runSplitQuery needs a way for the shard path to indicate targets are already interpolated.

title: Interpolating before querySupportsSplitting() can defeat the $__range split guard
body: Queries are now interpolated on line 299 before partition() calls querySupportsSplitting() on line 300. querySupportsSplitting() deliberately refuses to split queries containing $__range, $__range_s, or $__range_ms because those macros must be evaluated against the final request range (see the comment at lines 285-287). If applyTemplateVariables resolves those range macros from the request scoped vars, the token is gone by the time the guard runs, so a query that must not be split is split into daily chunks while keeping the full-range macro value baked into each chunk. That changes rate/count_over_time semantics at chunk boundaries and can return incorrect data. The range-variable check needs to run on the pre-interpolation expression, or range macros must be excluded from this early interpolation.

title: Queries that interpolate to an empty expression are no longer filtered out
body: The empty-expression filter runs before interpolation (lines 296-299), so a target whose whole expression is a variable, e.g. expr='$var', passes the filter and only becomes '' after applyTemplateVariables. Such a target is then classified and grouped as a normal (metric) query and sent downstream with an empty expression. If all targets interpolate to empty, runSplitQuery builds zero grouped requests and runSplitGroupedQueries() dereferences requests.filter(...)[0].partition after Math.max(...[]) , throwing a TypeError instead of completing with no data. The same regression is introduced in runShardSplitQuery(), which changed from interpolate-then-filter to filter-then-interpolate. Targets need to be filtered again after interpolation.

title: Shard-split queries are interpolated multiple times
body: runShardSplitQuery interpolates every target here, but splitQueriesByStreamShard (line 163) then passes those targets to runSplitQuery, which at querySplitting.ts:299 calls datasource.applyTemplateVariables again for every shard/time sub-request; the updated shard test even expects 5 applyTemplateVariables calls for one original query. Loki's applyTemplateVariables also injects request.filters adhoc filters into the stream selector and re-runs template replacement, neither of which is guaranteed idempotent: repeated passes can add the same adhoc matcher again and can re-expand $-sequences introduced by a first-pass variable value, besides re-parsing already-interpolated LogQL per chunk. Interpolation should be owned by one layer, e.g. the shard layer should be able to tell runSplitQuery its targets are already interpolated.

title: Split queries are interpolated again by datasource.runQuery for every chunk
body: The queries interpolated here are built into grouped sub-requests and executed via datasource.runQuery in runSplitGroupedQueries (line 180). Loki's runQuery backend path (DataSourceWithBackend.query) applies applyTemplateVariables again with the same scopedVars and request.filters before sending each chunk to the backend, so every split query is now interpolated at least twice, and three times on the shard path. As with the shard double-interpolation, the repeated adhoc-filter injection from request.filters and repeated templateSrv replacement of already-substituted values are not guaranteed idempotent and can corrupt or invalidly duplicate stream-selector matchers. The early interpolation for splitting decisions needs to be reconciled with the downstream one, rather than simply adding another pass.

title: Queries that interpolate to empty are no longer filtered out before sharding
body: The order was changed from interpolate-then-filter to filter-then-interpolate: lines 49-52 test the pre-interpolation expr, so a target such as '$SELECTOR' that resolves to an empty string was previously dropped but now survives into groupTargetsByQueryType, requestSupportsSharding/getSelectorForShardValues and fetchLabelValues with an empty stream selector. It is only dropped later by runSplitQuery's own pre-interpolation filter, which can leave that call with no grouped requests instead of the query simply being ignored as an empty query. Add a post-interpolation expr filter (and apply the same filter-after-interpolate ordering in runSplitQuery).

title: TestLogger.FromContext discards recorded logs
body: FromContext returns a brand-new TestLogger instead of the receiver or a logger sharing the receiver's recording state. LoggerMiddleware now logs through m.logger.FromContext(ctx), so a test that constructs it with a TestLogger and then inspects that original fake will always see zero InfoLogs and cannot verify the "Plugin Request Completed" log; the log is written to a discarded instance. FromContext should return the receiver (or a derived logger sharing the same Logs state).

title: No test covers contextual-logger propagation to LoggerMiddleware
body: This PR moves instrumentContext into a new middleware and makes LoggerMiddleware depend on it (it now obtains pluginId/endpoint/dsName/dsUID/uname only via logger.FromContext(ctx) instead of explicit log parameters), but no test is added for ContextualLoggerMiddleware and the renamed metrics test only asserts Prometheus metrics. A regression in instrumentContext (wrong endpoint/attributes) or in the middleware ordering in CreateMiddlewares would silently drop those fields from "Plugin Request Completed" logs without any test failing. Add a test that runs ContextualLoggerMiddleware before LoggerMiddleware and asserts the emitted log carries the contextual attributes.

title: TestLogger.FromContext discards all recorded logs
body: FromContext returns a brand-new TestLogger instead of the receiver or an instance sharing the receiver's recording state. LoggerMiddleware now logs through m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...), so a test that injects a TestLogger into LoggerMiddleware will observe zero InfoLogs on the injected logger because the log call is recorded on an orphaned instance. This makes the new logging path untestable with the provided fake; FromContext should return the receiver (or share its Logs state).

title: LoggerMiddleware silently loses identifying fields when used without ContextualLoggerMiddleware
body: logRequest no longer receives the PluginContext or endpoint and no longer adds pluginId, endpoint, dsName, dsUID, uname, or traceID itself; it now relies entirely on ContextualLoggerMiddleware having already enriched ctx. NewLoggerMiddleware's signature and contract give no indication of that new ordering dependency, so any existing or future decorator chain, test, or direct use of LoggerMiddleware without ContextualLoggerMiddleware immediately before it will emit 'Plugin Request Completed' logs missing the plugin/endpoint/datasource/user fields that LoggerMiddleware previously guaranteed on its own. The main CreateMiddlewares ordering happens to satisfy the dependency, but the middleware's standalone behavior is silently degraded.

title: No test covers the new contextual-logger propagation that logging now depends on
body: The PR moves endpoint/pluginId/dsName/dsUID/uname enrichment into the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware and makes LoggerMiddleware consume it via FromContext, but adds no test for NewContextualLoggerMiddleware or for the ContextualLoggerMiddleware -> LoggerMiddleware composition, and the renamed metrics test only asserts Prometheus metrics. A regression in instrumentContext, in the middleware ordering in CreateMiddlewares, or in Logger.FromContext would silently drop those fields from 'Plugin Request Completed' and downstream plugin logs with no failing test. Add a decorator-level test asserting the next client receives the enriched context and that the completed-request log carries the expected fields.

title: Streaming endpoints do not receive the contextual logger
body: SubscribeStream, PublishStream and RunStream pass the original context to next without calling instrumentContext, unlike QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth and CollectMetrics. These request types also carry a PluginContext, so any logging performed downstream via a contextual logger during streaming (including long-lived RunStream handlers) will lack endpoint, pluginId, dsName/dsUID and uname, making the extracted ContextualLoggerMiddleware incomplete and its behaviour inconsistent across endpoints.

title: TestLogger.FromContext discards the receiver's recorded logs
body: FromContext returns a brand-new TestLogger instead of returning the receiver or a logger sharing its state. LoggerMiddleware now logs through m.logger.FromContext(ctx) (logger_middleware.go:58), so a test holding the original TestLogger and asserting on InfoLogs will observe zero calls even though a log was emitted; the fake therefore no longer behaves like the real logger (which writes to the same underlying output) and will silently hide the new Plugin Request Completed log in tests.

title: Nil requests panic before LoggerMiddleware's nil guards can run
body: QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth and CollectMetrics dereference req.PluginContext without a nil check. LoggerMiddleware explicitly guards nil requests and passes them through (logger_middleware.go:63, 77, 90, 104), but in CreateMiddlewares the contextual middleware sits in front of it (pluginsintegration.go:160-161), so a nil request now panics in this middleware instead of reaching the guarded pass-through/downstream error handling.

title: No test covers contextual-logger propagation or the LoggerMiddleware field move
body: The refactor removes the explicit pluginId/endpoint/dsName/dsUID/uname fields from LoggerMiddleware.logRequest and relies entirely on ContextualLoggerMiddleware enriching the context earlier in the chain plus Logger.FromContext honouring it, yet the only renamed test still asserts Prometheus metrics and never checks the context seen downstream or the emitted Plugin Request Completed fields. A regression in middleware ordering or in FromContext (in either the real or fake logger) that drops those log fields would pass the whole suite undetected; a chain-level test for the new middleware is needed.

title: Failed device-limit check poisons the local cache and lets the device in on retry
body: tagDeviceUI writes the device key to localCache before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice and never removes it when that call fails. A new device over the limit is denied on its first request, but the cache entry remains for the 29-minute cache TTL; on its next request tagDeviceUI returns nil on the cache hit without touching the store, TagDevice returns nil, and Anonymous.Authenticate grants an identity. The configured limit is therefore bypassed after a single denied attempt on the same instance. Set the cache entry only after a successful store write, or delete it when CreateOrUpdateDevice returns an error.

title: Device limit is enforced by a non-atomic count-then-insert and can be exceeded concurrently
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice runs CountDevices in one DB session and, if the count is below the limit, performs the INSERT/UPSERT in a separate session with no transaction, lock, or other serialization. Concurrent first-time requests for distinct devices (across goroutines or Grafana instances sharing the database) can all observe count == limit-1 and all insert, exceeding the configured limit. The check-and-create needs to be atomic, e.g. inside a transaction with appropriate locking.

title: Provider signature changes are not reflected in wire generation, breaking the server build
body: ProvideAnonymousDeviceService now takes db.DB instead of anonstore.AnonStore and constructs the store itself, and ProvideAnonDBStore now takes an int64 deviceLimit that wire cannot supply. The checked-in pkg/server/wire_gen.go is not updated in this PR and still calls both providers with their old signatures, so the server package will not compile; the wire provider set also still needs to drop/replace ProvideAnonDBStore and be regenerated.

title: Anonymous authentication now blocks on the database with no timeout or panic isolation
body: Authenticate previously tagged the device in a goroutine with a 2-minute background-context timeout and panic recovery; it now calls TagDevice synchronously with the request context and no deadline. A slow or stalled device-store query (count plus upsert, now on the auth path) blocks anonymous authentication indefinitely, a client disconnect cancels the tagging via the request context, and a panic in tagging now propagates into authentication. Keep the synchronous enforcement needed for the limit, but bound it with a timeout context and recover from panics.

title: updateDevice can falsely report the limit reached for an existing MySQL device
body: updateDevice treats RowsAffected == 0 as ErrDeviceLimitReached. On MySQL, RowsAffected for UPDATE counts changed rows, not matched rows; when an already-known device is re-tagged (e.g. via another instance whose local cache is cold) within the same second and with unchanged client_ip/user_agent, the stored updated_at has second precision so nothing changes and MySQL reports 0. A legitimate, already-counted device is then denied as if it were new. Use a matched-row check (existence SELECT, or found-rows semantics) instead of relying on changed-row counts.

title: No test covers an existing device updating successfully while at the limit, or client-level denial
body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only verifies that a second, new device is rejected when the limit is 1. The other half of the feature branch—an already-registered device calling CreateOrUpdateDevice again while count >= limit must succeed via updateDevice—is untested, as is Anonymous.Authenticate returning an error (and no identity) on ErrDeviceLimitReached and unlimited behavior with limit 0 end to end (impl_test.go always uses a default cfg with limit 0). A regression in updateDevice would ship undetected.

title: New device_limit option is not added to default configuration or documentation
body: The PR reads [auth.anonymous] device_limit into Cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit but does not add it to conf/defaults.ini (or the configuration documentation). Operators have no discoverable way to learn the option exists or that 0 means unlimited and negative values are also treated as unlimited by the deviceLimit > 0 guard. Add the setting with its default and semantics to defaults.ini and the auth.anonymous docs.

title: Rejected devices are cached and allowed on retry
body: tagDeviceUI inserts the device into the 29-minute local cache before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice and does not evict the entry when that call fails. A new device rejected with ErrDeviceLimitReached therefore fails authentication once, but its next request hits the cache, TagDevice returns nil, and Anonymous.Authenticate issues an identity even though the device was never stored or counted. The device limit can be bypassed simply by retrying the same device ID.

title: Device-limit check is not atomic with device insertion
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice performs CountDevices in one DB session and the subsequent insert/upsert in another, without a transaction, lock, or atomic conditional insert. Concurrent requests, including requests handled by different Grafana instances sharing the database, can all observe a count below the limit and insert distinct devices, causing the configured limit to be exceeded.

title: Omitting the device ID bypasses the device limit
body: TagDevice returns nil when the X-Grafana-Device-Id header is absent, after which Anonymous.Authenticate still returns an anonymous identity. Any non-browser client, or a client that strips this voluntary header, can therefore use anonymous access without being counted or subjected to AnonymousDeviceLimit, undermining the limit as an access control.

title: Provider signature changes are not reflected in dependency-injection wiring
body: ProvideAnonymousDeviceService now requires db.DB instead of anonstore.AnonStore, while ProvideAnonDBStore now additionally requires a bare int64 that Wire cannot construct. The PR contains no regenerated wire_gen.go or wire-set update, so the existing generated injector that supplies the old arguments will no longer compile and Wire generation for the anonymous store provider cannot resolve int64.

title: Limit tests do not cover allowed existing devices or the authentication path
body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only checks sequentially that a second distinct device is rejected by the store. It does not verify that an already-counted device can still be updated when the count equals the limit, nor does it exercise AnonDeviceService.TagDevice or Anonymous.Authenticate with a non-zero configured limit (the service tests use a default cfg with limit 0), leaving the main enforcement and retry behavior untested.

title: New device_limit setting is not documented or added to sample configuration
body: The PR parses auth.anonymous device_limit but adds no entry to conf/defaults.ini or conf/sample.ini and no documentation update. Operators have no discoverable documentation for the new option, its units/scope (devices seen in the last 30 days), or that 0 means unlimited.

title: Rejected devices are cached and then allowed on the next request
body: tagDeviceUI inserts the device into localCache with SetDefault before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice, and it never evicts that entry when the store returns an error. A new device over the limit therefore fails once with ErrDeviceLimitReached, but its next request on the same instance within the 29-minute cache TTL hits the early cache return, TagDevice reports success, and Anonymous.Authenticate grants an identity even though the device was never inserted. Concurrent requests can also observe the cache entry set by an in-flight request that is later rejected. Set the cache only after a successful store write, or delete the entry on error.

title: Device-limit check and insert are not atomic
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice runs CountDevices in one database session and then performs the insert/upsert in a separate session, with no transaction, lock, or database constraint enforcing the maximum row count. Two concurrent requests for different new devices, on the same or different Grafana instances, can both observe count == deviceLimit-1 and both insert, exceeding the configured limit. The per-process local cache does not coordinate distinct device IDs or multiple instances. The count check and admission of a new device need to be made atomic, for example with a locking transaction or another database-enforced mechanism.

title: Provider signature changes are not reflected in dependency wiring
body: ProvideAnonymousDeviceService changes its third parameter from anonstore.AnonStore to db.DB, and ProvideAnonDBStore in anonstore/database.go additionally changes from accepting only db.DB to requiring an int64 deviceLimit. The checked-in Wire injector/provider wiring that calls these constructors is not updated or regenerated in this PR, so code generated/called with the old arguments no longer compiles and Wire has no ordinary injectable int64 binding for the new store parameter. Update and regenerate the wiring, or keep the store injectable and supply the configured limit through its existing provider wiring.

title: Anonymous authentication now blocks on device tagging without a timeout
body: Authenticate previously tagged devices in a goroutine with panic recovery and a two-minute background-context timeout. It now calls TagDevice synchronously with the request context and no timeout or recovery. A slow or blocked anon_device count/insert therefore stalls anonymous authentication for the full database/request duration, request cancellation can abort the limit decision, and a panic in tagging now propagates into request authentication instead of merely degrading tagging. Use a bounded context for the now-synchronous enforcement call and preserve appropriate panic handling.

title: New device_limit setting is absent from shipped configuration definitions
body: The PR parses auth.anonymous/device_limit into Cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit, but it does not add device_limit to conf/defaults.ini, the sample configuration, or the Grafana configuration documentation. Operators therefore cannot discover the new limit from the shipped configuration, and configuration/environment handling that enumerates known keys may not surface it consistently. Add the default and explanatory documentation alongside the existing auth.anonymous settings.

title: Device-limit tests do not cover allowed updates or the service authentication path
body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only verifies that a second distinct device is rejected by the store when the limit is 1. It does not verify the intended complementary behavior that the already-admitted device can still be updated while count >= limit, and no test exercises AnonDeviceService.TagDevice or Anonymous.Authenticate repeatedly after a rejection. Those missing cases leave both the updateDevice success path and service-level enforcement behaviour unverified. Add tests for updating the existing device at the limit and for repeated service-level requests from a rejected device.

title: Ticker change runs every cleanup job ten times more often
body: Changing the global cleanup ticker from 10 minutes to 1 minute affects all jobs in clean(), not only annotation cleanup: expired snapshots, dashboard versions, images, user invites, short URLs, and query history will also run ten times as often. This increases database and filesystem load and lock contention on every Grafana instance, is unrelated to the annotation deadlock fix described in the PR, and is not documented or made configurable. The interval should be reverted to 10 minutes or separately justified and scoped to annotations only.

title: Successful cleanup batches are logged as errors with full ID lists
body: The new cleanup paths at lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579 call r.log.Error unconditionally after successful fetches/deletes, passing a nil err and the entire ids slice (up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize, e.g. 32767 IDs in the new test). Normal cleanup will therefore emit multiple huge error-level log lines per batch per annotation type, flooding logs, triggering error alerting, and masking real failures. These should be Debug-level (or removed), should not log the full ID list, and errors should only be logged where they are actually returned.

title: deleteByIDs can exceed parameter limits on non-SQLite databases
body: For every database except the special-cased SQLite path, deleteByIDs builds a single DELETE with one placeholder per fetched ID, and the number of IDs is bounded only by the configurable AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize. PostgreSQL and MySQL prepared statements are limited to 65535 parameters, so a larger configured batch size that previously worked with the subquery DELETE will now fail on every batch and abort cleanup. The delete should be chunked into bounded groups for all dialects rather than only working around SQLite.

title: SQLite ID list construction is quadratic for large batches
body: The SQLite branch rebuilds the IN list with values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) inside the loop, copying the entire accumulated string on every iteration. For the 32767-ID batch exercised by the new test this is O(n^2) copying (gigabytes of intermediate copying) on each affected annotation type, undermining the large-batch support the branch is meant to add. Build the list with strings.Builder or strings.Join instead.

title: Global cleanup ticker shortened from 10 minutes to 1 minute without justification
body: The ticker that drives CleanUpService.clean() is changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute. This does not only affect annotation cleanup: the same clean() run executes temporary-file, snapshot, dashboard-version, image, user-invite, short-URL, and query-history cleanup. All of those jobs will now run ten times as often, increasing database and filesystem load on every Grafana instance, and the PR description gives no reason for this unrelated change. It looks like a leftover local-testing change and should be reverted or justified separately.

title: Successful cleanup batches are logged at Error level with the full ID list
body: The new batch loops in CleanAnnotations (lines 534, 537, 554, 557) and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags (lines 576, 579) call r.log.Error unconditionally, including on success where the logged err value is nil. Every batch of a routine cleanup will therefore emit error-level log lines, which pollutes logs, can trigger error alerting, and prints the entire ids slice (potentially tens of thousands of IDs for large batch sizes) on every iteration. These should be removed or downgraded to Debug and should not dump the full ID list.

title: Placeholder-limit workaround only handles SQLite, so large batches still fail on PostgreSQL/MySQL
body: deleteByIDs special-cases only SQLite when AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize exceeds 999; for all other databases it builds one DELETE ... WHERE id IN (?, ?, ...) with len(ids) bound parameters. PostgreSQL's extended protocol allows at most 65535 parameters per statement (MySQL has similar placeholder/packet limits), so a configured batch size above that now makes every cleanup batch fail, whereas the previous subquery-based DELETE had no parameter-count limit regardless of batch size. The workaround should be based on the actual number of IDs and the target dialect's limit, chunk the DELETE, or inline IDs for large batches on all dialects.

title: Split SELECT/DELETE for MaxCount can delete annotations that are back within the retention count
body: For MaxCount cleanup, IDs are selected with ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT batch OFFSET MaxCount and then deleted by ID in a separate, non-transactional statement. If one of the newest MaxCount annotations is deleted (e.g. via the annotation Delete API) between the SELECT and the DELETE, a fetched ID moves into the set that should now be retained, but it is still deleted, leaving fewer than MaxCount annotations. The old single-statement DELETE evaluated the offset atomically. The PR description only acknowledges under-deletion on concurrent inserts; this concurrent-delete path causes over-deletion beyond the configured retention policy.

title: SQLite inline ID list is built with repeated fmt.Sprintf string concatenation
body: In the SQLite large-batch branch, values is grown with fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) once per ID. This copies the entire accumulated string on every iteration, making building the IN list O(n^2); with the newly tested batch size of 32767 IDs the final string is hundreds of kilobytes and is re-copied tens of thousands of times. Use strings.Builder (or strconv.AppendInt into a []byte) to build the list in linear time.

title: Cleanup ticker reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute for all jobs without justification
body: This changes the interval for CleanUpService.Run from 10 minutes to 1 minute. That ticker drives every job in clean(), not only annotation cleanup: expired snapshots, dashboard versions, images, temp-user invites, short URLs, and query-history enforcement will now run 10x as often, increasing database and log load in every Grafana instance. The PR description only justifies splitting the annotation DELETE statements to avoid MySQL deadlocks and does not mention or justify this frequency change, so it looks like a leftover local-testing change and should be reverted or separately justified and scoped to annotations.

title: Normal cleanup batches are logged at Error level with the full ID list
body: CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags unconditionally call r.log.Error before and after every batch (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579), including successful batches and the final empty batch where err is nil and affected is 0. Normal periodic cleanup will therefore flood error logs, trigger error-based alerting/log pipelines, and serialize ID slices that can contain up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize (tested at 32767) entries per batch. These diagnostic messages should be Debug level, should not log the full ID slice, and errors should only be logged/returned when the batch actually fails.

title: Parameter-limit workaround only handles SQLite, regressing large batches on other databases
body: deleteByIDs binds one '?' placeholder per fetched ID for every database except the special-cased SQLite path at lines 608-613. The previous implementation used a subquery DELETE with no per-ID bind parameters. AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is configurable and this PR's own test raises it to 32767; a larger configured batch (over 65535 parameters) will now fail on PostgreSQL/MySQL with bind-parameter limits even though the old statement would have succeeded, aborting cleanup partway. The workaround should be based on len(ids) and the actual database's parameter limit, or IDs should be chunked/inlined for all affected dialects.

title: SQLite inline ID list is built with quadratic string concatenation
body: For SQLite with batch size over 999, deleteByIDs builds the IN list by repeatedly doing values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) in a loop. Each iteration copies the entire accumulated string, so building a list of up to batch-size IDs (32767 in the added test, applied repeatedly to annotations and orphaned tags) is O(n^2) in time and allocations and can make large cleanups and the new test very slow. Use strings.Builder (or chunk the deletes) instead of re-formatting the whole string per ID.

title: Async legacy writes inherit the request context and can be cancelled immediately
body: Create derives its 10-second legacy-write context from the incoming request context; the same pattern is used for Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection. Once the API handler finishes and returns the response, the request context is cancelled, so an in-flight legacy write can be aborted despite the 10-second timeout. This can silently leave legacy storage without the backup write that mode 3 is intended to provide. The context needs to be detached from request cancellation while preserving request values such as authentication.

title: Async legacy Create races with use of the returned object
body: Create passes the original obj to Legacy.Create in a goroutine after Storage.Create has returned created from that same input. Storage implementations may mutate obj or return an object aliasing it, while the caller will proceed to serialize or otherwise use created. The legacy store can therefore concurrently read or mutate shared object state, causing a data race or changing the response after unified storage has completed. The object should be deep-copied before launching the asynchronous legacy write.

title: Update reuses objInfo instead of propagating the unified-storage result to legacy
body: Update passes the same UpdatedObjectInfo independently to unified storage and then asynchronously to legacy storage, dropping the previous updateWrapper behavior. UpdatedObject will be computed a second time against legacy's old object, so the two stores can receive different content when their old objects or resource versions differ, and implementations that cache or mutate the decoded object can make the second computation incorrect. Legacy should receive the same updated object that unified storage accepted, as the previous implementation ensured.

title: Storage failures are recorded in the wrong duration metric
body: When Storage.Create fails, the code calls recordLegacyDuration instead of recordStorageDuration; Update has the same mistake on its storage-error path, and DeleteCollection records its asynchronous legacy result with recordStorageDuration. Storage and legacy latency/error dashboards and alerts will therefore attribute failures to the wrong backend and can hide unified-storage errors.

title: Delete uses the object name as the Prometheus kind label
body: The successful Delete path calls recordStorageDuration with name where the other methods pass options.Kind. Prometheus labels must be bounded; using a distinct resource name for every deleted object creates unbounded metric cardinality, increasing memory and query cost and breaking comparisons by kind. It should pass options.Kind like the error path and other methods.

title: Destroy does not wait for in-flight asynchronous legacy writes
body: Mode 3 launches fire-and-forget goroutines for legacy writes but keeps no WaitGroup or other tracking. Destroy immediately destroys both storages, so shutdown can terminate or close legacy storage while writes are still running, losing backup writes or causing use-after-destroy failures. Asynchronous work needs to be tracked and drained before the underlying storages are destroyed.

title: Mode 3 tests never verify the asynchronous legacy writes
body: The new tests invoke Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection but do not wait for or assert the legacy goroutines, and both stores share one testify mock with indistinguishable expectations. The tests therefore pass even if a legacy method is never called, is called with the wrong object, or fails asynchronously after the test returns. They need synchronization and separate assertions that each legacy operation eventually runs with the expected arguments.

title: Mode 3 playlist integration test assumes synchronous legacy visibility
body: The new mode 3 integration cases reuse doPlaylistTests, which creates or updates through the Kubernetes API and immediately reads the same data through the legacy playlist API. Mode 3 now writes to legacy in a background goroutine, so there is no ordering guarantee that the legacy rows exist when those immediate assertions run. This introduces intermittent integration-test failures unless the test polls for legacy visibility or the helper waits for asynchronous writes to settle.

title: Async legacy writes inherit the cancellable request context
body: Create derives the legacy goroutine's context from the incoming request context, and the same pattern is used by Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection. The API server can cancel that context as soon as Create returns the unified-storage response, which happens immediately after spawning the goroutine, so the legacy write will often run with an already-cancelled context and fail. This defeats the stated safety purpose of mode 3. The legacy context needs to be detached from request cancellation, for example with context.WithoutCancel plus its own timeout, while preserving needed values.

title: Unordered legacy goroutines can resurrect or lose objects
body: Every Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection launches an independent legacy goroutine with no per-resource ordering or queue. Rapid operations on the same object can therefore reach legacy storage out of order: a delete can run before the preceding create and leave a resurrected object, or an update can run before its create and be lost. The previous synchronous implementation preserved request order, so legacy storage can now silently diverge from unified storage.

title: Create shares the same object between the response and legacy goroutine
body: Create passes the original obj pointer to the asynchronous Legacy.Create while returning the unified-storage result to the caller. The storage implementation may have mutated obj, and the caller/API server may concurrently serialize or mutate the returned object while the goroutine reads the same underlying object, creating a data race. The legacy call can also observe storage-assigned fields such as resourceVersion that a legacy create does not expect. Legacy needs its own deep copy made before the goroutine is started.

title: Update recomputes the updated object separately for legacy storage
body: Update now passes the original objInfo to Legacy.Update after Storage.Update has already consumed it. Each storage will invoke UpdatedObject against its own old object, so transformations, defaults, timestamps, or other computed fields can differ between unified and legacy storage, and a stateful UpdatedObject implementation may fail or behave differently on the second call. The removed updateWrapper existed to compute the object once and give both stores the identical result; that guarantee needs to be restored for the legacy write.

title: Delete no longer cleans up legacy objects when unified delete reports NotFound
body: Delete now returns immediately for any Storage.Delete error. The previous implementation specifically tolerated NotFound and still attempted the legacy delete. An object that exists only in legacy storage, or whose unified copy was already removed, will now remain in legacy storage and can reappear if traffic is rolled back to a legacy-reading mode. NotFound from unified storage should still trigger the legacy deletion attempt.

title: Several dual-writer metrics are recorded against the wrong storage or label
body: When Storage.Create fails, Create calls recordLegacyDuration instead of recording a storage failure, and Update does the same at its storage-error path. DeleteCollection records the asynchronous legacy result with recordStorageDuration, while Delete's success path passes the resource name where other calls pass options.Kind as the kind label. This corrupts the mode-3 dashboards/error attribution and, for Delete, introduces a high-cardinality metric label containing object names.

title: Asynchronous legacy failures are silently swallowed
body: The legacy goroutines in Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection capture the legacy error only to update a duration metric and never log it. The previous synchronous implementation logged legacy write failures. Operators therefore get no object identity or error context when legacy storage starts diverging, making the safety copy unreliable and difficult to diagnose or reconcile.

title: Mode 3 tests never synchronize with or verify the async legacy writes
body: The new Create and Update tests register legacy mock expectations but return immediately after asserting only the unified-storage result; Delete and DeleteCollection do not meaningfully verify a legacy call at all. Nothing waits for the goroutines, calls AssertExpectations, or uses.Eventually, so a legacy write that never happens can still pass, while a goroutine running after the test finishes can produce racy or unexpected mock calls. The async behavior that defines mode 3 is therefore untested.

title: New mode 3 integration cases immediately assert legacy visibility despite async writes
body: The added file and unified-storage mode 3 cases reuse doPlaylistTests, which creates, updates, and deletes through the Kubernetes API and then immediately checks the legacy playlist API for the same state. Mode 3 performs legacy writes in fire-and-forget goroutines with no completion signal, so those legacy assertions race the asynchronous writes and will be flaky even if they usually win the race in local runs.

title: Asynchronous legacy writes inherit the cancellable request context
body: Create derives the legacy-write context with context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...) from the incoming request context, and Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection do the same. That parent is cancelled when the HTTP handler finishes, normally shortly after the unified-storage response is encoded, so the nominal 10-second timeout rarely applies. Legacy writes therefore race response completion and are frequently aborted after the client has received success, silently leaving unified storage and legacy storage diverged. The context needs to be detached from request cancellation while preserving required values before applying the timeout.

title: Asynchronous legacy Create races the caller on the same mutable object
body: Create passes obj to Storage.Create and then captures the same obj in a background goroutine while returning created to the API server. Storage implementations commonly mutate and return the passed object, so created may alias obj. The API server can encode or further mutate the returned object while Legacy.Create concurrently reads or mutates it, causing a data race and potentially changing the response or the object persisted to legacy storage. A deep copy must be made for the legacy write before returning, rather than sharing the request object with the goroutine.

title: Legacy Update re-runs UpdatedObjectInfo instead of writing the unified-storage result
body: Update passes the original objInfo to Legacy.Update after Storage.Update has already consumed it. The legacy store will invoke UpdatedObject a second time against its own old object, so fields derived from the old object, defaults, resource version, or other update logic can produce an object different from res, the object actually written to unified storage. The previous implementation used updateWrapper to give legacy storage exactly the unified-storage result; removing that wrapper reintroduces a consistency risk between the two stores.

title: A unified-storage Delete error abandons the legacy delete
body: Delete now returns immediately for every Storage.Delete error, including NotFound. An object that exists only in legacy storage, for example because it predates migration, a backfill missed it, or an earlier asynchronous create/update failed, will therefore never be deleted from legacy storage. The client receives an error based on unified storage while the legacy orphan remains and can reappear if the resource is later returned to a legacy-reading mode. The previous behavior still attempted the legacy delete when unified storage reported NotFound.

title: Mode 3 duration metrics are recorded against the wrong store or label
body: Several metric calls are misattributed: a Storage.Create failure at line 45 records recordLegacyDuration, a Storage.Update failure at line 129 also records recordLegacyDuration, the legacy DeleteCollection goroutine at line 166 records recordStorageDuration, and successful Delete at line 106 passes the object name instead of options.Kind as the kind label. This corrupts legacy-versus-storage latency and error measurements and, for Delete, creates a high-cardinality kind label containing user object names.

title: Mode 3 tests never verify the asynchronous legacy writes
body: The Mode 3 Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection tests assert only the synchronous unified-storage result and return without waiting for or asserting completion of the background legacy goroutine. They would pass if the legacy write were removed or always failed, and the unsynchronized goroutine can still access the shared mock and shared example objects after the test has finished, creating flaky behavior under the race detector. The tests need a synchronization mechanism and explicit assertions that each legacy method was called with the expected arguments.

title: Mode 3 playlist integration tests assume synchronous legacy visibility
body: The new mode 3 scenarios reuse doPlaylistTests, which immediately checks the legacy playlist APIs after Kubernetes create and update operations through helpers such as the legacy search check and getFromBothAPIs. Mode 3 performs legacy writes asynchronously with no completion signal, so those assertions race the background legacy write and can intermittently observe missing or stale legacy playlists even when the implementation eventually succeeds. The mode 3 scenarios need eventual-consistency polling for legacy assertions or a different set of expectations from the synchronous modes.

title: Cache is not rechecked after acquiring the write lock
body: GetWebAssets releases the read lock before acquiring the write lock, but never rechecks entryPointAssetsCache after acquiring it. Every goroutine that observed a nil cache during a cold start will therefore serialize on the write lock and repeat the manifest file read and parsing, overwriting the cache each time, while the exclusive lock also blocks fast-path readers for the duration of that I/O. On a burst of concurrent index requests at startup this defeats the cache for that burst and unnecessarily serializes disk I/O; recheck the cache inside the write lock (respecting Dev mode) and return the already-loaded value when another goroutine populated it.

title: No concurrent regression test exercises the claimed race fix
body: This change adds mutex synchronization around entryPointAssetsCache but adds no test that calls GetWebAssets from multiple goroutines. Sequential tests would not have triggered the original data race under the race detector, so removing or misplacing one of the new lock operations in the future would not be caught. Add a same-package test that resets the global cache, serves a valid assets-manifest fixture via cfg.StaticRootPath, hammers GetWebAssets concurrently in non-Dev mode, and is run with -race.

title: Cache is not rechecked after acquiring the write lock
body: The fast path checks the cache under RLock at lines 41-46, but after a goroutine waits for the exclusive lock at line 48 it unconditionally reloads the manifest and overwrites entryPointAssetsCache at line 69. Consequently, if several non-Dev requests arrive concurrently on a cold cache, every one of them performs the file read instead of all but the first reusing the newly populated cache. Add a second check after acquiring Lock (only for cfg.Env != setting.Dev, so Dev reload behavior is preserved) to return the populated cache.

title: No concurrent regression test for the race fix
body: The change adds synchronization to GetWebAssets but no test exercises concurrent calls, so CI running with -race has no coverage that would catch a regression of the reported data race on entryPointAssetsCache. Add a test that resets the global cache, serves a temporary assets-manifest.json, and calls GetWebAssets from many goroutines simultaneously (cold-cache non-Dev path, and ideally the Dev reload path), asserting all callers succeed with the same assets.

title: Cache is not re-checked after acquiring the write lock
body: Multiple goroutines can concurrently observe a nil entryPointAssetsCache under the read lock, then queue on the write lock at line 48. Because the locked section does not re-check the cache, every queued goroutine re-reads and parses assets-manifest.json, overwrites the cache, and blocks other callers while holding the exclusive lock. A cold-start burst therefore defeats the cache and serializes redundant file I/O. After acquiring the lock, return the cached value when cfg.Env is not Dev and the cache is now populated, while preserving the reload behavior in Dev mode.

title: No concurrent regression test for the data-race fix
body: The change synchronizes entryPointAssetsCache but adds no test that calls GetWebAssets concurrently, so CI running with the race detector has no new coverage for the simultaneous cache-miss/cache-hit path that previously raced. Add a same-package test using a valid temporary assets manifest and a non-Dev configuration that launches multiple concurrent GetWebAssets calls, properly resetting the global cache between tests, and verifies all callers succeed with the expected assets.

title: Legacy SQL-command entry point is not explicitly disabled
body: UnmarshalSQLCommand still constructs a SQLCommand through NewSQLCommand without any disabled/feature check. The newer ExpressionQueryReader is explicitly described as not yet replacing the existing transform.go query path, so this legacy path remains reachable. It is currently blocked only incidentally because sql.TablesList calls the new stub DB and fails, which is then reported as a generic invalid-SQL BadRequest. If the stub DB is later implemented or replaced, this entry point would re-enable SQL execution without passing through the reader's kill-switch and could re-expose the DuckDB RCE/LFI surface. Reject SQL explicitly in UnmarshalSQLCommand/NewSQLCommand, or in the service pipeline builder, with the same disabled/not-implemented error used by the reader.

title: No tests lock in that SQL expressions stay disabled
body: The change adds an early rejection for QueryTypeSQL and stubs out the SQL DB in pkg/expr/sql/db.go, but no test files are changed. There is therefore no regression test proving a SQL expression is rejected even when FlagSqlExpressions is enabled, and no updated/skipped coverage for the existing SQL parser/command tests whose TablesList/QueryFramesInto calls now always return 'not implemented'. Add tests for the disabled behavior on both query-parsing entry points and update or explicitly skip the now-obsolete DuckDB-backed SQL tests so CI demonstrates the CVE fix rather than merely failing or silently losing coverage.

title: SQL feature gate contains inverted dead logic and always returns false
body: enableSqlExpressions computes enabled as !IsEnabledGlobally(FlagSqlExpressions), then returns false both when enabled is true and when it is false. The feature-flag value therefore has no effect, the variable name and negation misrepresent the security intent, and the function unnecessarily dereferences h.features even though it can never return true; a reader constructed without feature toggles would panic on a SQL query instead of cleanly rejecting it. Replace this with an unconditional return false (with a comment explaining SQL expressions are disabled) or remove the helper and reject directly at the call site.

title: Legacy UnmarshalSQLCommand entry point is not explicitly disabled
body: The explicit SQL-expression rejection is added only to ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery in pkg/expr/reader.go, while UnmarshalSQLCommand here still accepts a SQL expression and forwards it to NewSQLCommand. It is currently blocked only incidentally because the stubbed sql.TablesList/RunCommands returns 'not implemented', producing a misleading 'error reading SQL command' BadRequest; there is no explicit disabled check or feature/feature-toggle awareness on this path. If the in-memory DB implementation is later restored, this entry point silently becomes functional again without passing through the reader.go gate. Reject SQL commands explicitly on this unmarshalling path as defense-in-depth.

title: No regression tests cover the disabled SQL-expression behavior
body: This security change makes RunCommands and QueryFramesInto always return 'not implemented', makes pkg/expr/sql.TablesList always fail, makes NewSQLCommand always fail, and makes the reader reject QueryTypeSQL, but the PR changes no _test.go files. Existing tests that expect table parsing or SQL execution to succeed will now fail or need skipping, and there is no new regression test proving a SQL expression is rejected even when FlagSqlExpressions is enabled (the CVE scenario) via both the reader path and UnmarshalSQLCommand. Add/update tests asserting the disabled behavior so a future refactor of enableSqlExpressions or the DB stub cannot silently re-enable the vulnerable path.

title: Legacy SQL command construction path is not explicitly disabled
body: UnmarshalSQLCommand still accepts a raw SQL expression and calls NewSQLCommand without any disabled/feature check. It currently fails only incidentally because sql.TablesList calls the stub DB's RunCommands and NewSQLCommand maps that 'not implemented' error to a BadRequest for invalid SQL. The kill switch is therefore not enforced at this entry point, produces a misleading error, and restoring a working DB/parser implementation would remove the only construction barrier on this path even though SQL expressions are supposed to be disabled. Add an explicit disabled check to UnmarshalSQLCommand/NewSQLCommand or remove those constructors while the feature is disabled.

title: enableSqlExpressions always returns false through inverted dead logic
body: The helper computes enabled as the negation of FlagSqlExpressions and then returns false both inside the if and after it, so the feature toggle has no effect and the logic reads as the opposite of its name. It also unnecessarily dereferences h.features: a reader constructed with nil toggles will panic on a SQL query instead of returning the intended disabled error. Replace this with an explicit unconditional disabled return with a comment, or implement the toggle check without negation.

title: No regression test covers the SQL-expression kill switch
body: This security change makes the reader reject SQL expressions and makes NewSQLCommand/TablesList/Execute fail through the stub DB, but no _test.go file is changed. Add tests proving that a SQL expression is rejected when FlagSqlExpressions is enabled through ReadQuery, that the raw-node UnmarshalSQLCommand/NewSQLCommand path cannot construct an executable command, and that Execute returns an error rather than running the query; otherwise a future refactor or DB restoration could silently re-enable the CVE-2024-9264 vulnerable path.

title: Concurrent BuildIndex calls for the same key are no longer serialized
body: BuildIndex no longer holds cacheMu while creating and populating the index; it only locks for the final cache assignment. Because GetIndex returns nil until that assignment, two concurrent getOrCreateIndex/Search calls for the same NamespacedResource can both build an index. For file-backed indexes both call bleve.New on the same directory, so one can fail or contend on the on-disk index; for memory indexes both build fully and the later assignment overwrites and leaks the earlier unclosed index. Add per-key synchronization/singleflight or a double-checked cache lookup so only one build per key runs while different keys still build in parallel.

title: Search init workers race on shared err and counter
body: Every errgroup closure in init assigns to the same outer err variable and increments totalBatchesIndexed without synchronization. Concurrent workers therefore data-race, and a failing build's error can be overwritten by a concurrent successful build before the failing closure returns it, letting startup proceed with a missing index and producing incorrect span counts. Use a closure-local err returned directly to errgroup and an atomic or mutex-protected counter.

title: Handlers no longer reject requests after Stop
body: All RPC handlers removed their s.Init(ctx) check, but Stop relies on mutating s.initErr to make subsequent Init calls return the stopping/stopped error. Create and the other handlers never consult initErr now, and they use the request context rather than the cancelled server context, so direct in-process callers can still read, write, delete, search, or use blobs after lifecycle Stop instead of failing fast. Keep a lightweight stopped/init-state check in handlers, separate from the sync.Once initialization.

title: Constructor returns no handle to clean up partially initialized services on Init failure
body: If s.Init fails after lifecycle initialization or after search.init has started its background watch goroutine, NewResourceServer returns nil without calling cancel or lifecycle Stop. The caller receives no server handle with which to clean up, so the opened backend and the search watch/poller (which uses context.Background) can keep running and repeated construction attempts can accumulate pollers. On Init error, stop/cancel whatever was started before returning the original error.

title: TotalDocs iterates the index cache without holding cacheMu
body: TotalDocs ranges over b.cache without RLock while BuildIndex now inserts into that map under a short Lock at the end of a build. Concurrent index creation (for example from the search watch goroutine handling a new namespace while init logs TotalDocs, or later lazy builds) can therefore race with this iteration, which the race detector flags and Go can turn into a fatal concurrent-map-iteration/write panic. Hold cacheMu.RLock for the iteration.

title: TotalDocs iterates the index cache without holding cacheMu
body: bleveBackend.TotalDocs ranges over b.cache without acquiring cacheMu, while BuildIndex now writes b.cache at the end of a potentially long concurrent build. Concurrent map iteration and map write can cause Go's fatal 'concurrent map iteration and map write' panic. This can be reached when searchSupport.init starts its watch goroutine before logging TotalDocs and a watch/search request lazily builds another index. TotalDocs should hold cacheMu.RLock for the iteration.

title: Concurrent BuildIndex calls for the same key are no longer serialized or deduplicated
body: BuildIndex previously held cacheMu for its whole duration; now it only locks when inserting the finished index and never re-checks whether the same NamespacedResource was built concurrently. Two concurrent Search/handleEvent calls through getOrCreateIndex can both miss GetIndex and build the same key: for file-backed indexes both use the same directory path, so one can fail on the already-open index, and for memory indexes one finished index is overwritten in the cache and leaked without Close. Add per-key/single-flight building or a double-checked cache lookup under an appropriate lock.

title: searchSupport.init has unsynchronized writes from errgroup workers
body: In searchSupport.init, every errgroup worker executes totalBatchesIndexed++ and assigns to the shared outer err variable (line 190). These concurrent unsynchronized writes are a data race, can lose counter increments for the span attribute, and make the shared err value racy/redundant because errgroup already collects worker return values. Use an atomic counter and a local error variable inside each worker.

title: NewResourceServer performs blocking index builds with an uncancellable background context
body: NewResourceServer now synchronously calls s.Init(ctx), but ctx is derived internally from context.Background and is only cancelled by server.Stop, which cannot be called until the constructor returns. A slow or hung GetResourceStats/ListIterator index build therefore blocks construction indefinitely with no caller-supplied startup context or timeout, and a search-index failure now prevents creation of the whole resource server including non-search operations. Pass a caller context/timeout into construction or otherwise make eager initialization cancellable.

title: Constructor does not clean up partial initialization on Init failure
body: When s.Init fails in NewResourceServer, the function returns nil, err without calling s.cancel or lifecycle Stop. Init may already have started side effects, notably searchSupport.init's background-context watch goroutine or a partially started watcher, but the discarded server gives the caller no handle to stop them. This leaks goroutines/pollers that continue consuming storage events after construction has failed; clean up the server context and started components on the error path.

title: Postgres storage-server integration coverage is disabled instead of fixed
body: The change adds an unconditional postgres skip to TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer just as the PR changes storage-server startup to eagerly initialize unified storage. That removes CI coverage for the eager Init/SQL path on one supported database backend, so a postgres-specific startup regression would not be caught. Fix the underlying postgres failure or keep the skip tied to a tracked, narrowly scoped condition.

title: Concurrent builds for the same index are no longer serialized
body: BuildIndex now only locks cacheMu when inserting the finished index, while GetIndex (lines 60-68) only checks the cache and has no in-flight tracking. Two concurrent Search/search-init/watch-event calls for the same not-yet-cached NamespacedResource can therefore both invoke BuildIndex, both run the document builder, and for file-backed indexes both call bleve.New on the same directory path at line 97. This can fail with an index-exists/lock error, double-count IndexTenants, leak the overwritten index without Close, or corrupt startup/search behaviour; previously GetIndex blocked on the read lock while a build held the write lock. Per-key in-flight deduplication (or equivalent) is needed, not just a short cache-insert lock.

title: TotalDocs iterates the index cache without holding cacheMu
body: TotalDocs ranges over b.cache without acquiring cacheMu.RLock, while BuildIndex now concurrently writes b.cache[key] under the write lock at lines 137-139 (and builds now run in parallel during startup and on-demand). Concurrent map iteration and map write is a Go data race and can trigger a fatal 'concurrent map iteration and map write' panic or race-detector failures. TotalDocs should snapshot or read the cache under RLock.

title: Parallel init workers share the outer err and counter without synchronization
body: In searchSupport.init, every errgroup worker executes 'totalBatchesIndexed++' and '_, _, err = s.build(...); return err' using variables captured from the enclosing scope. With initWorkers > 1 these are unsynchronized concurrent writes/reads: the race detector will flag them, the indexed count can lose increments, and one namespace's build error can be overwritten by another worker's result before it is returned, so init may report success despite a failed namespace build (or report another worker's error). Each worker should use a local err variable and an atomic/mutex-protected counter.

title: Postgres integration coverage for the changed startup path is disabled
body: The PR adds an unconditional skip for postgres in TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer, the integration test that exercises the storage-server target whose initialization this PR moves into NewResourceServer. Skipping it removes CI coverage for exactly the eager-init/startup behaviour on postgres and can hide a postgres-specific startup regression (the comment only says it fails in Drone but works locally). The failure should be diagnosed or tracked with a linked issue rather than silently skipped.

title: Call to non-existent no-argument isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()
body: UsernameForm.authenticate() calls isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() with no arguments, but the only method added to its superclass UsernamePasswordForm is isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user). There is no no-argument overload in UsernamePasswordForm or AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator, so this code does not compile and blocks building the services module and running any of the added tests.

title: Conditional passkeys now disabled for unidentified users, breaking initial discoverable login
body: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel) requires user != null, and it is used in authenticate() and in challenge(context, error, field). Previously conditional WebAuthn data was filled when no user had been identified, which is the normal first-login case for discoverable passkeys: the credential itself supplies the user. With the new predicate, opening the username/password page initially (context.getUser() == null) never calls webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(), so no challenge/RP data or conditional-UI form is rendered and automatic passkey login cannot happen; the same loss occurs after an invalid-username challenge where the user is null. The predicate should enable passkeys based on the realm/feature setting regardless of whether a user is already identified, while only restricting the listed authenticators for an identified user.

title: Call to non-existent no-argument isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() breaks compilation
body: UsernameForm.authenticate() calls isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() with no arguments, but the only method added in UsernamePasswordForm is isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user). UsernameForm, UsernamePasswordForm, and their superclasses define no no-argument overload, so this code does not compile and the services module cannot be built.

title: Passkey conditional UI is now disabled for initial login where no user is set yet
body: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel) requires user != null, and it gates fillContextForm() in authenticate() (line 115) and challenge(error, field) (line 137). On an initial UsernamePasswordForm login the context user is still null, including for discoverable-passkey login, so the WebAuthn challenge, RP ID and conditional-UI attributes are never put on the login form. This reverses the previous user==null behaviour instead of extending it to re-authentication, regressing first-login passkey authentication and removing passkeys from the form re-rendered after an initial-login error.

title: Call to non-existent no-argument isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() does not compile
body: UsernameForm.authenticate() calls isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() with no arguments, but the only method added to its superclass UsernamePasswordForm is isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user) at UsernamePasswordForm.java:160. There is no no-argument overload in UsernamePasswordForm, AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator, or the shown superclass chain, so this file fails compilation and the whole services module cannot build. The call should pass the relevant user, e.g. isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser()), or a no-argument overload must be defined.

title: Conditional passkeys are now only filled when a user is already known, breaking initial ID-less passkey login
body: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel) requires user != null, and authenticate() (line 115) and challenge(context,error,field) (line 137) now use it instead of the previous logic that filled WebAuthn data when no user was selected yet. On a first login through UsernamePasswordForm/UsernameForm no user is set, so WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator.fillContextForm() is never called, ENABLE_WEBAUTHN_CONDITIONAL_UI/challenge/RP data are not put on the login page, and discoverable (ID-less) passkeys cannot auto-login or be offered. The same applies after a failed password attempt in a normal login where the user is cleared. The helper must also return true for the not-yet-identified case (user == null) in addition to the re-authentication case.

title: Re-authentication passkey check does not verify the known user actually has a passkey credential
body: For a known user, isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() only checks that the realm/feature passkeys flag is on; it never checks user.credentialManager().isConfiguredFor(webauthnAuth.getCredentialType()). Because WebAuthnConditionalUIAuthenticator.shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators() now always returns false, fillContextForm() also no longer bails out when the user has no WebAuthn authenticators. Consequently every re-authenticating user in a passkeys-enabled realm, including password-only users, loses the UsernameForm skip-success shortcut (UsernameForm.java:47) and is presented with passkey conditional-UI/authenticate UI they cannot use, instead of going straight to password/broker re-authentication.

title: reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey test disables passkeys realm-wide instead of testing a user without a passkey
body: The test named reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey sets WebAuthnPolicyPasskeysEnabled to FALSE for the whole realm, so the absence of the webauth form only proves the realm flag is honoured. It does not cover the distinct and currently broken case of a passkeys-enabled realm with a user (test-user@localhost, who only has a password) who has no passwordless credential, which is the case a credential check in isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() needs to handle. Add/adjust the test to keep passkeys enabled in the realm while the re-authenticating user has no passkey and assert no passkey UI is shown and password re-authentication still works.

title: Update invalidation compares an organization-aware wrapped model against a raw model
body: update() obtains the original via getById(), which returns createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel(): for an IdP linked to an organization its isEnabled() is overridden to also require the organization (and the organization feature) to be enabled. registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate() then evaluates getLoginPredicate() on that wrapped original but on the raw updated model, while the JPA getForLogin query that populated the cache filters on the raw enabled flag. Example: an enabled, public IdP of a disabled organization is in the cached login list (raw enabled=true), but the wrapped original reports isEnabled()=false; disabling the IdP (updated enabled=false) makes both predicates false, so no login-cache invalidation is registered and the stale internal id remains in the cached getForLogin result, violating the contract that getForLogin returns only enabled login IdPs.

title: Shared getLoginPredicate() semantics changed to exclude private organization brokers
body: LoginFilter.getLoginPredicate() is a public SPI predicate previously defined purely by the LoginFilter values (enabled, not link-only, not hidden on login, matching getLoginSearchOptions()). This change additionally requires any organization-linked IdP to have kc.org.broker.public=true. That silently changes the meaning for every existing caller of the predicate, not just the new cache-invalidation code: a private organization broker that is legitimately usable once its organization is known (e.g. after organization identification) is now classified as never available for login, and the predicate no longer corresponds to the LoginFilter enum documented as containing all fields considered for login availability. The broker-public check should be local to the cache-invalidation decision instead of redefining the shared predicate.

title: Test cleanup registers removal of a literal "alias" instead of the created IdPs
body: In testCacheIDPForLogin the loop creates IdPs with aliases idp-alias-0..19 (and later idp-alias-20 at line 425) but registers cleanup as testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove, i.e. for an IdP literally named "alias" rather than the loop variable alias / the created alias. The created providers are therefore not removed (and removing the non-existent "alias" can itself fail during cleanup), leaving 21 extra IdPs in the shared test realm that can leak into other test methods of the class and make count-based cache assertions order-dependent and flaky.

title: getForLogin loses the delegate's deterministic ordering
body: The cached path collects identity-provider IDs into a Set and then builds a HashSet<IdentityProviderModel> (lines 244-254) before returning identityProviders.stream(). This discards the ordering of idpDelegate.getForLogin(), which concatenates realm-level providers before organization providers and otherwise follows the storage query order. Callers of getForLogin that do not explicitly sort (the login bean does, but other broker/manager callers may not) will now observe arbitrary, potentially call-varying ordering instead of the previous deterministic order.

title: New getLoginPredicate clause can NPE on a null config map
body: getLoginPredicate() now evaluates Boolean.parseBoolean(idp.getConfig().get(OrganizationModel.BROKER_PUBLIC)) for every identity provider whose organizationId is non-null, without checking getConfig() for null. IdentityProviderModel config is settable and can be null for models built from representations or by custom code. Previously the predicate only called isEnabled/isLinkOnly/isHideOnLogin and could not fail this way. In the new cache code this predicate is invoked from create/update/remove in InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider before the delegate operation runs, so a null-config organization-linked IdP would fail creation/update/removal with an NPE instead of being processed.

title: Login cache aggregates an unbounded entry per organization under three keys
body: cacheKeyForLogin creates only one cache key per FetchMode, while organizationId is stored as the searchKey inside a single IdentityProviderListQuery. Every distinct organizationId first seen for a mode therefore goes through the miss branch (lines 233-241), invalidates the whole shared object, and re-adds a new query copied from the previous one. In realms with many organizations this creates one retained ID set per organization ever queried under REALM_ONLY/ORG_ONLY/ALL, makes adding each new organization copy all previously cached variants, and means the REALM_ONLY cache also accumulates spurious per-organization entries even though that mode ignores organizationId. This is unbounded cache growth and invalidation churn proportional to the number of organizations.

title: New login-cache test cleans up a literal alias and never asserts cache-hit results
body: In testCacheIDPForLogin the cleanup registration uses testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias") instead of the created alias (idp-alias-<i>, and similarly idp-alias-20 at line 425), so the 21 created providers are not removed by cleanup and removal of the non-existent alias 'alias' may itself error during cleanup. Additionally, the test only asserts IdentityProviderListQuery sizes inside the cache; it never calls getForLogin a second time and asserts the aliases actually returned on a cache hit, so defects in the cached reconstruction path (for example wrong/missing providers returned via getById) would not be caught.

title: Update invalidation compares an organization-aware model against the raw updated model
body: update() obtains the original model through getById() (line 91), which returns the organization-aware wrapper whose isEnabled() is false whenever the linked organization is disabled. The JPA-backed getForLogin result, however, is based on the stored enabled/hideOnLogin/linkOnly/BROKER_PUBLIC fields and does not exclude IdPs merely because their organization is disabled. Therefore, for an IdP in a disabled organization that currently qualifies in the stored data, changing hideOnLogin or linkOnly to a disqualifying value makes both the wrapped original and the updated model fail getLoginPredicate(), so registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate() returns without invalidating any login cache. The stale cached ID remains and can reappear when the organization is re-enabled, even though the IdP is now hidden or link-only. The comparison should use the unwrapped stored model/fields rather than the organization-aware isEnabled() view.

title: Empty-string organizationId collides with the null organization cache key
body: getForLogin() uses "" as the IdentityProviderListQuery search key when organizationId is null, while a caller-supplied organizationId of "" is also non-null and is kept as "". Under the IdentityProviderStorageProvider contract these are different requests: null means IdPs from any organization, whereas "" is passed through as a specific organization-id search.
