body: update unconditionally sets group.visible based on whether params[:visible] equals 'true'. Any API client that updates only some fields, such as name, without also sending visible will unintentionally hide the group. This makes partial updates unsafe and changes the previous API behavior.

title: Admin groups API contract changed without compatibility
body: The previous admin groups API accepted a nested group payload, allowed usernames during create/update, and supported incremental membership changes via PATCH. The new controller expects flat parameters and separate membership endpoints. Existing clients or plugins using the old admin group API may fail or silently lose membership changes.

title: remove_member automatic-group spec uses the wrong HTTP verb
body: The automatic-group case for remove_member uses xhr :put, but the route is defined as DELETE and the successful remove_member spec uses DELETE. This test does not exercise the real HTTP verb/route and could miss routing regressions.

title: Unconditional call to custom ensure_loaded! will crash if fallbacks object is replaced
body: `set_locale` calls `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!`. That method is only defined on the new `FallbackLocaleList` class added in `config/initializers/i18n.rb`. If `I18n.fallbacks` is not that exact object (for example if an environment file, plugin, or test setup installs Rails' normal `I18n::Locale::Fallbacks`), this before_filter will raise NoMethodError on every request. Guard with `respond_to?(:ensure_loaded!)` or provide the method on the standard fallbacks object.

title: Only the current locale is loaded; fallback locales may be missing outside controllers
body: The accelerator loads only `config.locale` before calling the uncached translate. With `I18n::Backend::Fallbacks` enabled, a lookup can fall back to `SiteSetting.default_locale` and `:en`, but those locale files are only loaded by `FallbackLocaleList#ensure_loaded!`, which is called only from `ApplicationController#set_locale`. In background jobs, mailers, rake tasks, or initializers, fallback locales may remain unloaded, so fallbacks can return translation-missing strings. Zero-argument translations are cached, so a missing result can also be cached. Load the fallback chain in the translation path or wherever the locale is set.

title: Fallback list does not behave like a normal Hash
body: `FallbackLocaleList` subclasses `Hash` but overrides `[]` without storing entries. Hash methods such as `fetch`, `each`, `keys`, `key?`, and `to_h` will see an empty hash rather than the computed fallback arrays. If I18n or a plugin uses any of those methods on `I18n.fallbacks`, fallbacks can silently fail. Use a dedicated object implementing the expected interface or populate the hash.

title: Race in initialization of loaded-locales list
body: `ensure_loaded!` initializes `@loaded_locales` with `||=` outside `LOAD_MUTEX`, while `load_locale` mutates the array inside the mutex. On first concurrent uses, threads can race and overwrite or duplicate the loaded-locales list, causing redundant locale loading. Initialize and check the list under the same mutex or use a thread-safe collection.

title: No tests for fallback behavior
body: The change introduces server-side locale fallbacks and alters lazy locale loading, but adds no automated coverage. Tests should cover falling back from a user locale to the site default and English, behavior when the default locale changes, and translation outside controller requests such as jobs or mailers.

title: Fallback locales are not loaded automatically by I18n.translate
body: The new fallback support only loads fallback locale files when ApplicationController calls I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!. The accelerated translate method still loads only config.locale, while the backend fallback module resolves fallback locales at the backend level and will not trigger load_locale for them. Any translation performed outside a controller request (background jobs, mailers, rake tasks, middleware, I18n.with_locale blocks, or explicit locale options) can therefore miss the fallback locale files and return missing translations instead of falling back.

title: Translation cache key does not include the fallback default locale
body: Fallbacks now depend on SiteSetting.default_locale, but the cache key only contains the translation key, current locale, and backend object id. If the site default locale is changed, cached translations that were stored as fallbacks for other locales are not invalidated by this PR, so stale strings from the previous default locale can continue to be served until the LRU entry expires or I18n is reloaded.

title: Unsynchronized lazy initialization of @loaded_locales
body: ensure_loaded! initializes the shared @loaded_locales array with ||= outside LOAD_MUTEX, while translate and load_locale access the same variable from multiple threads. Concurrent first calls can assign or observe different arrays, losing loaded-locale state and causing duplicate locale loads. translate also reads @loaded_locales without a nil guard.

title: No tests for new global fallback behavior
body: This changes I18n fallback behavior for all server-side translations and interacts with the lazy-loading and caching accelerator, but no tests are added to verify the fallback order, loading of fallback locale files, cache invalidation when the default locale changes, or behavior outside controller requests.

title: Fallback locales are only loaded for controller requests
body: The accelerator loads translation data lazily, and `translate` only calls `load_locale(config.locale)`. The new fallback locales are loaded only by `FallbackLocaleList#ensure_loaded!`, which is invoked solely from `ApplicationController#set_locale`. Any server-side translation outside that controller path (background jobs, mailers, rake tasks, `I18n.with_locale` blocks, or errors before the filter) will not have the fallback locale YAML loaded, so missing keys may not actually fall back to `SiteSetting.default_locale` or `:en`.

title: Translation cache key omits fallback order/default locale
body: After this change, the result of a cached translation can depend on `SiteSetting.default_locale` (and the hardcoded `:en` fallback), but the cache key is only key + current locale + backend object id. If the default locale changes and `I18n.reload!` is not called, cached missing-key translations will continue to return the old fallback language. Include the fallback chain/default locale in the cache key or ensure invalidation on fallback changes.

title: Unconditional call to custom `ensure_loaded!` can raise
body: `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` assumes the fallbacks object is the custom `FallbackLocaleList`. If another initializer, plugin, or test replaces `I18n.fallbacks` with a standard fallback object, every request will raise NoMethodError. Consider calling it only when `I18n.fallbacks.respond_to?(:ensure_loaded!)`.

title: Fallback list ignores hash storage and assignments
body: `FallbackLocaleList` subclasses Hash but overrides `[]` to always recompute the chain and never consult stored entries. Normal fallback customization such as `I18n.fallbacks[:zh_TW] = [:zh_CN, :en]` will silently have no effect. If fallbacks are intended to be extensible, the class should merge stored/custom entries or expose an explicit extension point.

title: Unsynchronized initialization/read of @loaded_locales
body: `ensure_loaded!` initializes and checks `@loaded_locales` outside `LOAD_MUTEX`, while `load_locale` mutates the same array inside the mutex. Under multithreaded servers this can race, causing duplicate loads or lost/cleared loaded-locale state. Initialize the array in a thread-safe way and perform the check under the same mutex.

title: Denial cache key omits identity type, allowing cross-identity denials
body: Check builds the denial-cache key from namespace, user identifier, action, resource name, and parent folder only; the identity type is not included. Supported subjects include anonymous:0 and render:0, both of which parse to the identifier "0". A denied check for anonymous will therefore write a denial entry that a subsequent renderer check with the same action/resource/folder will hit, causing the renderer to be denied even though renderer permissions are hard-coded to allow dashboard/folder/datasource reads. The reverse is also possible. The denial key should include the identity type.

title: Denial cache key is ambiguous and can collide across resources
body: userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates name and parent with underscores. Resource and folder UIDs can contain underscores, so different (name, parent) tuples can produce the same key. For example, name="a_b" with parent="" and name="a" with parent="b" both serialize to the suffix "_a_b_". Because a denial-cache hit short-circuits the authorization check, a denial cached for one resource/folder combination can be incorrectly applied to another, causing authorized requests to be denied for the cache TTL. Use an unambiguous escaping, separator scheme, or hash of the fields.

title: Cached denial can continue to deny after permissions are granted
body: Check returns false immediately when a denial-cache entry exists, and denial entries are written after any failed full check with a 30-second TTL. If access is granted immediately after a denial, for example when permissions are added around dashboard/folder creation, subsequent checks for that exact resource will keep hitting the denial cache and will be denied until the TTL expires. This can still block access to newly created resources, which is the issue this PR is intended to fix. Consider invalidating negative entries on permission changes, avoiding negative caching in this path, or using a much shorter TTL.

title: Denial cache key omits identity type
body: Check builds the denial cache key from namespace, UserUID, action, name, and parent folder only, without including the identity type. validateSubject permits multiple identity types, and anonymous:0 and render:0 both parse to UserUID 0. A denied anonymous check can therefore write a denial cache entry that a later render:0 check hits, causing the renderer to be denied before getRendererPermissions can allow read access. The denial key must be scoped by identity type.

title: Unescaped underscore-separated denial cache keys can collide
body: userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates namespace, user UID, action, resource name, and parent folder with underscores and no escaping. If a resource or folder UID contains an underscore, different (name, parent) pairs can produce the same key; for example, name a_b with parent c collides with name a and parent b_c. Because this key stores authorization denials, a collision can cause a denial recorded for one resource/folder combination to be applied to a different resource, incorrectly denying access.

title: Negative denial cache can mask newly granted permissions
body: Check consults the denial cache before the newly added DB fallback and writes a denial entry whenever a permission check fails. The denial entry is not invalidated when permissions or folder relationships change. If the initial denial is caused by stale permissions, replica lag, or a stale folder tree cache, the denial entry continues to block subsequent checks until its TTL expires, even if a fresh database lookup would now allow access. This can delay access to newly created dashboards or folders and counteracts the fallback behavior added by this PR.

title: Denial-cache test does not prove the denial entry overrides permissions
body: The test sets the positive permission cache entry to {"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}. In checkPermission, only true scope-map entries grant access, so this cached value does not allow the request even if the denial cache is ignored. The test would still pass without the denial-cache lookup. To verify the denial cache, cache a true permission (or database permissions) and assert that the explicit denial entry still causes denial.

title: Denial cache key omits identity type
body: Check builds the denial-cache key from namespace, UserUID, action, name, and parent folder, but not IdentityType. Anonymous and renderer identities can both have UID 0, and user/service account UIDs may also overlap or be supplied in different forms. A denial cached for one identity type can therefore be returned for another identity type, skipping its permission lookup and causing incorrect access denials. Include the identity type in the denial cache key.

title: Negative cache key can collide because fields are joined with underscores
body: userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates name and parent with underscores and no escaping. Grafana resource and folder UIDs can contain underscores, so different name/parent pairs can produce the same key, for example name a_b with parent c and name a with parent b_c. A denial cached for one combination can then incorrectly deny another resource. Use an unambiguous encoding, hash, or separator that cannot appear in UIDs.

title: Denial cache is checked before positive permissions and never invalidated
body: The denial cache is consulted before any positive cached or database permissions and is only cleared by TTL. If a check is denied while permissions are being created or replicated, the denial entry remains and blocks subsequent checks even after the permission exists. This can keep a creator from accessing a newly created dashboard or folder for the TTL, which conflicts with the stated goal of the PR. Consider checking positive permissions before the denial cache, deleting denial entries when a fresh check allows, or not negative-caching checks for resources that may be in the process of being created.

title: Unauthorized checks can force repeated database permission queries
body: Check now falls back to getIdentityPermissions whenever the cached permission set does not explicitly allow the requested resource, even if the permission cache was just populated. Sequential checks for many distinct unauthorized resources will each trigger a full database permission query before their negative cache entry is written. This can substantially increase database load and can be amplified by authenticated enumeration. Consider limiting requeries, using cache age, or keeping cached-permission denials for non-existent resources.

title: Error-path test does not actually test an error
body: The test case named should return error if store fails does not set fakeStore.err and the test asserts require.NoError, so it never exercises the error path. Add an expected error flag and make the fake store fail for this case.

title: Missing React key for Grafana rule list items
body: In the rules map, the 'grafana' case returns GrafanaRuleListItem without a key prop, while the datasource and unknown cases do pass key. Because this list is incrementally appended during infinite scrolling, missing keys can cause incorrect React reconciliation, reused DOM/state, and hard-to-debug rendering bugs.

title: Delete action is hidden for ruler-less Grafana rules even when permitted
body: AlertRuleMenu computes canDelete from both ruler abilities and Grafana Prometheus abilities, but the Delete menu item is only rendered when rulerRule is truthy. In the new alert list view, Grafana rules are rendered from promRule only, so rulerRule is undefined. Users with delete permission will not see Delete, breaking the intended removal of ruler API dependency.

title: Silence menu item can be shown but clicking it does nothing for ruler-less rules
body: AlertRuleMenu renders the Silence notifications item based on canSilence, which can be true from Grafana Prometheus abilities, and handleSilence sets showSilenceDrawer to true. However SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer is only rendered when rule is a Grafana ruler alerting rule. In the ruler-less list view rule is undefined, so clicking Silence opens no drawer and the action silently fails.

title: Pause action unavailable for ruler-less Grafana rules despite computed ability
body: canPause can be true via useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities, but the pause menu item additionally requires rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule). In the new list view rulerRule is undefined for Grafana Prometheus rules, so Pause is not shown even though the ability hook says it is supported/allowed. This makes pause functionality regress when ruler requests are removed.

title: Federated ruler rules are no longer treated as immutable
body: useAllRulerRuleAbilities now hardcodes isFederated = false, whereas the previous combined-rule ability logic used isFederatedRuleGroup. Federated rules should be immutable in the UI, but this change can make edit/delete/duplicate abilities appear supported for federated ruler rules. Since useAllAlertRuleAbilities still delegates to this hook, existing views may inherit the regression.

title: skipToken does not actually skip Grafana abilities and can grant Duplicate incorrectly
body: useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities converts skipToken to undefined, but useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(undefined) still returns abilities such as Duplicate based on Grafana create permissions. In AlertRuleMenu, abilities from ruler and Grafana hooks are OR'ed, so non-Grafana rules could show Duplicate based on Grafana-internal permissions or when ruler abilities deny it. skipToken should result in all abilities being [false, false].

title: View link no longer includes returnTo navigation parameter
body: The removed GrafanaRuleLoader implementation created the rule view URL with returnTo, but GrafanaRuleListItem now builds /alerting/grafana/:uid/view without it. If the rule viewer or back-navigation logic still relies on returnTo to return to the list/folder context, this change will lose the return location.

title: Grafana rule key contains an extra trailing brace
body: getGrafanaRuleKey returns `grafana-${namespace.uid}-${groupName}-${rule.uid}}`, which includes a literal trailing '}' after the uid interpolation. This is likely a typo and produces malformed React keys if the helper is used for keys.

title: Clipboard write promise rejection is unhandled
body: copyToClipboard calls navigator.clipboard?.writeText(text).then(...) without a catch handler. If clipboard access is denied or fails, the promise rejection is unhandled and the user receives no feedback.

title: Inline actions arrays defeat memoization in ability hooks
body: AlertRuleMenu passes newly created action arrays to useRulerRuleAbilities and useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities on every render. Those hooks memoize based on the actions array identity, so the memoization is ineffective and abilities are recomputed for every rule row on re-renders, which may matter on large alert lists.

title: Test normalizes missing Delete action despite granting delete permissions
body: The test grants AlertingRuleDelete and folder delete permissions, then expects exactly four menu items and does not expect Delete. This encodes the current behavior where Delete is missing for ruler-less Grafana rules instead of validating the intended RBAC behavior. It also does not click Silence, which would expose the no-op drawer issue.

title: Stale comments/variable name about ruler preloading
body: The code and comments still refer to preloading ruler rules and use cacheAndRulerPreload, but the ruler prefetch was removed in this change. This is misleading for future maintainers.

title: Silence action is a no-op in the ruler-less Grafana rule list
body: In the new list view, RuleActionsButtons is rendered with only promRule and no ruler rule. AlertRuleMenu can show 'Silence notifications' because canSilence can be true from Grafana Prometheus abilities, and clicking it sets showSilenceDrawer. However, the silence drawer is only rendered when rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) is true; with rule undefined this condition never passes, so clicking Silence does nothing.

title: Pause menu item is hidden for Grafana rules in the ruler-less list view
body: AlertRuleMenu computes canPause from either ruler abilities or Grafana Prometheus abilities, but the Pause menu item is rendered only when rulerRule is a Grafana ruler rule. In the alert list view after removing ruler requests, rulerRule is undefined, so Pause will not be shown even when the user has permission to pause the Grafana rule.

title: Delete menu item is hidden for Grafana rules in the ruler-less list view
body: canDelete can be true from Grafana Prometheus abilities, but the Delete menu item is rendered only when rulerRule is truthy. In the ruler-less alert list view rulerRule is undefined, so users with delete permission cannot delete Grafana rules from the list. If deletion by UID is intended, this is a regression; if not, the ability should not be enabled.

title: skipToken does not disable Grafana abilities and can enable Duplicate incorrectly
body: useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities converts skipToken to undefined and calls useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(undefined). That hook does not return all-false abilities for undefined; Duplicate becomes supported and allowed if the user has Grafana rule create permission. Because AlertRuleMenu ORs Grafana abilities with ruler abilities, non-Grafana rules may show Duplicate based on unrelated Grafana permissions.

title: Federated rule groups are no longer treated as immutable
body: useAllRulerRuleAbilities hardcodes isFederated = false, while previous CombinedRule logic used isFederatedRuleGroup to mark federated rule groups as immutable. Federated Mimir rules may now incorrectly appear editable, deletable, pausable, or duplicatable.

title: Grafana recording rules lose pause/restore/delete-permanently abilities
body: useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities gates Pause, Restore, and DeletePermanently on isAlertingRule. The previous ruler-based ability logic applied these actions to Grafana-managed rules generally, and Grafana recording rules expose isPaused. This change will hide pause/restore/permanent-delete actions for Grafana recording rules.

title: Grafana rule list items are rendered without a React key
body: In FilterViewResults.rules.map, the computed key is passed to DataSourceRuleLoader and UnknownRuleListItem, but the Grafana branch returns GrafanaRuleListItem without a key. This can cause React list reconciliation warnings and may cause component state to be reused by the wrong rule row when the list updates.

title: Grafana rule key contains an extra closing brace
body: getGrafanaRuleKey returns `grafana-${namespace.uid}-${groupName}-${rule.uid}}`, which adds an unintended trailing closing brace to every generated key. This appears to be a typo and produces malformed keys.

title: Tests assert the limited ruler-less menu instead of covering missing actions
body: The GrafanaGroupLoader menu test grants delete permission but asserts exactly four menu items, omitting Delete and Pause, and does not exercise the Silence action. This masks the ruler-less view regressions where Delete/Pause are missing and Silence can be a no-op.

title: Component comment still says Ruler endpoint is used
body: GrafanaGroupLoader's JSDoc says it loads an evaluation group from Prometheus and Ruler endpoints, but the Ruler query was removed in this change. The comment should be updated to reflect that only the Prometheus endpoint is used.

title: Silence menu item can be shown but the silence drawer never opens for ruler-less rules
body: In the ruler-less list flow, RuleActionsButtons receives only promRule. AlertRuleMenu can therefore show the 'Silence notifications' item based on Grafana Prometheus abilities, and clicking it sets showSilenceDrawer to true. However, the drawer is only rendered when rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) is true, and rule is undefined in this flow. The result is a visible, clickable Silence action that does nothing. The drawer should be rendered from the Prometheus rule data or the menu item should be hidden/disabled when no ruler rule is available.

title: Grafana list items are rendered without a React key
body: FilterViewResults maps over rules and computes a key for each item, but in the 'grafana' case it returns GrafanaRuleListItem without key={key}. The datasource and unknown branches do pass a key. Missing React keys can cause reconciliation warnings and incorrect reuse of component state across list items when results are appended or updated.

title: skipToken does not produce neutral Grafana abilities
body: useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities converts skipToken to undefined and still evaluates useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities. With an undefined rule, some abilities are not neutral: for example Duplicate can become supported and allowed based on global Grafana create permissions. This can make actions appear in contexts where there is no Grafana rule, such as non-Grafana Prometheus rules or missing promRule data. skipToken should return [false, false] for all requested actions.

title: Federated rules are no longer treated as immutable
body: useAllRulerRuleAbilities hard-codes isFederated = false, and the deprecated useAllAlertRuleAbilities wrapper no longer checks the original rule group with isFederatedRuleGroup. Previously, federated rules were considered immutable and update/delete/duplicate actions were hidden. After this change, federated rules may be shown as editable or deletable in the UI, which is a permission/contract regression unless federation support is intentionally being removed.

title: Delete is not rendered for Grafana Prometheus-only rules even when allowed
body: canDelete is computed from either ruler abilities or Grafana Prometheus abilities, but the Delete menu item is only rendered when canDelete && rulerRule. In the ruler-less alert list view rulerRule is undefined, so users with delete permission will never see Delete for Grafana rules. If deletion is intended to remain available after removing ruler fetches, this condition needs to support Prometheus-only rules.

title: Grafana rule key contains an extra closing brace
body: getGrafanaRuleKey returns a string ending with an extra '}' after rule.uid. The key is currently not used in the Grafana branch because the key prop is missing, but the malformed key will be confusing if reused later.

title: Clipboard copy promise has no rejection handler
body: navigator.clipboard?.writeText(text).then(...) does not handle promise rejection. If clipboard access is denied or fails, the app can produce an unhandled promise rejection and the user receives no feedback. A catch handler should be added.

title: Inline action arrays defeat memoization in ability hooks
body: AlertRuleMenu passes new array literals to useRulerRuleAbilities and useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities on every render. Those hooks memoize their result based on the actions array reference, so the mapped abilities are recomputed on every render for every row. Extracting the action list to a stable constant would avoid unnecessary work in large rule lists.

title: Sharded queries are interpolated twice
body: runShardSplitQuery applies template variables to each target before passing them to splitQueriesByStreamShard. That code later calls runSplitQuery, and runSplitQuery now unconditionally applies template variables again to request.targets. As a result, already-interpolated queries, including ones that have had shard selectors injected, are interpolated a second time. Template interpolation is not guaranteed to be idempotent: variable values that contain template syntax, ad-hoc filter placeholders, or other variable-like text can be expanded or modified again, producing incorrect LogQL queries or duplicated filters. It also adds unnecessary work for every shard/time-split subrequest.

title: Empty queries produced by interpolation are not filtered
body: runSplitQuery filters targets on query.expr before calling applyTemplateVariables, but it does not filter again after interpolation. If a raw expression is a non-empty variable such as `$selector` and interpolation resolves it to an empty string, the target remains in the query list and can be grouped and sent to Loki as an empty expression. This can create unnecessary or failing subrequests. The mapped queries should be filtered again after interpolation.

title: Step-splitting test uses the wrong request object and mutates shared state
body: The test creates `req` as a shallow copy of `request`, sets `req.targets[0].step = '10s'`, but then calls `runSplitQuery(datasource, request)` instead of `runSplitQuery(datasource, req)`. It only passes because the shallow copy shares the same targets array/object, so the mutation leaks into the shared outer `request`. This makes the test order-dependent and can affect later tests. It should use the intended request object and avoid mutating shared test state.

title: Sharded queries are interpolated twice
body: runSplitQuery now maps every target through datasource.applyTemplateVariables. runShardSplitQuery already interpolates the same targets at public/app/plugins/datasource/loki/shardQuerySplitting.ts:52 before calling runSplitQuery for each shard group at public/app/plugins/datasource/loki/shardQuerySplitting.ts:163. As a result, targets can be passed through applyTemplateVariables multiple times. Template replacement and ad-hoc filter injection are not guaranteed to be idempotent: filters may be appended twice and variable values containing '$' may be expanded again, producing incorrect or invalid LogQL. Consider adding an option to skip interpolation for already-interpolated subrequests or centralizing interpolation in one place.

title: Queries that interpolate to an empty expression are no longer removed
body: runShardSplitQuery filters query.expr before calling applyTemplateVariables, while the previous code interpolated first and then filtered empty expressions. If a query expression is a variable that resolves to an empty string, the target now survives interpolation with an empty expr and is passed into sharding/splitting. This can cause empty stream selectors, invalid shard queries, or unnecessary label-value lookups. runSplitQuery has the same ordering issue at public/app/plugins/datasource/loki/querySplitting.ts:298; filter again after interpolation.

title: runSplitQuery re-interpolates already interpolated shard-split queries
body: runSplitQuery now unconditionally applies datasource.applyTemplateVariables to every target. It is also called from shardQuerySplitting.ts after runShardSplitQuery has already applied template variables and after interpolateShardingSelector has rewritten the expression. This causes template replacement to run twice on the same query. Template replacement is not generally idempotent: dollar signs introduced by variable values or by the first interpolation can be treated as variables on the second pass, corrupting the LogQL expression or silently dropping text. It can also reapply variable/filter substitution multiple times. Consider an internal non-interpolating split path or a flag to skip interpolation when targets are already interpolated.

title: $__range splitting guard is evaluated after interpolation
body: querySupportsSplitting relies on isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr), and the comment says queries using $__range must not be split. Because the targets are now passed through applyTemplateVariables before this check, any $__range or ${__range} macro that is replaced will no longer be present in expr, so the query will be classified as splittable. This can split queries that were explicitly meant to be excluded and produce incorrect range vectors or results. The exclusion should be based on the raw query expression, or range macros must be preserved until after the check.

title: Queries that interpolate to empty are no longer filtered out
body: runShardSplitQuery filters query.expr before calling applyTemplateVariables, whereas the previous implementation interpolated first and then filtered. If a target has an expression such as a template variable that resolves to an empty string, it now passes the filter, is grouped/sharded, and can be sent to Loki as an empty query. The same missing post-interpolation filter exists in querySplitting.ts. Filter hidden/empty queries again after interpolation.

title: Missing interpolation edge-case tests for $__range and empty results
body: The new interpolation tests only cover $__auto and $step. They do not verify that queries containing $__range remain excluded from splitting after interpolation, nor that queries whose expression interpolates to an empty string are skipped. These are the edge cases made more fragile by moving interpolation to the start of the splitting pipeline.

title: Trace ID is no longer added to plugin request logs
body: The previous LoggerMiddleware explicitly appended a traceID field from tracing.TraceIDFromContext to plugin request logs. After this refactor, LoggerMiddleware relies on contextual attributes added by ContextualLoggerMiddleware, but instrumentContext only adds endpoint, pluginId, datasource name/UID, and user login. As a result, plugin request logs can lose trace correlation unless some other middleware independently injects the trace ID.

title: TestLogger.FromContext returns a throwaway logger
body: TestLogger.FromContext returns a brand-new TestLogger instead of the receiver or a child logger that shares the same recorded Logs. Since LoggerMiddleware now emits logs via logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...), tests using this fake will record those messages on an unreachable object, making it impossible to assert logging behavior and allowing regressions to pass silently.

title: No tests cover the new contextual logging middleware
body: This PR moves request-scoped logging context into a new middleware and changes LoggerMiddleware to depend on that context, but the only test change is renaming the metrics middleware test. There is no coverage verifying that ContextualLoggerMiddleware injects the expected fields or that LoggerMiddleware emits them, so regressions in logging fields are likely to be missed.

title: Metrics middleware mutates a shared instance when wrapping next
body: NewMetricsMiddleware creates one MetricsMiddleware and the returned middleware function assigns imw.next = next each time it is applied. If the same ClientMiddleware is applied more than once, all returned clients share the same MetricsMiddleware and the last assignment overwrites the next handler. This can route requests through the wrong chain and creates a potential data race. A new middleware instance should be created for each next client.

title: Adding FromContext to Logger is a breaking interface change
body: The exported Logger interface now requires FromContext. Any external implementation of this interface will fail to compile after this change. Only the in-repo fake is updated, so if this package is consumed outside the repository this is an API break that should be called out or handled compatibly.

title: Plugin request logs lose the traceID field
body: The previous LoggerMiddleware explicitly appended traceID from the tracing context to the plugin request log entry. This change removes that explicit field and relies on Logger.FromContext, but the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware only adds endpoint, pluginId, datasource, and user fields. Unless the underlying logging infrastructure independently injects trace IDs, plugin backend request logs will no longer include traceID, reducing trace/log correlation.

title: Metrics middleware reuses a single mutable wrapper across middleware applications
body: NewMetricsMiddleware creates one MetricsMiddleware instance and the returned middleware assigns imw.next = next each time it is applied. Middleware factories should return a new wrapper per next while sharing the registered Prometheus collectors. If this middleware is applied more than once, the chains share and overwrite next, which can cause incorrect request routing or data races.

title: TestLogger.FromContext discards logs and contextual fields
body: TestLogger.FromContext returns a brand-new TestLogger instead of the receiver or a child logger that records into the same captured log fields. Since LoggerMiddleware now emits logs through logger.FromContext(ctx), tests using TestLogger cannot observe those log messages or their contextual key/value pairs.

title: No tests for the new contextual logger middleware or FromContext logging
body: The PR introduces ContextualLoggerMiddleware and changes LoggerMiddleware to rely on Logger.FromContext, but the only changed test is the renamed metrics middleware test. There is no coverage verifying that the request context is enriched with the expected attributes or that LoggerMiddleware emits those attributes, so regressions in middleware ordering or missing fields would not be detected.

title: Adding FromContext to the exported Logger interface is a breaking change
body: The exported log.Logger interface now requires FromContext(context.Context) Logger. Any implementation of this interface outside this package will fail to compile after this change. If this interface is considered a public or stable contract, this needs a compatibility plan or explicit release note.

title: Plugin request logs no longer include traceID
body: The previous LoggerMiddleware explicitly appended `traceID` from `tracing.TraceIDFromContext` to the log parameters. This change removes that field, and the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware only adds endpoint, plugin ID, data source, and user fields. Unless an earlier middleware independently injects traceID into the contextual logger, plugin request log lines will no longer contain traceID, weakening trace correlation.

title: TestLogger.FromContext discards logs and context
body: TestLogger.FromContext returns a brand-new TestLogger instead of a logger that shares the receiver's recorded log state or carries contextual attributes. Because LoggerMiddleware now logs via `logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...)`, tests injecting TestLogger will not observe emitted log records on the original fake, and contextual fields added by ContextualLoggerMiddleware cannot be verified. The fake should return a child/logger that records into the same state or preserves context.

title: MetricsMiddleware is a shared mutable middleware instance
body: NewMetricsMiddleware creates one *MetricsMiddleware and the returned middleware function mutates `imw.next` each time it is applied, returning the same instance. If the middleware value is used to build more than one client chain, or applied concurrently, the `next` field can be overwritten or raced, causing requests from one chain to be dispatched to another chain's next client. Middleware factories should construct a new wrapper per `next` or avoid mutable shared state.

title: No tests for new contextual logger middleware
body: The PR introduces ContextualLoggerMiddleware and changes LoggerMiddleware to rely on `FromContext`, but the only changed test is a rename of the metrics middleware test. There are no tests verifying that QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, and CollectMetrics contexts are enriched with endpoint/plugin/data source/user attributes, or that stream endpoints are intentionally excluded. Without such tests, future changes can silently drop contextual log fields.

title: Failed device tagging is cached, allowing anonymous device limit bypass
body: In tagDeviceUI, the local cache entry for a device ID is written before the database upsert. If CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, the entry is not removed. Anonymous.Authenticate fails the first request, but a retry with the same X-Grafana-Device-Id header gets a cache hit, TagDevice returns nil, and the request is authenticated even though the device was not stored and the configured limit should block it. The same caching of failed operations also hides transient database errors for the cache TTL.

title: Client-controlled device ID can exhaust the anonymous device limit
body: The anonymous device identifier is supplied by the client in the X-Grafana-Device-Id header. With device_limit enabled, unauthenticated callers can create arbitrary unique device IDs until the configured number of active devices is reached. Those attacker-created records remain active for the 30-day window, after which new legitimate devices receive ErrDeviceLimitReached and cannot authenticate, causing a denial of service for new anonymous users.

title: Device-limit check and insert are not atomic
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice first runs CountDevices and then, if the count is below the limit, executes the upsert as a separate operation. There is no transaction, row lock, or conditional insert, so concurrent new devices can all pass the count check and insert. The active device count can therefore exceed device_limit under normal concurrent traffic.

title: Device limit adds synchronous database work to anonymous authentication
body: The PR changes anonymous device tagging from an asynchronous goroutine to a synchronous step in Authenticate. When device_limit is enabled, each uncached device performs a COUNT over anon_device and an upsert before the request can proceed. For high-traffic anonymous instances, especially if updated_at is not efficiently indexed, this can add significant latency and database load to anonymous authentication.

title: Frontend type for anonymousDeviceLimit does not match backend JSON
body: GrafanaConfig declares anonymousDeviceLimit as number | undefined, but the Go FrontendSettingsDTO uses a non-pointer int64 without omitempty, so the backend always sends a number, with 0 meaning unlimited. Frontend code that checks for undefined to determine whether a limit is configured will not work; the contract should either use a pointer/omitempty or document 0 as unlimited.

title: Negative device_limit silently disables the limit
body: device_limit is read with MustInt64(0) and enforcement only occurs when the value is greater than zero. A negative configuration value is accepted and silently treated as unlimited, which can hide operator mistakes. The setting should be validated as non-negative.

title: No tests cover device-limit failures in AnonDeviceService
body: The tests cover successful tagging and a store-level limit, but do not exercise AnonDeviceService.tagDeviceUI when CreateOrUpdateDevice fails. In particular there is no test that a failed device-limit attempt is not cached, which is the behavior that allows the limit bypass in impl.go.

title: Device limit can deny service to anonymous users and be exhausted by clients
body: Authenticate fails when TagDevice returns anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached. The device ID comes from the client-supplied X-Grafana-Device-Id header, so a client can send many unique device IDs until the configured limit is reached; afterwards anonymous requests from new device IDs can be rejected. This turns a tracking/storage limit into an anonymous-access outage. If the limit is meant to cap stored devices, new devices should probably be left untracked but still authenticated; if it is meant to cap access, it needs server-side identity and abuse protection.

title: Local cache is populated before device persistence and not rolled back on error
body: tagDeviceUI inserts the device key into localCache before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice. If CreateOrUpdateDevice fails, for example with ErrDeviceLimitReached or a transient database error, the key remains cached for 29 minutes. Subsequent requests for the same device then return nil from the cache, suppressing the original error and treating the device as tagged although no row was written. In the limit case this can make the first request fail but later retries succeed, producing inconsistent enforcement and incorrect device tracking.

title: Limit check and insert are not atomic
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice counts active devices and, if below the limit, performs a separate upsert. Under concurrent requests, multiple new device IDs can observe count < deviceLimit and then all insert, exceeding the configured limit. If the limit is intended to be hard, enforcement needs an atomic conditional insert, transaction, or database constraint.

title: Anonymous authentication now blocks on device-tag database work
body: TagDevice was previously invoked asynchronously with its own timeout, but Authenticate now performs it synchronously on the request context. For uncached devices this executes a COUNT query and an upsert before the anonymous identity is returned, adding database latency to anonymous page loads and API calls and making anonymous authentication more sensitive to database slowness.

title: Device limit is bypassed when the device header is omitted
body: TagDevice returns nil immediately if X-Grafana-Device-Id is absent, and Anonymous.Authenticate then succeeds. Because the header is optional and client-controlled, a client can avoid the device-limit check entirely by not sending it. If the limit is intended to restrict anonymous devices or sessions, absence of the header should not silently bypass the limit.

title: No-limit value is serialized as 0 while frontend expects undefined
body: FrontendSettingsDTO.AnonymousDeviceLimit is a non-pointer int64, so the frontend settings JSON always contains anonymousDeviceLimit: 0 when no limit is configured. The TypeScript type is number | undefined and the runtime default is undefined. Frontend code that distinguishes undefined from 0 may interpret no limit as an explicit zero limit. Use a pointer/omitempty or make the frontend contract explicit that 0 means unlimited.

title: Negative device_limit is silently treated as unlimited
body: AnonymousDeviceLimit is read with MustInt64(0) and the store only enforces values greater than zero. A negative configuration value, likely a typo, is accepted and disables the limit instead of failing validation or being clamped to zero.

title: Device-limit tests do not cover updating an existing device at the limit
body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only verifies that a second new device is rejected when limit=1. It does not verify that an existing active device can still be updated after the limit is reached, nor that stale devices behave as intended. These are the main enforcement paths and should be covered.

title: Failed device-limit writes are cached, allowing the limit to be bypassed
body: tagDeviceUI stores the device ID in localCache before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice. If the store returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, TagDevice propagates the error and the first anonymous authentication fails, but the cache entry remains. For the cache TTL (29 minutes), subsequent requests with the same device ID return nil from tagDeviceUI without checking the limit or persisting the device, so Anonymous.Authenticate succeeds. This allows a device rejected by the limit to access anonymously and makes the limit ineffective. Cache only after successful persistence or delete the cache entry on error.

title: Device limit check and insert are not atomic
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice performs a separate COUNT(*) to check the active-device limit and then runs the upsert in another session without a transaction or lock. Concurrent requests from distinct new device IDs can both observe count < device_limit and then insert, exceeding the configured limit. If device_limit is intended as a hard bound, enforce it atomically (for example with a conditional insert/update, transactional locking, or a database constraint/trigger).

title: COUNT query is executed in the authentication path when the limit is enabled
body: When device_limit is greater than zero, every anonymous request that misses the local cache runs COUNT(*) over anon_device during authentication before upserting. On instances with many anonymous devices, this can add latency and database load. Consider a cheaper enforcement strategy, such as an approximate cached counter or a conditional write that avoids a separate count query.

title: No tests cover device-limit failures through TagDevice/authentication
body: The added store test checks that a second device is rejected when the limit is 1, but there is no service-level test for TagDevice with a configured AnonymousDeviceLimit. In particular, nothing verifies that a limit-reached error blocks anonymous authentication and that a failed write is not cached, which is the interaction that allows the limit to be bypassed. Add integration tests with a non-zero device limit and repeated requests for the same device ID.

title: Cleanup interval changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute
body: The background cleanup loop now runs all cleanup jobs every minute instead of every 10 minutes. This is a global behavior change that affects more than annotation cleanup and can substantially increase DB and filesystem load; it looks accidental or at least undocumented.

title: Error-level logging of every cleanup batch and full ID list
body: CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags log at Error level for every successful batch, include the full IDs slice, and log err=nil. With small batch sizes, large backlogs, or the 1-minute cleanup ticker, this can flood logs, create very long log lines, and trigger error-based alerts. These should be Debug/Trace and should not log full ID lists.

title: Batch loop may stop early if selected rows are deleted concurrently
body: The fetch-then-delete implementation treats a DELETE that affects zero rows as completion. If another process deletes all IDs selected in a batch between fetchIDs and deleteByIDs, affected will be 0 even though more eligible rows remain, so cleanup stops for this cycle. Consider looping until fetchIDs returns no IDs.

title: SQLite IN list is built with O(n^2) string concatenation
body: When avoiding SQLite parameter limits, the code builds the IN clause by repeatedly calling fmt.Sprintf with the previous string. For large batch sizes this causes quadratic allocations/copying and can slow cleanup; a strings.Builder or joined list would be safer.

title: Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute without explanation
body: This change makes the entire background cleanup loop run every minute instead of every 10 minutes. It affects all cleanup jobs, not just annotation cleanup, and is not described in the PR. This can significantly increase database and filesystem load, and if a cleanup pass takes longer than one minute, queued ticks can cause passes to run back-to-back. Unless this is intentional, it should be reverted or made configurable.

title: Normal cleanup paths log at Error level and dump full ID lists
body: The new cleanup code calls Error-level logging on every successful batch, including batches that find zero rows, and includes the full ids slice in the log entry. Because batch sizes can be large, this can produce very large log lines and constant error-level noise during normal operation. These logs should be Debug or Info, and should likely log only counts or truncated IDs. Similar logging occurs later in the same file for count-based annotation cleanup and tag cleanup.

title: SQLite inline ID list is built with repeated Sprintf, causing O(n^2) copying
body: In the SQLite branch, the IN-list is constructed by repeatedly appending to the previous string with fmt.Sprintf. For large batches this repeatedly copies a growing string and becomes O(n^2) in the number of IDs. With batch sizes in the tens of thousands, this can cause noticeable CPU and memory overhead. Use strings.Builder or strings.Join instead.

title: Only SQLite is protected against parameter limits
body: For non-SQLite databases, deleteByIDs builds a single DELETE ... WHERE id IN clause with one placeholder per ID. The code special-cases SQLite's parameter limit but does not chunk or otherwise protect other databases from driver or database placeholder limits. If AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is configured very large, the generated statement may exceed those limits and fail. Consider chunking deletes by a safe limit for all supported databases or validating the batch size.

title: Fetch-then-delete can delete annotations that are no longer excess for max-count cleanup
body: The max-count cleanup first selects IDs to delete and then deletes them in a separate statement. If newer annotations are deleted between the SELECT and DELETE, the selected older IDs may move inside the retained MaxCount set, so the job can delete annotations that would now be among the newest retained rows. If this best-effort behavior is intentional, it should be documented; otherwise the deletion needs a stronger consistency check.

title: Cleanup interval changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute
body: The background cleanup ticker is reduced from time.Minute*10 to time.Minute*1. This makes every cleanup job (temp files, snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, invites, short URLs, query history) run ten times more frequently. The PR description only discusses the annotation deletion strategy, so this looks like a debugging/test leftover and can add significant database and filesystem load in production.

title: Normal cleanup progress is logged at Error level with full ID lists
body: CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags log at Error level on every batch (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579), including the full ids slice and a nil err. In normal operation this produces error-level log spam and can create very large log lines when batch sizes are large, which may trigger alerting or log-pipeline pressure. These should be Debug/Info and should not log entire ID lists.

title: Batch loop can exit early when fetched IDs were deleted concurrently
body: untilDoneOrCancelled stops when the callback returns affected == 0. After splitting SELECT and DELETE, a batch can fetch a non-empty set of IDs and then deleteByIDs can return 0 because another process deleted those rows between the two statements. More rows may still satisfy the cleanup condition, but the loop exits and cleanup is postponed. Completion should be based on whether the fetch returned an empty batch, or on fetched count, not solely on rows affected.

title: Single DELETE IN clause can exceed non-SQLite parameter limits
body: deleteByIDs builds one DELETE with one placeholder per fetched ID and only special-cases SQLite's 999 parameter limit. AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is configurable, so on databases such as PostgreSQL/MySQL (around 65535 parameters) or MSSQL (around 2100 parameters) a large batch can generate too many bind parameters and make cleanup fail. The delete should be chunked or dialect parameter limits should be handled.

title: SQLite inline ID list is built with quadratic string concatenation
body: For SQLite, deleteByIDs builds the IN-list by repeatedly formatting the growing string with fmt.Sprintf. Each iteration copies the entire existing string, making the operation O(n^2) in the batch size. With the newly tested batch size of 32767, or larger configured values, this can cause unnecessary CPU and memory usage during cleanup. Use strings.Builder or strings.Join.

title: Asynchronous legacy writes use the request context and will be canceled when the request finishes
body: Create derives the background legacy-write context from the incoming request context using context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...). The same pattern is used in Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection. When the HTTP handler returns, the request context is canceled, so the child context is also canceled even though the legacy write is intended to continue asynchronously. This can abort legacy writes immediately after the API response is sent, defeating mode 3's dual-write safety behavior and causing divergence between unified storage and legacy storage. Use a detached context such as context.WithoutCancel(ctx), or a dedicated background context that preserves values but not cancellation.

title: Fire-and-forget legacy writes are unordered and untracked
body: Each write path launches an independent goroutine to create, update, delete, or delete-collection in legacy storage. There is no ordering, queue, mutex, wait group, or lifecycle tracking. Concurrent operations on the same object may complete in legacy storage in a different order than they were applied to unified storage, for example a delete arriving before a create or an old update arriving after a newer update. This can leave legacy storage inconsistent with unified storage. Destroy may also run while these goroutines are still active. If legacy writes are meant to be a safe fallback, they should be serialized per object or managed by a tracked background worker.

title: Background legacy-write goroutines do not recover from panics
body: The asynchronous legacy write paths use bare goroutines without panic recovery. Because legacy writes are secondary and best-effort in mode 3, a panic in legacy storage code or serialization should not crash the whole API server process. Add a deferred recover in these goroutines and log/metric the failure.

title: Legacy update is performed with the original UpdatedObjectInfo instead of the object written to unified storage
body: After Storage.Update succeeds, the code asynchronously calls Legacy.Update with the same rest.UpdatedObjectInfo. Legacy.Update will re-evaluate UpdatedObject against the legacy store's current object, which may produce a different result than the update that was applied in unified storage, especially for patches, defaults, generated fields, or resourceVersion handling. Mode 3 treats unified storage as the source of truth, so legacy should receive the final object returned by Storage.Update. The previous implementation wrapped the updated object for the legacy call; removing that wrapper creates a real risk of silent divergence between unified storage and legacy storage.

title: Legacy create uses the original request object instead of the created object
body: After Storage.Create succeeds, the asynchronous Legacy.Create call is made with the original obj rather than the created object returned by unified storage. If unified storage assigns a name, UID, creation timestamp, defaults, or otherwise changes the object, legacy storage may create a different object identity or fail validation. To mirror unified storage, the legacy create should use the created object's identity and spec, clearing any fields that are invalid on create such as resourceVersion if needed.

title: Storage Delete errors, including NotFound, prevent legacy cleanup
body: Delete returns immediately when Storage.Delete fails, so Legacy.Delete is never attempted. The previous implementation treated NotFound specially and still attempted deletion from legacy storage. If an object exists only in legacy storage, or remains there after unified storage no longer has it, this change can leave stale legacy data that may reappear if the dual-writer mode changes. The same issue exists for DeleteCollection, where any storage error skips legacy cleanup. At minimum, NotFound from unified storage should still trigger legacy deletion.

title: Delete storage duration metric uses object name as kind label
body: In Delete, the success path records storage duration with name as the third argument: d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage). Other methods pass options.Kind for that label. This puts the resource name into the kind metric label, producing incorrect metrics and potentially high-cardinality series, breaking dashboards or alerts that aggregate by kind. It should pass options.Kind.

title: Storage create failures are recorded as legacy duration
body: When Storage.Create fails, the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage). This misattributes a unified-storage failure and latency to legacy storage. Operators relying on dual-writer metrics will see false legacy errors and missing storage errors. Use recordStorageDuration for the storage operation.

title: Storage update failures are recorded as legacy duration
body: When Storage.Update fails, the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage). This misattributes a unified-storage failure and latency to legacy storage. Use recordStorageDuration for the storage operation so mode 3 metrics correctly distinguish unified storage failures from legacy failures.

title: Legacy DeleteCollection failure is recorded as storage duration
body: In the asynchronous DeleteCollection goroutine, the error from d.Legacy.DeleteCollection is recorded with d.recordStorageDuration. This misattributes legacy latency and errors to unified storage. Use recordLegacyDuration for the legacy operation.

title: Asynchronous legacy write failures are not logged
body: In Create, errors from Legacy.Create are only reflected in a metric. The same applies to the asynchronous legacy operations in Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection. Since mode 3 writes to legacy storage as a safety measure, silent failures make it difficult to diagnose divergence. Log the error with the object kind, name or identifier, and operation before recording the metric.

title: Delete stores the base logger in the context instead of the enriched logger
body: Delete creates log := d.Log.WithValues(...), but then sets ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log), discarding the added values for downstream logging. Any code that uses klog.FromContext(ctx) inside Storage.Delete or Legacy.Delete will miss the name, kind, and method fields. It should use ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, log).

title: Mode 3 unit tests do not wait for or verify asynchronous legacy writes
body: TestMode3_Create calls dw.Create and returns immediately, but the legacy create happens in a goroutine. The tests do not synchronize with that goroutine, do not assert that legacy methods were actually called, and use a shared mock for both legacy and unified storage, so calls to either store are indistinguishable. As a result, the tests can pass even if asynchronous legacy writes are skipped, canceled, reordered, or otherwise broken. Similar gaps exist for Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection. Add synchronization and explicit assertions that legacy storage receives the expected calls.

title: Mode 3 integration test assumes immediate legacy consistency despite asynchronous legacy writes
body: The added mode 3 scenarios run doPlaylistTests, which performs create/update/delete operations through the Kubernetes API and then immediately checks the legacy playlist API. In mode 3, legacy writes are asynchronous, so the legacy store may not yet reflect the change. This makes the integration test flaky and also masks eventual-consistency behavior. The test should poll or otherwise wait for legacy convergence, or mode 3 tests should use a synchronous/test-only legacy write path.

title: Async legacy writes inherit the request context and will be canceled when the request returns
body: In Create, the goroutine derives a 10-second context from the incoming request context with context.WithTimeoutCause. Because Create returns immediately, the HTTP request context is canceled when the request completes, canceling the child context and likely abortting Legacy.Create. The same pattern is used in Delete (line 110), Update (line 135), and DeleteCollection (line 163). This defeats the purpose of the asynchronous legacy safety write. Use a detached context, such as context.WithoutCancel(ctx) or a background context carrying only needed values, plus the timeout.

title: Fire-and-forget legacy writes are not ordered
body: All write operations start an independent goroutine to write to legacy and do not sequence those writes. Rapid create/update/delete requests for the same object can cause legacy operations to run out of order, for example update before create, delete before create, or create after delete. This can leave the legacy store inconsistent even though unified storage is correct. Since mode 3 is intended to keep legacy as a safe fallback, these writes need per-resource ordering or another synchronization mechanism.

title: Async legacy create may use the same runtime.Object that is returned to the client
body: Create launches Legacy.Create in a goroutine with the same obj that was passed to Storage.Create. If Storage.Create mutates obj or returns it as created, the API server may serialize the returned object concurrently while the goroutine reads or mutates the same runtime.Object in Legacy.Create. runtime.Object instances are not generally safe for concurrent use. Pass a deep copy to the asynchronous legacy write.

title: Legacy update is recomputed from objInfo instead of mirroring the unified-storage result
body: In Update, after Storage.Update succeeds, the async Legacy.Update is called with the original rest.UpdatedObjectInfo. Legacy.Update will typically fetch the current legacy object and call UpdatedObject again, so the legacy object may be computed from divergent legacy state or from a request-scoped or non-idempotent UpdatedObjectInfo. The previous implementation precomputed the updated object and passed the unified result to legacy. The new code can write a different object to legacy than the one stored in unified storage. Pass an UpdatedObjectInfo that returns the object returned by Storage.Update, preferably a deep copy.

title: Legacy delete is skipped when unified delete returns NotFound
body: Delete returns immediately for any Storage.Delete error, including NotFound. The previous mode 3 behavior tolerated NotFound from unified storage and still attempted Legacy.Delete, allowing cleanup of stale legacy objects. With this change, an object that exists only in legacy will not be removed, leaving orphaned data in the legacy store even though the API returns NotFound.

title: Storage failures are recorded as legacy duration metrics
body: In Create, when Storage.Create fails, the code calls recordLegacyDuration with the storage start time. The same happens in Update at line 129. This attributes unified-storage latency and errors to the legacy store and fails to record a storage duration for the failed storage operation. Metrics and alerts for legacy and storage error rates will be incorrect.

title: Delete success metric uses the object name as the kind label
body: In Delete, the successful storage duration is recorded with name as the third argument, while other calls use the kind. If that metric argument is the kind label, this emits a per-resource-name label value. That breaks aggregation and can create high-cardinality metrics. Use the resource kind, not the object name.

title: DeleteCollection records legacy async duration as a storage metric
body: In DeleteCollection's goroutine, after Legacy.DeleteCollection completes, the code calls recordStorageDuration. This records the legacy store's async duration and error state as if it were unified storage. Legacy failures will be invisible as legacy failures and storage metrics will be double-counted or incorrectly marked failed. This should call recordLegacyDuration.

title: Delete puts the wrong logger into the context
body: Delete builds log with name, kind, and method values, but then sets the context to klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log) instead of klog.NewContext(ctx, log). As a result, downstream logging from Storage.Delete and Legacy.Delete loses the request-specific fields, making debugging harder.

title: Asynchronous legacy write failures are not logged
body: The goroutines for Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection only record a metric when the legacy operation fails; they do not log the error or identify the affected object. Since the API returns success to the client even if the legacy safety write fails, operators have little information to detect or diagnose divergence. Add error logging for asynchronous legacy failures.

title: Destroy does not wait for in-flight asynchronous legacy writes
body: DualWriterMode3.Destroy destroys both Storage and Legacy immediately, but write methods launch untracked goroutines that may still be using Legacy. On shutdown or mode change, those goroutines may fail or panic because the underlying storage has been closed. Track pending asynchronous writes and wait or cancel them during Destroy.

title: Mode 3 unit tests do not synchronize or verify asynchronous legacy writes
body: TestMode3_Delete calls dw.Delete, which launches a goroutine to call Legacy.Delete, but the test neither sets a mock expectation for Legacy.Delete nor waits or asserts that it happened. DeleteCollection has the same issue, and Create/Update tests set legacy expectations but return without waiting or asserting that the asynchronous calls occurred. This makes the tests racy: they may pass before the goroutine runs, or an unexpected mock call may panic later. They also do not actually verify the mode 3 asynchronous legacy-write behavior.

title: Mode 3 integration test races with asynchronous legacy writes
body: The added mode 3 subtest runs doPlaylistTests, which creates, updates, and deletes objects through the k8s API and then immediately checks the legacy /api/playlists endpoints. In mode 3, writes to legacy are asynchronous fire-and-forget goroutines, so the legacy endpoints may not yet reflect the change. Without polling or waiting, the integration test is flaky and can pass or fail depending on goroutine scheduling.

title: Async legacy writes use the request context and will be canceled when the request finishes
body: DualWriterMode3.Create starts a goroutine to write to legacy storage and derives its context from the incoming request context via context.WithTimeoutCause. When the API request handler returns, the request context is canceled, which cancels the async legacy write. The same pattern exists in Delete (line 110), Update (line 135), and DeleteCollection (line 163). Since mode 3 is explicitly asynchronous, the legacy operation should use a detached context, for example context.WithoutCancel plus a timeout, or a background context with copied logger/values; otherwise legacy writes may be aborted before completion.

title: Asynchronous legacy writes can execute out of order
body: Each mutating operation spawns an independent goroutine for the legacy write with no sequencing, completion tracking, retry, or backpressure. A client can issue update or delete immediately after create; the legacy update/delete may execute before the legacy create, fail, or a delayed legacy create may recreate an object after a delete. This makes the legacy store inconsistent and can resurrect deleted objects despite mode 3 being intended as a safe dual-write fallback. A per-resource serialized queue or other ordering guarantee is needed.

title: Legacy update re-evaluates the update instead of writing the unified storage result
body: In Update, after Storage.Update succeeds, the goroutine calls Legacy.Update with the original rest.UpdatedObjectInfo. Legacy.Update will retrieve the legacy object's current state and invoke objInfo.UpdatedObject against that state. For patch-style updates, or if the legacy store is behind, this can produce a different result than the unified update or fail. The previous implementation wrapped the object returned by the unified update so legacy received the exact final object. Passing the original objInfo risks inconsistent legacy data and unsafe use of request-scoped update info after the request completes.

title: Legacy object is not deleted when unified delete returns NotFound
body: Mode3.Delete returns immediately if Storage.Delete returns any error, including NotFound, so it never attempts Legacy.Delete. If an object exists only in legacy storage because of earlier async failure, mode transition, or legacy-only residue, deleting it through the API will leave the legacy object behind. The prior behavior still attempted legacy deletion when unified deletion returned NotFound.

title: Async legacy create uses the original object without a deep copy
body: The Create goroutine passes the same runtime.Object to Legacy.Create that was passed to Storage.Create and may be the same object returned to the caller. Kubernetes storage strategies can mutate objects during create, and the response may be serialized while the legacy goroutine is running. This can cause data races or inconsistent legacy writes. Use runtime.DeepCopyObject, preferably copying the final object that should be written to legacy, before starting the goroutine.

title: Several duration metrics are recorded with the wrong store
body: Several metric calls record the wrong backend. In Create, a Storage.Create failure calls recordLegacyDuration at line 45. In Update, a Storage.Update failure calls recordLegacyDuration at line 129. In DeleteCollection, the async Legacy.DeleteCollection result calls recordStorageDuration at line 166. This mislabels storage failures as legacy failures and legacy latency as storage latency, breaking dashboards and alerts.

title: Delete storage duration metric uses object name as kind label
body: In Delete, the successful storage duration is recorded with the object name as the kind label: d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage). The metric expects the resource kind, not the object name. This creates inconsistent labels and can cause high-cardinality metric series for every deleted object name. Use options.Kind like the other methods.

title: Destroy can run while async legacy writes are still in flight
body: Destroy closes both Storage and Legacy immediately, but Mode 3 methods start detached goroutines that can continue to call Legacy for up to 10 seconds. If shutdown or Destroy happens while those goroutines are running, they may use closed storage, fail, or race. Track outstanding goroutines with a WaitGroup or worker pool and wait for them in Destroy.

title: Mode 3 integration test checks legacy APIs immediately after asynchronous writes
body: The added mode 3 integration subtest runs doPlaylistTests, which creates, updates, and deletes through the k8s API and immediately queries legacy endpoints. Because mode 3 writes to legacy asynchronously, those immediate legacy reads can race and make the test flaky. The test needs polling or eventual-consistency checks for mode 3, or it should not assert synchronous legacy visibility.

title: Mode3 tests race with asynchronous legacy writes and do not verify them
body: The Mode 3 unit tests invoke mutating methods that start goroutines but do not wait for or assert the legacy calls. In TestMode3_Delete at line 230 and TestMode3_DeleteCollection at line 284, no legacy mock expectation is configured, yet the async goroutine will call Legacy.Delete or Legacy.DeleteCollection; this can panic or produce nondeterministic results. Even where expectations exist, tests do not verify async behavior. Add synchronization and AssertExpectations.

title: Legacy async failures are only counted, not logged
body: Async legacy errors are only passed to metrics. For example, if Legacy.Create fails in the goroutine, there is no log entry; the old synchronous code logged such failures. Silent legacy-write failures make divergence and operational problems hard to detect. Log the error with object kind/name and cause.

title: Delete puts the base logger in context instead of the method-specific logger
body: Delete builds a logger with name, kind, and method values, but then sets the context logger to d.Log instead of that enriched log. Downstream code using klog.FromContext will not see the method-specific fields. Use ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, log).

title: Duplicate and unrelated go.work.sum entries added
body: The go.work.sum diff adds a duplicate checksum line for github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery@v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod and several unrelated dependency hashes. This appears accidental or should be split from the feature change. Regenerate go.work.sum to avoid unintended lockfile changes.

title: Missing cache re-check after acquiring write lock
body: GetWebAssets reads entryPointAssetsCache under RLock, releases the lock, and then acquires the write lock without re-checking whether another goroutine has already populated the cache. In non-development mode this allows multiple concurrent initial callers to all perform the manifest load sequentially. More importantly, a caller that observed a nil cache before another goroutine populated it can still run the load path and, if that load fails, the unconditional assignment at line 69 can overwrite a valid cached value with nil. Re-check entryPointAssetsCache after acquiring the write lock for non-dev mode, and/or avoid replacing a valid cache when the reload fails.

title: Global write lock held during manifest I/O
body: The write lock acquired at line 48 is held while reading assets-manifest.json from disk, and would also be held during the CDN HTTP request if that path were enabled. This serializes all GetWebAssets callers during I/O; in development mode, where the cache fast path is bypassed, every request can be forced through this locked file read. Consider performing I/O outside the lock, using singleflight, or only locking when publishing the cached result.

title: Cache is not re-checked after acquiring the write lock
body: GetWebAssets reads entryPointAssetsCache under RLock, then acquires the exclusive lock without re-checking the cache. In non-dev mode, goroutines that observed a nil cache before another goroutine populated it will all proceed to reload the manifest after acquiring the lock. If one of those delayed reloads fails, it assigns nil to entryPointAssetsCache and can replace a previously valid cached value, causing subsequent requests to fail or reload repeatedly. Re-check `cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil` immediately after Lock and return the existing cache.

title: Exclusive mutex is held during file/CDN I/O
body: The deferred entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Unlock() means the global exclusive lock is held while reading assets-manifest.json from disk and, if the CDN path is enabled, while making an HTTP request. This serializes all GetWebAssets callers during potentially slow I/O; a slow CDN or filesystem stall can block all web-asset responses. Load the assets outside the critical section, or use singleflight/once, and only update the cache under the lock.

title: Typo in error message
body: The error message says 'asssets-manifest' with three s's; it should be 'assets-manifest'.

title: Cache is not rechecked after acquiring the write lock
body: GetWebAssets reads entryPointAssetsCache under RLock, releases the lock, and then acquires the exclusive lock without checking the cache again. In non-dev mode, multiple goroutines that observed a nil cache can all proceed to load the manifest; a later goroutine can overwrite a cache that was already populated by an earlier goroutine. If that later load fails, it can replace a valid cached value with nil. Recheck entryPointAssetsCache after Lock and return the existing value before doing I/O in non-dev mode.

title: Failed loads overwrite the cache with nil
body: The function assigns entryPointAssetsCache = result unconditionally, even when err != nil and result is nil. Combined with the missing re-check after acquiring the write lock, a stale initialization that errors can clear a previously populated cache. Unless explicit invalidation is intended, the cache should only be updated when the load succeeds.

title: SQL command construction path is not disabled by feature gate
body: UnmarshalSQLCommand still creates a SQLCommand via NewSQLCommand without checking whether SQL expressions are disabled. In this PR the operation fails only because the new sql.DB stub returns 'not implemented' from TablesList/RunCommands.
