Consider not caching denials for resources that don't yet exist, or checking the permission cache/DB before the denial cache when the denial entry is close to expiry.

title: Every Check that misses the permission cache now hits the database
body: When cached permissions exist but do not grant access to the requested resource, the code falls through to `getIdentityPermissions` which queries the database. In a scenario where a user has many permissions cached but repeatedly requests access to resources they don't have (e.g., probing different dashboard UIDs), each unique resource will trigger a full DB permission query before the denial cache is populated. The denial cache mitigates repeated requests for the same resource, but the first request per resource always hits the DB. For high-cardinality workloads this could increase DB load significantly compared to the previous behavior where a cached permission set was authoritative.

title: List uses potentially stale cached permissions without DB fallback
body: The `List` method uses `getCachedIdentityPermissions` and, on a cache hit, returns the cached permission set directly without falling through to the database. In contrast, `Check` now falls through to the DB when the cached permissions don't grant access. This asymmetry means a newly created dashboard might pass a `Check` (via DB fallback) but not appear in a `List` response until the permission cache expires. If the UI relies on `List` to populate navigation or search results, users may not see their newly created resources even though `Check` would allow access.

title: Denial cache key construction is ambiguous and can produce collisions
body: userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates namespace, userUID, action, name, and parent using underscores as separators, but these components can themselves contain underscores. For example, userPermDenialCacheKey("org-1", "u1", "dashboards:read", "my_dash", "folder1") produces the same key as userPermDenialCacheKey("org-1", "u1", "dashboards:read", "my", "dash_folder1"). A denial cached for one resource would incorrectly deny access to a different resource. Consider using a separator that cannot appear in UIDs/names (e.g., a null byte or a structured encoding), or hashing the components individually.

title: Denial cache can block access to a resource immediately after it is created
body: The denial cache is checked first (line 117) and returns deny immediately if hit, without re-checking the database. If a user's request for a not-yet-existing resource is denied and that denial is cached (line 154), then the resource is created (granting the user permission), subsequent checks for up to shortCacheTTL (30 seconds) will still return deny from the stale denial cache entry. This partially undermines the PR's stated goal of letting creators access newly created dashboards/folders, particularly in UI flows that may pre-check permissions before creation completes.

title: Every denied request that misses the denial cache triggers a full DB permission query
body: When the permission cache is hit but does not contain the requested scope (i.e., the user has some permissions but not for this specific resource), the code falls through to getIdentityPermissions which queries the database. Previously the cached permission set was authoritative for both allow and deny. Now, every check for a resource not in the cached set hits the DB until the denial cache entry is written. In high-cardinality environments (many users checking many distinct resources they lack access to), this can significantly increase database load during the initial warm-up period before denial cache entries are populated.

title: permissionCacheUsage metric incremented as 'false' even when permission cache was hit but simply didn't allow
body: At line 137, s.metrics.permissionCacheUsage.WithLabelValues("false", ...) is incremented whenever the code falls through the cached-permission check, including the case where getCachedIdentityPermissions succeeded (err == nil) but checkPermission returned false. This conflates 'cache miss' with 'cache hit but denied', making it harder to distinguish actual cache effectiveness from the expected deny-after-hit path. The metric label 'false' suggests a cache miss, but it was actually a cache hit that simply didn't grant access.

title: Denial cache key is ambiguous due to underscore separator
body: The `userPermDenialCacheKey` function concatenates fields with underscores: `namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent`. Since resource UIDs (name, parent) can themselves contain underscores, different (name, parent) tuples can produce the same key. For example, name="a_b" with parent="" produces the same key as name="a" with parent="b". A denial cached for one resource would incorrectly deny access to a different resource. This can cause false authorization denials for users who should have access.

title: Denial cache key uses raw UserUID which may differ from resolved UID used in permission cache
body: The denial cache key at line 116 uses `checkReq.UserUID` (the raw value parsed from the subject, e.g. a numeric ID like "123"), while the permission cache in `getCachedIdentityPermissions` uses `userIdentifiers.UID` (the resolved UID string like "abc-def"). If the same user is referenced by numeric ID in one request and by UID string in another, the denial cache will not hit for the second request, reducing cache effectiveness. The denial should be cached using the resolved UID to be consistent with the permission cache key.

title: Denial cache test uses unrealistic permission cache value and doesn't prove precedence over an allow
body: The test 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' sets `map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}` in the permission cache. In production, `getScopeMap` only ever stores `true` values, so a `false` value is never present. The comment says 'Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked' but a `false` value would not grant access anyway (`checkPermission` checks `scopeMap[...]` which evaluates to false). To properly test that the denial cache takes precedence over a granting permission cache entry, the test should set `map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": true}` and verify the response is still denied.

title: Pause button will never render in list view because it requires rulerRule to be defined
body: The pause menu item rendering condition on line 123 requires `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)` to be true. When this component is used from the alert list view (the stated goal of this PR), `rulerRule` is undefined because ruler API calls have been removed. Even though `canPause` may be true via the `grafanaPauseSupported && grafanaPauseAllowed` path, the additional guard `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)` will always be false when `rulerRule` is undefined, so the pause button will never appear in the list view.

title: Delete button will never render in list view because it requires rulerRule to be truthy
body: The delete menu item on line 165 is guarded by `canDelete && rulerRule`. When coming from the alert list view (where ruler API calls have been removed), `rulerRule` will be undefined, so the delete button will never render even if the user has delete permissions determined via the `grafanaDeleteSupported && grafanaDeleteAllowed` path. This makes the delete action inaccessible from the list view.

title: Silence drawer will not open when rulerRule is undefined (list view scenario)
body: The SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer is conditionally rendered with `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) && showSilenceDrawer`. When `rule` (the RulerRuleDTO) is undefined—which is the case in the list view where ruler calls are removed—clicking 'Silence notifications' in the menu will set `showSilenceDrawer` to true but the drawer will never render because the type guard fails. The user clicks the button and nothing visible happens.

title: Extra closing brace in template literal produces incorrect key
body: The function `getGrafanaRuleKey` returns `grafana-${namespace.uid}-${groupName}-${rule.uid}}` — note the trailing double `}}`. The extra closing brace becomes part of the key string, producing keys like `grafana-abc-group1-uid1}` instead of `grafana-abc-group1-uid1`. While this won't cause a crash, it produces incorrect key values and could cause issues if these keys are used for deduplication or comparison elsewhere.

title: Missing key prop on GrafanaRuleListItem in list rendering
body: In the `rules.map()` callback, the `key` variable is destructured from `ruleWithOrigin` on line 152, but it is not passed as a `key` prop to `<GrafanaRuleListItem>` on line 157. The `DataSourceRuleLoader` on line 165 correctly receives `key={key}`, but the Grafana case does not. React will fall back to using index-based reconciliation, which can cause rendering bugs when the list order changes or items are added/removed.

title: Federated rule group check removed, causing regression for Mimir federated rules
body: In `useAllRulerRuleAbilities`, `isFederated` is now hardcoded to `false` with a TODO comment. Previously, `useAllAlertRuleAbilities` (which now delegates to this function) checked `isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)`. This means federated rule groups in Mimir/Cloud data sources will no longer be treated as immutable—users may see Edit/Delete buttons for federated rules that should be protected. The `RuleGroupIdentifierV2` type doesn't carry federation information, so this data is lost in the refactoring.

title: Leftover development comment '// duplicate' in production code
body: Line 289 has a trailing comment `// duplicate` on the `useIsGrafanaPromRuleEditable` call that appears to be a leftover development note. It should be removed before merging.

title: Pause menu item will never render in list view because rulerRule is undefined
body: The condition `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)` will always be false when `rulerRule` is undefined, which is the case when AlertRuleMenu is used from the alert list view (the primary motivation of this PR). Even though `canPause` may be true via the grafana prom rule abilities path, the menu item is gated on `rulerRule` being a valid Grafana ruler rule. Users will see no Pause option in the list view despite having permission.

title: Delete menu item will never render in list view because rulerRule is undefined
body: The condition `canDelete && rulerRule` requires `rulerRule` to be truthy. In the list view (the primary use case this PR targets), `rulerRule` is undefined, so the Delete menu item will never appear even when the user has delete permissions via the grafana prom rule abilities. The `handleDelete` callback also expects a `RulerRuleDTO` argument, so this needs a redesign to work without ruler data.

title: Silence drawer will never open from list view because ruler rule type check fails
body: The condition `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` on line 104 will be false when `rule` is undefined (which is the case in the list view where only `promRule` is provided). The user can click 'Silence notifications' in the dropdown menu (since `canSilence` can be true via grafana abilities), which sets `showSilenceDrawer` to true, but the `SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer` component will never render because the guard condition fails. The user experiences a non-functional menu item.

title: Federated rule check hardcoded to false is a regression for Mimir/Loki federated groups
body: The previous implementation checked `isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)` which inspected `source_tenants` on the rule group. The new code hardcodes `isFederated = false` with a TODO comment. This means federated Mimir/Loki rules will now incorrectly show Edit, Delete, Pause, and Duplicate actions that should be disabled for federated rules. The `RuleGroupIdentifierV2` type passed to `useAllRulerRuleAbilities` does not carry the `source_tenants` information needed to make this determination.

title: Extra closing brace in Grafana rule key generation
body: The template literal `grafana-${namespace.uid}-${groupName}-${rule.uid}}` has a trailing extra `}` character. While this won't cause a functional failure (it's just a React key), it produces inconsistent key values and may cause confusion during debugging. Should be `grafana-${namespace.uid}-${groupName}-${rule.uid}`.

title: useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities invokes sub-hooks with API calls even when skipToken is passed
body: When `skipToken` is passed to `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` (e.g., for non-Grafana rules in AlertRuleMenu), the hook still calls `useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(undefined)` which unconditionally invokes `useGrafanaRulesSilenceSupport()` (making an RTK Query call to get alertmanager configuration status) and `useCanSilenceInFolder(undefined)`. Since React hooks cannot be conditionally called, every non-Grafana rule in the list view triggers these unnecessary API calls and hook invocations, potentially causing performance degradation on pages with many data-source-managed rules.

title: Redundant type narrowing makes promAlertingRule always equal to rule
body: Inside the `if (prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule))` block, the expression `rule && rule.type === PromRuleType.Alerting ? rule : undefined` is redundant because the outer condition already guarantees `rule.type === PromRuleType.Alerting` and `rule` is truthy. `promAlertingRule` will always equal `rule`. While not a runtime bug, it obscures intent and the `undefined` branch is dead code.

title: Silence drawer will never open when rulerRule is undefined (new list view)
body: When `rule` (rulerRule) is undefined — which is the case in the new alert list view that no longer fetches ruler data — the condition `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` evaluates to false. This means even though `canSilence` can be true (via the prom rule abilities path in AlertRuleMenu) and the user can click 'Silence notifications' in the dropdown menu, the `SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer` will never render because `showSilenceDrawer` is gated behind the rulerRule type check. The user clicks the menu item and nothing happens.

title: Pause menu item will never render when rulerRule is undefined despite canPause being true
body: The `canPause` variable can now be true via the `grafanaPauseSupported && grafanaPauseAllowed` path (when promRule is a Grafana rule and rulerRule is undefined). However, the render condition on line 123 additionally requires `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)`, which returns false when `rulerRule` is undefined. This means in the new list view (where ruler is not fetched), the Pause button will never appear even though the ability system says the user can pause the rule. The `MenuItemPauseRule` component also requires a `rulerRule` prop, so a deeper refactor is needed to support pause without ruler data.

title: Delete menu item will never render when rulerRule is undefined despite canDelete being true
body: Similar to the Pause issue: `canDelete` can be true via the grafana prom rule abilities path, but the render condition `{canDelete && rulerRule && (...)}` requires `rulerRule` to be truthy. In the new list view where ruler data is not fetched, `rulerRule` is undefined, so the Delete menu item will never appear. Additionally, `handleDelete` is called with `rulerRule` as an argument (line 172), so the delete flow itself depends on having a ruler rule object.

title: Federated rule check removed from useAllRulerRuleAbilities, allowing edit/delete of federated rules
body: The old `useAllAlertRuleAbilities` checked `isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)` to determine if a rule was in a federated group (which should make it immutable). The refactored `useAllRulerRuleAbilities` hardcodes `isFederated = false` with a TODO comment. Since `useAllAlertRuleAbilities` (marked deprecated but still used via `useAlertRuleAbility`) now delegates to `useAllRulerRuleAbilities`, federated rules in Mimir/Cloud data sources will incorrectly appear as editable and deletable in the old list view and rule details view until the TODO is addressed.

title: Inline actions array in useMemo dependency defeats memoization
body: In `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` (and `useRulerRuleAbilities`), the `actions` parameter is included in the `useMemo` dependency array. All call sites (e.g., AlertRuleMenu.tsx line 73-79) pass an inline array literal, which creates a new reference on every render. This causes the useMemo to recompute every render, negating the memoization benefit. Consider using a stable reference (e.g., a constant array or JSON-serialized key) or removing `actions` from deps and using a ref.

title: Redundant type narrowing creates unnecessary undefined assignment
body: Inside the `if (prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule))` block, the code does `const promAlertingRule = rule && rule.type === PromRuleType.Alerting ? rule : undefined`. The outer type guard already narrows `rule` to `GrafanaPromAlertingRuleDTO`, so this inner check is always true and `promAlertingRule` can never be undefined. While not a runtime bug, it makes the code misleading — a reader might think `promAlertingRule` could be undefined and that the subsequent `promAlertingRule?.state` and `promAlertingRule?.totals` optional chaining is necessary, when in fact `rule` itself could be used directly.

title: Double interpolation: queries are interpolated in runShardSplitQuery and again in runSplitQuery
body: runShardSplitQuery now calls datasource.applyTemplateVariables on each query (line 52), then passes the already-interpolated queries to splitQueriesByStreamShard, which calls runSplitQuery (line 163). runSplitQuery (querySplitting.ts line 299) also calls datasource.applyTemplateVariables on its input targets. This means every query going through the shard splitting path is interpolated twice. If an interpolated variable value contains text that resembles a template variable (e.g., a label value containing `$`), the second interpolation pass could corrupt the query or produce unexpected results. The tests pass only because the mock replace function is idempotent on already-replaced strings, but real-world variable values may not be.

title: Filtering by expr before interpolation changes behavior for variables that resolve to empty strings
body: The previous code called interpolateVariablesInQueries first, then filtered by query.expr. The new code filters by query.expr first (line 50), then interpolates (line 52). If a query has expr set to a variable like '$myVar' that interpolates to an empty string, the old code would filter it out after interpolation, but the new code lets it through the filter (since '$myVar' is truthy) and then interpolates it to an empty string. This empty-expr query will then be passed downstream and potentially sent to the backend, causing errors or unexpected behavior. The same issue exists in querySplitting.ts line 298.

title: Double interpolation when shard splitting delegates to runSplitQuery
body: runShardSplitQuery() now interpolates queries at line 52 via applyTemplateVariables(). It then passes these already-interpolated targets to runSplitQuery() at line 163. However, runSplitQuery() (in querySplitting.ts, line 299) also calls applyTemplateVariables() on its input targets. This means queries going through the shard splitting path are interpolated twice. While this may be idempotent for simple variable substitutions, it is wasteful and could produce incorrect results if a variable's resolved value contains text that matches another variable pattern (e.g., a label value containing `$` followed by text). Consider adding an option to runSplitQuery to skip interpolation, or restructuring so interpolation happens only once.

title: Test mock mutates the input query object, masking potential double-interpolation issues
body: The mock for applyTemplateVariables at line 56-58 mutates the query object in place (`query.expr = query.expr.replace(...)`) and returns the same reference. If the production code were to call applyTemplateVariables twice on the same object (which now happens due to the double interpolation path through runSplitQuery), this mutation-based mock would silently succeed on the second call (replacing an already-replaced string is a no-op), hiding the double-interpolation bug. A more robust mock would return a new object, making it easier to detect if interpolation is applied more than once.

title: Interpolation before `isQueryWithRangeVariable` check defeats the guard against splitting `$__range` queries
body: The new `.map((query) => datasource.applyTemplateVariables(...))` on line 299 interpolates all template variables (including `$__range`, `$__interval`, etc.) before the `partition` on line 300 calls `querySupportsSplitting`. That function (line 282–288) relies on `isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr)` to detect expressions containing `$__range` and exclude them from splitting, because the backend would otherwise interpolate `$__range` with the incorrect sub-range. After interpolation, `$__range` is already replaced with a concrete duration string, so `isQueryWithRangeVariable` returns false and the query is incorrectly classified as splittable. This can produce wrong results for any query using `$__range` in a range selector (e.g., `rate(metric[$__range])`). The interpolation should happen after the splitting eligibility check, or the check should be performed on the original uninterpolated targets.

title: Double interpolation when shard splitting delegates to `runSplitQuery`
body: `runShardSplitQuery` now interpolates targets at line 52 via `datasource.applyTemplateVariables`. The interpolated targets are then passed through `splitQueriesByStreamShard` → `runNextRequest` → `runSplitQuery` (line 163), which interpolates them a second time at its own line 299. While often idempotent, this can produce incorrect results if a template variable's resolved value itself contains template syntax (e.g., a variable whose value is `${other_var}`), and it adds unnecessary work on every sub-request. The fix should either skip interpolation in `runSplitQuery` when called from the shard-splitting path (e.g., via an option flag), or remove the early interpolation from `runShardSplitQuery` and rely solely on `runSplitQuery` to interpolate.

title: traceID no longer included in log output
body: The previous implementation explicitly extracted the trace ID via `tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false)` and appended it to `logParams`. This has been removed, and the new `ContextualLoggerMiddleware.instrumentContext` does not include the trace ID in the contextual attributes it sets on the context. Unless the infra log layer's `FromContext` implementation independently extracts the trace ID from the span context (which is not guaranteed by the code shown), log messages will no longer contain the `traceID` field. This is a silent observability regression that could break log-based dashboards, alerts, or trace-to-log correlation.

title: TestLogger.FromContext discards all contextual state
body: `TestLogger.FromContext` returns a brand-new `NewTestLogger()` with no connection to the context or the original logger. This makes it impossible to write meaningful tests that verify the `ContextualLoggerMiddleware` is properly enriching the logger via context. Any test calling `FromContext` will get a logger with zero recorded calls, regardless of what was set in the context. Consider returning `f` itself (or a copy that records which context it was called with) so tests can assert on contextual propagation.

title: Adding FromContext to Logger interface is a breaking change
body: The `Logger` interface in `pkg/plugins/log` gains a new required method `FromContext(ctx context.Context) Logger`. Any external or internal code that implements this interface (outside of the two implementations updated here) will fail to compile. Since this package is under `pkg/` and may be imported by plugins or other Grafana modules, this is a breaking API change that should be called out in the PR description or changelog.

title: Stream operations not enriched with contextual logger
body: `SubscribeStream`, `PublishStream`, and `RunStream` do not call `instrumentContext`, so the context passed downstream for stream operations will lack the plugin ID, endpoint, data source, and user attributes. If any downstream middleware or the plugin SDK itself uses `FromContext` for logging during stream operations, those log lines will be missing contextual information. This is inconsistent with the other four operations and may lead to confusing or incomplete logs for streaming plugins.

title: Potential nil pointer dereference if FromContext returns a nil *ConcreteLogger
body: In `FromContext`, the type assertion `d.l.FromContext(ctx).(*log.ConcreteLogger)` will succeed with `ok=true` if the underlying method returns a nil `*ConcreteLogger` stored in an interface. In that case, `concreteInfraLogger` is nil, and the returned `grafanaInfraLogWrapper{l: nil}` will panic on any subsequent logging call (e.g., `d.l.Debug(...)`). A nil check on `concreteInfraLogger` after the type assertion would prevent this.

title: TestLogger.FromContext discards contextual attributes, making contextual logging untestable
body: `TestLogger.FromContext` always returns a brand-new `TestLogger` with no contextual state. This means tests that use `TestLogger` cannot verify that contextual attributes (set via `log.WithContextualAttributes`) are actually propagated to the logger. Since `LoggerMiddleware.logRequest` now relies on `FromContext` to produce log output with contextual fields, there is no way to assert in tests that the correct context (pluginId, endpoint, etc.) appears in log entries. The fake should store and return contextual data from the context.

title: No unit tests for the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware
body: The new `ContextualLoggerMiddleware` is a new middleware that enriches the request context with contextual logging attributes, but no test file is included in this PR. There is no verification that `instrumentContext` correctly populates the context with the expected keys (endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID, uname) or that the middleware correctly delegates to the next client for all endpoints.

title: LoggerMiddleware loses traceID in log output
body: The previous implementation of `logRequest` explicitly extracted `traceID` from the context via `tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false)` and included it in `logParams`. This logic was removed in this PR. The `ContextualLoggerMiddleware.instrumentContext` function does not add the traceID to the contextual attributes either. As a result, the traceID will no longer appear in the 'Plugin Request Completed' log line, which is a regression in observability for correlating logs with traces.

title: traceID is no longer included in plugin request log output
body: The previous implementation of `logRequest` explicitly extracted the traceID from the context via `tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false)` and appended it to `logParams`. This code has been removed, and the new `ContextualLoggerMiddleware.instrumentContext` does not add traceID to the contextual logger attributes. As a result, the `traceID` field will no longer appear in 'Plugin Request Completed' log messages, which is a regression that reduces observability and makes it harder to correlate logs with traces.

title: Adding `FromContext` to the `Logger` interface is a breaking change
body: The `Logger` interface now requires a `FromContext(ctx context.Context) Logger` method. Any external or third-party implementations of this interface (e.g., custom plugin loggers) will fail to compile after this change. Since the PR is described as a chore/rename, this silent interface expansion may surprise consumers. Consider whether this should be a separate interface or introduced with a deprecation/migration path.

title: `NewMetricsMiddleware` returns a closure that mutates a shared `MetricsMiddleware` instance
body: `NewMetricsMiddleware` creates a single `*MetricsMiddleware` and the returned `ClientMiddlewareFunc` mutates `imw.next` each time it is invoked. If this middleware is applied to multiple plugin clients (which is the typical case—one middleware chain per plugin), all clients share the same `MetricsMiddleware` and the `next` field will point to whichever client was wired last. This means requests for one plugin may be forwarded to the wrong next client. This is a pre-existing pattern from the old `InstrumentationMiddleware`, but it remains a correctness bug.

title: Stream methods (`SubscribeStream`, `PublishStream`, `RunStream`) do not enrich the context
body: The `ContextualLoggerMiddleware` does not call `instrumentContext` for `SubscribeStream`, `PublishStream`, or `RunStream`. If the `LoggerMiddleware` (or any downstream middleware) logs during these calls, the contextual logger will lack plugin/endpoint information. While this matches the previous behavior of the old `InstrumentationMiddleware`, it's worth noting as a gap now that contextual logging is explicitly separated into its own middleware.

title: `TestLogger.FromContext` discards contextual attributes, making it impossible to test contextual logging
body: `TestLogger.FromContext` always returns a fresh `NewTestLogger()`, discarding any contextual attributes that were stored in the context. Tests that use `TestLogger` cannot verify that contextual attributes (pluginId, endpoint, etc.) are properly propagated through the middleware chain to the final log call. A test-capable implementation should capture or expose the contextual attributes for assertion.

title: Local cache set before DB write allows bypassing device limit
body: In `tagDeviceUI`, the local cache entry is set (line 87: `a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{})`) before `CreateOrUpdateDevice` is called. If `CreateOrUpdateDevice` returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached` (because the device is new and the limit is hit), the error propagates and authentication fails. However, the cache entry persists for 29 minutes. On the very next request from the same device, `tagDeviceUI` will find the cache hit at line 83 and return nil immediately, never reaching the database. This means the device limit is effectively bypassed after the first rejected attempt — the second request within the cache TTL will authenticate successfully despite the device not existing in the database.

title: TOCTOU race between CountDevices and INSERT allows exceeding device limit
body: In `CreateOrUpdateDevice`, the check `count >= s.deviceLimit` (line 115) and the subsequent INSERT (lines 122-153) are not atomic. Under concurrent load, multiple goroutines can each observe `count < deviceLimit`, then all proceed to INSERT, causing the actual number of devices to exceed the configured limit. A transactional approach or database-level constraint would be needed to enforce the limit reliably.

title: TagDevice moved from async goroutine to synchronous authentication path
body: Previously `TagDevice` was called in a goroutine with a 2-minute timeout, making it fire-and-forget so database latency did not block authentication. Now it runs synchronously in the `Authenticate` method. Every anonymous request will wait for the database round-trip (including the `CountDevices` query when a limit is set) before authentication completes. Under high anonymous traffic or database latency spikes, this directly increases request latency for all anonymous users.

title: ErrDeviceLimitReached returned for non-limit scenarios in updateDevice
body: In `updateDevice`, `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned whenever `rowsAffected == 0`. This can also occur when the device exists in the database but its `updated_at` falls outside the BETWEEN window (e.g., the device was last seen more than 30 days ago). In that case the error is semantically wrong — the device is known but stale, not blocked by a limit. This could cause confusing error handling upstream and might incorrectly block a returning device whose record simply aged out of the window.

title: Duplicated anonymousDeviceExpiration constant risks drift
body: The constant `anonymousDeviceExpiration = 30 * 24 * time.Hour` is now defined independently in both `anonstore/database.go` (line 16) and `api/api.go` (line 18). If one is updated without the other, the API listing window and the store's expiration logic will diverge silently. This should be a single shared constant.

title: TOCTOU race condition between device count check and insert
body: In `CreateOrUpdateDevice`, the code first calls `CountDevices` to check if the limit is reached, then proceeds to INSERT if below the limit. Between these two operations, concurrent requests can also pass the count check and insert, causing the actual number of devices to exceed the configured `deviceLimit`. Under high concurrency (e.g., many new anonymous users arriving simultaneously), the limit can be significantly exceeded. Consider using a database-level constraint, an atomic INSERT with a subquery check, or a SELECT ... FOR UPDATE pattern to make the check-and-insert atomic.

title: COUNT query executed on every non-cached anonymous request when device limit is set
body: When `deviceLimit > 0`, every call to `CreateOrUpdateDevice` (i.e., every anonymous request not served by the 29-minute local cache) executes a `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM anon_device WHERE updated_at BETWEEN ...` query. On a busy instance with many anonymous users, this adds a full table scan (or index scan) to the critical authentication path. Consider caching the count result for a short period or using an approximate count mechanism.

title: TagDevice changed from async to synchronous, adding latency to every anonymous authentication
body: Previously, `TagDevice` was called in a goroutine with its own timeout, so it did not block the authentication response. Now it is called synchronously on the request context. When `deviceLimit > 0`, this adds at least one COUNT query (and potentially an INSERT or UPDATE) to the critical path of every anonymous request. This increases authentication latency for all anonymous users, even those whose devices are already known. The local cache mitigates this for repeat requests within 29 minutes, but first requests and cache-expired requests will pay the full cost.

title: updateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached for devices that exist but have stale updated_at
body: The `updateDevice` function's WHERE clause includes `updated_at BETWEEN ? AND ?` with a 30-day window. If a device exists in the database but its `updated_at` is older than 30 days (e.g., it was last seen 31 days ago but not yet cleaned up by the background job which runs every 2 hours with a 61-day retention), the UPDATE will affect 0 rows and return `ErrDeviceLimitReached`. The device exists but cannot be updated, and the error message doesn't distinguish this case from a truly new device being rejected. This is a minor semantic issue but could cause confusion in debugging.

title: TypeScript type says `number | undefined` but backend always sends a number
body: The `anonymousDeviceLimit` field is typed as `number | undefined` in the TypeScript interface, but the Go DTO uses `int64` without `omitempty`, meaning it will always be serialized as a JSON number (0 when unset). The frontend will never receive `undefined` for this field. If the intent is to distinguish 'no limit configured' from 'limit is 0', the Go struct should use a pointer type with `omitempty`, or the TypeScript type should just be `number`.

title: TOCTOU race between CountDevices and INSERT allows exceeding device limit
body: In `CreateOrUpdateDevice`, the device count is checked with `CountDevices` and then, if below the limit, an INSERT is performed in a separate database call. Between these two operations, concurrent requests can also pass the count check and insert, causing the actual device count to exceed the configured limit. Under high concurrency (common for anonymous access), the limit becomes a soft guideline rather than a hard cap. Consider using a single atomic query (e.g., INSERT ... WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) ...) < limit) or a database-level constraint.

title: Local cache is set before DB write succeeds, causing inconsistent auth behavior on device limit rejection
body: In `tagDeviceUI`, the local cache entry is set on line 87 (`a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{})`) before `CreateOrUpdateDevice` is called on line 93. If `CreateOrUpdateDevice` returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, the error propagates and the user is rejected on the first request. However, the cache entry persists for 29 minutes. On the next request from the same device, the cache hit on line 83 causes `tagDeviceUI` to return nil (success), and the user is authenticated. This means the first request is rejected but subsequent requests within the cache window succeed, creating inconsistent and confusing behavior. The cache should only be set after a successful DB write.

title: TagDevice is now synchronous in the authentication hot path, adding latency to every anonymous request
body: Previously `TagDevice` was called in a goroutine with a 2-minute timeout, so it never blocked the authentication response. Now it runs synchronously within `Authenticate`, meaning every anonymous request incurs a database round-trip (and potentially two: one for COUNT and one for INSERT/UPDATE) before the user receives a response. This adds latency to the critical authentication path for all anonymous users, and if the database is slow, it can cause request timeouts or pile-ups.

title: updateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when device simply doesn't exist, conflating two different failure modes
body: When the device limit is reached and `updateDevice` is called for a device that has never been seen (or was cleaned up), `rowsAffected` is 0 and `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned. This is functionally correct for enforcing the limit, but the error message is misleading for logging and debugging: the device wasn't rejected because an existing device hit a limit—it was rejected because it's a new device and the limit is full. More importantly, if a device was cleaned up by `DeleteDevicesOlderThan` but the client still sends its device ID, the user will be permanently locked out with a confusing error, even though the device no longer occupies a slot. Consider distinguishing 'device not found' from 'limit reached' or documenting this behavior.

title: TypeScript type says `number | undefined` but Go int64 always serializes as a number (0 when unset)
body: The `anonymousDeviceLimit` field is typed as `number | undefined` in the frontend TypeScript interface, but the Go DTO uses `int64` without `omitempty`, which means it will always serialize as `0` in JSON when no limit is configured—never as `null` or absent. Frontend code checking for `undefined` to determine if a limit is active will not work correctly; it should check for `0` instead, or the Go struct should use a pointer type with `omitempty`.

title: No test verifying that an existing device can still be updated when the limit is reached
body: `TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` only tests that a *new* device is rejected when the limit is reached. There is no test confirming that an *existing* device (one already in the database) can still successfully update its record when the limit is reached. This is the happy path for the `updateDevice` function and is critical to verify—without it, a regression could silently lock out all anonymous users once the limit is hit.

title: Cleanup ticker interval reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute, affecting all cleanup jobs
body: The ticker interval was changed from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`. This increases the execution frequency of ALL cleanup jobs (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, user invites, short URLs, query history) by 10x, not just annotation cleanup. The PR description only discusses fixing annotation deadlocks and does not mention intentionally changing the global cleanup cadence. This appears to be a debugging or testing change left in accidentally. Running all cleanup jobs every minute will significantly increase database load and may ironically cause more lock contention.

title: Error-level logging used for normal operational messages
body: Lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579 all use `r.log.Error(...)` to log routine operational information (e.g., 'Annotations to clean by time', 'cleaned annotations by time', 'Tags to clean'). At this point in the code, `err` is nil (errors were already checked and returned above). Using Error level for non-error conditions will pollute error monitoring and alerting systems in production, making it harder to identify real issues. These should be `r.log.Debug` or `r.log.Info`.

title: Logging all annotation IDs can produce extremely large log entries
body: The log statements include `"ids", ids` which serializes the entire slice of fetched IDs. With `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` configured up to 32767 (as tested), this produces log lines containing tens of thousands of integers on every batch iteration. This will cause significant log volume and potential performance issues in production. Consider logging only the count or a truncated sample of IDs.

title: Loop may terminate prematurely when IDs are fetched but already deleted by concurrent processes
body: In `untilDoneOrCancelled`, the loop exits when `affected == 0`. With the new split approach, it's possible that `fetchIDs` returns a non-empty list of IDs, but by the time `deleteByIDs` executes, those rows have already been deleted by another process (e.g., a concurrent cleanup instance or explicit user deletion). In this case `affected` is 0 and the loop stops, even though more eligible rows may exist. While the next cleanup cycle will handle them, with the original 10-minute interval this could mean a 10-minute delay in cleanup. The 1-minute ticker change may have been an attempt to mitigate this, but the root cause is that the termination condition should be based on whether `fetchIDs` returned results, not whether the delete affected rows.

title: Cleanup ticker reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute without explanation
body: The ticker interval for the entire cleanup service was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute. This affects all cleanup jobs (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, user invites, short URLs, query history), not just annotations. The PR description does not mention this change, suggesting it may be a debugging leftover. Running all cleanup jobs 10x more frequently will significantly increase database load in production, especially now that annotation cleanup performs multiple round-trip queries per batch.

title: Normal operational logging uses Error level
body: Lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579 all use `r.log.Error(...)` to log routine cleanup progress (e.g., "Annotations to clean by time", "cleaned annotations by time"). These are not errors — they represent normal operation. In production, this will flood error-level logs and trigger false alerts in monitoring systems that alert on error log volume. These should be `Debug` or `Info` level.

title: SQLite parameter limit check uses batch size instead of actual ID count
body: The condition `r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > sqliteParameterLimit` checks the configured batch size rather than `len(ids)`. If the batch size is configured above 999 but fewer IDs are actually returned (e.g., only 50 rows match), the code unnecessarily inlines IDs into the SQL string instead of using parameterized queries. The check should be `len(ids) > sqliteParameterLimit` to correctly decide based on the actual number of parameters that will be bound.

title: Race between fetchIDs and deleteByIDs may cause premature loop termination
body: Because fetchIDs and deleteByIDs run in separate sessions (no shared transaction), another process could delete the fetched IDs between the SELECT and DELETE. If this happens for an entire batch, `deleteByIDs` returns 0 affected rows, and `untilDoneOrCancelled` terminates the loop — even if more annotations still qualify for cleanup. The code comment acknowledges under-deletion from concurrent inserts, but this scenario (concurrent deletes causing early termination) means the cleanup may stop prematurely and not resume until the next scheduled cycle. With the ticker now at 1 minute this is less impactful, but worth documenting.

title: Test uses explicit IDs that may conflict across test runs on shared databases
body: The `createTestAnnotations` function now sets `ID: int64(i + 1)` explicitly. If tests run against a shared database where the auto-increment sequence has advanced past these IDs (e.g., from a previous partial run or parallel test), the explicit IDs could conflict. The cleanup between subtests deletes all rows, but if a test panics before cleanup runs, subsequent runs may fail with duplicate key errors. Using the database's auto-increment (as the old code did) would be more robust.

title: Normal operational messages logged at ERROR level
body: Lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579 all use `r.log.Error(...)` to log routine cleanup progress (e.g., how many IDs were fetched, how many rows were affected). These are not errors—they represent normal successful operation. In production, this will flood the error log with thousands of entries per cleanup cycle, making it harder to identify real errors and potentially triggering false alerts on error-rate monitoring. These should be `r.log.Debug` or `r.log.Info`.

title: Cleanup interval reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute without explanation
body: The ticker interval is changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, causing all cleanup jobs (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, user invites, short URLs, query history) to run 10× more frequently. This increases database load across all cleanup operations, not just annotations. If the intent is only to run annotation cleanup more often to compensate for smaller batch sizes, this change is overly broad. The PR description does not justify this change.

title: SQLite parameter limit check uses configured batch size instead of actual ID count
body: The condition `r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > sqliteParameterLimit` checks the configured batch size rather than `len(ids)`. If the batch size is configured above 999 but a particular batch returns fewer than 999 IDs (e.g., near the end of cleanup), the code still inlines the values into the SQL string instead of using parameterized queries. While functionally correct, this is inconsistent: on non-SQLite databases the same small batch would use parameters. More importantly, if a future database introduces a similar parameter limit, this pattern would need to be replicated. The check should be `len(ids) > sqliteParameterLimit`.

title: cutoffDate is interpolated directly into SQL string without parameterization
body: The `cutoffDate` integer is embedded into the SQL condition via `fmt.Sprintf` (`created < %v`). While the value is internally computed and not user-controlled, this bypasses the database driver's parameter binding. If the `fetchIDs`/`deleteByIDs` pattern is extended in the future to accept externally-influenced conditions, this pattern becomes a SQL injection vector. Using a parameterized query (passing cutoffDate as a bind parameter) would be safer and more consistent with the rest of the codebase.

title: Wrong metric function called on storage error in Create
body: When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` instead of `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`. This means storage failures are recorded under the legacy metric, corrupting both the legacy and storage duration metrics and making it impossible to correctly monitor storage health.

title: Wrong logger placed into context in Delete
body: The code builds `log` with name, kind, and method values on line 96, but then on line 97 inserts `d.Log` (the bare logger without those values) into the context via `klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)`. This means any downstream code that retrieves the logger from the context will not see the structured fields. It should be `klog.NewContext(ctx, log)`.

title: Wrong label value passed as kind in Delete success metric
body: On the success path of Delete, `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes `name` (the resource name) as the kind parameter. Every other call in this file passes `options.Kind` for that position. This will produce metric labels with the object name instead of the resource kind, leading to high-cardinality metrics and inconsistency with other operations.

title: Wrong metric function called on storage error in Update
body: When `d.Storage.Update` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` instead of `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`. This misattributes storage errors to the legacy metric, the same class of bug as in Create.

title: Wrong metric function called for legacy write in DeleteCollection goroutine
body: Inside the async goroutine that writes to legacy storage, the code calls `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)` instead of `d.recordLegacyDuration(err != nil, ...)`. This means legacy delete-collection durations are recorded as storage durations, corrupting both metrics.

title: Async legacy writes derive context from request context and will be cancelled when the request completes
body: In Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection, the goroutines that asynchronously write to legacy storage derive their timeout context from the request context (`ctx`). In Go's HTTP server, the request context is cancelled once the handler returns and the response is written. Since these goroutines are fire-and-forget, the parent request context will typically be cancelled almost immediately after the function returns, causing `context.WithTimeoutCause` to also cancel. This means the legacy writes will likely fail with a context cancellation error before completing, defeating the purpose of the async safety-net write. The goroutines should use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (Go 1.21+) or `context.Background()` as the parent.

title: Tests do not verify that legacy storage is actually called asynchronously
body: The mode 3 tests set up mock expectations for legacy Create/Update/Delete but never assert that those mocks were actually called (e.g., via `m.AssertExpectations(t)` or a wait/sleep). Since the legacy writes happen in goroutines, the tests may pass even if the goroutine never executes or panics. This means the core dual-write behavior is not actually verified by the unit tests.

title: Wrong metric function called on Storage.Create error
body: When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` instead of `d.recordStorageDuration(...)`. This records a unified storage failure under the legacy metric, producing misleading observability data and making it impossible to correctly monitor storage vs legacy error rates.

title: Wrong metric function called on Storage.Update error
body: When `d.Storage.Update` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` instead of `d.recordStorageDuration(...)`. This is the same class of bug as the Create method: a unified storage failure is recorded under the legacy duration metric, corrupting monitoring data.

title: Wrong metric function called for legacy DeleteCollection result
body: Inside the goroutine that asynchronously writes to legacy storage for DeleteCollection, the code calls `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy)` instead of `d.recordLegacyDuration(...)`. This records the legacy operation's outcome under the storage metric, inverting the observability semantics.

title: Inconsistent metric label: `name` used instead of `options.Kind`
body: In the Delete method's success path, `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object `name` (e.g. "foo") as the kind label instead of `options.Kind`. Every other call in the file uses `options.Kind` for this parameter. This will produce metrics with incorrect kind labels, making dashboards and alerts based on kind unreliable.

title: Delete method sets context logger to `d.Log` instead of enriched `log`
body: Line 96 creates `log := d.Log.WithValues("name", name, "kind", options.Kind, "method", method)` but line 97 sets `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` using the base logger without the added values. The enriched `log` variable is only used for the error message on line 102, but any downstream code that extracts the logger from context will miss the name/kind/method fields. This should be `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, log)`.

title: Async legacy writes derive from request context and may be silently cancelled
body: All async goroutines (Create, Delete, Update, DeleteCollection) create a timeout context derived from the incoming request context (`ctx`). If the HTTP request completes and its context is cancelled before the goroutine executes, the derived context is immediately done and the legacy write silently fails. Since mode 3's stated purpose is to write to legacy 'as a safe measure', these writes should use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` or `context.Background()` to ensure they are not tied to the request lifecycle.

title: Tests do not verify that async legacy writes actually execute
body: The mode 3 tests set up mock expectations for legacy Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection but never wait for or assert that the goroutines actually ran. Since the legacy writes are fire-and-forget goroutines, the tests can pass even if the goroutines never execute (e.g., due to context cancellation or scheduling). The tests should use synchronization (e.g., a WaitGroup, channel, or eventually-style assertion) to confirm the legacy mock was called.

title: Async goroutines use request context that will be cancelled after response is sent
body: All async goroutines (Create line 51, Delete line 110, Update line 135, DeleteCollection line 163) derive their timeout context from the parent request context via `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`. Once the HTTP handler returns and the response is sent, the request context is cancelled, which will immediately cancel the child context. This means the asynchronous legacy writes will almost certainly fail with a context cancellation error, defeating the purpose of the dual-write safety net. The goroutines should use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (Go 1.21+) or `context.Background()` with any necessary values copied over.

title: Create records legacy duration metric on storage error instead of storage duration
body: On line 45, when `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`. Since this is measuring the duration of the storage operation that just failed, it should call `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)` instead. This will produce incorrect metrics, attributing storage failures to the legacy store.

title: Update records legacy duration metric on storage error instead of storage duration
body: On line 129, when `d.Storage.Update` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`. This should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)` since it is measuring the failed storage operation. This produces incorrect metrics.

title: DeleteCollection async goroutine records storage duration instead of legacy duration
body: On line 166, inside the async goroutine that performs the legacy delete-collection, the code calls `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy)`. Since this is measuring the legacy operation, it should call `d.recordLegacyDuration(...)` instead. This will produce incorrect metrics, attributing legacy store latency to the storage store.

title: Delete success metric passes `name` as kind parameter instead of `options.Kind`
body: On line 106, `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object `name` (e.g. "foo") where the `kind` parameter is expected (e.g. "Playlist"). All other calls in this file pass `options.Kind` in this position. This will produce metrics with incorrect kind labels, making them useless for aggregation by resource kind.

title: Delete sets context logger to d.Log instead of the enriched log variable
body: On line 97, `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` uses the base logger `d.Log` instead of the locally enriched `log` variable (defined on line 96 with name, kind, and method values). This means any logging within the Storage.Delete call or the async goroutine will lack the structured context fields that all other methods include, making debugging harder.

title: Tests cannot verify async legacy writes succeed or fail appropriately
body: The unit tests for Mode3 (Create, Delete, Update, DeleteCollection) set up mock expectations for legacy store calls but have no mechanism to wait for or assert that the asynchronous goroutines actually execute. Since the legacy writes happen in goroutines, the tests may pass even if the goroutines never run or fail immediately due to context cancellation. Consider using synchronization (e.g., channels or WaitGroup) in tests, or at minimum adding a test that verifies the legacy mock was called after a short delay.

title: Missing double-check after acquiring write lock (classic double-checked locking omission)
body:
After releasing the RLock and before acquiring the write Lock, another goroutine may have already computed and stored the result in `entryPointAssetsCache`. When the current goroutine finally acquires the write lock, it proceeds to re-read the manifest file (or make an HTTP request) redundantly. In production (non-dev) mode with concurrent requests at startup, this means multiple goroutines will serialize on the write lock and each perform the same expensive I/O. The standard fix is to re-check the cache immediately after acquiring the write lock:

```go
entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()
defer entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Unlock()

if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil {
    return entryPointAssetsCache, nil
}
```

This is the well-known double-checked locking pattern; without the second check the cache provides no benefit under concurrent access until the first writer finishes.

title: Missing re-check of cache after acquiring write lock (incomplete double-checked locking)
body: After releasing the RLock and before acquiring the write Lock, another goroutine may have already populated `entryPointAssetsCache`. The code does not re-check the cache after acquiring the exclusive lock at line 48. In non-dev mode, this means multiple goroutines that simultaneously observe a nil cache will all serialize on the write lock and each redundantly perform the expensive file I/O (reading and parsing assets-manifest.json). The standard double-checked locking pattern requires re-checking the condition after upgrading to the write lock: after line 49, add `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` to avoid redundant work during startup bursts.

title: Missing double-check after acquiring write lock allows thundering herd
body:
After releasing the RLock (line 43) and before acquiring the write Lock (line 48), another goroutine may have already populated `entryPointAssetsCache`. When multiple goroutines all observe a nil cache during the RLock phase (e.g., at startup), they all proceed to acquire the write lock and each one redundantly recomputes the value (file I/O or HTTP request) sequentially. The standard double-checked locking pattern requires re-checking the cache after acquiring the exclusive lock:

```go
entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()
defer entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Unlock()
if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil {
    return entryPointAssetsCache, nil
}
```

Without this, N concurrent requests at startup will perform N redundant manifest reads instead of 1.

title: enableSqlExpressions contains confusing dead logic that could be accidentally re-enabled
body: The function `enableSqlExpressions` always returns `false`, but the logic is written in a misleading way: the variable `enabled` is assigned the *negation* of the feature flag check (`!h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(...)`), so `enabled` is `true` when the flag is OFF. Both branches return `false`, making the feature flag check dead code. For a security-critical function that disables a feature to prevent RCE (CVE-2024-9264), this should be as unambiguous as possible (e.g., simply `return false` with a comment explaining why). The current form risks a future developer misreading the inverted logic and 'fixing' it to actually respect the feature flag, which would re-introduce the vulnerability.

title: TablesList still constructs SQL and calls RunCommands on the stub, producing a misleading error path
body: `TablesList` in `parser.go` still builds a SQL string via `fmt.Sprintf("SELECT json_serialize_sql('%s')", rawSQL)` and calls `duckDB.RunCommands(...)`, which now always returns `errors.New("not implemented")`. While this is safe (it will always error), the function performs unnecessary string manipulation including a single-quote replacement (`strings.Replace(rawSQL, "'", "''", -1)`) on user input before discarding it. If the intent is to fully disable this path, the function should return an error immediately without processing user input, reducing attack surface and making the intent clearer.

title: enableSqlExpressions has misleading logic that always returns false regardless of feature flag
body: The function `enableSqlExpressions` contains a negation (`!h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(...)`) and an if-branch, but both the if-branch and the fallthrough return `false`. This means the feature flag check is entirely inert—the function always returns false. While this is the intended security behavior (always disable SQL expressions), the code reads as if it has a logic bug. A future maintainer might 'fix' what appears to be an inverted condition or dead code, accidentally re-enabling the vulnerable path. A clearer implementation would be `return false` with a comment referencing CVE-2024-9264, making the intent unmistakable and reducing the risk of accidental re-enablement.

title: Error message 'sqlExpressions is not implemented' is misleading for a deliberately disabled feature
body: The error returned when a user attempts a SQL expression query says 'sqlExpressions is not implemented', but the feature was implemented and is now intentionally disabled due to a critical security vulnerability (CVE-2024-9264). Users or developers debugging this may be confused into thinking the feature was never built. A message like 'sqlExpressions is disabled' or 'sqlExpressions is not available' would be more accurate and less likely to lead someone to try to 'implement' it again.

title: No tests verify that SQL expressions are blocked
body: This PR disables a feature that had a critical RCE/LFI vulnerability (CVE-2024-9264), but no test is added to assert that `ReadQuery` returns an error for `QueryTypeSQL`. Without a test, a future refactor could silently remove the guard or change the code path, re-exposing the vulnerability. A unit test calling `ReadQuery` with a SQL-type query and asserting the error would provide a regression safety net for this security fix.

title: Stub DB lacks documentation explaining it is a security mitigation
body: The new `DB` struct and `NewInMemoryDB` function replace the real DuckDB-backed implementation as a security fix, but there is no comment explaining why all methods return 'not implemented'. Without context, a developer might think this is incomplete work and attempt to re-implement the DuckDB integration, potentially reintroducing the vulnerability. A package-level or function-level comment referencing the CVE and the intentional disabling would prevent this.

title: enableSqlExpressions contains misleading dead-code logic that could be accidentally re-enabled
body: The function `enableSqlExpressions` always returns false, but does so through confusing conditional logic with a misleadingly named variable. The variable `enabled` is actually the *negation* of the feature flag (`!h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(...)`), and both branches return false. A future maintainer might interpret the `if enabled { return false }` branch as a bug (since the else path also returns false) and 'fix' it by returning true, inadvertently re-enabling the vulnerable code path. For a security-critical kill switch, the function should simply be `return false` with a comment explaining why, eliminating any ambiguity.

title: Error message 'sqlExpressions is not implemented' is misleading for a deliberately disabled feature
body: The error returned when a user attempts a SQL expression query says 'sqlExpressions is not implemented'. The feature *was* implemented and has been intentionally disabled due to CVE-2024-9264. This message may confuse users and operators into thinking it's a missing feature rather than a security-driven removal. A message like 'sqlExpressions has been disabled' or referencing the security advisory would be more accurate and actionable.

title: Removing coarse lock from BuildIndex allows concurrent builds for the same key, risking file-based index corruption
body: The previous code held `cacheMu.Lock()` for the entire `BuildIndex` function, which serialized all index builds. The new code only locks around the final cache write. This means two concurrent callers (e.g., a search request and a watch event handler both calling `getOrCreateIndex` for a namespace that wasn't pre-built during init) can simultaneously execute `BuildIndex` for the same key. When `size > b.opts.FileThreshold`, both goroutines will call `bleve.New(dir, mapper)` on the same directory path, which can corrupt the index or return errors. Even for memory-based indexes, duplicate work is performed and one index is silently discarded. A per-key lock or a singleflight/deduplication mechanism is needed to prevent concurrent builds for the same key.

title: History and Origin methods will panic with nil pointer dereference when search is not configured
body: `s.search.History(ctx, req)` and `s.search.Origin(ctx, req)` are called without checking whether `s.search` is nil. The `Search` method (line 916) correctly checks `if s.search == nil` before delegating, but `History` and `Origin` do not. If `opts.Search.Resources` is nil or `opts.Search.Backend` is nil (causing `newSearchSupport` to return nil), the server is created successfully but calling History or Origin will panic. The removed `Init` calls did not protect against this either, but since this PR is modifying these exact methods, it would be appropriate to add the nil check.

title: TotalDocs iterates over cache map without holding the read lock
body: `TotalDocs()` ranges over `b.cache` without acquiring `b.cacheMu.RLock()`. Since `BuildIndex` now writes to `b.cache` under a brief lock (lines 137-139), there is a data race between a concurrent `BuildIndex` writing to the map and `TotalDocs` iterating it. This can cause a runtime panic ('concurrent map iteration and map write'). The `TotalDocs` method should acquire `b.cacheMu.RLock()` before iterating.

title: Data race on totalBatchesIndexed incremented from multiple goroutines
body: In `searchSupport.init()`, `totalBatchesIndexed` is a local `int` variable that is incremented (`totalBatchesIndexed++`) inside `group.Go` closures which run concurrently (up to `s.initWorkers` goroutines). This is a data race. It should be an `atomic.Int64` or the increment should be moved after `group.Wait()` by collecting results.

title: NewResourceServer now blocks on full index build, changing startup behavior and contract
body: `NewResourceServer` now calls `s.Init(ctx)` which builds all search indexes synchronously before returning. For large deployments, this could significantly increase startup time and may exceed caller timeouts or health check deadlines. The PR description acknowledges this question ('Does anything else depend on initializing US lazily?') but there is no mechanism (e.g., a context with a configurable timeout, or an option to skip eager init) to control this behavior. Callers that previously had a fast `NewResourceServer` followed by lazy initialization may now experience startup failures if index building takes too long.

title: Removing the lock around BuildIndex introduces a TOCTOU race for concurrent builds of the same key
body: The original code held `cacheMu.Lock()` for the entire `BuildIndex` call, which prevented two goroutines from building the same index concurrently. The new code only locks when writing to the cache at the end. This means two concurrent callers of `getOrCreateIndex` (in search.go) can both observe a nil index from `GetIndex`, both invoke `BuildIndex` for the same `NamespacedResource`, and both fully build the index. The second write to `b.cache[key]` silently overwrites the first, orphaning the first index. This wastes resources and can produce subtle inconsistencies if the two builds observe slightly different data. A per-key synchronization mechanism (e.g., `golang.org/x/sync/singleflight`) would preserve the concurrency improvement across different keys while preventing duplicate builds for the same key.

title: Init failure in NewResourceServer leaks the cancel function and any partially-initialized resources
body: When `s.Init(ctx)` fails at line 258, `NewResourceServer` returns an error without calling `cancel()` (the context cancel func created at line 229). This leaks the context and any goroutines or resources tied to it. Additionally, if `newSearchSupport` succeeded (allocating a builder cache, etc.) but `Init` subsequently fails, those resources are never cleaned up. The `cancel()` should be called (or deferred with a success check) before returning the error.

title: Data race on totalBatchesIndexed incremented from multiple errgroup goroutines without synchronization
body: The variable `totalBatchesIndexed` is a plain `int` that is incremented (`totalBatchesIndexed++`) inside `group.Go` closures that run concurrently (up to `s.initWorkers` goroutines). This is a data race under the Go memory model. While this is pre-existing code, the PR's change to propagate `ctx` through this function makes it a good opportunity to fix. Use `atomic.Int64` or collect results from the errgroup instead.

title: History and Origin methods will panic with nil pointer dereference when search is not configured
body: If `opts.Search.Resources` is nil in `ResourceServerOptions`, `s.search` remains nil. The `Search` method correctly checks for this (`if s.search == nil`), but `History` (line 924) and `Origin` (line 929) call `s.search.History(...)` and `s.search.Origin(...)` without a nil check, which will panic. Previously the `s.Init(ctx)` call was present (though it also wouldn't have prevented this), but now that these are the only guards removed, the nil dereference is the immediate failure mode for any deployment without search configured.

title: Data race on `totalBatchesIndexed` and `err` in concurrent goroutines
body: Inside `searchSupport.init()`, the `group.Go` closures concurrently increment `totalBatchesIndexed` (line 189) and assign to the outer `err` variable (line 190) without synchronization. Since `group.SetLimit(s.initWorkers)` allows multiple goroutines to run in parallel, both of these are data races (undefined behavior in Go). The `err` race is especially dangerous: multiple goroutines write to the same variable, and although `group.Wait()` returns the first error independently, the shared `err` is still being raced on. `totalBatchesIndexed` should use `atomic.Int64` or be collected after `group.Wait()`, and the inner `err` should be a local variable (use `:=` or a new declaration) rather than assigning to the outer `err`.

title: Removing the lock from BuildIndex allows concurrent builds for the same key, risking file-index conflicts
body: The old code held `cacheMu` for the entire `BuildIndex` call, which serialized all index builds and prevented two goroutines from building the same key simultaneously. The new code only locks around the final cache write. If two goroutines call `getOrCreateIndex` for the same `NamespacedResource` concurrently (e.g., two search requests for a namespace not yet indexed), both will see `nil` from `GetIndex`, both will call `BuildIndex`, and for file-based indexes (`size > FileThreshold`) both will call `bleve.New(dir, mapper)` on the same directory. `bleve.New` returns an error if the path already exists, causing one of the requests to fail. A per-key lock or a `singleflight`-style mechanism is needed to prevent duplicate concurrent builds for the same key.

title: TotalDocs() iterates cache map without holding the read lock
body: `TotalDocs()` ranges over `b.cache` without acquiring `cacheMu.RLock()`. Since `BuildIndex` writes to `b.cache` (now with only a brief lock around the write), concurrent calls to `TotalDocs` and `BuildIndex` constitute a data race on the map. This is a pre-existing issue but is made more likely to trigger by this PR's change to finer-grained locking, which increases the window during which `BuildIndex` can be called concurrently. Adding `b.cacheMu.RLock()`/`RUnlock()` around the iteration would fix it.

title: Integration test unconditionally skipped for postgres
body: The test `TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer` now skips all postgres runs with a TODO comment. Since the PR moves initialization to startup (a significant behavioral change), losing postgres coverage for the storage server module increases the risk of undetected regressions in that database backend. The skip should be temporary and tracked, or the root cause should be fixed before merging.

title: Call to non-existent zero-argument method `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()`
body: `UsernameForm.authenticate()` calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` with no arguments, but the only such method defined in the parent class `UsernamePasswordForm` is `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` which requires a `UserModel` parameter. There is no zero-argument overload anywhere in the class hierarchy shown. This will cause a compilation error.

title: WebAuthn conditional UI no longer initialized on first login (user == null)
body: The `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` method requires `user != null` to return true. In `authenticate()`, when the user has not yet been identified (first login), `context.getUser()` is null, so `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled` returns false and `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context)` is never called. Previously, WebAuthn setup was performed inside the `else` branch (user == null). This means the WebAuthn conditional UI (autocomplete passkey) will not be available on the initial login page, breaking first-time passkey login. The same issue affects the `challenge(context, error, field)` override at line 137, where error pages during first login will also lack WebAuthn setup.

title: WebAuthn not re-initialized on error during first login attempt
body: The overridden `challenge(AuthenticationFlowContext context, String error, String field)` method now calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())` which requires a non-null user. During a first login attempt with an invalid username, `context.getUser()` will be null (the user lookup failed), so WebAuthn conditional UI attributes will not be set on the error page. The original code explicitly checked `context.getUser() == null` to handle this case. Users who mistype their username on the first login will lose the ability to use passkeys on the error page.

title: Missing @Override annotation on shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators
body: The method `shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators` overrides the method introduced in `WebAuthnAuthenticator` but lacks the `@Override` annotation. While not a bug, this makes it harder for the compiler to detect if the parent method signature changes, and is inconsistent with the `fillContextForm` override on line 42 which does have `@Override`.

title: Call to non-existent no-arg method isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()
body: The code calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` without arguments, but the only such method defined in the parent class `UsernamePasswordForm` is `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` which requires a `UserModel` parameter. No no-arg overload exists in `UsernameForm`, `UsernamePasswordForm`, or `AbstractUsernameFormAuthenticator` (all shown in full). This will fail to compile. The call likely needs to be `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())` or a separate no-arg convenience method needs to be added.

title: WebAuthn conditional UI no longer set up during initial login (user is null)
body: The `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())` check requires `user != null`, but during initial login `context.getUser()` is null. The previous code (`webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled()`) was inside the `else` branch (user == null) and correctly set up the WebAuthn challenge for initial login. With this change, `fillContextForm` is never called during initial login, so no WebAuthn challenge is generated and the browser cannot perform the passkey ceremony. This breaks the discoverable-key auto-login flow (e.g., `PasskeysOrganizationAuthenticationTest.webauthnLoginWithDiscoverableKey` expects automatic login on initial page load). The condition should likely be `webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled()` (without the user != null requirement) or should handle both cases separately.

title: Inverted condition in challenge() breaks WebAuthn on initial-login error pages
body: The overridden `challenge(context, error, field)` now calls `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())` which requires user != null. The previous code was `context.getUser() == null && webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled()` — it set up WebAuthn when user was null (initial login errors). During initial login with a wrong password, `context.getUser()` is null at the time `challenge()` is called (the user is only set in context after successful password validation), so WebAuthn will no longer appear on the error page. This means a user who mistypes their password on the combined username/password form can no longer recover by using a passkey.

title: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled conflates 'passkeys enabled' with 'user is set'
body: The method `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` returns `webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled() && user != null`. This conflates two independent concerns: whether the passkeys feature is enabled, and whether a user is present in the context. Callers in `authenticate()` and `challenge()` need different semantics (initial login has no user but still needs WebAuthn; re-authentication has a user and also needs WebAuthn). A clearer design would separate the feature-enabled check from the user-presence check, or provide distinct methods for each scenario.

title: Call to non-existent no-arg method `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()`
