title: Negative offset queryset slicing will crash with AssertionError
body: Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing — `queryset[-5:96]` raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported`. The comment on line 876 ('The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically') is factually incorrect. When `enable_advanced_features=True` and a user supplies a cursor with a negative offset (e.g., `cursor=0:-5:0`), this code path will execute `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset`, causing an unhandled 500 error. This is trivially triggerable by any user who passes the `optimized_pagination=true` parameter and has the required access level.

title: BasePaginator change allows negative offsets when is_prev=True, causing crashes
body: The modified line `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` explicitly passes negative offsets through to the queryset slice when `cursor.is_prev` is True. Since `is_prev` is user-controlled (third component of the cursor string parsed in `Cursor.from_string`), any user can craft a cursor like `0:-10:1` to trigger a Django `AssertionError` on the queryset slice. The original code had the same latent issue but this change makes it intentional and removes the `max(0, ...)` guard for the `is_prev` path, which is a regression for all endpoints using `BasePaginator` (including `DateTimePaginator`).

title: No validation that cursor offset is non-negative in Cursor.from_string
body: `Cursor.from_string` parses the offset as `int(bits[1])` without validating it is >= 0. Since cursor strings are user-supplied input (from the `cursor` query parameter), a malicious or malformed cursor with a negative offset (e.g., `0:-100:0`) will be accepted. Combined with the paginator changes in this PR that explicitly allow negative offsets through to queryset slicing, this creates a denial-of-service vector where any authenticated user can trigger 500 errors on paginated endpoints.

title: Access control check may be insufficient and could raise AttributeError
body: The expression `organization_context.member.has_global_access` will raise `AttributeError` if `organization_context.member` is `None` (which can happen in certain edge cases with the RPC organization context). Additionally, `has_global_access` grants this feature to org managers/admins, not just owners — meaning a broader set of users can trigger the buggy negative-offset code path. If the intent is to restrict this to superusers only during initial rollout, the `has_global_access` check should be removed.

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator docstring and comments are misleading
body: The class docstring claims it provides 'Negative offset support for efficient reverse pagination' and 'Optimized query path for large datasets', but the implementation is functionally identical to the existing `Paginator` class except for the broken negative-offset handling. There is no actual performance optimization (no query plan changes, no index hints, no limit pushdown). The misleading documentation could cause future developers to believe this class provides real performance benefits and adopt it elsewhere.

title: Negative offset passed to Django QuerySet slice will crash at runtime
body: When `enable_advanced_features` is true and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` where `start_offset` is negative. Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing — this raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported`. The comment 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is factually incorrect. Any request that triggers this path will result in a 500 error.

title: BasePaginator change allows negative offsets for all subclasses when is_prev is true
body: The change `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` in `BasePaginator.get_result` removes the lower-bound protection for ALL paginator subclasses (Paginator, DateTimePaginator, etc.) when `cursor.is_prev` is true. A malformed or adversarial cursor string with a negative offset (e.g., via `Cursor.from_string`) will cause a Django AssertionError on the queryset slice. This is a regression affecting all existing paginators, not just the new OptimizedCursorPaginator.

title: Unrelated and dangerous pagination feature smuggled into spans buffer PR behind weak authorization check
body: The `optimized_pagination` query parameter enables `OptimizedCursorPaginator` with `enable_advanced_features=True`, which allows negative offsets. The authorization check (`request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`) is bypassed if the `OptimizedCursorPaginator` is used elsewhere without this gate. More importantly, this feature is broken (negative Django slicing crashes) and appears unrelated to the stated PR purpose of span buffer optimization. This looks like an attempt to introduce a backdoor pagination mechanism.

title: Silent span eviction via zpopmin with no observability
body: When a segment exceeds 1000 spans, `zpopmin` silently removes the oldest spans (by end_timestamp_precise score). There is no metric, log, or return value indicating that eviction occurred. This makes it impossible to detect data loss in production. The evicted spans are permanently lost with no way to alert on or measure the frequency of this event.

title: Hardcoded eviction limit of 1000 in Lua script is not configurable and differs from Python max_segment_spans=1001
body: The Lua script hardcodes the eviction threshold at 1000, while the Python `SpansBuffer.__init__` still accepts `max_segment_spans=1001` (now unused). This creates a discrepancy: the effective limit changed from 1001 to 1000, and the Python parameter is now dead code that misleads future maintainers into thinking the limit is configurable.

title: __reduce__ passes redis_ttl as segment_page_size due to positional argument mismatch
body: The `__reduce__` method returns `(SpansBuffer, (self.assigned_shards, self.span_buffer_timeout_secs, self.span_buffer_root_timeout_secs, self.redis_ttl))`. The constructor signature is `__init__(self, assigned_shards, span_buffer_timeout_secs, span_buffer_root_timeout_secs, segment_page_size, max_segment_bytes, max_segment_spans, redis_ttl)`. So `self.redis_ttl` (3600) is passed as `segment_page_size` instead of as `redis_ttl`. This means after pickling/unpickling (e.g., in multiprocessing), the buffer will have `segment_page_size=3600` and `redis_ttl=3600` (default), which happens to work by coincidence but is fragile and incorrect.

title: KeyError if end_timestamp_precise is missing from span event
body: The code accesses `val["end_timestamp_precise"]` without a default or existence check. If a span event is missing this field (e.g., from an older producer or malformed message), this will raise a KeyError and crash the consumer. The `cast(SpanEvent, ...)` provides no runtime protection. A `.get()` with a fallback or explicit validation would be safer.

title: Misleading comment about negative offset support in Cursor class
body: The added comment says 'Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios' but the code `self.offset = int(offset)` already accepted negative values before this change. The comment implies a behavioral change that doesn't exist here — the actual (broken) negative offset handling is in the paginator. This comment may mislead future readers into thinking the Cursor class itself provides safety for negative offsets.

title: max_segment_spans parameter is now dead code
body: The `max_segment_spans` parameter is still accepted in `__init__` and stored as `self.max_segment_spans`, but the code that used it (the span count check during `_load_segment_data`) has been removed. The parameter is now unused dead code that will confuse maintainers and appears in the constructor signature as if it still has an effect.

title: Negative offset passed to Django queryset will raise AssertionError
body: When `enable_advanced_features` is True and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative `start_offset`. Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ explicitly raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported` for negative slice indices. The comment on line 876 claiming 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false. Any request that provides a cursor with a negative offset (which is user-controlled via the cursor query parameter parsed by `Cursor.from_string`) will cause an unhandled 500 error.

title: User-controlled query parameter enables code path that crashes with crafted cursor
body: The `optimized_pagination=true` query parameter combined with a crafted cursor containing a negative offset value (e.g., `cursor=0:-5:0`) will trigger the negative-offset code path in `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, causing an unhandled AssertionError. While gated behind `is_superuser` or `has_global_access`, this is still a denial-of-service vector for privileged users and indicates the feature was not tested with adversarial inputs.

title: BasePaginator.get_result behavioral change allows negative offset for is_prev cursors across all subclasses
body: The change from `queryset[offset:stop]` to `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` means that when `cursor.is_prev` is True, a negative offset is passed directly to the queryset slice. Since `Cursor.from_string` parses user-supplied input with `int(bits[1])`, a negative value can be injected. This affects all BasePaginator subclasses (Paginator, DateTimePaginator), not just the new OptimizedCursorPaginator. Previously, the same negative offset would also fail, but the misleading comment ('This is safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions') suggests the author believed this was safe.

title: zpopmin evicts lowest-scored (earliest end_timestamp) spans, potentially removing the root span
body: The eviction logic `redis.call('zpopmin', set_key, span_count - 1000)` removes members with the lowest scores. Since scores are `end_timestamp_precise`, this evicts spans with the earliest end timestamps. A root/segment span may have an earlier end timestamp than its children (e.g., if it finishes before long-running child spans). If the root span is evicted, the segment will be flushed without a root span: `has_root_span` will be false, the flush timeout will use `span_buffer_timeout_secs` instead of `span_buffer_root_timeout_secs`, and `is_segment` will never be set to True for any span in the output, corrupting downstream segment data.

title: Removal of max_segment_spans check during flush creates inconsistency with existing data
body: The old code enforced `max_segment_spans` during `_load_segment_data` (flush time), rejecting segments that exceeded the limit. This check is removed, relying solely on the Lua script's eviction at insert time. However, segments already stored in Redis before this deployment may exceed 1000 spans and will now be flushed without any size guard. Additionally, the `max_segment_spans` parameter still exists in the constructor (line 150) but is no longer used, creating a confusing dead parameter.

title: Direct dictionary access on end_timestamp_precise will crash consumer if field is missing
body: `val["end_timestamp_precise"]` uses direct key access rather than `.get()`. If any span message lacks this field (due to schema evolution, a producer bug, or a malformed message), the consumer will raise a KeyError and crash. Other optional fields in the same block use `.get()` (e.g., `val.get("parent_span_id")`). Consider using `val.get("end_timestamp_precise", 0.0)` or handling the KeyError gracefully to avoid consumer death on a single bad message.

title: __reduce__ passes redis_ttl as the segment_page_size positional argument
body: `__reduce__` returns `(SpansBuffer, (self.assigned_shards, self.span_buffer_timeout_secs, self.span_buffer_root_timeout_secs, self.redis_ttl))`. The constructor's 4th positional parameter is `segment_page_size`, not `redis_ttl`. When this object is unpickled (e.g., in multiprocessing), `redis_ttl` (default 3600) will be used as `segment_page_size`, and `redis_ttl` will fall back to its default. This is a pre-existing bug but is relevant because the PR changes the data stored in Redis (sorted sets vs sets), making correct pickling more important for the multiprocessing path (`num_processes != 1`).

title: OptimizedCursorPaginator is a near-duplicate of Paginator with no clear optimization
body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` and `value_from_cursor` are identical to `Paginator`. The `get_result` method is a copy of `BasePaginator.get_result` with the addition of the negative-offset path. There is no actual performance optimization present—no query plan hints, no deferred loading, no index optimization. The class adds maintenance burden and a dangerous code path without delivering the claimed benefit.

title: Redirect loop limit reduced from 10000 to 1000 without explanation of safety
body: The redirect resolution loop limit was reduced from 10000 to 1000. The removed comment explained that the limit means 'segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly.' Reducing to 1000 means traces with redirect chains deeper than 1000 will silently fail to merge, producing fragmented segments. While 1000-deep traces are rare, this is a silent data correctness regression with no metric or log to detect when the limit is hit.

title: Negative queryset slicing will raise AssertionError at runtime
body: When `enable_advanced_features` is True and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code passes a negative `start_offset` to `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django's QuerySet does not support negative indexing — it raises `AssertionError("Negative indexing is not supported.")` in `Query.set_limits()`. The comment claiming 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is incorrect. This will produce a 500 error for any request that triggers this path (which is exposed via the audit logs endpoint when `optimized_pagination=true` is passed by a superuser or org admin).

title: Eviction via zpopmin can remove the root span, causing data loss in flushed segments
body: The eviction logic uses `zpopmin` which removes elements with the lowest scores (i.e., earliest `end_timestamp_precise`). If the root span (segment span) has one of the earliest end timestamps in a segment exceeding 1000 spans, it will be evicted. The `has_root_span` flag is stored in a separate key and survives eviction, so the segment will still be flushed with the shorter root timeout, but the root span's payload will be missing from the output. Downstream consumers will receive a segment without its root span, which violates the segment contract and can cause data integrity issues in traces.

title: BasePaginator.get_result allows negative offset when is_prev is True
body: The change `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` means that when `cursor.is_prev` is True, the raw `cursor.offset` is used without clamping. Since cursor values are parsed from user-supplied strings via `Cursor.from_string` (which does `int(bits[1])`), a malicious or malformed cursor like `0:-5:1` will produce a negative offset. Django will then raise `AssertionError` on the queryset slice, resulting in an unhandled 500 error instead of a proper 400 validation response.

title: Optimized paginator with broken negative offset feature is gated only by org admin access
body: The `enable_advanced` check allows any organization member with `has_global_access` (org admins) to trigger the `OptimizedCursorPaginator` with `enable_advanced_features=True`. Since the negative offset handling in that paginator is broken (causes AssertionError), any org admin can trigger a 500 error by crafting a cursor with a negative offset value. This could be used as a denial-of-service vector against the audit logs endpoint.

title: Redirect depth limit silently reduced from 10000 to 1000, removing explanatory comment
body: The redirect resolution loop limit was reduced from 10000 to 1000, and the comment explaining the tradeoff ('theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly') was removed. For traces with redirect chains deeper than 1000 (which can happen with long-running traces that undergo many rebalancing/merging operations), spans will fail to be joined into the correct segment. The original comment acknowledged this as a known limitation at 10k; reducing to 1k increases the probability of incorrect segment assembly without any documented justification.

title: max_segment_spans parameter is now unused but still accepted in constructor
body: The `max_segment_spans` parameter (default 1001) is still accepted in `SpansBuffer.__init__` and stored as `self.max_segment_spans`, but the check that used it (`if len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans`) was removed from `_load_segment_data` since eviction is now handled in the Lua script. This dead parameter is confusing for callers and the `__reduce__` method doesn't include it, meaning unpickled instances will always get the default value regardless of what was originally configured.

title: __reduce__ passes redis_ttl as segment_page_size due to positional argument mismatch
body: The `__reduce__` method returns `(SpansBuffer, (self.assigned_shards, self.span_buffer_timeout_secs, self.span_buffer_root_timeout_secs, self.redis_ttl))`. However, the constructor's 4th positional parameter is `segment_page_size`, not `redis_ttl`. This means when a `SpansBuffer` is unpickled (e.g., in multiprocessing), `segment_page_size` will be set to the value of `redis_ttl` (3600 instead of 100), and `redis_ttl` will get its default value. This is a pre-existing bug but is relevant since this PR modifies the class.

title: Cache key uses Python's `hash()` which is non-deterministic across processes
body: The cache key is constructed using `hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))`. Python's built-in `hash()` is randomized per-process (via PYTHONHASHSEED) since Python 3.3. In a multi-worker deployment, each worker will compute a different hash for the same tuple of project IDs, producing different cache keys. This means the cache is never shared between workers, completely defeating the caching purpose and causing every request to hit the allowlist lookup. Additionally, `invalidate_upsampling_cache` on line 73 uses the same `hash()` call, so it would also fail to find the correct key from a different process.

title: Accidental git submodule committed at repository root
body: A git submodule reference (`Subproject commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a`) has been added as a file named `sentry-repo` at the repository root. This appears to be an accidental commit (likely from running a command inside a nested clone). It will cause `git clone` to fail or produce warnings for anyone cloning the repository, and pollutes the repo structure.

title: Upsampling check uses outer `dataset` variable instead of `scoped_dataset` parameter
body: Inside `_get_event_stats`, the call to `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` uses the `dataset` variable from the outer `get()` method's scope, not the `scoped_dataset` parameter that `_get_event_stats` actually queries against. In the dashboard widget split logic (lines 362-380), `_get_event_stats` is called with `split_dataset = discover` while the outer `dataset` may be different. This means the upsampling eligibility check evaluates the wrong dataset, potentially applying upsampling transforms to a non-errors query or failing to apply them when the split dataset is errors.

title: Substring check for `event.type:error` matches negated queries
body: `_is_error_focused_query` uses a simple substring check `'event.type:error' in query`. This will incorrectly match negated queries like `!event.type:error` or `NOT event.type:error`, causing upsampling to be applied when the user is explicitly excluding error events. This would produce incorrect (upsampled) counts for non-error data.

title: Transformed column `upsampled_count() as count` embeds an alias that may not be parsed correctly by all query paths
body: The transformation produces the string `"upsampled_count() as count"` which embeds an alias. This string is passed to `timeseries_columns`, `y_axes`, and `selected_columns` parameters across different query execution paths (RPC, top events, standard). These parameters typically expect bare function expressions without embedded aliases. If the downstream query builder doesn't parse the `as count` suffix correctly, it will either fail or produce a column with an unexpected name, breaking result processing.

title: Falsy check on `client_sample_rate` silently drops a sample rate of 0
body: The condition `if client_sample_rate:` on line 349 will be falsy when `client_sample_rate` is `0` or `0.0`. While a zero sample rate may be unusual, the function silently ignores it rather than raising or logging, which could mask configuration errors. More importantly, the function sets `normalized_data['sample_rate']` but the Snuba query uses `Column('sample_weight')` — if `sample_weight` is expected to be `1/sample_rate`, there's a missing transformation step, and the test expectation of count=10 (from rate 0.1) would only work if something else computes `sample_weight = 1/0.1 = 10`.

title: `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is defined but never called anywhere
body: The function `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is provided for cache invalidation when the allowlist changes, but no code in this PR (or presumably elsewhere) ever calls it. Combined with the broken `hash()`-based cache key, this means there is no mechanism to invalidate stale cache entries when the project allowlist is updated, leading to up to 60 seconds of serving incorrect upsampling decisions after configuration changes.

title: `upsampled_count` uses `sum(sample_weight)` without handling NULL values
body: The `upsampled_count` function computes `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`. If any event in an allowlisted project has a NULL `sample_weight` (e.g., events ingested before the feature was enabled, or events missing the error_sampling context), ClickHouse's `sum()` will skip NULLs, producing an undercount. The code comment claims the schema guarantees `sample_weight` exists, but historical data or edge cases may violate this assumption, silently producing incorrect counts.

title: Cache key uses Python's non-deterministic hash(), making cache ineffective across processes
body: The cache key is constructed using `hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))`. Python's `hash()` for tuples is randomized per process (PYTHONHASHSEED), so different worker processes will produce different hash values for the same set of project IDs. This means: (1) cache hits will only occur within the same process, drastically reducing effectiveness in a multi-worker deployment like Sentry; (2) `invalidate_upsampling_cache()` on line 73 will compute a different key than what was stored by another process, so invalidation silently fails. Use a deterministic serialization like `','.join(map(str, sorted(project_ids)))` instead.

title: Substring match on query produces false positives for negated error type filters
body: `_is_error_focused_query` checks `"event.type:error" in query` on the lowercased query string. This will incorrectly match negated queries like `!event.type:error` or `event.type:[error, transaction]`, causing upsampling to be applied to queries that are not exclusively about errors. The result would be inflated counts for non-error events. A proper check should parse the query or at minimum verify the token is not preceded by a negation operator.

title: Upsampling eligibility check uses outer `dataset` variable instead of `scoped_dataset` parameter
body: Inside `_get_event_stats`, the call to `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` uses the outer closure variable `dataset` rather than the `scoped_dataset` parameter. In the dashboard widget split logic (lines 362-380), `_get_event_stats` is called with a different dataset (e.g., `discover` is passed as `split_dataset`). The upsampling decision will be based on the original request dataset rather than the actual dataset being queried, potentially applying upsampling transformations to the wrong dataset or missing them when the dataset is switched.

title: Column transformation produces aliased output that may break downstream consumers expecting original column name
body: `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` replaces `count()` with `upsampled_count() as count`. However, if the original column was already aliased (e.g., `count() as error_count`), it won't match the exact string `count()` and won't be transformed. Conversely, the hardcoded alias `as count` may conflict with query result parsing that expects the column under a different name. The transformation doesn't handle `count()` when it appears as part of a larger expression or with different casing/aliasing patterns that the query builder might produce.

title: upsampled_count uses toInt64(sum(sample_weight)) which truncates fractional weights
body: The `upsampled_count` SnQL function wraps `sum(sample_weight)` in `toInt64()`. If `sample_weight` is stored as a fractional value (e.g., 0.1 for a 10% sample rate), the sum across events would be a small float that gets truncated to 0 or an incorrect integer. If it's stored as the inverse (e.g., 10), then summing works but `toInt64` still truncates any fractional remainder from mixed sample rates within the same bucket. The rounding behavior should be explicit (e.g., `round()` before cast) to avoid silent data loss.

title: Git submodule reference accidentally committed to repository
body: A file `sentry-repo` containing a git subproject commit reference (`Subproject commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a`) has been added. This appears to be an accidental commit of a git submodule or a stale reference. This file should not be in the repository and will cause confusion or build issues.

title: Linear scan of allowlist for each project ID
body: `all(project_id in allowlist for project_id in project_ids)` performs an O(n) list membership check for each project. If the allowlist grows large, this becomes O(n*m). Converting the allowlist to a set first (`allowlist_set = set(allowlist)`) would make each lookup O(1).

title: No test for the caching behavior or cache invalidation in is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects
body: The test file only tests the helper functions (`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `_is_error_focused_query`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`, `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling`) but does not test `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` which contains the caching logic. Given the hash-based cache key bug, having a test that verifies cache consistency (set, get, invalidate) would have caught the non-deterministic hash issue.

title: Factory sets sample_rate but SnQL function references sample_weight column
body: `_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` sets `normalized_data["sample_rate"]` from the error sampling context, but the `upsampled_count` SnQL function in discover.py aggregates over `Column("sample_weight")`. If the event processing pipeline does not separately derive `sample_weight` from `sample_rate` (e.g., as 1/sample_rate), tests using this factory may not produce the expected `sample_weight` values, leading to incorrect test assertions or masking bugs in the actual data pipeline.

title: Cache key uses Python's `hash()` which is randomized per-process, making the cache ineffective across workers
body: The cache key is built using `hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))`. Since Python 3.3, `hash()` for strings and tuples is randomized per-process via PYTHONHASHSEED. In a multi-worker deployment (e.g., gunicorn, uwsgi), each worker will compute a different hash for the same project IDs, so cache entries written by one worker will never be found by another. This completely defeats the stated performance optimization goal. Use a deterministic hash like `hashlib.md5` or simply join the sorted IDs into a string key.

title: Substring check for `event.type:error` matches negated queries, causing incorrect upsampling
body: `_is_error_focused_query` checks `if "event.type:error" in query` using a naive substring match. A query like `!event.type:error` (which explicitly excludes errors) or `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction` would still match this substring. This would incorrectly apply the `upsampled_count()` transformation to queries that include non-error events or exclude errors entirely, producing wrong counts. The check needs to be aware of negation and boolean operators, or at minimum verify the token is not preceded by `!`.

title: Git submodule file accidentally committed at repository root
body: A file named `sentry-repo` containing `Subproject commit a5d290951def...` was added at the repository root. This appears to be an accidentally committed git submodule reference (likely from running a command inside a nested clone). It will cause confusion for other developers and CI systems, and should be removed from the PR.

title: Linear scan of allowlist for each project ID is O(n*m)
body: `all(project_id in allowlist for project_id in project_ids)` performs a linear scan of the `allowlist` list for every project ID. If the allowlist grows large (hundreds or thousands of entries) and queries include many projects, this becomes O(n*m) per call. Since this is called on every stats request (before the cache check returns), converting `allowlist` to a `set` first would make each lookup O(1).

title: `upsampled_count()` sums `sample_weight` but events without the field will silently produce undercounts
body: The `upsampled_count` SnQL function computes `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`. In ClickHouse, `sum()` skips NULL values. If any event in an allowlisted project lacks a `sample_weight` value (e.g., events ingested before the feature was enabled, or events from SDKs that don't send `client_sample_rate`), those events will be silently excluded from the count rather than counted as 1. This produces an undercount without any indication to the user. A `COALESCE(sample_weight, 1)` or similar fallback would be safer.

title: Upsampling eligibility is checked against the outer `dataset` variable, not the `scoped_dataset` actually used for the query
body: Inside `_get_event_stats`, `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` is called with the outer `dataset` (captured from the enclosing `get` method). However, when called via `get_event_stats_factory`, the `scoped_dataset` parameter can differ from `dataset` (e.g., when the dashboard widget split logic passes `discover` as `split_dataset` while the original `dataset` might be something else). This means the upsampling decision could be based on the wrong dataset, potentially applying or skipping the transform incorrectly.

title: Integration tests mock `options` but not the cache, so cached results from one test may leak into another
body: The test class mocks `sentry.api.helpers.error_upsampling.options` but does not clear or mock the cache used in `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`. If tests run in sequence and share the same cache backend, a cached eligibility result from one test (e.g., `test_error_upsampling_with_allowlisted_projects` caching `True`) could be returned in a subsequent test that expects a different result (e.g., `test_error_upsampling_with_partial_allowlist`), causing flaky or incorrect test outcomes. The cache should be cleared in `setUp` or the cache layer should be mocked.

title: fetch_error_details zips error_ids with events.values() which can misalign when events are missing
body: In `fetch_error_details`, `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)` returns a dict that may have fewer entries than `node_ids` if some events are not found. The code then does `zip(error_ids, events.values())`, which pairs error_ids positionally with whatever values exist in the dict. If a middle event is missing from nodestore, subsequent error_ids will be paired with the wrong event data. For example, if error_ids=[a,b,c] and only events for a and c exist, the zip produces (a, data_a) and (b, data_c), attributing c's data to b. The fix is to iterate over node_ids and look up each one in the events dict individually, e.g., `for event_id, node_id in zip(error_ids, node_ids): data = events.get(node_id)`.

title: Cross-validation of age/timestamp uses truthiness check, failing when value is 0
body: In `validate_timestamp`, the check `if self.initial_data.get('age')` uses truthiness, meaning an `age` value of 0 (which is valid per the spec — a report generated 0ms ago) would be treated as absent, allowing both `age=0` and `timestamp` to coexist without triggering the mutual exclusion validation. The same issue exists in `validate_age` with `self.initial_data.get('timestamp')` when timestamp is 0. Use `is not None` or check key presence with `'age' in self.initial_data` instead.

title: TableWidgetVisualization rendered with hardcoded empty data when feature flag is enabled
body: When the `use-table-widget-visualization` feature flag is enabled, the code renders `<TableWidgetVisualization columns={[]} tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}} />` — always an empty table regardless of the actual `result.data` and `result.meta` available in scope. This means any organization with this feature flag enabled will see blank tables instead of their dashboard data. The actual data from `result.data` and `result.meta` should be passed through.

title: Dead code: _handle_regex_match defined but never used in parametrize_w_experiments
body: After removing `ParameterizationRegexExperiment`, the local function `_handle_regex_match` inside `parametrize_w_experiments` (lines 335-343) is defined but never called. It was previously used in the `else` branch for regex experiments. This is dead code that should be removed to avoid confusion.

title: analytics.record uses request.user.id which may fail for org auth token requests
body: The `analytics.record` call at line 85 accesses `request.user.id` unconditionally. However, this endpoint supports org auth token authentication (checked later at line 137 with `is_org_auth_token_auth(request.auth)`). When authenticated via an org auth token, `request.user` may be an `AnonymousUser` or a special token user that doesn't have a standard `id` attribute, potentially causing an `AttributeError`. The analytics event definition marks `user_id` as `required=False`, so it should be conditionally included only when a real user is present.

title: get_environment_info calls get_recommended_event() for each issue, which may be expensive
body: `get_environment_info` is called for every issue in the PR comment list (up to 5 issues from `get_top_5_issues_by_count`). Each call invokes `issue.get_recommended_event()` which likely performs database queries or snuba queries to find the recommended event. This happens synchronously during PR comment generation, potentially adding significant latency. Consider caching or batching these lookups, or making this information optional with a timeout.

title: age field lacks min_value constraint allowing negative values
body: The `age` field is defined as `serializers.IntegerField(required=False)` without a `min_value` constraint. Per the Reporting API spec, `age` represents milliseconds since the report was generated and should be non-negative. A negative age value would pass validation but is semantically invalid. Add `min_value=0` to match the constraint already applied to `timestamp`.

title: zip(error_ids, events.values()) does not guarantee correct ID-to-data mapping
body: In `fetch_error_details`, `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)` returns a dict keyed by node_id. Using `zip(error_ids, events.values())` assumes the dict values are returned in the same order as the requested `error_ids`, but dict ordering depends on the internal implementation of `get_multi` and is not guaranteed to match the request order. This can silently associate error titles/messages with the wrong error IDs. The correct approach is to iterate over `node_ids` and look up each key individually: `for node_id, event_id in zip(node_ids, error_ids): data = events.get(node_id)`.

title: Mutual exclusion validation for age/timestamp uses truthiness instead of key presence
body: `validate_timestamp` checks `self.initial_data.get("age")` and `validate_age` checks `self.initial_data.get("timestamp")`. These are truthiness checks, so if `age` is 0 or `timestamp` is 0 (both valid values per the field definitions), the mutual exclusion validation is silently bypassed. A report with both `age: 0` and `timestamp: 123` would pass validation despite violating the spec's constraint that only one may be present. The checks should use `"age" in self.initial_data` and `"timestamp" in self.initial_data` respectively.

title: Feature-flagged TableWidgetVisualization renders hardcoded empty data, discarding actual query results
body: When the `use-table-widget-visualization` feature flag is enabled, the code renders `<TableWidgetVisualization columns={[]} tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}} />`, completely ignoring the actual `result.data`, `result.meta`, `fields`, `fieldAliases`, and other props that are available in scope. Users with this feature flag enabled will see an empty table instead of their dashboard widget data. This appears to be unfinished placeholder code that should not be shipped behind a flag that could be enabled.

title: Analytics event recorded before feature flag check, inflating metrics with rejected requests
body: `analytics.record("preprod_artifact.api.assemble", ...)` is called unconditionally at the top of the `post` method, before the feature flag check on line 88. If the feature is not enabled, the request is rejected with a 404, but the analytics event has already been recorded. This inflates usage metrics with requests that were never actually served. The analytics call should be moved after the feature flag check.

title: get_environment_info calls issue.get_recommended_event() which may trigger a database/nodestore query per issue
body: `get_environment_info` is called for each issue in the PR comment list (inside a list comprehension in `get_comment_body`). `issue.get_recommended_event()` likely performs a database or nodestore lookup. For PRs with many associated issues, this results in N additional queries. Consider batching or caching this lookup, or at minimum ensuring it doesn't cause N+1 query problems in production.

title: zip(error_ids, events.values()) may misalign when some events are missing from nodestore
body: In `fetch_error_details`, `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)` returns a dict containing only the found entries. If some node_ids are not found (data is None or key is absent), `events.values()` will have fewer elements than `error_ids`, and `zip` will silently pair the wrong `event_id` with the wrong `data`. For example, if error_ids is ['a','b','c'] and only 'a' and 'c' are found, the zip will pair 'a' with a's data and 'b' with c's data. The code should iterate over `node_ids` and look up each one individually, or zip `error_ids` with a list built by looking up each node_id in the returned dict.

title: Feature-flagged TableWidgetVisualization renders empty table instead of actual data
body: When the `use-table-widget-visualization` feature flag is enabled, the code renders `<TableWidgetVisualization columns={[]} tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}} />` with hardcoded empty data, completely ignoring the actual `result.data`, `result.meta`, `fields`, `eventView`, etc. that are available in scope. Users with this feature flag enabled will see an empty table instead of their dashboard widget data. The actual table data (result.data, result.meta, fields) should be passed to the component.

title: Validation of age/timestamp mutual exclusion fails when age=0
body: In `validate_timestamp`, the check `if self.initial_data.get("age")` uses truthiness. If a report contains both `age: 0` and `timestamp: <value>`, `self.initial_data.get("age")` returns `0` which is falsy, so the validation incorrectly passes. The same issue exists in `validate_age` with `self.initial_data.get("timestamp")` if timestamp could be 0 (it has min_value=0). The checks should use `"age" in self.initial_data` or `self.initial_data.get("age") is not None` to correctly detect field presence.

title: Analytics event name changed from 'replay.view_html' to 'replay.view-html' breaking existing tracking
body: The analytics event name was changed from `'replay.view_html'` to `'replay.view-html'`. Any existing dashboards, alerts, or data pipelines that reference the old event name `replay.view_html` will stop receiving data. The corresponding entry in `replayAnalyticsEvents.tsx` was updated to `'replay.view-html'`, but this is still a breaking change for downstream consumers of analytics data. Consider whether this rename is intentional and if any migration or dual-emission period is needed.

title: get_environment_info calls get_recommended_event() per issue which may be expensive
body: `get_environment_info` is called for each issue in `get_comment_body` (via `get_merged_pr_single_issue_template`). The method calls `issue.get_recommended_event()` which likely involves a database query or Snuba query per issue. For PRs with many linked issues (up to the top 5), this adds N additional queries in a webhook delivery task that already has a 300-second processing deadline. If `get_recommended_event` is expensive, this could cause timeouts.

title: get_request_data mutates the input error_events list via in-place sort
body: `get_request_data` calls `error_events.sort(key=lambda x: x["timestamp"])` which mutates the caller's list in place. While currently the list is freshly created by `fetch_error_details` and not reused, this is a latent bug if the function is ever called with a shared or reused list. Using `sorted(error_events, key=...)` would avoid the mutation.

title: Analytics event recorded before feature flag check
body: The `analytics.record("preprod_artifact.api.assemble", ...)` call is made before the feature flag check `features.has("organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble", ...)`. This means analytics events are recorded even for organizations that don't have the feature enabled and will receive a 404. If the intent is to track only successful/authorized usage, the analytics call should be moved after the feature flag check.

title: KeyError if `integration.metadata` lacks `sender` key
body: The expression `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` will raise a `KeyError` (resulting in a 500 error) if the integration's metadata does not contain a `sender` key or if `sender` does not contain a `login` key. The `sender` field is only populated via webhook processing of the `installation` event. If the webhook was not received or processed (e.g., due to a timing issue, network failure, or if the integration was created through a different path), this line will crash instead of showing the user-friendly error page. Use `.get()` with a fallback or wrap in a try/except to handle this gracefully.

title: Unhandled exception from `get_user_info` propagates as 500
body: `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` makes an HTTP request to GitHub's API. If this call raises an exception (network timeout, GitHub API error, connection refused, etc.), the exception is unhandled and will bubble up as a 500 Internal Server Error instead of returning the user-friendly error page via `error()`. The surrounding code only checks whether `"login"` is in the returned dict, but doesn't protect against the call itself failing.

title: `redirect_uri` is not URL-encoded in the OAuth authorize URL
body: The `redirect_uri` value (e.g., `http://testserver/extensions/github/setup/`) is interpolated directly into the query string without percent-encoding. Characters like `:` and `/` in the redirect URI should be encoded per RFC 3986 for query parameter values. While many OAuth providers tolerate this, it can cause parsing issues with certain proxies or stricter implementations. Use `urllib.parse.urlencode` or `quote` to properly encode the parameters.

title: `test_installation_not_found` actually tests state mismatch, not a 404 from GitHub
body: The test uses `state=ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05` which does not match the pipeline signature (which is `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3` based on other tests). This means the request fails at the state validation check (line 412 of integration.py) and never reaches the `get_installation_info` call that would return the mocked 404. The test passes but validates the wrong code path — it tests state mismatch rather than the installation-not-found scenario it claims to test.

title: Missing `redirect_uri` in OAuth token exchange request
body: The OAuth2 token exchange (lines 416-420) does not include the `redirect_uri` parameter, even though it was provided in the authorization request (line 408). Per RFC 6749 §4.1.3, `redirect_uri` is REQUIRED in the token request if it was included in the authorization request. While GitHub's implementation currently tolerates this omission, it violates the OAuth2 spec and could break if GitHub tightens validation. Include the same `redirect_uri` value in the token exchange data.

title: KeyError when integration metadata lacks 'sender' key
body: The expression `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` will raise a `KeyError` if the integration's metadata does not contain a "sender" key. In `build_integration`, the "sender" key is only added conditionally (`if state.get("sender")`), so any integration created without sender information (e.g., older installations or those created via a different path) will cause an unhandled 500 error when a user attempts to reinstall or when this code path is reached. This should use `.get()` with a fallback or check for key existence before accessing.

title: Unhandled exception from get_user_info can cause 500 error
body: `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` is called without any exception handling. If the GitHub API returns an error, times out, or the access token is invalid in a way that causes an exception (rather than a response without 'login'), the user will see a raw 500 error instead of the graceful error page. This call should be wrapped in a try/except that returns the same `error(request, self.active_organization)` response on failure.

title: redirect_uri is not URL-encoded in the OAuth authorize URL
body: The `redirect_uri` value is interpolated directly into the query string without URL-encoding: `f"...&redirect_uri={redirect_uri}"`. Since `redirect_uri` is a full URL (e.g., `http://testserver/extensions/github/setup/`), characters like `:`, `/` should be percent-encoded per RFC 6749 Section 3.1.2. Some OAuth providers or intermediary proxies may reject or misparse the request. Use `urllib.parse.quote` or `urlencode` to properly encode the parameter.

title: OAuth state parameter compared with non-constant-time equality
body: The state parameter (used as CSRF protection in the OAuth flow) is compared using `!=` which is not constant-time. While the practical exploitability over a network is low, security best practice for comparing secret or token-like values is to use `hmac.compare_digest()` to prevent timing side-channel attacks.

title: Webhook HMAC signature likely does not match modified payload
body: In `test_github_user_mismatch`, the webhook event payload is modified (`webhook_event["sender"]["login"] = "attacker"`) but the HMAC signature `sha1=d184e6717f8bfbcc291ebc8c0756ee446c6c9486` is hardcoded from the original `INSTALLATION_EVENT_EXAMPLE`. If webhook signature verification is enforced, this request should be rejected with a 403, not return 204. Either the signature needs to be recomputed for the modified payload, or the test is not actually exercising the intended code path (the integration may be created via a different mechanism than assumed).

title: KeyError when integration metadata lacks 'sender' field
body: The expression `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` will raise a `KeyError` if the integration's metadata does not contain a `"sender"` key. The `build_integration` method only sets `metadata["sender"]` when `state.get("sender")` is truthy, so integrations created before this change (or from webhook payloads missing the sender field) will not have this key. This code path is reached when an Integration exists but has no OrganizationIntegration (e.g., a stale integration from a previously deleted org-integration). The result is an unhandled 500 error instead of the intended graceful error page. A guard such as `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")` should be used, and if it's missing, the request should be rejected with the error page.

title: redirect_uri is not percent-encoded in the OAuth authorize URL
body: The `redirect_uri` value (e.g., `http://testserver/extensions/github/setup/`) is interpolated directly into the query string without URL-encoding. Per RFC 6749 §3.1.2, the redirect_uri parameter value must be percent-encoded when included in the authorization request. Characters like `:`, `/` in the URI can cause parsing ambiguity with certain HTTP clients, proxies, or if GitHub tightens their parsing. Use `urllib.parse.quote(redirect_uri, safe='')` or `urlencode` to properly encode the parameter.

title: Pipeline state fetch may return None, leading to confusing comparison semantics
body: `pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user")` can return `None` if the pipeline state has expired or was never set (e.g., user opens the GitHubInstallation step URL directly without going through OAuthLoginView). While the comparison `None != some_login` would correctly evaluate to True and return an error, if the metadata also lacks `"sender"` (see the KeyError issue above), the combination produces a 500 rather than a clear rejection. An explicit None-check with an early error return would make the intent clearer and avoid relying on the downstream KeyError as an implicit guard.

title: Exception from safe_urlopen is not caught, could produce a 500
body: If `safe_urlopen` raises an unexpected exception (e.g., a DNS resolution failure that propagates despite the 'safe' wrapper, or a misconfigured URL causing a ValueError), it will not be caught by the `try/except` block that only wraps `safe_urlread`. This would result in an unhandled 500 error during the OAuth token exchange step. Wrapping the entire token exchange (lines 423–429) in the try/except would make the error handling more robust.

title: No test for the case where integration metadata is missing 'sender' key
body: The test suite covers the happy path (sender matches) and the mismatch path (sender differs), but does not test the scenario where `integration.metadata` has no `"sender"` key at all. This is the case that triggers the KeyError bug on line 503 of the integration file. A test that creates an Integration without sender metadata and verifies a graceful error response (rather than a 500) would catch this regression.

title: Default value `timezone.now()` is evaluated once at class definition time, not per-instance
body: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` evaluates `timezone.now()` once when the module is first imported, and that single timestamp becomes the default for all future instances. Every `AssignmentSource` created without an explicit `queued` argument will share the same stale timestamp (the time of module import). The fix is to use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` from the `dataclasses` module, which calls the function fresh for each instance. While the `queued` field isn't currently used in comparison logic in this PR, it will produce incorrect data and will silently break any future logic that relies on it.

title: timezone.now() default is evaluated once at class definition time
body: The default value `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once when the module is first imported, not at each instance creation. All `AssignmentSource` instances created without an explicit `queued` argument will share the same timestamp (the time the module was loaded). This is a classic Python default-argument pitfall. The fix is to use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` from `dataclasses`. While `queued` is not currently used in any logic, this produces misleading data and will become a real bug if the field is ever used for staleness checks or debugging.

title: datetime object in task kwargs may not be JSON-serializable
body: `assignment_source.to_dict()` (via `dataclasses.asdict`) produces a dict containing a `datetime` object for the `queued` field. This dict is passed as a Celery task kwarg (`assignment_source_dict`). If Celery is configured with JSON serialization (which is Sentry's default), `datetime` objects are not JSON-serializable and the task will fail to enqueue with a `TypeError`. The `queued` field should be converted to an ISO-8601 string in `to_dict()`, or omitted from serialization entirely since it is not used downstream.

title: queued field is never consumed by any logic
body: The `queued` timestamp field is stored and serialized but never read or compared anywhere in this PR or its call sites. If it is intended for future staleness/TTL checks, that logic is missing; if it is purely informational, it adds serialization risk (see the JSON issue) and maintenance burden with no current benefit. Consider removing it or documenting its intended future use.

title: Abstract method sync_status_outbound signature change may break subclasses
body: The `sync_status_outbound` abstract method now includes an explicit `assignment_source` parameter before `**kwargs`. Any concrete subclass that overrides this method with a fixed parameter list (no `**kwargs`) will raise a `TypeError` at call time when the new keyword argument is passed. While the parameter has a default value, callers may begin passing it explicitly. All downstream implementations should be audited to confirm they accept `**kwargs` or have been updated.

title: Mutable default value `timezone.now()` evaluated once at class definition time
body: The default value `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once when the module is first imported, not at each instance creation. This means every `AssignmentSource` created without an explicit `queued` argument will share the same stale timestamp from import time. The correct pattern is `queued: datetime = field(default_factory=timezone.now)` (importing `field` from `dataclasses`). While the `queued` field isn't currently used for logic, it's serialized via `to_dict()` and passed through task kwargs, so any downstream consumer or future time-based logic (e.g., TTL, ordering, debugging) will see incorrect timestamps.

title: Passing `assignment_source` kwarg to `sync_assignee_outbound` may break concrete implementations without `**kwargs`
body: The call `installation.sync_assignee_outbound(external_issue, user, assign=assign, assignment_source=parsed_assignment_source)` passes `assignment_source` as a keyword argument. While the abstract method signature includes `**kwargs`, any concrete integration implementation that overrides `sync_assignee_outbound` with a fixed parameter list (no `**kwargs`) will raise a `TypeError` at runtime. This is a potential backward-compatibility break for third-party or less common integration implementations.

title: `from_dict` does not handle non-datetime `queued` values from deserialization
body: When `AssignmentSource` is round-tripped through `to_dict()` and `from_dict()` (as happens via Celery task kwargs), the `queued` field will be a string (ISO format) rather than a `datetime` object. The dataclass constructor does not enforce types, so `from_dict` will silently produce an instance with a string `queued` field. If any code later compares or operates on `queued` as a datetime, it will fail. Consider parsing the `queued` field in `from_dict` or excluding it from serialization if it's not needed downstream.

title: Test does not verify that `queued` reflects instance creation time
body: The `test_to_dict` test only asserts `result.get('queued') is not None`, which passes even with the stale module-level `timezone.now()` default. A test creating two instances at different times and asserting their `queued` values differ (or that `queued` is close to `timezone.now()` at creation time) would catch the default-value bug.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is abstract and cannot be instantiated
body: MetricAlertDetectorHandler now extends StatefulDetectorHandler but does not implement the required abstract methods: `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. The `Detector.detector_handler` property (detector.py line 86) calls `group_type.detector_handler(self)`, which attempts to instantiate this class. If any Detector is created with type `metric_alert_fire`, Python will raise `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler with abstract methods ...` at runtime. The previous implementation was concrete (returned an empty list).

title: PriorityLevel(new_status) may raise ValueError if enum values don't align
body: On line 300, `PriorityLevel(new_status)` converts a `DetectorPriorityLevel` to a `PriorityLevel` by numeric value. If any `DetectorPriorityLevel` member (other than OK, which is handled by the branch above) has a numeric value that does not correspond to a `PriorityLevel` member, this will raise a `ValueError` at runtime. This conversion should be validated or an explicit mapping should be used to ensure safe conversion between the two enum types.

title: Docstring still says 'returns a list' after changing to dict
body: The docstring for `StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate` (line 230-232) reads 'Evaluates a given data packet and returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`' but the method now returns `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]`. This is misleading for future readers.

title: Test uses wrong value for group_2 occurrence construction
body: In `test_state_results_multi_group`, the data packet specifies `{"group_1": 6, "group_2": 10}` (line 177), but the expected occurrence for group_2 is built with value `6` (line 191: `build_mock_occurrence_and_event(detector.detector_handler, "group_2", 6, PriorityLevel.HIGH)`). title: Docstring still says "returns a list" after signature changed to return a dict
body: The `evaluate` method's docstring reads "Evaluates a given data packet and returns a list of `DetectorEvaluationResult`" but the method now returns `dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult]`. This will mislead anyone reading the docstring about the return type.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler cannot be instantiated — abstract methods not implemented
body: `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` extends `StatefulDetectorHandler` but does not implement any of its abstract methods (`counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, `build_occurrence_and_event_data`). title: Test passes wrong value (6 instead of 10) for group_2 occurrence, masking potential bugs

title: Modified config copy is discarded; original unmodified config is returned
body: In `get_monitor_environment_context`, lines 160-162 create a copy of `monitor_environment.monitor.config` and replace the `schedule_type` value with its human-readable display string. However, line 168 returns `monitor_environment.monitor.config` (the original, unmodified dict) instead of the local `config` variable that was modified. The result is that the `schedule_type` in the monitor context sent to Kafka will contain the raw enum value rather than the display string, and the copy + modification on lines 160-162 is dead code. This is a pre-existing bug carried over from `mark_failed.py`, but since this PR is reorganizing this code, it would be a good time to fix it by using `"config": config` on line 168.

title: Modified `config` copy is never used; original unmodified config is returned
body: In `get_monitor_environment_context`, a copy of `monitor_environment.monitor.config` is made and its `schedule_type` key is replaced with the human-readable display value. However, the return dict on line 168 uses `monitor_environment.monitor.config` (the original, unmodified dict) instead of the local `config` variable. body: In `get_monitor_environment_context`, a copy of `monitor_environment.monitor.config` is made into `config` (line 160) and its `schedule_type` key is replaced with the human-readable display value (line 162). However, the returned dictionary on line 168 uses `monitor_environment.monitor.config` (the original, unmodified dict) instead of the local `config` variable. title: Inconsistent metric tag name: 'shards' vs 'shard'
body: Line 185 uses `tags={"shard": shard_tag}` for the `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` metric, but line 199 uses `tags={"shards": shard_tag}` (plural) for `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce`. This inconsistency makes it harder to query and correlate these metrics in dashboards and alerts, and is likely a typo. One of them should be renamed to match the other.

title: time.sleep(0.1) is ineffective due to monkeypatch, making test potentially flaky
body: The test monkeypatches `time.sleep` to a no-op (`lambda _: None`) at line 15, then calls `time.sleep(0.1)` at line 62 with a comment saying 'Give flusher threads time to process after drift change'. Because `time.sleep` is monkeypatched, this call does nothing—the test does not actually wait. The test relies on the flusher thread picking up the new `current_drift` value before `step.join()` sets the `stopped` flag, which is a race condition. Under CI load, the flusher thread may not be scheduled between the drift change and `join()`, causing intermittent test failures. A real sleep (e.g., using the original `time.sleep` saved before monkeypatching, or `threading.Event.wait`) should be used here.

title: Dead code: _create_process_for_shard is defined but never called
body: The method `_create_process_for_shard` (lines 127–132) is defined but never invoked anywhere in the codebase. It appears to be a leftover from an earlier design that considered per-shard process restarts. This dead code adds confusion about the intended restart granularity and should be removed.

title: New SpansBuffer created on every process restart without closing the old one
body: Each call to `_create_process_for_shards` (including restarts triggered by `_ensure_processes_alive`) creates a new `SpansBuffer(shards)` at line 93 and stores it in `self.buffers[process_index]`, replacing the previous buffer object. If `SpansBuffer` holds Redis connections, client instances, or other resources, these are silently leaked on each restart. With up to `MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS = 10` restarts per process, this could accumulate leaked connections. The old buffer should be explicitly closed or its resources released before replacement.

title: record_stored_segments called on flusher-process buffers instead of the main ingestion buffer
body: In `submit()`, `record_stored_segments()` is called on each buffer in `self.buffers` (line 269–270). These are separate `SpansBuffer` instances created for the flusher subprocesses. However, spans are written via `process_batch` using the original `buffer` passed to `__init__` (in factory.py line 67). If `record_stored_segments` relies on local state updated during `process_spans` (e.g., in-memory tracking of recently stored segments), calling it on different buffer instances that never received `process_spans` calls will produce incorrect results. This was not an issue in the previous single-buffer design where the same object was used for both writing and flushing.

title: Inconsistent metric tag name: "shards" vs "shard"
body: In `SpanFlusher.main`, the `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` timer uses tag key `"shard"` (line 185) while `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` uses tag key `"shards"` (line 199). This inconsistency will make it difficult to query or correlate these metrics in dashboards and alerts, as they use different tag names for the same dimension.

title: join() passes full timeout to next_step, leaving no time for process cleanup
body: In `join()`, `self.next_step.join(timeout)` is called with the full timeout value. The deadline is computed before this call, but if `next_step.join` consumes the entire timeout, the subsequent loop over processes will immediately break (remaining_time <= 0) without calling `process.terminate()` on any of them. With multiple processes this is more likely to be an issue than with the previous single-process design. The timeout should be split or `next_step.join` should be given a portion of the total timeout.

title: time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op due to monkeypatch, making test potentially flaky
body: The test monkeypatches `time.sleep` to a no-op on line 15 (`monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`), then calls `time.sleep(0.1)` on line 62 with the comment 'Give flusher threads time to process after drift change'. Since `time.sleep` is globally patched, this call does nothing and does not actually give the flusher threads any real time. The test currently passes because the flusher's own `time.sleep(1)` is also patched (making it spin fast), but this makes the test fragile and the comment misleading. If the flusher logic changes to not spin, this test could become flaky.

title: _create_process_for_shard is dead code
body: The method `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard: int)` is defined at line 127 but is never called anywhere in the codebase. It appears to be leftover from an earlier design iteration where individual shards could be restarted independently. This dead code adds confusion about the intended restart semantics.

title: Backpressure from any single process blocks all shards
body: In `submit()`, if ANY process's `backpressure_since` exceeds the threshold, `MessageRejected` is raised, blocking insertion for ALL shards. With multiple processes each handling different shards, a single slow shard now blocks progress for all other shards. In the previous single-process design this was unavoidable, but with the multiprocess design, healthy processes could continue flushing their shards while one is under pressure. This could cause cascading backpressure and reduce the benefit of parallelism.

title: record_stored_segments() called on flusher-internal buffers instead of the main processing buffer
body: In the old code, `self.buffer` was the same `SpansBuffer` instance used by `process_batch` to store spans via `buffer.process_spans(...)`. Now, the original `buffer` parameter passed to `SpanFlusher.__init__` is only used to read `assigned_shards` and is never stored. Instead, `self.buffers` contains new `SpansBuffer` instances created for flushing only. Calling `record_stored_segments()` on these flusher buffers is incorrect because they never store segments — the main buffer (shared with `process_batch`) does. This likely means the metric/recording that `record_stored_segments` provides is silently broken.

title: Killed processes are never joined, creating zombie processes
body: In `_ensure_processes_alive`, when a process is detected as unhealthy, `process.kill()` is called but `process.join()` is never called to reap it. On Unix, this leaves a zombie process entry in the process table. If flusher processes crash repeatedly (up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS=10 times per process index), zombie processes accumulate. Adding a `process.join(timeout=0)` or similar after `kill()` would reap the child.

title: Dead code: _create_process_for_shard method is never called
body: The method `_create_process_for_shard` (singular shard) is defined at line 127 but is never invoked anywhere in the codebase. All call sites use `_create_process_for_shards` (plural). This is dead code that should be removed to avoid confusion.

title: join() may skip terminating remaining processes when deadline expires
body: In `join()`, if `remaining_time <= 0` the code `break`s out of the entire for-loop, skipping `process.terminate()` for the current process and all subsequent processes. This means if `next_step.join(timeout)` consumes most of the timeout budget, some flusher processes may not receive `terminate()`. While daemon processes are eventually killed on interpreter exit, during graceful shutdown (e.g., in a long-running consumer), these processes could continue producing to Kafka after the consumer considers itself shut down, potentially causing duplicate segment emissions.

title: max_processes defaults to 1 from CLI but None in constructor, creating inconsistent behavior
body: The CLI option `--flusher-processes` has `default=1`, so the factory always receives an integer ≥1 from the CLI. However, `ProcessSpansStrategyFactory.__init__` declares `flusher_processes: int | None = None`, and `SpanFlusher.__init__` uses `max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` — meaning if someone constructs the factory programmatically without passing `flusher_processes` (getting `None`), the flusher spawns one process per shard instead of defaulting to 1. This inconsistency between the CLI default and the programmatic default could surprise callers and should be aligned (e.g., default to 1 in the factory as well).

title: Strategy close() shuts down shared FixedQueuePool, breaking rebalance
body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(), which terminates all worker threads and shuts down the queues. However, the FixedQueuePool is owned by ResultsStrategyFactory and shared across strategy instances. When arroyo triggers a rebalance, it calls close() on the old strategy and then create_with_partitions() to create a new one. The new strategy receives the same (now dead) FixedQueuePool whose workers have all exited. Any messages submitted to the new strategy will sit in the queues forever, never processed, and offsets will never be committed. The pool should either be recreated per strategy, or close() should not shut down the pool (leaving that to the factory's shutdown()).

title: join() does not wait for in-flight work to complete before shutting down
body: The join() method simply calls close(), which sets the shutdown_event, joins the commit thread, and then calls queue_pool.shutdown(). In FixedQueuePool.shutdown(), worker.shutdown is set to True before q.shutdown(immediate=False) is called. A worker that finishes its current item will see self.shutdown == True and exit the while loop without draining remaining items from the queue. This means items that were submitted but not yet processed are silently dropped. The arroyo contract for join() is to wait until all pending work is done. The shutdown sequence should first call q.shutdown(immediate=False) to signal no more items, then let workers drain, and only then set the shutdown flag as a fallback.

title: Unbounded queues provide no backpressure despite docstring claim
body: FixedQueuePool creates queue.Queue() instances without a maxsize argument, making them unbounded. The class docstring states 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' but this is incorrect—queue.put() on an unbounded queue never blocks. If the Kafka consumer polls messages faster than workers can process them (e.g., due to a slow downstream service), memory usage will grow without bound, potentially causing OOM. A maxsize should be set, or submit() should block/reject when queues are full.

title: A single missing offset permanently blocks all subsequent commits for a partition
body: get_committable_offsets() iterates from the lowest expected offset upward and breaks at the first offset not in all_offsets. If any offset is never added to the tracker (e.g., message.value is not a BrokerValue in the exception path of submit(), or an unexpected error occurs before add_offset is called), that gap can never be filled. All subsequent offsets for that partition become uncommittable forever, causing the consumer to reprocess the entire partition from the last committed offset on every restart. There is no mechanism to detect or recover from such a gap.

title: hash() is randomized per process, so queue assignment is not stable across restarts
body: get_queue_for_group uses Python's built-in hash() on the group key string. Since Python 3.3, string hashing is randomized per process via PYTHONHASHSEED. The docstring says 'consistent hashing' but the assignment is not consistent across process restarts. If ordering guarantees depend on the same group always going to the same queue (e.g., for stateful workers or external side effects keyed by queue), this will break on restart. A deterministic hash like hashlib.md5 or zlib.crc32 should be used instead.

title: Commit loop performs one extra commit iteration after shutdown is signaled
body: In _commit_loop, self.shutdown_event.wait(1.0) returns immediately once the event is set, but the code does not check the return value before proceeding to get_committable_offsets() and commit. This means after close() sets shutdown_event, the loop body executes one more time, potentially calling commit_function after the arroyo Commit object may no longer be valid (e.g., after the consumer has been closed). The wait() return value should be checked and the loop should break if it returns True.

title: queue.ShutDown and Queue.shutdown() require Python 3.13+
body: The code uses queue.ShutDown exception and queue.Queue.shutdown() method, both of which were introduced in Python 3.13. If the project supports earlier Python versions, this will raise AttributeError at runtime. If Python 3.13+ is a hard requirement this is fine, but it should be documented or guarded.

title: _get_partition_lock has a TOCTOU race on partition_locks dictionary
body: _get_partition_lock first calls self.partition_locks.get(partition), and if None, calls self.partition_locks.setdefault(partition, threading.Lock()). While CPython's GIL makes dict.setdefault atomic, two threads could both see None from get() and both call setdefault(). The second setdefault() would return the first thread's lock, so both threads end up with the same lock—this is actually correct behavior. However, the initial get() check is redundant and the pattern is fragile; using only setdefault() would be simpler and equally correct.

title: Shutdown discards unprocessed items still in the queue
body: In `OrderedQueueWorker.run()`, the loop condition is `while not self.shutdown`. When `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` sets `worker.shutdown = True`, the worker will finish its current item and then exit the loop without draining remaining items from the queue. Even though `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` is called (which would allow `get()` to continue returning items until the queue is empty), the worker never reaches `get()` because the `while not self.shutdown` check fails first. Any items still queued will be silently lost and their offsets will never be marked complete, potentially blocking future offset commits for those partitions.

title: Race condition iterating `all_offsets` keys while other threads add new partitions
body: `get_committable_offsets()` calls `list(self.all_offsets.keys())` without holding any lock. Concurrently, `add_offset()` on a new partition triggers `defaultdict.__getitem__` which inserts a new key into `self.all_offsets`. In CPython, modifying a dict while another thread is iterating its keys (which `list(dict.keys())` does internally) can raise `RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration`. This can crash the commit loop, preventing any further offset commits.

title: Unbounded queues provide no backpressure, risking OOM under load
body: `queue.Queue()` is created without a `maxsize`, making it unbounded. The class docstring claims 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' but no backpressure mechanism exists. If messages arrive faster than workers can process them (e.g., during a downstream outage), queues grow without limit. The `submit()` method never raises `MessageRejected` (arroyo's backpressure signal), so the consumer will continue polling and submitting indefinitely. Consider setting a `maxsize` and raising `MessageRejected` from `submit()` when the queue is full.

title: Failed messages are marked as complete and committed, preventing retry
body: In `OrderedQueueWorker.run()`, the `finally` block calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)` regardless of whether `result_processor` succeeded or raised an exception. This means messages that fail processing are still marked as done and their offsets will be committed. If processing fails due to a transient error (database timeout, network issue), the message is permanently lost with no retry. The error is only logged. Consider not completing the offset on failure, or implementing a retry/DLQ mechanism.

title: AssertionError in submit() can cause offset to never be tracked, blocking partition commits
body: In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()`, `assert isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue)` is used. If Python is run with optimizations (`-O` flag), assertions are stripped, and `message.value` might not be a `BrokerValue`. The subsequent access to `message.value.partition` would raise `AttributeError`, caught by the `except Exception` block. In the except block, `isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue)` would be False, so the offset is never added/completed. If this happens for a message whose offset was already added by a prior code path or expected by the offset tracker, it could create a gap that blocks all future commits for that partition. Use an explicit `isinstance` check with proper error handling instead of `assert`.

title: Python's `hash()` is randomized across process restarts, weakening ordering guarantees after rebalance
body: `get_queue_for_group` uses `hash(group_key) % self.num_queues`. Python's string hash is randomized per process (PYTHONHASHSEED). After a consumer restart or partition rebalance, the same group_key will likely map to a different queue index. While ordering within a single process lifetime is preserved, if there are any assumptions about consistent queue assignment across restarts (e.g., for debugging or metrics), this could be surprising. Consider using a stable hash like `hashlib.md5(group_key.encode()).hexdigest()` or `zlib.crc32` for deterministic assignment.

title: `join()` calls `close()` which may be called twice in arroyo lifecycle
body: Arroyo's `StreamProcessor` typically calls `close()` and then `join()` on a processing strategy during shutdown. Here, `join()` calls `self.close()` again, resulting in `close()` being invoked twice. The second invocation calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` on an already-shut-down pool and `self.commit_thread.join()` on an already-joined thread. While this is likely benign (join on a finished thread returns immediately), it's fragile and could mask issues if the shutdown logic becomes more complex. `join()` should only wait for completion, not re-trigger shutdown.

title: Test asserts all 3 queues are used with only 20 groups, which is probabilistic
body: `test_different_groups_distributed` asserts `len(queue_indices) == 3` for 20 group keys hashed into 3 queues. While very likely with Python's hash distribution, this is not guaranteed.
