body: ensure_loaded! can cause additional locale files to be loaded after I18n.translate has already cached a result. The LRU cache key includes only the key, current locale, and backend object id, and ensure_loaded! does not clear @cache. If a translation is looked up before its fallback locales are loaded, the cached missing string can continue to be returned even after the fallback data becomes available.

title: Non-thread-safe initialization and check of @loaded_locales
body: ensure_loaded! performs `@loaded_locales ||= []` and checks membership outside LOAD_MUTEX, while load_locale mutates the same array inside the mutex. In a multithreaded server this can race, causing lost or duplicate loaded-locale markers or reads while the array is being modified. The check/load sequence should be synchronized or use a thread-safe data structure.

title: Custom fallback list ignores stored fallback mappings and locale hierarchy
body: FallbackLocaleList subclasses Hash but overrides [] to always compute [locale, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en] without consulting stored hash entries. Any fallback mappings added by Rails or plugins will be ignored. It also does not provide standard parent-locale fallback such as fr_CA to fr unless that parent is the site default or English, which can cause avoidable missing translations.

title: No tests for fallback behavior with lazy loading and caching
body: The change introduces custom fallbacks, modifies lazy locale loading, and interacts with a global translation cache, but no specs cover these behaviors. Tests should verify fallback to default/English, loading of fallback locales outside controllers, and that cached missing translations are not served after fallback locales are loaded.

title: Translation cache key ignores dynamic fallback chain
body: The LRU cache key only contains the translation key, current locale, and backend object id. This PR makes fallback resolution depend on SiteSetting.default_locale (and always :en). If two requests use the same I18n.locale but have different default locales (for example in multisite, or after an admin changes default_locale without a full I18n cache clear), a fallback translation cached for one context can be returned for another, serving the wrong language until the cache is cleared or evicted. Include the fallback chain/default locale/site identifier in the cache key, or invalidate this cache when fallback inputs change.

title: Fallback locales are only ensured loaded for controller requests
body: I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded! is called only in ApplicationController#set_locale. The translate accelerator lazily loads only the current locale inside I18n.translate, so fallback target locales (site default and :en) are not loaded in mailers, Sidekiq jobs, rake tasks, console, middleware, or any code path that translates without passing through this controller filter. In those contexts, missing translations will not fall back and may return translation-missing strings or raise instead. Fallback locales should be ensured whenever I18n.locale is set or inside the translate path.

title: translate still assumes @loaded_locales is initialized
body: The new ensure_loaded! method initializes @loaded_locales, but translate still calls @loaded_locales.include?(config.locale) without initializing it. If any code calls I18n.translate before ensure_loaded!, reload!, or load_locale has run, this will raise NoMethodError on nil. translate should use a memoized/synchronized accessor or initialize @loaded_locales before checking it.

title: Locale-loaded flag initialization is not synchronized
body: @loaded_locales ||= [] in ensure_loaded! happens outside LOAD_MUTEX. On first concurrent use, multiple threads can race on assignment; one thread can overwrite the array after another has recorded loaded locales, causing duplicate locale loading or transient inconsistent state. Initialization and checks of @loaded_locales should be done under LOAD_MUTEX or through a synchronized memoized accessor.

title: No tests for new fallback/loading behavior
body: This PR changes global I18n fallback order, lazy locale loading, and request-time loading, but adds no specs covering: missing translations falling back to SiteSetting.default_locale and :en; loading of fallback locales outside controllers; or cache invalidation when default_locale changes. Without tests, regressions in fallback behavior or cache staleness are likely.

title: Denial cache key is not scoped by identity type
body: In Service.Check, permDenialKey is built from namespace, user identifier, action, resource name, and parent folder, but not the identity type. validateSubject permits anonymous and render-service identities, and both can have the identifier "0" (e.g. anonymous:0 and render:0). A denied anonymous check will therefore write a negative cache entry under the same key used by a render:0 check for the same resource. A subsequent renderer check can hit that denial cache entry and return Allowed:false before getRendererPermissions is evaluated, even though the renderer is hard-coded to read all dashboards/folders. Similar cross-identity denials are possible between other identity types if identifiers are not globally unique. The denial cache key should include the identity type, or renderer/anonymous checks should bypass this denial cache.

title: Denial cache key concatenation can collide
body: userPermDenialCacheKey joins namespace, userUID, action, name, and parent with underscores and no escaping. If any of these fields can contain underscores (for example user-supplied dashboard/folder UIDs), distinct authorization checks can produce the same cache key. For example, name="a" and parent="b_c" produces the same key as name="a_b" and parent="c". Because this cache stores negative authorization decisions, such a collision can cause a denial for one resource to incorrectly apply to another resource. Use an unambiguous separator/encoding, or hash length-prefixed fields.

title: Negative caching can continue denying access after permission is granted
body: Service.Check stores a denial in permDenialCache for shortCacheTTL (30 seconds) whenever the database check denies access. There is no invalidation when permissions are added or changed. If a permission is granted immediately after a denial—for example during dashboard/folder creation, permission propagation, or a read-before-write race—subsequent checks can hit the denial cache and keep rejecting the user until the TTL expires. This can reintroduce the same inability to access newly created resources that this PR is trying to fix.

title: Denial-cache test does not actually seed an allowed cached permission
body: In TestService_CacheCheck, the subtest "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" claims to prove that the denial cache overrides cached permissions, but it seeds permCache with map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}. checkPermission treats a false value as no permission, so the check would be denied even if the denial cache were ignored. To verify that an explicit denial entry overrides a cached allow, the test should seed the permission cache with true for that scope.

title: Errors from cached identity lookup are treated as cache misses
body: getCachedIdentityPermissions can return real errors from GetUserIdentifiers for user/service-account subjects, but Service.Check only proceeds with the cached path when err == nil and otherwise falls through as though it were a cache miss. It then calls getIdentityPermissions, which repeats GetUserIdentifiers. This can duplicate database work during failures, add latency, and emit misleading cache-miss metrics instead of distinguishing cache lookup failures from ordinary cache misses.

title: Denial cache key does not include identity type
body: Check builds the negative-cache key from namespace, checkReq.UserUID, action, name, and parent. UserUID is only the identifier part of the subject and does not include the identity type returned by validateSubject. Different identity types can share the same identifier, for example anonymous:0 and render:0 in the tests, or user/service-account numeric identifiers. Because the denial cache is consulted before identity-specific permission logic, a denial cached for one identity can be returned for another. For example, an anonymous denial for dashboards:read on a dashboard can cause the render service to be denied even though it is hard-coded to allow dashboard reads. Include IdentityType, or the full subject, in the denial cache key and canonicalize the identifier.

title: Denial cache key can collide because fields are joined with underscores
body: userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates namespace, user identifier, action, resource name, and parent with underscore separators and without escaping. These fields can be empty and identifiers such as dashboard/folder UIDs may contain underscores, making the boundary between fields ambiguous. Different (user, action, name, parent) tuples can therefore produce the same cache key, causing a denial entry for one tuple to incorrectly deny another tuple. Use an unambiguous key encoding, such as escaped fields, base64/hash encoding, or a separator that cannot appear in the values.

title: Cached denial can hide newly granted permissions for its TTL
body: A denied Check is stored in permDenialCache for 30 seconds. Subsequent checks hit this entry and return deny before the new logic that re-queries the database when a cached permission set lacks the requested resource. If a permission is granted or a resource is created immediately after a check was denied for the same namespace/user/action/name/parent, the user can remain denied until the TTL expires. This can still break immediate access to newly created dashboards or folders in races or with client-generated UIDs. Consider invalidating negative entries on permission changes or avoiding negative caching for create/read-after-create paths.

title: Denial-cache override test uses a deny permission instead of an allow
body: The test sets permCache to map[string]bool{'dashboards:uid:dash1': false} while the comment says it should allow access to prove the denial cache entry is used. With a false permission the request would be denied even if the denial cache were ignored, so the test does not verify that a denial-cache entry overrides a positive cached permission. The cached permission should be set to true to make the assertion meaningful.

title: Denial cache key omits identity type, allowing denials to leak between identities
body: userPermDenialCacheKey is built only from namespace, userUID, action, name, and parent folder. validateSubject permits multiple identity types, and different identities can have the same identifier string. For example, 'anonymous:0' and 'render:0' both parse to userUID "0". If an anonymous check for 'dashboards:read' on a dashboard is denied, the denial is cached under a key like ns.perm_0_dashboards:read_<dash>_. A subsequent renderer check for the same dashboard will hit this denial cache at line 117 and be denied before getRendererPermissions can return its built-in read access. The denial cache key must include the identity type (and ideally a normalized internal identity ID) to avoid cross-identity wrongful denials.

title: Cached denial can persist after permission is granted
body: When a permission check reaches the database and denies access, the result is cached in permDenialCache for shortCacheTTL (30 seconds). There is no invalidation when permissions change. If the first check for a newly created dashboard/folder happens before the new permission is visible (for example due to read-replica lag or asynchronous permission provisioning), the denial is cached. Subsequent checks within the TTL hit the denial cache and skip the database requery, leaving the creator unable to access the newly created resource for up to the TTL. This reintroduces the same class of staleness problem the PR is trying to fix.

title: Denial cache key construction is ambiguous because fields are joined with underscores
body: userPermDenialCacheKey concatenates namespace, userUID, action, name, and parent using '_' as a separator. Dashboard/folder UIDs can contain underscores, so different combinations of name and parent can produce identical cache keys. For example, name='a_b' with parent='c' yields the same key suffix as name='a' with parent='b_c'. Because this cache stores negative authorization decisions, a key collision can cause a denial for one resource/folder combination to be incorrectly applied to another resource. The key should be constructed with unambiguous escaping/encoding or by hashing the separate fields.

title: Tests do not cover denial-cache isolation by identity type or grant-after-denial behavior
body: TestService_CacheCheck only pre-seeds a denial entry for a user and checks that it denies access. It does not verify that denial entries are scoped by identity type, so it would not catch a denial for anonymous affecting the renderer identity. It also does not verify behavior when a permission is granted after a denial has been cached. Since the denial cache is a new authorization decision path, tests should cover cross-identity isolation and stale-denial scenarios.

title: Missing React key for GrafanaRuleListItem in filtered list
body: FilterViewResults maps rules to list items and computes a unique key for each rule, but in the origin === 'grafana' branch the returned GrafanaRuleListItem does not receive a key prop. React will emit missing-key warnings and may reconcile list items by position, which can cause wrong or retained component state, such as open dropdowns or silence drawers, when the filtered list updates.

title: Silence action is shown but does nothing for Prometheus-only Grafana rules
body: The new list item supplies only promRule to RuleActionsButtons, so rule is undefined. AlertRuleMenu can still render 'Silence notifications' because canSilence includes Grafana Prometheus rule abilities. Clicking it sets showSilenceDrawer to true, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer is only rendered when rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) is true. With no ruler rule the drawer never appears, so the Silence action is dead UI.

title: Delete and pause actions are hidden for prom-only Grafana rules despite computed abilities
body: AlertRuleMenu computes canDelete and canPause from both ruler abilities and Grafana Prometheus abilities, but the Delete menu item is guarded by rulerRule and the Pause item requires a Grafana ruler rule. In the new alert list view Grafana rules are rendered from Prometheus data without a ruler rule, so users who have delete or pause permission according to the new Grafana abilities will not see these actions. Delete appears especially likely to be intended because the delete modal can be opened from the rule identifier alone.

title: skipToken does not disable Grafana Prometheus rule abilities
body: useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities converts skipToken to undefined, but useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(undefined) still produces real abilities. In particular, Duplicate is allowed when the user has Grafana alert-rule create permission, regardless of the actual rule. Because AlertRuleMenu ORs these abilities with ruler abilities, this can show Duplicate for non-Grafana, missing, or plugin-provided rules where the Grafana hook should be inert.

title: Federated rule groups are no longer treated as immutable
body: useAllRulerRuleAbilities hardcodes isFederated = false, replacing the previous isFederatedRuleGroup check. Federated ruler rule groups should be immutable, but this change makes update, delete, pause, and restore appear supported for them if the user has permissions, regressing UI/RBAC behavior for federated cloud rules.

title: Abilities memo is invalidated by a new canSilence tuple each render
body: useCanSilence returns a new [supported, allowed] array on every render, and that tuple is included in the useMemo dependency array of useAllRulerRuleAbilities. The memo therefore recomputes on every render, which can add noticeable overhead when these hooks are invoked for many rows in the rule list.

title: Extra closing brace in Grafana rule key
body: getGrafanaRuleKey returns a template string ending in ${rule.uid}}, so the generated key contains an unintended trailing closing brace. This does not crash React but makes keys incorrect and can confuse debugging or key-based assumptions.

title: Clipboard write promise rejection is not handled
body: copyToClipboard calls navigator.clipboard.writeText(...).then(...) without a catch handler. If the Clipboard API rejects, for example due to browser permissions or an insecure context, the result is an unhandled promise rejection.

title: RuleDetails RBAC tests assert contradictory behavior
body: Tests named 'Should not render Edit/Delete button for users with the update/delete permission' mock useIsRuleEditable with isEditable or isRemovable true and then assert the buttons are absent, without granting the corresponding permissions. This likely tests the wrong condition and can pass even if the RBAC button visibility logic is broken.

title: Grafana list items are rendered without a React key
body: In FilterViewResults, rules.map destructures a key and passes it to DataSourceRuleLoader and UnknownRuleListItem, but for origin === 'grafana' it returns GrafanaRuleListItem without key={key}. In an infinite-scroll list this can cause React reconciliation problems and duplicate/incorrect DOM reuse when new pages are appended.

title: Typo adds an extra '}' to Grafana rule keys
body: getGrafanaRuleKey returns `grafana-${namespace.uid}-${groupName}-${rule.uid}}`, which appends an unintended trailing curly brace to every Grafana rule key. The key may still be unique, but this is a typo that can make keys harder to debug and suggests the template literal was not intended to end with `}}`.

title: Silence menu item can be shown but the silence drawer never opens in the Prometheus-only list
body: AlertRuleMenu now computes silence support from Grafana Prometheus rule abilities, so in the new list view where only promRule is supplied the 'Silence notifications' menu item can be rendered. However RuleActionsButtons only mounts SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer when rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) is true, and rule is undefined in this flow. Clicking Silence therefore sets local state but renders no drawer, making the action silently do nothing.

title: Delete action is hidden for Prometheus-only Grafana rules even when allowed
body: AlertRuleMenu computes canDelete from both ruler abilities and Grafana Prometheus abilities, but the Delete menu item is only rendered when rulerRule is truthy. In the new alert list flow GrafanaRuleListItem/RuleActionsButtons supplies only promRule, so users with delete permission will not see Delete even though canDelete can be true and the delete handler in RuleActionsButtons can operate using the rule identifier alone.

title: Pause action is not rendered for Prometheus-only Grafana rules although pause ability is computed
body: canPause can become true from useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities, but MenuItemPauseRule is only rendered when a rulerRule is present. Since the new list view removes ruler data and passes only promRule, pause becomes unavailable even though the new Grafana Prometheus ability hook reports it as supported/allowed. If pause truly requires ruler data, the ability should not be reported as supported; otherwise the pause menu item needs a Prometheus-rule-compatible implementation.

title: Federated ruler rules are no longer treated as immutable
body: useAllRulerRuleAbilities hard-codes isFederated = false, while the previous useAllAlertRuleAbilities implementation used isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group). The deprecated useAllAlertRuleAbilities now delegates to this hook, so existing callers that pass CombinedRule lose the federated check. Federated Mimir rule groups may now be considered editable/deletable/pausable/duplicable, exposing actions that should be unsupported and potentially allowing users to attempt mutations they should not be allowed to perform.

title: Menu test asserts Silence item exists but never exercises the action
body: The test clicks More and asserts that the Silence menu item is present, but it does not click the item or verify that a silence drawer opens. Because the new Prometheus-only list item has no ruler rule, the current implementation renders the Silence menu item but does not mount the corresponding drawer, so this test can pass while the user-visible action is broken.

title: Silence menu item can be shown but clicking it does nothing when only a Prometheus rule is provided
body: GrafanaRuleListItem renders RuleActionsButtons with only promRule and no ruler rule. AlertRuleMenu can render the 'Silence notifications' item because canSilence is now also computed from the Grafana Prometheus rule abilities. Clicking that item sets showSilenceDrawer to true, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer is only rendered when rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) is true. When rule is undefined, this condition is false, so the drawer is never rendered and the visible Silence action is a no-op.

title: skipToken does not neutralize Grafana Prometheus rule abilities
body: useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities converts skipToken to undefined and calls useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities. That hook does not treat an undefined rule as absent: when loading is false it sets MaybeSupported to AlwaysSupported, so abilities such as Duplicate can become [true, true] based only on permissions. AlertRuleMenu ORs these Grafana abilities with ruler abilities, which can incorrectly enable Duplicate for non-Grafana rules, missing rules, or rules that should be unsupported. A skip token should result in [false, false] for all requested actions.

title: Federated rule groups are no longer treated as immutable
body: useAllRulerRuleAbilities hard-codes isFederated = false, and the deprecated useAllAlertRuleAbilities now delegates to it. Previously useAllAlertRuleAbilities used isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group) to make federated rules immutable. After this change, federated Mimir rules may be considered editable, deletable, pausable, or restorable, exposing actions that should be disabled and risking modification of rules that are intended to be read-only.

title: Missing React key for GrafanaRuleListItem in filtered rule list
body: In FilterViewResults, the datasource and unknown rule branches pass key={key}, but the Grafana branch returns GrafanaRuleListItem without a key. React will emit missing-key warnings and may reuse list-item state incorrectly when the list changes. The available key variable should be passed to GrafanaRuleListItem.

title: Menu test verifies Silence item exists but does not exercise it
body: The test asserts that the Silence notifications menu item is rendered, but it never clicks the item or asserts that a silence drawer opens. This misses the current bug where the Silence action is visible in the Prometheus-only list view but does nothing when clicked because no ruler rule is available.

title: Extra closing brace in Grafana rule key
body: getGrafanaRuleKey returns a template string ending with an extra `}`, producing keys like `grafana-<namespaceUid>-<groupName>-<ruleUid>}`. This is likely a typo and makes generated keys harder to debug; the trailing extra brace should be removed.

title: Clipboard write promise rejection is unhandled
body: copyToClipboard calls navigator.clipboard?.writeText(text).then(...) without a catch handler. If the clipboard write fails, the promise rejection is unhandled and the user receives no feedback. A rejection handler should be added, ideally with an error toast or fallback.

title: Component comment still says ruler endpoint is used
body: GrafanaGroupLoader's comment says it loads an evaluation group from Prometheus and Ruler endpoints, but the ruler query was removed in this PR. The component now only polls the Prometheus endpoint. The comment and the nearby expectedRulesCount comment referencing Ruler responses should be updated.

title: Stale comment about preloading ruler rules
body: After removing the alertRuleApi.util.prefetch('getGrafanaRulerGroup') call, the comment still says this step preloads ruler rules and improves UX by avoiding waiting for each group to load. The remaining code only upserts Prometheus query data, so the comment is misleading.

title: Queries that interpolate to empty strings are not filtered out
body: runSplitQuery filters targets on query.expr before calling applyTemplateVariables. If a target's raw expression is a non-empty variable that interpolates to an empty string, it is not discarded. It can then be grouped and sent to Loki as an empty query; if all targets become empty, the grouped requests array is empty and runSplitGroupedQueries can fail (Math.max over an empty array and undefined longest partition). Filter again after interpolation.

title: Shard splitting now filters empty expressions before interpolation
body: runShardSplitQuery changed from interpolating targets before filtering out empty expressions to filtering expressions first and interpolating afterwards. A query whose raw expr is a non-empty variable but whose interpolated expression is empty will no longer be discarded. This is a behavior regression and can create invalid shard queries or empty request groups. Add a filter after applyTemplateVariables.

title: Already interpolated/sharded queries are interpolated again by runSplitQuery
body: runShardSplitQuery interpolates targets at the start and later calls runSplitQuery for each shard group. runSplitQuery now unconditionally interpolates targets again. The updated tests expect applyTemplateVariables to be called multiple times for one query in the shard flow. Because applyTemplateVariables receives request.filters and template replacement is not necessarily idempotent, repeated interpolation can duplicate ad-hoc filters or alter already-interpolated values containing '$'. This can change or corrupt the shard-modified query. Avoid re-interpolating already interpolated targets or make the operation explicitly idempotent.

title: Targets are interpolated here and again inside runSplitQuery
body: runShardSplitQuery interpolates each target with applyTemplateVariables at line 52, then later calls runSplitQuery for each shard cycle (line 163). runSplitQuery now also unconditionally interpolates its targets (querySplitting.ts line 299). This repeats template interpolation for the same queries many times in the shard-splitting path. That adds avoidable work and assumes applyTemplateVariables is idempotent; repeated interpolation can also change queries if substituted values contain template-like syntax. Consider interpolating once and skipping interpolation in runSplitQuery when called from shard splitting.

title: Queries that interpolate to an empty expression are not filtered out
body: runSplitQuery filters targets with `.filter((query) => query.expr)` before calling applyTemplateVariables. If a query expression is a template variable that interpolates to an empty string, the empty expression remains after interpolation and is still partitioned/grouped and passed to datasource.runQuery. This can send invalid empty Loki queries. A filter should be applied after interpolation to drop targets whose interpolated expr is empty.

title: Empty interpolated expressions are no longer filtered before sharding
body: The previous code interpolated queries before filtering out empty expressions. The new code filters `query.expr` before interpolation, so a target whose raw expr is a variable that resolves to an empty string is kept and passed into the shard-splitting pipeline. This can cause unnecessary shard-label lookups for an empty selector and can produce subrequests with no valid targets; runSplitGroupedQueries assumes at least one request and can fail when given an empty request list. Filter after interpolation here as well.

title: Sharded queries are interpolated twice
body: runShardSplitQuery() maps every target through datasource.applyTemplateVariables() at line 52, then later executes each shard group through runSplitQuery(). runSplitQuery() was changed to also map every incoming target through datasource.applyTemplateVariables() in querySplitting.ts line 299. As a result, sharded expressions are interpolated again after the __stream_shard__ matcher has been injected. The added test even expects five interpolation calls for one target. Template interpolation is not guaranteed to be idempotent; repeated calls can duplicate ad-hoc filters or reinterpret variable syntax introduced by the first interpolation. Interpolation should be performed in only one layer.

title: Queries that interpolate to empty expressions are not skipped
body: runSplitQuery() filters targets on query.expr before calling applyTemplateVariables(). If a raw expression is a template variable that resolves to an empty string, the target passes the non-empty filter, becomes empty after interpolation, and is still grouped and sent to Loki. This can create invalid empty queries. Add a non-empty expr filter after interpolation; the same problem exists in runShardSplitQuery().

title: Shard splitting keeps targets that become empty after interpolation
body: runShardSplitQuery() filters request.targets by the raw query.expr before interpolation. A target whose expression is a variable that expands to an empty string will still enter splitQueriesByStreamShard(), potentially causing shard-label lookups for an empty selector and sending an empty query downstream. Targets should be filtered again after applyTemplateVariables().

title: Plugin request logs no longer include traceID
body: The previous logRequest implementation explicitly extracted traceID via tracing.TraceIDFromContext and appended it to the log fields. The refactored code removes that logic, and the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware only adds endpoint, pluginId, datasource, and user fields. There is no replacement in this change, so plugin request logs emitted by LoggerMiddleware may lose trace correlation.

title: TestLogger.FromContext discards captured logs and context
body: LoggerMiddleware now logs through logger.FromContext(ctx). The test fake responds by returning a brand-new TestLogger, so messages logged through the contextual logger are not recorded on the original fake and contextual state is lost. This makes it difficult or impossible to assert log output from code paths that use FromContext and can hide regressions in tests.

title: NewMetricsMiddleware mutates a shared middleware instance
body: NewMetricsMiddleware creates a single *MetricsMiddleware and the returned ClientMiddlewareFunc sets imw.next = next each time it is applied. If the same middleware value is used to wrap more than one client, or is applied concurrently, the next field can be overwritten, causing requests to be forwarded to the wrong client or creating a data race. Middleware constructors should create a new wrapper per application or avoid mutable shared state.

title: Adding FromContext to Logger is an interface break
body: The exported Logger interface now requires FromContext(context.Context) Logger. Any existing implementation of this interface outside this package will fail to compile until updated, making this change a backward-incompatible API change.

title: No tests verify the new contextual logger enrichment
body: The PR introduces a middleware whose purpose is to enrich the request context and changes LoggerMiddleware to depend on that enrichment, but there are no tests verifying that QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, or CollectMetrics contexts receive the expected attributes or that LoggerMiddleware logs them. Given the fake logger's FromContext currently discards contextual logs, this behavior can regress silently.

title: TestLogger.FromContext discards log output
body: TestLogger.FromContext returns a brand-new TestLogger instead of the receiver or a child linked to the receiver. Since LoggerMiddleware now logs via logger.FromContext(ctx).Info, any log emitted in tests using TestLogger will be recorded on an object the test cannot inspect, making assertions on logged messages impossible. Return the same TestLogger, or a child that propagates recorded logs back to the original fake.

title: Metrics middleware mutates a shared instance when applied
body: NewMetricsMiddleware creates one MetricsMiddleware and the returned ClientMiddlewareFunc sets imw.next and returns that same instance. If this middleware is ever applied more than once, for example when reusing a middleware slice to build multiple decorators, the shared next field will be overwritten and earlier decorator chains will route requests to the wrong downstream client. Create a per-chain wrapper or avoid mutating shared state.

title: Adding FromContext to Logger is a breaking interface change
body: The exported Logger interface gains a new FromContext method. Any existing implementation of this interface outside this package, including downstream forks, enterprise code, or tests, will no longer compile. If this package is intended to be implementable outside the repository, this should be treated as an API break or introduced in a compatible way.

title: Plugin request logs lose traceID field
body: The previous logRequest implementation explicitly appended traceID from tracing.TraceIDFromContext to the plugin request log fields. This change removes that code and the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware only injects endpoint, pluginId, datasource, and user attributes. Unless another middleware outside this diff injects traceID into the log context, Plugin Request Completed logs emitted by LoggerMiddleware will no longer contain traceID, reducing trace/log correlation.

title: NewMetricsMiddleware mutates a shared middleware instance when wrapping next client
body: NewMetricsMiddleware creates a single *MetricsMiddleware and returns a ClientMiddlewareFunc that sets imw.next = next each time it is applied. If the middleware is applied more than once or to multiple client chains, all chains share the same MetricsMiddleware and overwrite each other's next client, causing requests to be dispatched to the wrong downstream client. Concurrent application can also race on the next field. Returning a new MetricsMiddleware per next, while sharing the registered metric collectors, would avoid this.

title: Adding FromContext to Logger interface is a breaking API change
body: The exported log.Logger interface now requires FromContext(context.Context) Logger. Any external implementation of this interface will fail to compile until updated. The PR updates in-repo implementations, but this is still an API/contract break for consumers of pkg/plugins/log.

title: TestLogger.FromContext returns a logger that does not record into the original fake
body: TestLogger.FromContext returns NewTestLogger(), discarding the receiver's recorded log state. Code under test that calls logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...) will emit logs to a new fake that the test cannot inspect, so assertions on the original TestLogger will miss those messages. This makes the fake unsuitable for verifying LoggerMiddleware's FromContext-based logging.

title: No tests for the new contextual logger middleware
body: The PR moves request-scoped log attributes from the metrics/instrumentation middleware into a new ContextualLoggerMiddleware and changes LoggerMiddleware to rely on FromContext, but only renames the existing metrics middleware test. There is no automated test that ContextualLoggerMiddleware adds the expected attributes or that LoggerMiddleware logs them, so regressions in context propagation or log fields can go unnoticed.

title: Device limit can be bypassed by omitting the client-supplied device header
body: TagDevice returns nil when X-Grafana-Device-Id is empty, and Anonymous.Authenticate only rejects authentication when TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Because the device ID header is supplied by the client, an anonymous client can omit it and avoid being counted or blocked, while normal UI clients that send the header are limited. The configured device_limit therefore cannot reliably cap anonymous devices.

title: Local cache is populated before persistence, allowing blocked devices to bypass the limit on retry
body: tagDeviceUI stores the device key in the local cache before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice. If CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, or any other database error, the cache entry is not removed. For the cache TTL, subsequent requests with the same device ID hit the cache and TagDevice returns nil without touching the database, so Anonymous.Authenticate succeeds. A device that was initially rejected by the device limit can therefore retry and bypass the limit, and database failures are also hidden.

title: Device-limit check is not atomic with the insert/update
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice enforces the limit by running SELECT COUNT(*) and then, in a separate step, inserting or updating the device. There is no transaction, lock, or conditional database operation tying the count check to the write. Concurrent anonymous requests for new devices can all observe count below device_limit and then all insert new rows, causing the number of active anonymous devices to exceed the configured limit.

title: Unauthenticated clients can exhaust the device limit and deny access to new devices
body: Device IDs come from the unauthenticated X-Grafana-Device-Id header. When device_limit is enabled, an attacker can send many requests with unique device IDs to fill the active anon_device count. Once the limit is reached, Anonymous.Authenticate rejects unknown devices, so legitimate new anonymous devices can be denied access. This makes the limit exploitable as a denial-of-service vector.

title: Device tagging is now synchronous on the anonymous authentication path
body: TagDevice was moved from a background goroutine into Anonymous.Authenticate. When device_limit is non-zero, each uncached device triggers a COUNT query plus a database write before the anonymous identity is returned. This adds latency to anonymous requests and can become a performance hotspot on instances with many anonymous devices.

title: Missing test that existing devices can still update when the limit is reached
body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only verifies that a second, unknown device is rejected when the limit is 1. It does not verify that an existing active device can still be updated after the limit is reached. Since returning anonymous devices should remain authenticated, a regression in updateDevice could lock out existing devices without being caught.

title: untagDevice logs the wrong error variable
body: In untagDevice, when DeleteDevice fails the log statement uses the incoming err variable instead of errD, the error returned by DeleteDevice. As a result, the logged error is unrelated to the actual delete failure.

title: Failed device tagging is cached, allowing device-limit bypass
body: tagDeviceUI adds the device ID to localCache before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice and does not remove it when the store returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. The first request for a new device after the limit is reached fails authentication, but the cache entry remains for 29 minutes; subsequent requests hit the cache and return nil without a database check, so the unregistered device is authenticated. Set the cache only after a successful write or delete it on error.

title: Device limit check is not atomic with insert/update
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice first counts active devices and then performs the upsert in a separate database session. Concurrent first-time requests from multiple new devices can all observe count below the configured limit and then all insert, causing the active anonymous device count to exceed the limit. If this is intended as a hard cap, enforcement must be atomic, for example via a transaction with locking or a conditional insert.

title: Limit tests do not cover existing-device updates or retry/cache behavior
body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only checks that inserting a second new device fails when the store limit is 1. It does not verify that an already-registered device can still be updated after the limit is reached, nor does it exercise the higher-level TagDevice flow where the local cache can bypass the limit. Add coverage for updating an existing device at the limit and for the service-level cache path.

title: Failed device tagging is cached, allowing device-limit bypass
body: tagDeviceUI stores the device ID in localCache before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice and does not remove it when CreateOrUpdateDevice fails. If the database returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, the first request is rejected, but the cache entry remains for about 29 minutes. A retry with the same X-Grafana-Device-Id hits the cache, tagDeviceUI returns nil, Anonymous.Authenticate succeeds, and the device is allowed despite never being admitted under the limit. This makes the configurable limit ineffective after one failed retry per device ID and also masks transient DB errors.

title: Device limit is checked non-atomically before insert
body: CreateOrUpdateDevice counts active anonymous devices and then performs the insert/upsert in a separate statement without a transaction, row lock, or conditional insert. Under concurrent requests from new device IDs, multiple callers can observe count < deviceLimit and all insert, causing the stored active device count to exceed the configured limit.

title: Device tagging DB queries are now synchronous in anonymous authentication
body: Anonymous.Authenticate now calls TagDevice synchronously. When device_limit is enabled and a device is not in the local cache, this executes a COUNT over anon_device plus an insert/update before authentication completes. Unique device IDs can force this path on every request, adding latency to anonymous logins and creating a DB load vector that did not exist when tagging ran asynchronously with a timeout.

title: Missing X-Grafana-Device-Id bypasses the device limit
body: TagDevice returns nil immediately when the X-Grafana-Device-Id header is absent, and Anonymous.Authenticate then returns an anonymous identity. Because the limit is only enforced for requests that supply this client-controlled header, a client can avoid being counted or blocked simply by omitting the header. If the limit is intended to cap anonymous access, this is a bypass.

title: untagDevice logs the wrong error variable
body: When anonStore.DeleteDevice fails, untagDevice logs the outer err variable, which has already been checked to be nil, instead of errD returned by DeleteDevice. The resulting log message does not contain the actual deletion error.

title: Negative device_limit is silently treated as unlimited
body: AnonymousDeviceLimit is read with MustInt64(0), and anonstore only enforces the limit when deviceLimit > 0. A negative configuration value therefore disables limiting instead of being rejected or clamped to zero, which can hide operator mistakes.

title: No tests cover device-limit enforcement and cache interaction
body: The updated tests use setting.NewCfg(), whose AnonymousDeviceLimit defaults to 0, and assert TagDevice never errors. There is no test that a limit-reached failure is returned consistently on retries, that the local cache does not mask a failed create, or that existing active devices can still update when the limit is reached.

title: Cleanup job interval changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute
body: Run now schedules the full cleanup suite every minute instead of every 10 minutes. This affects all cleanup jobs, not just annotation cleanup, and can increase database and filesystem load tenfold. The PR description only discusses changing annotation cleanup queries, so this looks accidental or at least undocumented. If intentional, it should be called out and possibly gated or configurable; otherwise revert to the previous 10-minute interval.

title: Normal cleanup batches are logged at Error level with full ID lists
body: CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags log successful batch fetches and deletes with r.log.Error (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579) and include the entire ids slice plus a nil err value. This will generate error-level noise for normal operation and can emit very large log entries or cause large allocations when the batch size is large. Use debug or info logging and log only counts or a truncated sample of IDs.

title: Cleanup loop may finish early if a fetched batch is deleted before the DELETE runs
body: untilDoneOrCancelled stops when a batch reports zero affected rows. With the new fetch-then-delete approach, another process can delete all IDs returned by fetchIDs before deleteByIDs executes; deleteByIDs then returns 0 even though other rows still match the cleanup condition. The job will return and defer remaining deletions to a later cycle. Consider continuing when len(ids) > 0, with a retry cap, or otherwise distinguishing 'no rows fetched' from 'fetched rows already deleted'.

title: SQLite IN-list construction is quadratic and unbounded
body: deleteByIDs builds the SQLite IN clause by repeatedly formatting into a growing string. For large batches (the test uses 32767 IDs) this copies the entire string on each iteration and can be slow and memory-heavy; very large batches may also exceed SQLite SQL-length limits, and non-SQLite databases have placeholder limits that are not guarded. Use strings.Builder or strings.Join, and consider chunking deletes by a safe maximum.

title: Test cleanup is registered after inserting test data
body: In TestIntegrationAnnotationCleanUp, the t.Cleanup that deletes annotation and annotation_tag rows is registered after createTestAnnotations and the initial assertions. If those assertions fail before registration, the shared test database is left dirty and subsequent subtests may fail spuriously. Register the cleanup before creating data or use a guaranteed truncation step.

title: Cleanup logs success paths at Error level and prints full ID lists
body: CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags call r.log.Error on normal execution, including when no rows are selected, and include the full ids slice. This happens on every batch and will produce error-level log noise and potentially very large log lines even when cleanup is healthy. These logs should be debug or info and should not log full ID lists by default.

title: Cleanup interval changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute
body: The cleanup ticker now runs all cleanup jobs every minute instead of every 10 minutes. This affects snapshots, dashboard versions, images, invites, short URLs, query history, and annotations, not just the annotation deadlock fix. This can substantially increase database and filesystem load and may be accidental. If intentional, it should be explained or configurable; otherwise it should be reverted.

title: SQLite inline ID list is built quadratically
body: In the SQLite fallback, the IN-list is built by repeatedly assigning values = fmt.Sprintf with the previous full string. This creates and copies a growing string on every iteration, giving O(n^2) allocations and CPU usage for large batches such as 32767 IDs. Use strings.Builder or strings.Join instead.

title: Non-SQLite bind-parameter limits are not handled
body: deleteByIDs only special-cases SQLite's parameter limit. PostgreSQL has a 65535 bind-parameter limit, and other databases or drivers may have statement-size limits. If AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is configured above such a limit, the generated DELETE with one placeholder per ID will fail and cleanup will stop. Chunking deletes by a safe maximum parameter count would make this robust across supported databases.

title: Max-count cleanup can delete rows that are no longer excess
body: For MaxCount cleanup, IDs are selected with OFFSET MaxCount in one session and deleted in another session without rechecking the current ordering. If newer annotations are deleted between the SELECT and DELETE, the selected older IDs may now be within the newest MaxCount annotations, but they are still deleted. The previous single-statement delete evaluated selection and deletion atomically. If this behavior is acceptable, it should be documented; otherwise the delete should re-validate the condition.

title: Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute
body: The background cleanup loop now runs every minute instead of every 10 minutes. This change affects all cleanup jobs, not just annotation cleanup, and can substantially increase filesystem and database load. The PR description does not mention this cadence change; if it is accidental it should be reverted, and if intentional it should be justified and preferably configurable.

title: Routine cleanup operations are logged at Error level with full ID lists
body: CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags log normal batch progress using Error level and include the full ids slice and a nil error. With large batch sizes (the added test uses 32767) and the cleanup ticker now running every minute, this can flood logs, produce misleading error entries, and add unnecessary CPU/log throughput. These should be Debug/Trace logs and should avoid emitting full ID lists.

title: SQLite inline IN list is built with quadratic string concatenation
body: deleteByIDs builds the SQLite inline IN list by repeatedly doing values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v). For large batches this copies the growing string on every iteration, causing O(n^2) allocations and CPU. Use strings.Builder or strings.Join instead.

title: Only SQLite parameter limit is handled for large IN lists
body: For non-SQLite databases, deleteByIDs builds a DELETE ... WHERE id IN (...) statement with one bind parameter per ID. Only SQLite is special-cased. If AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is configured larger than the placeholder/bind limit of the target database (for example MySQL or PostgreSQL limits around 65535 parameters), the DELETE can fail and halt cleanup. Consider chunking deletes into a universally safe size instead of relying solely on the SQLite check.

title: Asynchronous legacy writes are derived from the request context
body: In Create, and similarly in Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection, the background goroutine creates a timeout context from the incoming request context. Request contexts are normally canceled when the HTTP handler returns, so the 10-second timeout does not make the legacy write independent. The legacy operation may be canceled immediately after the API response is sent, causing mode 3 to skip the intended asynchronous legacy write. A detached context, with logger/values copied, should be used instead.

title: Legacy Create uses the original request object instead of the created object
body: Mode3.Create passes the original obj to Legacy.Create after Storage.Create has returned created. Storage may assign name, UID, resourceVersion, annotations, or defaults, and created is the canonical object that unified storage accepted. Passing the original object, rather than a deep copy of created, can create a different object in legacy storage or cause concurrent use of a mutable object. This can make legacy storage diverge from unified storage.

title: Legacy Update reuses the request UpdatedObjectInfo instead of the unified result
body: Mode3.Update calls Storage.Update with objInfo and then asynchronously calls Legacy.Update with the same objInfo. Legacy.Update will normally evaluate objInfo against the legacy store's current object, so patches, strategic merges, or resource-version-dependent updates can produce a different result or fail. To keep legacy consistent, the legacy update should receive an UpdatedObjectInfo that returns the exact object returned by Storage.Update, preferably a deep copy.

title: Unordered background goroutines can leave legacy storage inconsistent
body: Each write operation starts an independent goroutine to write to legacy storage without sequencing, queueing, or per-resource locking. Rapid create/update/delete operations can be applied to legacy out of order, for example a legacy delete can run before a legacy create or an older update can overwrite a newer one. Because mode 3 keeps legacy as a fallback, this can resurrect deleted objects or leave stale data if legacy is later used.

title: Delete does not attempt legacy deletion when unified delete returns NotFound
body: DualWriterMode3.Delete returns immediately on any Storage.Delete error, including NotFound. The previous behavior tolerated NotFound from unified storage and still attempted to delete from legacy storage. With the new behavior, objects that are already absent from unified storage but still present in legacy cannot be cleaned through the API, leaving orphaned legacy data.

title: Delete success metric uses the object name as the kind label
body: In DualWriterMode3.Delete, the successful storage-duration metric is recorded with name as the third argument, while other call sites pass options.Kind. This labels the metric with the object name instead of the resource kind, producing incorrect aggregations and potentially unbounded metric cardinality.

title: Several mode 3 metrics record the wrong store
body: When Storage.Create fails, recordLegacyDuration is called at line 45; when Storage.Update fails, recordLegacyDuration is called at line 129; and the asynchronous Legacy.DeleteCollection result is recorded with recordStorageDuration at line 166. These record the duration or error state of the wrong store, making mode 3 observability misleading.

title: Background legacy writes are detached and untracked
body: Mode 3 launches a new goroutine for every write with no wait group, queue, or shutdown coordination. Destroy can close Storage and Legacy while background writes are still running, which may cause failures or panics if the underlying stores are closed. There is also no backpressure, so a slow legacy backend can cause unbounded goroutine growth.

title: Asynchronous legacy write failures are not logged
body: The background create, update, delete, and delete-collection paths only record a metric when the legacy operation fails. They do not log the error or cause. Because these writes are asynchronous and can fail due to cancellation, timeouts, conflicts, or backend errors, operators will have no actionable logs to diagnose legacy divergence.

title: Delete puts the base logger into the context instead of the enriched logger
body: In DualWriterMode3.Delete, a logger is created with name, kind, and method fields, but the context is set with klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log) instead of that enriched logger. Downstream code logging from the context will miss those fields, unlike the other mode 3 methods.

title: Mode 3 unit tests do not synchronize or set expectations for async legacy calls
body: Mode3 methods start goroutines that call LegacyStorage, but the unit tests neither wait for those goroutines nor assert whether legacy was called. For example, TestMode3_Delete calls Delete without setting a Legacy.Delete expectation, so the asynchronous call can hit the mock unexpectedly and race with test completion. Create and Update tests set legacy expectations but never verify them, so they can pass even if the asynchronous legacy write never happens.

title: Mode 3 integration tests check legacy APIs synchronously despite asynchronous legacy writes
body: The added mode 3 subtests run doPlaylistTests, which creates, updates, and deletes through the Kubernetes API and then immediately reads the legacy playlist API. In mode 3 the legacy write happens asynchronously, so these checks are racy. Without polling or retry for mode 3, the integration test can flake or hide failures where the legacy write never completes.

title: Async legacy writes derive from the request context and will be canceled when the request returns
body: In Create, the background goroutine creates a timeout context from the incoming request context: ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...). When the Create handler returns, the HTTP request context is normally canceled, so the derived context is canceled immediately and Legacy.Create will often fail with context canceled. This defeats the purpose of mode 3's asynchronous legacy write. The same pattern is used in Delete (line 110), Update (line 135), and DeleteCollection (line 163). A detached context, such as context.WithoutCancel or a background context carrying only logger/values, should be used for background writes.

title: Delete skips legacy deletion when unified delete returns NotFound
body: Delete returns immediately for any error from Storage.Delete, including NotFound. The previous mode 3 behavior explicitly tolerated NotFound from unified storage and still attempted Legacy.Delete. With this change, an object that exists only in legacy storage, or was removed from unified storage but not legacy storage, will never be deleted from legacy storage. This can leave stale legacy data that reappears if the system is rolled back to a mode that reads from legacy storage.

title: Legacy update receives the original UpdatedObjectInfo instead of the object written to unified storage
body: Update passes the same rest.UpdatedObjectInfo to Storage.Update and later to Legacy.Update. Legacy.Update will therefore recompute the candidate object using the legacy store's current object, which may differ from the unified store's state. This can cause resource-version conflicts or write a different object to legacy storage than the one persisted in unified storage. The previous implementation wrapped the object returned by unified storage so that legacy storage received the exact resulting object; removing that breaks dual-write consistency.

title: Mode 3 unit tests do not wait for or assert asynchronous legacy writes
body: TestMode3_Create calls dw.Create and then asserts immediately, but the legacy write happens in a goroutine. The test does not synchronize with that goroutine or assert mock expectations, so it can pass even if Legacy.Create is never called, is called after the test finishes, or fails. The same issue exists for the Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection tests. These tests do not actually verify the asynchronous legacy-write behavior introduced by mode 3.

title: Mode 3 integration test asserts legacy state immediately after asynchronous writes
body: The new mode 3 subtest runs doPlaylistTests, which checks the legacy /api/playlists endpoints immediately after creating, updating, or deleting objects through the Kubernetes API. For example, it lists legacy playlists right after Kubernetes creates and calls getFromBothAPIs after updates. In mode 3, writes to legacy storage are asynchronous, so these assertions can race. The test should poll or otherwise wait for eventual consistency in mode 3, or avoid synchronous legacy assertions for asynchronous dual-write modes.

title: Delete success metric uses the resource name as the kind label
body: On successful Storage.Delete, the code records d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage). Elsewhere the third parameter is the resource kind, but here the object name is passed. This produces incorrect metric labels and can create high-cardinality metrics by putting per-resource names into a label intended to hold a kind. It should use the resource kind, such as options.Kind, consistently.

title: DeleteCollection records legacy background duration as storage duration
body: In DeleteCollection's asynchronous goroutine, after calling d.Legacy.DeleteCollection, the code calls d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy). This attributes the legacy operation's duration and error status to unified storage metrics. It should call d.recordLegacyDuration instead.

title: Storage create failures are recorded as legacy durations
body: When d.Storage.Create fails, Create calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage). This attributes a unified-storage failure and duration to the legacy store, corrupting metrics. Update has the same issue at line 129, where a Storage.Update failure is recorded with recordLegacyDuration.

title: Asynchronous legacy write failures are not logged or reconciled
body: In Create's background goroutine, the error from Legacy.Create is only passed to a metric; there is no logging, retry, queue, or reconciliation. If the legacy write fails because of timeout, conflict, or legacy-store outage, unified and legacy storage can silently diverge. The same fire-and-forget pattern exists in Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection. Since legacy writes are described as a safety measure, failures should at least be logged and ideally tracked or retried.

title: Background legacy writes are unordered and unbounded
body: Each write method launches an independent goroutine to update legacy storage. There is no per-resource sequencing, locking, queue, or concurrency limit. A fast sequence of create/update/delete operations can be applied to legacy storage out of order, for example a delete running before a create or an older update overwriting a newer one. This can leave legacy storage inconsistent even if every individual background call succeeds.

title: Delete puts the base logger into context instead of the enriched logger
body: Delete constructs log := d.Log.WithValues("name", name, "kind", options.Kind, "method", method), but then sets ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log). Any logging inside Storage.Delete or Legacy.Delete that uses the context logger will miss the added name/kind/method values. The context should be set to log, not d.Log.

title: Benign legacy delete NotFound errors are counted as failures
body: In the asynchronous Delete path, any error returned by Legacy.Delete is recorded as a failure via d.recordLegacyDuration(err != nil, ...). If the object is already absent from legacy storage, NotFound is a benign condition, but it will be counted as a legacy error metric. The previous implementation ignored NotFound for legacy deletes; the new code should do the same for metrics and logging.

title: Asynchronous legacy writes inherit the request context and may be canceled immediately
body: In Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection, the goroutine that writes to legacy storage derives its context from the incoming request context. When the API request completes, that context is canceled, so the asynchronous legacy create/update/delete/delete-collection can be canceled before it finishes. Mode 3 depends on these asynchronous writes to keep legacy storage in sync, so this can silently drop legacy writes. Use a detached context for the asynchronous operation, preserving only logging/values, not request cancellation.

title: Legacy update reuses the original UpdatedObjectInfo after it was already used by unified storage
body: Update calls Storage.Update with the provided rest.UpdatedObjectInfo and then passes the same objInfo to Legacy.Update asynchronously. UpdatedObjectInfo can be request-scoped or one-use, and it may compute the new object from the old object in the store that calls it. Legacy storage may therefore fail, consume an already-consumed payload, or apply the update to a different legacy state, producing a different object than unified storage. For dual-write convergence, legacy should receive the already-updated object returned from Storage.Update, ideally through a wrapper or deep copy.

title: Delete does not attempt legacy deletion when unified storage returns NotFound
body: Delete returns immediately if Storage.Delete fails, including when the object is not found in unified storage. In mode 3, legacy storage may still contain a stale copy, and this code path will never clean it up. The previous behavior tolerated NotFound from unified storage and still attempted the legacy delete. Skipping legacy deletion on NotFound can leave divergent legacy objects permanently.

title: DeleteCollection does not attempt legacy deletion when unified storage returns an error
body: DeleteCollection returns immediately if Storage.DeleteCollection fails, so Legacy.DeleteCollection is not attempted. If unified storage reports an error or has already removed the collection while legacy storage still contains objects, the legacy data will remain and the stores will diverge. For mode 3 dual-write cleanup, legacy deletion should still be attempted where appropriate, especially when the unified store reports the collection is already absent.

title: Async legacy create uses the original object without copying it
body: Create passes the same runtime.Object pointer to the asynchronous Legacy.Create call that was passed to Storage.Create. Storage implementations commonly mutate the object during create, and legacy storage may also mutate it. Returning to the caller while a background goroutine continues to use or mutate the same object can cause data races and inconsistent objects. The object should be deep-copied before being handed to the asynchronous legacy writer.

title: Delete success metric uses the object name as the kind label
body: After a successful unified-storage delete, recordStorageDuration is called with name as the kind label instead of options.Kind. This corrupts the metric's kind dimension and can introduce high-cardinality labels because every object name becomes a separate metric label value. The call should use options.Kind, as in the other methods.

title: Storage create failure is recorded as a legacy-store duration
body: When Storage.Create fails, Create records the duration with recordLegacyDuration using the storage start time. This reports a unified-storage failure under legacy-store metrics, making storage and legacy latency/error metrics incorrect. It should call recordStorageDuration.

title: Storage update failure is recorded as a legacy-store duration
body: When Storage.Update fails, Update records the duration with recordLegacyDuration using the storage start time. This mislabels unified-storage update failures as legacy-store update failures. It should call recordStorageDuration.

title: Legacy delete-collection duration is recorded as a storage duration
body: In the asynchronous DeleteCollection goroutine, the result of Legacy.DeleteCollection is recorded with recordStorageDuration. This reports legacy-store delete-collection latency/errors under unified-storage metrics. It should call recordLegacyDuration.

title: Delete puts the base logger into the context instead of the enriched logger
body: Delete builds log with name, kind, and method values, but then sets the context logger to d.Log instead of log. Downstream code that extracts the logger from ctx will miss the request-specific fields, making debugging harder. The context should be set with log.

title: Every write starts an unbounded goroutine for legacy replication
body: Create, Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection each start a new goroutine for the legacy write. There is no queue, worker pool, semaphore, or other backpressure mechanism. If legacy storage is slow or unavailable, write traffic can create a large number of blocked goroutines, increasing memory use and potentially destabilizing the process.

title: Destroy does not wait for outstanding asynchronous legacy writes
body: Destroy closes both Storage and Legacy immediately, but mode 3 may still have outstanding goroutines calling Legacy.Create, Legacy.Update, Legacy.Delete, or Legacy.DeleteCollection. Those goroutines can then operate on destroyed storage, causing errors or panics. The dual writer should track outstanding asynchronous writes and wait for them, or at least cancel and drain them, during Destroy.

title: Asynchronous legacy write failures are not logged
body: The asynchronous legacy paths only record metrics when the legacy operation fails; they no longer log the error. Since mode 3 returns success to the client as soon as unified storage succeeds, legacy failures are otherwise invisible. This makes diagnosing divergence between unified and legacy storage difficult. Errors from asynchronous legacy writes should be logged, ideally with the object identity and operation.

title: Unit tests do not synchronize with or verify asynchronous legacy writes
body: Mode 3 methods start background goroutines, but the unit tests return immediately after calling Create, Delete, Update, or DeleteCollection. There is no WaitGroup, channel, or injectable executor to wait for the legacy call. Some tests set legacy mock expectations but never assert them, while Delete and DeleteCollection do not set legacy expectations at all, so background mock calls may occur after the test finishes or panic as unexpected calls. These tests do not reliably prove that legacy writes happen.

title: Mode 3 integration test assumes immediate legacy consistency despite asynchronous writes
body: The new mode 3 integration test runs the same playlist CRUD suite, which creates/updates/deletes objects through the Kubernetes API and then immediately checks the legacy API. In mode 3, legacy writes are asynchronous, so the legacy API may not yet reflect the change. Without polling/eventual-consistency waits, this test can be flaky and may fail or pass for timing reasons rather than correctness.

title: Cache is not rechecked after acquiring the write lock
body: In GetWebAssets, the cache pointer is checked under RLock, the read lock is released, and then the write lock is acquired without rechecking entryPointAssetsCache. In non-dev mode, multiple concurrent requests during a cold start can all observe a nil cache and proceed past the early return. After one goroutine populates the cache, the others will still reload the manifest and then unconditionally assign entryPointAssetsCache = result. This causes redundant I/O while holding the mutex and, if one of those later reloads fails, it can overwrite a freshly populated valid cache with nil. The code should recheck the cache after acquiring the write lock and return the existing value when appropriate, or use sync.Once/singleflight for initialization.

title: Missing cache recheck after acquiring the write lock
body: In GetWebAssets, the cache pointer is read under RLock and then the lock is released before acquiring the write lock. After acquiring `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()`, the function does not recheck whether another goroutine has already populated `entryPointAssetsCache`. In non-development mode, concurrent first-time callers can therefore all observe a nil cache, then each sequentially reload `assets-manifest.json` and overwrite the cache. This causes unnecessary file I/O (and could cause repeated CDN requests if that path is ever enabled). Recheck `cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil` immediately after acquiring the write lock and return the cached value if present.

title: Missing cache recheck after acquiring write lock
body: GetWebAssets uses a double-checked locking pattern but only reads entryPointAssetsCache before taking the write lock. If another goroutine populates the cache between the RUnlock and Lock, this goroutine still reloads assets and overwrites entryPointAssetsCache at line 69. If that reload fails, a valid cached value can be replaced with nil; even when it succeeds, it causes redundant disk reads. After acquiring the write lock, re-check `cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil` and return the existing cached value.

title: Exclusive lock held while loading assets from disk/CDN
body: The write lock is held for the entire load path, including readWebAssetsFromCDN/readWebAssetsFromFile and cfg.GetContentDeliveryURL. This serializes all callers on a cache miss and, in dev mode, on every call; if the CDN path is ever enabled, a slow network request would block all GetWebAssets callers. Consider loading outside the lock, for example with singleflight, and publishing the result under the lock.

title: No automated test that SQL expressions are rejected
body: The PR adds a security gate that rejects QueryTypeSQL, but no unit test verifies the rejection, including when FlagSqlExpressions is enabled. Without a regression test, a future refactor could remove or weaken the gate and reintroduce the vulnerable SQL expression path.

title: enableSqlExpressions is a no-op with misleading flag logic
body: enableSqlExpressions computes enabled as the negation of FlagSqlExpressions and then returns false in both branches, so the feature flag has no effect. If the intent is to disable SQL expressions unconditionally, the conditional check is misleading and should be simplified; if the intent was to respect the flag, the logic is incorrect.

title: User-facing error says SQL expressions are not implemented rather than disabled
body: The rejected QueryTypeSQL path returns the error 'sqlExpressions is not implemented', but the feature is intentionally disabled for security reasons. This message can confuse users/operators, especially while the feature flag still exists.

title: No automated test that SQL expressions are disabled
body: The security fix rejects QueryTypeSQL in ReadQuery, but the PR adds no unit test asserting that a SQL expression query fails, including when featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions is enabled. Because this is a regression guard for a critical RCE/LFI issue, a future refactor could accidentally re-enable the SQL path without detection.

title: Feature-flag check in enableSqlExpressions is dead and misleading
body: enableSqlExpressions computes enabled as the negation of FlagSqlExpressions but then returns false in both branches, so the feature toggle has no effect and the conditional is dead. If the intent is a permanent disable, the function should simply return false; otherwise the inverted logic can mislead future changes about how the flag controls SQL expressions.

title: Empty SQL result NoData value is overwritten
body: In SQLCommand.Execute, when frame.Rows() == 0 the code sets rsp.Values to mathexp.NoData but immediately overwrites rsp.Values with mathexp.TableData. As a result the no-data handling branch has no effect, and empty SQL results would be returned as table data if SQL expressions were re-enabled.

title: SQL expression gate is hard-coded off and feature-flag logic is misleading
body: enableSqlExpressions computes enabled as the negation of FlagSqlExpressions but returns false in both branches, so the feature flag has no effect. If the intent is to disable SQL expressions unconditionally for the CVE fix, replace this with an explicit return false and a comment; otherwise the dead toggle logic is misleading and could be incorrectly modified later.

title: No regression test that SQL expressions are rejected
body: The PR rejects QueryTypeSQL in ReadQuery and stubs the DuckDB implementation, but adds no test verifying that SQL expression queries are rejected, including when FlagSqlExpressions is enabled. A regression test is needed to ensure the vulnerable path cannot be accidentally re-enabled.

title: Possible nil pointer dereference when creating an unload threshold command fails
body: In the threshold query branch, unloading.Invert is set before checking the error returned by NewThresholdCommand. If NewThresholdCommand returns an error and a nil command, this will panic while parsing a threshold query with an unload evaluator when FlagRecoveryThreshold is enabled. Check err before using unloading.

title: History and Origin can panic when search is not configured
body: `server.History` calls `s.search.History(...)` and `server.Origin` calls `s.search.Origin(...)` without checking whether `s.search` is nil. `NewResourceServer` can leave `s.search` nil when search resources are not configured or when `SearchOptions.Backend` is nil (`newSearchSupport` returns nil, nil). A gRPC History or Origin request in that configuration will dereference a nil pointer and panic. `Search` has a nil guard, but History and Origin do not.

title: Startup index-build goroutines share and race on the outer err variable
body: In `searchSupport.init`, each errgroup closure assigns to the outer `err` variable via `_, _, err = s.build(...)` and then returns it. Multiple index-build goroutines run concurrently and write to the same variable, causing a data race. This can also cause one goroutine's error to be overwritten by another goroutine's success, so `Init` may report success even though an index build failed. Each closure should use its own local error variable.

title: Unsynchronized increment of totalBatchesIndexed in concurrent startup builds
body: `totalBatchesIndexed++` is executed inside errgroup goroutines without any synchronization. Multiple goroutines can increment the same integer concurrently, which is a data race and can produce an incorrect value in the `namespaced_indexed` span attribute. Use an atomic counter or protect the counter with a mutex.

title: Events written during initial index build can be missed permanently
body: `searchSupport.init` builds all initial indexes first and only afterward calls `WatchWriteEvents` to start consuming new events. The resource version returned by `build`/`ListIterator` is discarded. Any writes committed between the initial listing for a namespace and the creation of the watch subscription are not applied to the newly built index. Because startup indexing can take a long time, this creates a potentially large window where the search index can become stale until another write happens for the same resource.

title: Search event loop does not handle a closed watch channel
body: The event loop started by `searchSupport.init` receives from the watch channel with `v := <-events` and does not check whether the channel is closed. The SQL backend closes its event channel on shutdown. After closure, this loop receives nil repeatedly and calls `handleEvent` with a nil event, causing a nil-pointer dereference on `evt.Type` or a tight loop. The loop also uses `context.Background()` and has no graceful shutdown path.

title: Broadcaster pipe does not handle a closed backend event channel
body: In `server.initWatcher`, the goroutine that pipes backend watch events reads `v := <-events` without checking the channel's ok value and then accesses `v.Type` and `v.ResourceVersion`. If the backend closes the event channel, as the SQL backend does when stopped, this dereferences a nil event and panics, or spins on a closed channel. A closed-channel check and shutdown path are needed.

title: BuildIndex no longer serializes builds for the same index key
body: `bleveBackend.BuildIndex` now performs the full index build without holding `cacheMu` or any per-key lock, and only locks briefly to write the cache. Concurrent calls for the same `NamespacedResource` can both observe no cached index from `GetIndex` and then build indexes simultaneously. This can create duplicate indexes, overwrite the cache without closing the previous index, and for file-based indexes can attempt to open/build the same directory concurrently, causing errors or corruption. A per-key lock, singleflight mechanism, or cache re-check under lock is needed.

title: TotalDocs iterates the index cache without locking
body: `bleveBackend.TotalDocs` iterates over `b.cache` without acquiring `cacheMu`, while `BuildIndex` writes to the same map under the lock. Concurrent calls to `TotalDocs` and index builds can cause a concurrent map read/write race, which can crash the process.

title: Constructor leaks resources when Init fails
body: `NewResourceServer` creates a cancelable context and then calls `s.Init(ctx)`.
