body: Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id) is used without filtering provider='github' (also at line 494). If external_id is unique only per provider, an ID collision with another integration provider can return the wrong Integration or raise MultipleObjectsReturned. That can cause false 'installed on another org' errors, wrong sender metadata being checked, or crashes. Add provider=GitHubIntegrationProvider.key to these queries.

title: installation_id can be changed after the OAuth step
body: GitHubInstallation.dispatch takes installation_id from request.GET in preference to the value bound during the OAuth step and overwrites pipeline state with it. After OAuth has completed, a URL can therefore retarget the pipeline to a different installation_id without re-validating that choice against the OAuth flow. Combined with the missing validation for absent Integration rows, this allows an installation_id to be switched mid-pipeline. If the query parameter must be accepted for direct installs, compare it with the bound state or fail when they differ, and validate the installer for the final installation_id.

title: OAuth exchange failures can raise 500s
body: safe_urlopen and get_user_info are not wrapped in the same exception handling as the token-response parsing. A network failure, timeout, non-200 response, or GitHub API error during token exchange/user-info fetch will bubble up as a 500 instead of rendering the installation-failed page. Catch the expected HTTP/API errors and return error(...).

title: OAuth authorize URL parameters are not URL-encoded
body: The GitHub authorize URL is constructed with an f-string instead of URL encoding the query parameters. redirect_uri (and any future parameters) is inserted raw, which can produce an invalid authorize URL if it contains reserved characters and is generally error-prone. Build the query string with urllib.parse.urlencode.

title: Tests do not cover missing sender metadata or absent Integration rows
body: test_github_user_mismatch only covers the case where a webhook-created Integration has metadata.sender.login. There are no tests for the security-relevant paths where metadata.sender is absent or where no Integration row exists before installation. Those paths currently crash or bypass the user-match check, so add regression tests for them.

title: Unsafe access to metadata['sender']['login'] can cause a 500
body: GitHubInstallation.dispatch compares the OAuth-authenticated user to integration.metadata['sender']['login']. Many legitimate Integration rows may not have metadata.sender (for example, integrations created before this change, installations where the webhook has not populated sender, or first-pass installations as shown in the tests). In those cases this direct subscripting can raise KeyError or TypeError and return a 500 instead of the intended graceful error page. The code should use safe lookups and fail closed when sender login is missing.

title: User mismatch validation is skipped when the Integration row does not exist
body: The new security check only runs after an Integration row exists. When Integration.DoesNotExist is raised, the view returns pipeline.next_step() without verifying that github_authenticated_user matches the installer. If the installation webhook that records sender is delayed, fails, or has not created/updated the Integration yet, the advertised mismatch validation is bypassed and an installation_id could potentially be completed by a different authenticated GitHub user. The flow should fail closed or otherwise verify installer identity before creating the integration.

title: Query-string installation_id can override the pipeline-bound installation_id
body: GitHubInstallation.dispatch uses request.GET.get('installation_id', pipeline.fetch_state('installation_id')), which lets a query-string parameter overwrite any installation_id already stored during the OAuth step. This weakens the binding between the GitHub OAuth identity and the installation ID. If an installation_id has already been bound in pipeline state, the view should use that value or require the query parameter to match it rather than silently allowing it to be swapped.

title: OAuth token exchange omits redirect_uri
body: The authorization request includes redirect_uri, but the access-token exchange sends only code, client_id, and client_secret. Omitting redirect_uri prevents Sentry from explicitly binding the code exchange to the callback URL used in the authorize step. This matters if the GitHub OAuth app can have multiple callback URLs or if a code could be obtained through another registered redirect URI. The same redirect_uri should be included in the token exchange.

title: OAuth exchange and user-info fetch can raise 500 instead of showing the intended error
body: safe_urlopen and get_user_info are called without exception handling; only parsing the response body is wrapped. Network timeouts, connection errors, HTTP errors, or exceptions raised by get_user_info will bubble up and produce a 500 instead of the intended installation-failed error page. The token exchange and user-info fetch should be wrapped and return error() on failure. Also treat an empty access_token as missing, not merely absent.

title: Authorize redirect URL is built without URL encoding
body: The GitHub authorize URL is constructed with an f-string, interpolating client_id, state, and redirect_uri directly into the query string. redirect_uri should be URL-encoded to avoid malformed or rejected URLs when reserved characters are present, and to make the construction robust to future changes. Use urllib.parse.urlencode to build the query parameters.

title: Redirect can be built with installation_id=None
body: If GitHub redirects with setup_action=install but without an installation_id, installation_id is None and is passed directly to reverse('integration-installation', args=[provider_id, installation_id]). This can generate a URL containing the literal None or cause a reverse/404 failure. The view should handle a missing installation_id with a graceful redirect or error page.

title: AssignmentSource default timestamp is fixed at import time
body: queued: datetime = timezone.now() in a dataclass evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time, so every AssignmentSource created without an explicit queued receives the same stale timestamp. Use field(default_factory=timezone.now). This makes the recorded time incorrect and can mislead any future logic or metrics based on it.

title: Cycle guard suppresses all outbound syncs for an integration, not just the triggering issue
body: should_sync returns False whenever the source integration id matches the target installation's integration id, but AssignmentSource does not identify the triggering external issue. If a group is linked to multiple external issues from the same integration, an inbound assignment from one issue suppresses outbound sync to all of them, leaving the other linked issues with stale assignees. Consider carrying and checking the external issue id/key, or explicitly accepting this limitation.

title: AssignmentSource is serialized with a raw datetime and deserialized without coercion
body: to_dict uses asdict, so the Celery kwargs built in sync_group_assignee_outbound contain queued as a datetime object. That is not a plain JSON-safe value; if the task serializer stringifies it, from_dict will later construct an AssignmentSource whose queued is a string rather than a datetime. Serialize queued to an ISO string, or omit it, and parse it back in from_dict.

title: Source-integration outbound tasks are still enqueued and discarded later
body: sync_group_assignee_outbound enqueues sync_assignee_outbound for every linked external issue even when assignment_source identifies the source integration. Tasks for source-integration issues will only exit after fetching ExternalIssue, Organization, integration, and installation and checking should_sync. In rapid webhook scenarios this still creates avoidable Celery load; filtering out source-integration external issues before enqueuing would be more efficient.

title: Missing coverage for deassign suppression and cross-integration sync
body: The added tests only cover assignment suppression for a matching integration. There is no test that deassignment with a matching AssignmentSource is also suppressed, nor that assignments sourced from one integration are still propagated to a different integration. Those are the main behaviors changed by this PR, so regressions could go unnoticed.

title: AssignmentSource.queued default is evaluated once at import time
body: In a Python dataclass, a plain default value is evaluated when the class is defined. `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` therefore assigns the same module-import timestamp to every AssignmentSource created without an explicit `queued` value, including `from_integration()` and `from_dict()` when `queued` is omitted. This makes the timestamp stale and misleading for diagnostics or any future dedupe/TTL logic. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` instead.

title: Celery kwargs receive a dict containing a datetime object
body: `sync_group_assignee_outbound` passes `assignment_source.to_dict()` as Celery task kwargs. `AssignmentSource.to_dict()` uses `dataclasses.asdict()`, so the `queued` field remains a `datetime` object. Task payloads should be JSON-safe primitives; depending on the Celery serializer this can make `apply_async` fail, or it can be serialized to a string that `AssignmentSource.from_dict()` does not convert back to a datetime. Serialize `queued` explicitly, for example as an ISO-8601 string, and normalize it in `from_dict`.

title: Task assumes all installations accept the new should_sync argument
body: The outbound task now calls `installation.should_sync("outbound_assignee", parsed_assignment_source)` and later passes `assignment_source` to `sync_assignee_outbound`. Integrations or plugins that still implement the previous one-argument `should_sync` or a `sync_assignee_outbound` method without `**kwargs` will raise TypeError at runtime. If custom or third-party integrations are supported, this signature change needs compatibility handling or documentation.

title: No test that deassignment from the same integration is suppressed
body: The added tests cover assignment with a matching AssignmentSource, but the deassignment path also accepts and forwards `assignment_source`, including from `sync_group_assignee_inbound`. There is no test asserting that `GroupAssignee.objects.deassign(..., assignment_source=AssignmentSource.from_integration(integration))` does not trigger outbound sync to that same integration.

title: AssignmentSource default queued timestamp is evaluated once at import time
body: The dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now(). Python evaluates this default when the class is defined, so every AssignmentSource created without an explicit queued value receives the same import-time datetime instead of the current time. This makes the field misleading for debugging and incorrect for any future logic that relies on it. Use field(default_factory=timezone.now).

title: AssignmentSource.to_dict emits a datetime into Celery task kwargs
body: sync_group_assignee_outbound passes assignment_source.to_dict() as the assignment_source_dict kwarg for the sync_assignee_outbound task. to_dict uses dataclasses.asdict, which leaves queued as a datetime object. Task kwargs are serialized across process boundaries; if the Celery serializer is JSON or another non-pickle serializer, this can raise TypeError and prevent the sync task from being enqueued. Even if it serializes to a string, AssignmentSource.from_dict does not parse it back into a datetime. Serialize queued to an ISO string, omit it, or explicitly handle conversion in from_dict.

title: from_dict silently discards invalid assignment source and fails open
body: AssignmentSource.from_dict catches TypeError and ValueError and returns None. The outbound cycle-prevention logic treats None as no source, so a malformed or partially serialized payload can cause outbound sync to run and potentially recreate the sync loop this PR is trying to prevent. At minimum, log or metric this failure; consider stricter validation or safer fallback behavior.

title: Cycle suppression blocks all outbound syncs for the source integration, not just the source issue
body: should_sync returns False whenever sync_source.integration_id matches the installation's integration, regardless of which external issue triggered the inbound change. If a Sentry group is linked to multiple external issues belonging to the same integration, an inbound assignment change from one issue suppresses outbound assignment updates to all other linked issues in that integration. This can leave linked external issues inconsistent. If the intent is only to avoid echoing back to the originating issue, AssignmentSource should also carry the external issue key and the check should be per issue.

title: New task keyword argument is not backward compatible with older workers
body: The Celery task sync_assignee_outbound now accepts assignment_source_dict, and producers immediately include it in apply_async kwargs. During a rolling deploy, a worker running the previous task signature will receive an unexpected keyword argument and fail with TypeError, causing sync tasks to error or retry. If task producers and workers can be deployed independently, additive task signature changes need compatibility handling or deploy-order guarantees.

title: Missing coverage for deassignment with a matching assignment source
body: The added tests cover assignment with a matching AssignmentSource, but there is no test that GroupAssignee.objects.deassign(..., assignment_source=AssignmentSource.from_integration(integration)) suppresses outbound sync to the same integration. Since the PR changes the deassign path as well, this path should also be covered.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is still abstract and cannot be instantiated
body: MetricAlertDetectorHandler subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler but does not implement the required abstract members counter_names, get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values, and build_occurrence_and_event_data. Because Detector.detector_handler instantiates group_type.detector_handler(self), any detector with type 'metric_alert_fire' will raise TypeError when processed instead of safely returning no results.

title: get_state_data crashes for stateful handlers with no counters
body: StatefulDetectorHandler.get_state_data only populates counter_updates when self.counter_names is truthy, but then unconditionally accesses counter_updates[gk] for every group key. A stateful handler with no counters (counter_names = []) will raise KeyError as soon as it evaluates a packet with any group key. Use a per-group default empty dict instead.

title: Occurrences are emitted before detector state is committed
body: process_detectors emits occurrences/status changes via create_issue_occurrence_from_result before handler.commit_state_updates() persists dedupe and detector state. If the commit to Redis/DB fails after a successful produce, a retry/reprocessing of the same packet can see the old state and emit duplicate occurrences. This is a data-integrity risk now that stateful detectors produce real occurrences.

title: Docstring still says evaluate returns a list
body: StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate now returns dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult], but the docstring still says it returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult. This misdocuments the new contract.

title: get_group_key_values return annotation does not allow None/DetectorGroupKey keys
body: get_group_key_values is annotated as returning dict[str, int], but the rest of the code and tests use DetectorGroupKey keys, including None. The annotation should be dict[DetectorGroupKey, int] (or the actual key type) to match the runtime contract.

title: Test builds expected occurrence for the wrong group key
body: TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe builds the expected occurrence for group key 'val1' but then evaluates group key 'group_key'. The expected result therefore does not validate the occurrence/fingerprint for the actual group key; the test can only pass if occurrence equality ignores that difference.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is still abstract and will crash when instantiated
body: StatefulDetectorHandler requires implementations of counter_names, get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values, and build_occurrence_and_event_data. MetricAlertDetectorHandler only contains pass, so it remains abstract. Detector.detector_handler instantiates group_type.detector_handler(self), so any detector using this type will raise TypeError instead of being evaluated.

title: get_state_data crashes for stateful detectors with no counters
body: If a StatefulDetectorHandler defines an empty counter_names list, the `if self.counter_names:` block is skipped and `counter_updates` remains an empty dict. The later `counter_updates=counter_updates[gk]` raises KeyError for every group key. The method should default to an empty dict per group key when there are no counters.

title: evaluate docstring still says it returns a list
body: StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate now returns dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult], but the docstring says it returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult. This can mislead implementers and callers.

title: Produced occurrences will always use hardcoded project_id 1
body: StatefulDetectorHandler now builds IssueOccurrence and StatusChangeMessage using self.detector.project_id, but Detector.project_id is a temporary property that always returns 1. If this code path is enabled for real detectors, issues and status changes will be associated with the wrong project.

title: test_dedupe expects an occurrence for the wrong group key
body: The test builds the expected occurrence for group key 'val1' but then evaluates and asserts a DetectorEvaluationResult for group key 'group_key'. The actual handler will build an occurrence/fingerprint for 'group_key', so the assertion is either wrong or fails to verify the correct fingerprint. The helper should be called with 'group_key'.

title: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is abstract but registered as a detector handler
body: MetricAlertDetectorHandler subclasses StatefulDetectorHandler but does not implement the abstract members counter_names, get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values, and build_occurrence_and_event_data. MetricAlertFire.detector_handler points to this class, and Detector.detector_handler instantiates group_type.detector_handler(detector). Any attempt to get the handler for a metric_alert_fire detector will raise TypeError instead of evaluating or safely no-oping. Either implement the required methods, provide safe stubs, or do not register this handler until it is concrete.

title: get_state_data raises KeyError when counter_names is empty
body: In StatefulDetectorHandler.get_state_data, counter_updates is initialized to {} and only populated if self.counter_names is truthy. Later DetectorStateData is constructed with counter_updates[gk] for every group key. If a subclass legitimately has counter_names == [], this raises KeyError for the first group key, making such a stateful detector unusable. Use a default mapping such as counter_updates.get(gk, {}) or always populate defaults for every requested group key.

title: Dedupe marker is advanced before validating condition group
body: evaluate_group_key_value calls enqueue_dedupe_update(group_key, dedupe_value) before checking self.condition_group. process_detectors later calls commit_state_updates even when evaluate returns no results, so a packet that was skipped because the detector has no condition group still persists the new dedupe value. If the missing condition group is temporary or corrected later, that packet will never be re-evaluated, potentially losing alert transitions. The dedupe update should probably only be committed after the packet has actually been evaluated, or at least not when skipping for invalid configuration.

title: Occurrences are emitted before state updates are committed
body: process_detectors calls create_issue_occurrence_from_result for every result and only afterwards calls handler.commit_state_updates(). If producing one of the occurrences or the subsequent state commit fails, the dedupe/state changes are not persisted. On retry the same packet will be evaluated again, and any occurrences already produced before the failure can be emitted again. Since this PR makes detector handlers produce real IssueOccurrence/StatusChangeMessage payloads, this path can create duplicate issues unless occurrence identifiers are guaranteed idempotent.

title: get_group_key_values type annotation excludes supported None group key
body: StatefulDetectorHandler.get_group_key_values is annotated as returning dict[str, int], but DetectorGroupKey is used throughout as an optional key and the tests pass {None: ...}. The abstract signature should be dict[DetectorGroupKey, int], or otherwise document None as a valid key, so subclasses and type checkers match the runtime behavior.

title: evaluate docstring still says it returns a list
body: StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate's docstring says it returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult, but the method now returns a dict keyed by DetectorGroupKey. This can mislead implementers about the contract introduced by this PR.

title: Expected occurrence is built for the wrong group key
body: In TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe, the test evaluates evaluate_group_key_value with group_key 'group_key', but the expected occurrence is built with build_mock_occurrence_and_event(handler, 'val1', ...), giving it a fingerprint for 'val1'. If IssueOccurrence equality includes fingerprint, this test will fail; if equality ignores fingerprint, the test does not verify that the produced occurrence corresponds to the evaluated group key. The expected occurrence should be built with the same group_key being evaluated.

title: Monitor context returns raw config instead of the prepared config copy
body: get_monitor_environment_context() creates a copy of monitor.config and rewrites schedule_type to the human-readable display value, but then returns monitor_environment.monitor.config instead of the modified config variable. As a result, the monitor context attached to issue occurrences still contains the raw schedule_type value, and the display transformation is silently lost. The function should return the modified config object.

title: Monitor status transition and incident creation are not atomic
body: try_incident_threshold() saves MonitorEnvironment.status as ERROR before creating or fetching the MonitorIncident, and these operations are not wrapped in a transaction. If get_or_create fails or the process crashes after the status save, the monitor environment can remain in ERROR state without an active incident. Subsequent failed check-ins then take the ERROR branch, find active_incident=None, skip occurrence creation, and still return True, causing incidents/occurrences to be silently lost. The status change and incident creation should be made atomic or ordered so a failed incident-creation step cannot strand the monitor environment.

title: Threshold check-in selection can be nondeterministic for identical timestamps
body: When evaluating failure_issue_threshold > 1, previous check-ins are ordered only by -date_added before slicing. If multiple check-ins share the same date_added, the database may return them in an unspecified order. This can change which check-ins are included in the threshold window, which starting check-in is recorded on the incident, and what failure reason/evidence is generated. Adding a deterministic tie-breaker such as -id would make the selection stable.

title: get_failure_reason() does not handle an empty status counter
body: get_failure_reason() filters check-in statuses through HUMAN_FAILURE_STATUS_MAP, but if no check-ins match, status_counts is empty. The code only special-cases a total count of 1, so it falls through to get_text_list([]) and produces a malformed message such as a leading-space ' check-ins detected'. Current callers generally pass failed statuses, but the helper is now in a shared module and should defensively handle an empty counter.

title: Modified monitor config copy is discarded in context
body: `get_monitor_environment_context` copies `monitor_environment.monitor.config` and replaces `schedule_type` with the human-readable display value, but the returned context uses `monitor_environment.monitor.config` instead of the modified `config`. The normalization is therefore lost, so the emitted monitor context contains the raw `schedule_type` value rather than the intended display value.

title: Failure threshold can be triggered without enough failed check-ins
body: In try_incident_threshold, when failure_issue_threshold is greater than 1, the code slices the latest check-ins to at most the threshold but never verifies that it actually obtained failure_issue_threshold check-ins. If a monitor with threshold 3 has only one failed check-in, previous_checkins will contain one failure, the OK-check will pass, and the code will set the environment to ERROR and create a MonitorIncident. This creates incidents and issue occurrences before the configured failure threshold is reached. A length check such as returning False when len(previous_checkins) < failure_issue_threshold is needed before changing status or creating the incident.

title: Modified monitor config copy is discarded when building event context
body: get_monitor_environment_context copies the monitor config and replaces schedule_type in the local config variable with the human-readable display value, but the returned dictionary uses monitor_environment.monitor.config instead of the modified local config. As a result, the prepared schedule_type display value is discarded and the emitted monitor context still contains the raw config value. The returned dict should use the modified config variable.

title: Previous check-in selection is nondeterministic when timestamps tie
body: The query that selects previous check-ins orders only by -date_added. If multiple check-ins have identical date_added values, the subset chosen at the threshold boundary and the selected starting_checkin can be nondeterministic. Adding a tie-breaker such as -id would make the threshold evaluation stable.

title: Occurrences may be created in arbitrary order for threshold check-ins
body: previous_checkins is explicitly reversed into oldest-to-newest order, but the later queryset uses filter(id__in=...) without an order_by. The resulting MonitorCheckIn rows may be returned in arbitrary order, so create_incident_occurrence can be invoked in a different order than the check-ins being represented. If occurrence ordering or detection_time ordering matters, preserve the original ordering when fetching the check-ins.

title: join() can skip terminating some flusher processes when timeout expires
body: SpanFlusher.join iterates over multiple flusher processes and breaks out of the loop as soon as the remaining deadline is <= 0. If the deadline is reached before later processes are visited, those processes are never terminated. Also, `deadline = time.time() + timeout if timeout else None` treats timeout == 0 as no deadline, so join can block indefinitely. During shutdown or rebalance this can leave flusher processes running or hang the consumer.

title: Restart path kills unhealthy process but never ensures it has exited
body: _ensure_processes_alive calls process.kill() for an unhealthy process and immediately creates a replacement without joining or otherwise verifying the old process has exited. The old process object is replaced, which can leak zombie/process resources. If the old worker is not actually dead (or in the thread-based test mode, where threads cannot be killed), two workers may flush the same shards concurrently, risking duplicate Kafka production and confusing buffer state.

title: Unvalidated --flusher-processes value can crash or silently change behavior
body: The new --flusher-processes option accepts any integer. A negative value reaches SpanFlusher, where num_processes becomes negative and process_to_shards_map is empty; the subsequent shard assignment then raises KeyError during consumer startup. A value of 0 is silently treated as “use one process per assigned shard” because of `max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)`. The option should validate the allowed range or document the sentinel behavior.

title: Inconsistent metric tag key: shards vs shard
body: The wait_produce timer is tagged with `shards`, while the produce timer and segment_size_bytes metric use `shard`. This inconsistency will make metrics harder to query and can silently break dashboards/alerts that expect a single tag name for flusher shard attribution.

title: Docstring overstates one-process-per-shard behavior
body: The class docstring says the flusher creates one process per shard, but the implementation creates min(max_processes, len(assigned_shards)) processes and may assign multiple shards to one process. The CLI default is also 1 process, so the documented behavior does not match the default or the configurable behavior.

title: join() can leave flusher processes running when timeout expires
body: SpanFlusher.join computes a deadline and, if remaining time is <= 0 before waiting on a process, breaks out of the process-wait loop. This skips `process.terminate()` for the remaining processes. In addition, `deadline = time.time() + timeout if timeout else None` treats a timeout of 0 as no timeout. During shutdown or rebalance with a small timeout, flusher processes may outlive join(), causing leaked processes and possible duplicate flushing/production.

title: Unhealthy flusher worker is replaced without ensuring the old worker stopped
body: _ensure_processes_alive kills a multiprocessing worker (and does nothing for threads created when `produce_to_pipe` is set), then immediately creates a replacement without waiting for the old worker to exit or cleaning up the old process object. If the old worker is still running, it can continue flushing the same shards and shares the same health/backpressure Values with the replacement, which can cause duplicate Kafka production, Redis state races, and leaked process handles.

title: Omitted flusher_processes defaults to one worker per shard, inconsistent with CLI default
body: SpanFlusher treats `max_processes=None` as `len(buffer.assigned_shards)`, while the CLI option defaults to 1. Any non-CLI construction of ProcessSpansStrategyFactory or SpanFlusher that omits `flusher_processes` will spawn one process/thread per shard instead of the previous single flusher, which can unexpectedly create many workers and connections. The default should be explicit and consistent, or documented.

title: --flusher-processes accepts invalid non-positive values
body: The new `--flusher-processes` option is declared as plain `type=int` with no lower bound. A negative value reaches SpanFlusher, where `num_processes` becomes negative and `process_to_shards_map` is empty, causing shard assignment to fail. A value of 0 is also silently coerced by `max_processes or len(...)`. Validate the option with something like `click.IntRange(min=1)`.

title: Added sleep in test is ineffective because time.sleep is monkeypatched
body: test_basic globally monkeypatches `time.sleep` to a no-op, then calls `time.sleep(0.1)` to give flusher threads time to process. The patched call does not actually wait, so the test is not synchronizing deterministically with the flusher and may become flaky. Use an unpatched sleep or poll for a deterministic condition.

title: join() can leave flusher processes running when timeout expires
body: SpanFlusher.join breaks out of the process cleanup loop when the deadline has expired, so flusher processes are not terminated. If next_step.join(timeout) consumes the whole timeout, or the deadline expires while waiting for one process, remaining background flushers keep running after join returns. Because they continue to poll Redis and produce to Kafka, a rebalance or restart can leak processes and duplicate segments. Terminate all processes even after timeout, and preferably join them after termination.

title: Unhealthy flusher worker is replaced without ensuring it has stopped
body: In _ensure_processes_alive, an unhealthy worker is killed only if it is a multiprocessing.Process, and the code does not wait for it to exit before creating a replacement. For threading.Thread workers, used when produce_to_pipe is set, there is no way to stop the old thread at all. The old worker can therefore continue flushing the same shards while the replacement runs, causing duplicate Kafka production or conflicting Redis updates. Ensure the old worker has terminated, or fence it, before starting a new one.

title: Health timestamp is not updated during long flush or produce cycles
body: SpanFlusher.main updates healthy_since once per loop before producing and waiting for Kafka futures. If flush_segments, produce, or future.result takes longer than spans.buffer.flusher.max-unhealthy-seconds, submit/_ensure_processes_alive will classify the process as hung and kill/restart it mid-flush. That can duplicate partially produced segments. Update the heartbeat during long flush/produce operations or include produce wait time in health reporting.

title: Added synchronization sleep is patched out and does not wait
body: test_basic monkeypatches time.sleep to a no-op for the whole test, then calls time.sleep(0.1) to wait for flusher threads. That call returns immediately, so the intended synchronization does not happen. If the test depends on the flusher observing the drift change, it remains racy and may pass or fail depending on scheduling. Use the original sleep, patch only the flusher's sleep, or wait for a deterministic condition.

title: --flusher-processes accepts non-positive values
body: The new --flusher-processes option is an unbounded int. A negative value is passed to SpanFlusher, where num_processes can become negative; with assigned shards the subsequent process/shard mapping can fail with a confusing KeyError instead of a clear CLI validation error. Use click.IntRange(min=1) or validate the value in the factory/flusher.

title: Inconsistent metric tag key: shards vs shard
body: The wait_produce timer is tagged with shards, while the adjacent produce timer and segment_size_bytes metric use shard. This splits the metric dimension and can break dashboards or alerts that expect a consistent tag name. Use the same tag key for all flusher metrics, for example shard.

title: Docstring says one process per shard, but processes are capped and shared
body: The SpanFlusher docstring says it creates one process per shard, but the implementation creates min(max_processes, len(assigned_shards)) processes and assigns multiple shards to the same process when max_processes is smaller. The CLI default is 1, so the actual behavior is not one process per shard. Update the docstring and help text to describe the actual process-sharing behavior.

title: Strategy close shuts down the factory-shared FixedQueuePool
body: ResultsStrategyFactory creates one FixedQueuePool in __init__ (result_consumer.py line 133) and reuses it for every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close/terminate/join shuts that pool down, stopping worker threads and closing the queues. Arroyo closes the old strategy on partition revocation/reassignment, so after a rebalance the factory will create new strategies around an already shut-down pool. New messages then cannot be processed, and enqueue attempts may fail or be dropped. The pool lifecycle must match the strategy lifecycle, or the pool must be recreated on each assignment.

title: Unbounded worker queues provide no backpressure
body: Each worker queue is created as queue.Queue() with no maxsize, and FixedQueuePool.submit puts items unconditionally. If workers are slower than the consumer—exactly the slow-item case this PR is trying to address—the consumer will keep polling and enqueuing full Kafka payloads without bound. poll() only emits a gauge and does not block or raise. This can cause unbounded memory growth. Use bounded queues, block in submit, or apply backpressure in poll.

title: Offsets are completed and can be committed even when processing fails
body: OrderedQueueWorker.run marks the offset complete in finally, so an exception from result_processor still allows the offset to become committable. ResultProcessor.__call__ in result_consumer.py also swallows all exceptions and only logs them. The result is that failed results can be committed and never retried, contradicting the strategy docstring claim that offsets are committed only after successful processing. This can silently drop uptime results. Failures should prevent completion, or be routed to retry/DLQ.

title: submit() marks offsets complete when it cannot enqueue/process a message
body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit catches all exceptions and, if the message has a BrokerValue, immediately adds and completes the offset. This includes decoder/grouping errors and failures from queue_pool.submit, such as submitting to a shut-down queue. The message is not processed, but its offset becomes committable. That turns transient or operational errors into silent data loss. Errors should be surfaced, retried, dead-lettered, or should block the consumer rather than completing the offset.

title: OffsetTracker iterates all_offsets while other threads mutate it
body: OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets iterates list(self.all_offsets.keys()) without a global lock, while add_offset can concurrently insert new partition keys from the consumer thread. Concurrent mutation of the partition dictionary can cause RuntimeError during iteration or inconsistent snapshots. Protect the partition set with a global lock, or copy/modify it under a lock.

title: Shutdown stops workers before draining queues and join ignores its timeout
body: FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets worker.shutdown = True before shutting down the queues, so each worker exits after finishing its current item instead of draining remaining queued work. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join(timeout) calls close() and ignores the timeout, forcibly shutting down the pool. Queued items are dropped on shutdown/rebalance instead of being processed up to the requested timeout. It should wait_until_empty(timeout) and only stop workers after draining or after the timeout expires.

title: Uses Python 3.13-only queue.ShutDown/Queue.shutdown APIs
body: OrderedQueueWorker catches queue.ShutDown, and FixedQueuePool.shutdown calls q.shutdown(immediate=False). These APIs were added in Python 3.13. If this consumer runs on an older supported Python version, shutdown will not work correctly: Queue.shutdown will raise AttributeError (caught and logged), workers may never be woken from queue.get(), and exception handling can fail. Add a fallback for older Python versions or explicitly enforce Python 3.13+.

title: decode_payload asserts on FilteredPayload instead of handling it
body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy's decoder type accepts KafkaPayload | FilteredPayload, but ResultsStrategyFactory.decode_payload begins with assert not isinstance(payload, FilteredPayload). Any FilteredPayload message therefore raises AssertionError, which SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit treats as a generic submission error and logs. Filtered payloads should be handled explicitly by returning None so they can be skipped without exception/log spam.

title: WorkItem retains the full Kafka message though it is unused
body: WorkItem stores the original Message[KafkaPayload | FilteredPayload], but only partition and offset are used for offset tracking; the message field is never read. With unbounded queues, this unnecessarily retains full Kafka payloads in memory. Remove the unused message field or store only the required metadata.

title: max_workers is not validated for thread-queue-parallel mode
body: FixedQueuePool is created with num_queues=max_workers or 20. This treats 0 as 20, but negative values are passed through. A negative num_queues creates no queues and later hash(group_key) % num_queues or queue lookup can fail. Validate that max_workers/num_queues is a positive integer when using thread-queue-parallel.

title: Strategy.close shuts down the factory-wide FixedQueuePool
body: ResultsStrategyFactory creates one FixedQueuePool in __init__ and passes the same pool to every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close is called by Arroyo when a strategy is torn down, including on partition revocation/rebalance, and it calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(). The factory never recreates the pool, so the next create_with_partitions() returns a strategy that submits to shutdown queues with stopped workers. New messages will not be processed, offsets will never complete, and commits will stall. The strategy should not own/shut down a shared pool, or the factory must recreate/reset the pool when a strategy closes.

title: Unbounded work queues provide no backpressure
body: FixedQueuePool creates queue.Queue() with no maxsize and submit() puts work items unconditionally. The processing strategy's poll() only emits metrics, so Arroyo has no signal to slow down or pause consumption. If workers are slower than the input rate, queue depth grows without bound and the process can exhaust memory. The docstring's claim of natural backpressure is not true with unbounded queues.

title: Shutdown flag prevents workers from draining queued items
body: FixedQueuePool.shutdown first sets worker.shutdown = True for every worker and then calls queue.shutdown(immediate=False). OrderedQueueWorker.run checks while not self.shutdown before each get, so a worker that has just finished an item will exit instead of continuing to drain the queue. Queued work items are therefore abandoned during graceful shutdown, even though immediate=False is intended to allow draining. The pool should rely on queue.shutdown/ShutDown to stop workers after the queues are empty, or only set the flag after draining.

title: Close stops the commit loop before draining workers
body: close() sets the shutdown event and joins the commit thread before calling queue_pool.shutdown(). The commit thread therefore exits after one final commit before the worker threads have drained the queues. Any offsets completed while the workers drain during shutdown are not committed. terminate() has the same ordering issue. The final commit should happen after the pool has drained, or the commit loop should remain alive until after pool shutdown.

title: OffsetTracker iterates all_offsets while other threads can add partitions
body: get_committable_offsets() iterates over list(self.all_offsets.keys()) without a global lock, while add_offset() can create new partition keys concurrently from the submit thread. If a new partition is first seen while this iteration is running, the dictionary can change size during iteration and raise RuntimeError, causing the commit loop to log an error and skip committing for that interval. A global lock around partition registration/key copying is needed.

title: Failed work items are marked complete and committed
body: OrderedQueueWorker.run completes the offset in finally even when result_processor raises, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit also completes offsets when decoding/grouping/enqueueing fails. This means exceptions are acknowledged and eventually committed rather than retried or sent to a DLQ. For uptime results, transient failures can drop data unless at-most-once processing is explicitly intended.

title: FilteredPayload is handled by an assertion in the queue path
body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy passes FilteredPayload values to ResultsStrategyFactory.decode_payload, which asserts that the payload is not FilteredPayload. The assertion is caught by submit() and treated as an unexpected error, logging Error submitting message to queue and completing the offset. Filtered payloads should be handled explicitly by returning None so filtered messages are skipped without error logs.

title: Uses Python 3.13-only queue.ShutDown/Queue.shutdown
body: OrderedQueueWorker.run catches queue.ShutDown and FixedQueuePool.shutdown calls Queue.shutdown(immediate=False). These were added in Python 3.13. On earlier Python versions, Queue.shutdown does not exist, so shutdown errors are swallowed and worker threads can remain blocked in get(); also evaluating except queue.ShutDown while handling another exception can raise AttributeError. If the service is not guaranteed to run on Python 3.13, this breaks graceful shutdown and error handling.

title: Error-handling test asserts the opposite of the implementation behavior
body: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling mocks ResultProcessor.__call__ to raise and asserts that no offsets are committed. The implementation completes offsets in the worker's finally block even when the processor raises, so the contiguous offsets are eligible to be committed by the commit loop. The test therefore asserts behavior the code does not implement and is also timing-dependent on the one-second commit loop. Either the test should expect the commit, or the consumer should not complete/commit failed work.

title: Strategy shuts down the shared FixedQueuePool, breaking later strategy instances
body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(), but the pool is created by ResultsStrategyFactory and is shared across strategies. Arroyo may close a strategy during a rebalance and then create a new strategy from the same factory. Once close() has shut down the shared pool, worker threads are stopped and queues are closed, so the next strategy will submit to a dead pool. Its submit() exception handler can then mark offsets complete without processing. This can silently drop messages after any rebalance. The strategy should not shut down a factory-owned pool, or a new pool should be created per strategy.

title: join() ignores its timeout and does not drain queued work before stopping commits
body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join() simply calls close(), ignoring the timeout argument. close() stops the commit thread before queue_pool.shutdown() drains remaining queued items, and it never waits for queues or outstanding offsets to become empty. As a result, work processed during shutdown may never have its offsets committed, and shutdown can still block for fixed internal timeouts rather than respecting the requested join timeout.

title: Shutdown flag can cause queued work items to be dropped
body: FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown = True before allowing queues to drain. OrderedQueueWorker.run() loops on while not self.shutdown, so if a worker is processing an item when shutdown begins it will exit after that one item even if its queue still contains pending work. Although q.shutdown(immediate=False) is intended to permit graceful draining, the worker flag prevents that and can discard queued messages without processing or committing them.

title: Failed work items are marked complete and become eligible for commit
body: OrderedQueueWorker.run() catches exceptions from the result processor and still calls offset_tracker.complete_offset() in the finally block. ResultProcessor.__call__ also swallows exceptions. Therefore a result that fails processing is treated as completed and can be committed, despite the strategy documentation saying offsets are committed only after successful processing. A transient failure, such as a database or downstream outage, can permanently lose results with no retry or DLQ.

title: OffsetTracker iterates shared partition dictionary while other threads may add partitions
body: OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets() iterates list(self.all_offsets.keys()) without a global lock, while add_offset() may concurrently create new partition entries in self.all_offsets from the submit thread. This can cause dictionary-changed-size-during-iteration errors or missed partitions in the commit loop. Per-partition locks protect individual offset sets but do not protect the partition key collection itself.

title: Unbounded queues provide no backpressure despite documented guarantee
body: FixedQueuePool creates queue.Queue() instances with no maxsize and submit() puts work unconditionally. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.poll() only emits metrics and never applies backpressure. The class documentation claims natural backpressure when queues fill up, but unbounded queues never fill. If workers are slower than the consumer, messages and full Kafka payloads will accumulate in memory without bound and can OOM the process.

title: FilteredPayload is handled through the generic exception path
body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() passes FilteredPayload messages to the decoder. When used with ResultsStrategyFactory.decode_payload(), that decoder asserts the payload is not FilteredPayload, causing an AssertionError that is caught by the generic except branch and logged as 'Error submitting message to queue'. This turns normal filtered messages into exception log spam and relies on exception handling for control flow. FilteredPayload should be explicitly treated as a skipped/completed offset before decoding.

title: Error-handling test is flaky and asserts behavior opposite to the implementation
body: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling mocks the result processor to raise for the first message and then asserts that no offsets were committed. However, the worker catches processing exceptions and marks the failed offset complete, so once the commit loop ticks the implementation will commit past the failed message. The test only waits briefly and may pass or fail depending on whether the 1-second commit loop runs before the assertion. It does not reliably validate the intended behavior and masks the fact that failed items are committed.
